RELIEF in the most DISTRESSED DISTRICTS. 



Mr. Tkbtely.4n to Mr. S. Jones Loyd, Chairman of the British Association. 

Treasury, August 20, 1847. 

In order that there may he no misunderstanding on a subject which has Arrangements with 
many wide and peculiar bearings, I thiuk it will be safe to recapitulate in Brituu Asso- 

wviting the substance of what I stated to Messrs. Prescott, Spring Rice, and 
Cane, on the subject of Count Strzelecki’s plan for disposing ol‘ the balance of 
your fund. 

I recommended that you should not form any new independent machinery, 
which you might find it difficult to man^e, and which would produce the ini- 
pressiou that the lavish cliaritable system of last season was intended to be 
renewed; but that you should select, through the Poor Law Commissioners, a 
certain number of Unions in which there is reason to believe tliat the rate]iayers 
will not be able to meet their liabilities, and that you should appropriate from 
time to tipie such sums as the Poor Law Commissioners may recommend, for 
the purpose of assisting in giving out-door relief in certain districts of these 
Unions ; the expenditure for this object being conducted under the special super- 
intendence of the Assistant Poor Law Commissioners, who would take care that 
no misappropriation took place. 

This plan is substantially the same as that which was last recommended by 
Count Strzelecki ; and it would be attended with the double advantage of 
limiting the relief afforded by the Association, to those parts of the country 
which are undoubtedly the most distressed, and of supporting and strengthening 
the administration of the Poor Law, which is the great point of all. 

The further condition should be annexed, that the Poor Law Commissioners 
should be able to certify that the ratepayers were making such exertions as 
could reasonably be expected from them ; and then I think every practicable 
security will have been taken that the bounty of which the Association is the 
organ, will be bestowed aright. 



Minutes of a Meeting of the British Association, on the 26th of August, 1847- 
It was resolved : — 

1 . That the Committee is prepared to act upon the recommendation contained 
in Mr. Trevelyan s letter, read at the last meeting of the Board, in gi\'ing tem- 
porary out-door relief in those Unions or districts of Unions in which there is 
good reason to apprehend that the rate-payers may not be able immediately to 
meet their liabilities, and in which, therefore, extreme distress may arise. 

2. That Mr. Trevelyan be requested to obtain from the proper authorities in 
Ireland, a list of those Unions in which it is expected that distress of the cha-

Mr. Trevelyan to Mr. Twisleton. 

August'S,^, 1847. 

I HAVE the pleasure of sending you a copy of resolutions which were 
come to yesterday by the Committee of the British Relief Association, and of 
the letter from me to Mr. Jones Loyd referred to in them. 

You will find tliat the Committee have resolved to appropriate the balance 
of the fund at their disposal for the relief of distress in Ireland, in such a 
maimer as will support and assist the operation of the Poor Law, at the same 
time that it will accomplish the object of the subscribers, by ajipropriating their 
money in aid of those districts in wliich the greatest distress jirevails. 

This letter will be delivered to you by Count Strzclecki, the confidential 
agent of the Association, and after you have ascertained the wishes of the Lord 
Lieutenant on the subject, and have conferred with the Count and Sir R. Routh, 
I shall be obhged to you to inform me whether you are prepared to co-operate 
in the execution of this plan, either in the manner in which it has b^n above 
stated, or with any modifications that may be suggested by you ; and I will 
communicate the result to the Association, after which your correspondence on 
the subject iriU be with the Association and their authorized agents. 

The Committee of the Association wish to obtain from you, as soon as you 
can furnish it, a list of the Unions to wliich you would recommend that assist- 
ance should be given from time to time ^ the occasion requires (it beino- 
mtended that the grants of the Association shall be sti-ictly limited to those 
particular Unions), as well with a view to enable Sir R. Routh to have the 
depots ready, as for other more important reasons which will be obvious to 
you.

1 BEG to enclose you the accompanying co})v of a letter I this morning

The subject of affording assistance to schools has been partially under the 
notice of the Committee for some time, but nothing hitherto has b^n decided ; 
the Count has in this letter re-opened the q^uestion, and resumed his arguments 
in its favour, and the subject will be taken into consideration, and be finally

Count Stezelecki to the Hon. Secretakies of tb3 Britisu Association. 

Agency of the British Association in Ireland. 

Reynold's Hotel, Duilin, October 24, 1S47. 

The melancholy accounts which I receive from the provinces compel me to bring again 
{he subject of the destitute children under j-our consideration. 

Ill my late communications I have directed your attention to the painful forms under wliich 
the life of the unhappy children presented itself to me last winter, and to the actual and future 
effects which the physical and moral degradation to which they are exposed, through hunger 
and nakedness, has and will have upon the fato of the country. 

I have told you also that the Temporary Relief Act, and }irivate and chaintablc donations, 
wliile meeting fully the destitution of the full-grown people, had seldom been instmmental in 
alleviating that ot the helpless children, who, in the general run and scramble for food, have 
been left behind hungry by' the way ; and I have added, that, seeing a separate distribution of 
food to them as necessary as that of screening them (the girls particularly) dining the day 
from the afflicting scenes in which they had been partly spectators, partly actors, I had, with 
your permission and sanction, tried this separate system of relief in Westport : and conscious 
that schools in general will be the most systematic and beneficial machinery for the issue of 
such relief, 1 had placed, in the first instance. 600 girls of the Roman Catholic persuasion, 
under the charge of the Sisters of Charity ; 700 boy's of tlie same persuason, under the super- 
intendence of the Catholic dean in Westport; and then to the children thus placed, and to those 
I found already in two Protestant schools of Westport and Louisburgh, amounting to 160, I 
have distributed clothing, and secured one meal daily, of which the cost averaged one-third of 
a jienay per head. 

That this assistance afforded to children through the medium of schools, whether Protestant 
or Catholic, secured to the community of Westport advantages beyoud those at first contem- 
plated, is borne out by the fact that the Finance Committee of that Union, composed of Pro- 
testants, Presbyterians, and Catholics, with Lord Sligo as their chairman, passed, on the I6th 
of September, a vote of thanks to the Association, in which, after acknowlwging the general 
benefit of the assistance afforded to the Union, they conclude by stating, “And while the 
wants of the destitute were thus provided for. an additional obligation was conferred upon us 
by the maintenance of our juvenile population in the several schools we were enabled to keep 
open ; and thereby not alone relieve their physical wants, but extend the blessings of education, 
so necessary for the well-being of society.” 

Now, impressed with the impending evils of destitution in the approaching winter, I have 
begged of you that I may be allowed to extend to otlier equally distressed districts in Ireland 
that system of separate relief which so well answered in Westport. 

The rarious arrangements contingent upon the above, w'hicli I transmitted to you in my late 
communications, and which I now will resume, consist in affording food and clothing to chddren 
through the medium of schools, and iii confining the sy'steni to those of the 22 Unions (specified 
in my letter of tlie 11th instant) in which such assistance will he Jound practicahle and accept- 
able-, and as, according to the last resolution of the Committee, and the concurrence of Her 
Majesty’s Government, the above Unions will be entitled to efficient relief when such will be 
claimed by the authorities, the proposed plan, therefore, as far as fbotl goes, will consist merely 
in determining that one-fifth, one-sixth, or one-seventh of the food granted to each of the U nions 
should go for the benefit of children. 

As regards clothing, which is of paramount necessity and importance, next to food, a couple of 
thousand pounds set apart for this object will be of the greatest charity ; and if invested through 
the agency of Dublin Ladies’ Reproductive and Industrial Society, would prove of a double 
benefit; for that Society, of which the Honourable Mrs. Newcombs and Mrs. Humphrey 
Lloyd are the active members, succeeded most wonderfully in fostering native industry amongst 
the females of Ireland, as their stores of frieze, flannels, drugget, and such like, attest, and are 
fully competent and capable to undertake the making and the furnishing of any articles of 
clothing required. 

And as to each of the 22 Unions there is being appointed a separate inspector under the 
Poor Law, it will be optional with the Committee either to confine to his instrumentality alone 
the allocation of both food and clothing, or to associate with him one Protestant and one 
Catholic gentleman, and invest them with tlie administration of the bounty which may be granted 
to children.

‘ ■ both Catholic and Protestant gentlemen upon tlie subject, and every one confessed that, in 

these extraordinary and exceptional times, when nakedness and hunger araoncrst children threaten

Count Strzelecki to the Poor Law Inspector of each of the 22 Unions. 

Agency of the British Relief Association in Ireland, 
Reynolds Hotel, Dublin, 
November 6, 184-7. 

The Committee of the British Relief Association are deeply concerned 
in the fate of the unhappy children in the twenty-two Unions, returned as the 
most destitute in Ireland, to eacli of -which a separate Inspector has been ap- 
pointed, and are anxious to secure to them relief in food and clothing during- 
this and the ibrthcoming season of trial and misery. ° 

The Committee are of opinion that this can be effected more advantageously, 
and -with more chance of success, through the medium of the already existing 
schools, than in any other way ; and their "wish being, above all other consider^ 
ations, to afford relief to the hungry and the naked, and thus mitigate, as mudi 
as it lies in their power, the physical and moral deterioration of the rising 
generation, it is but just that schools belonging to every persuasion should be 
placed on an equal footing as regards participation in the bounty, and be dealt 
-\vith according as they are more or less in need of relief; considering, moreover, 
that such mode of proceeding with, all schools alike will not be open to any -well- 
grounded objection on the score of favouring one religious persuasion above 
another. 

The extent of clothing is not yet determined upon. The nature of food 
is to consist of a ration of rye bread, a higher standard of nourishment than 
Indian meal stirabout, and a porringer of -w^arm broth, seasoned with salt and 
pepper. 

The supply of rye meal, the expense of making bread, and that of meat and 
bones lor broth, will be undertaken and defrayed by the Agent of the British 
Relief Association in Dublin. 

The Committee having obtained for the above system of relief the appro- 
bation of the head authorities, are now anxious to apply its provisions to 
your Union, towards -which object they solicit your valuable assistance and co- 
operation. 

As a preliminary step, I would beg of you to communicate to me, at your 
earliest convenience, a list of the schools in the Union, with the number of 
children they actually contain, and the number they could conveniently accom- 
modate. 

I sh^l then be ready to place at your disposal the necessary grants and 
means for supply of food, the detailed issue of -which may be conveniently 
carried out through the charitable aid of the clergy, school-inspectors, and 
school-masters. 

It will be optional with you either to take upon yourself alone the allocation 
of grants to the different schools in the Union, or to act in concert with one 
Protestant and one Catholic gentleman of your own selection, should you see 
such association necessary. 

The securing to children one of the most essential elements of a school — the 
u taught to pray for — w'ill be the duty of the Agent 

of the British Relief Association ; the rest of the work must naturally depend 
upon you and the benevolent persons of your Union ; I mean that diffusion of 
order, cleanliness, and those branches of industry and domestic economy 
amo^st boys and girls, in which the Scotch industrial schools of Aberdeen 
and Dundee have set such noble examples, and which, particularly in Ireland, 
are of paramount importance to instruction. 

Any of your suggestions towards securing to this charitable scheme all the 
benefits which it is capable of procuring, will be received by me with due 
regard and consideration.

By the last arrangement between Her Majesty’s Government and the seiMted Umons’for 
Committee of the British Relief Association, it was agreed that the assistance their info.mation 
of the Association should be confined to the 22 Unio3is in the west of Ireland, . pa^e 

in wliich alone, according to the best information which the Government has 
been able to obtain, it is not in the po-wer of the rate-payers to relieve the whole 
of the impending destitution. 

I shall, therefore, request that you null be pleased to communicate to the 
Inspectors of the above 22 Unions that that assistance will be granted to the

out their own arrangements, and when it is clearly ascertained and certified by 
the Inspector that these efforts have been made, and that the extent of distress 
really exceeds all their powers of relief duly and fully exerted. 

The assistance of the Association will consist in rye-meal, and the rations arc

The rations will be determined by the Poor Law' Commissioners, and a return 
in lal)Our exacted for it by the Inspector, if practicable. 

The expenditure and accounts for grants in money and food given by tlie- 
Association, will be reported and sent to the Poor Law Commission. Conse- 
quent upon the nature of food wdth which the poor are to be rationed, the 
necessary number of ovens which are required will be built at the expense of 
Her Majesty’s Treasury ; and it is highly desirable that the Inspector of each 
Union should, at his earliest convenience, report to the Agent of the British Relief 
Association in Dublin how many ovens will be needed in his Union, the 
required size, the kind of fuel for which they are adapted, and the probable 



cost of their erection. 



Count Strzelecki to Mr. Trevelyan. 

Reynolds' Hotel, DuUln, November 9, 1S47- 
I keep my issues within the bounds of great economy, and am reser\-ing 
our resources and power for a more advanced period of the winter, when the 
distress will have actually developed itself, and when our efficient relief will 
be more beneficial, and more appreciated. 

Tlie appointment of special Inspectors to the 22 Unions, the formation of the 
depots, and the queries relating to the erection of ovens, gave rise to some 
absurd expectations amongst the people about the extent of our gratuitous relief 
and assistance, wliich I found it necessary to sober down. Consequently I have 
acquainted the Inspectors, through the medium of the Poor Law' Commission, 
that the present reduced fund of the Association has compelled me to confine 
all future assistance to those Unions only in which it is clearly ascertained that 
all the efforts of the Poor Law Guardians had been made in developing their 
own arrangements, and that the extent of destitution really exceeds the local 
power of relief duly and fully exerted. I added, also, that any demand for 
relief by the Inspectors ivill be considered to have a stronger claim, where, in 
addition to the proved destitution, and want of local means to relieve it, a 
system of olitaining some return from the people in useful work can and will he 
organized. 

Meanwhile, to meet any extreme cases of destitution in the poorest dis- 
tricts, as in Bantry, BelmuUet, Glenties (island of Arranmore),^ I have placed 
10(J^. with each of the officers, so tliat every possible precaution is taken to 
promote the developement of the Poor Law provisions, as also to pre\'ent deaths 
occurring from starvation. 

I am very glad that my suggestion to the Committee as regards the relief to 
children in food and clothing was approved of. This kind of relief, besides 
being necessary and just, as charity, is more impressive upon the minds of the 
people here, and is more highly appreciated by them than a general issue of 
rations. It -will also lessen considerably the pressure upon the Union Work- 
houses, and make room for the able-bodied, which is of no less value. 

I am in daily communication with Sir R. Routh and hlr. Twisleton, and 
througli their respective channels you will be informed of every particular 
worth knowing as connected with the doings of the Association in Ireland.

of Guardians the absolute necessity of their making vigorous efforts to compel (he

To the Clerk to the Guardians of each Union. 

Circular as to the Appointment, Duties, &c., of Relieving Officers. 

Poor Law Commission Office, DuUin, 

Sir, Juhj 16, 1817. 

The Poor Law CommUaoners are desirous of calling the attention of Boards of 
Guardians to those clauses of the Irish Relief Extension Act, which relate to the appointment 
of a class of functionaries hitherto unknown in Ireland, who are called Relieving Officers. As 
the approaching discontinuance of advances under the Temporary Relief Act renders it 
necessary to bring those clauses into operation with the least possible delay, the Com- 
missioners now call upon Boards of Guardians to issue advertisements for candidates. 
At the same time, it is proposed in the present. Circular, to state, for general information, the 
nature of the duties which Relieving Officers will have to perform, the qualifications which they 
should possess, the amount of salary which tliey should receive, and the number which siiould 
be appointed for each Union. 

1. Kverv Relieving Officer will have a district of an Union assigned to him ; and all appli- 
cations within that district for relief from the Poor Rates will have to be made to him in the 
fimt instance. It will be his duty forthwith to examine into the circumstances of every case, by 
visiting the home of the applicant, and by making all necessary inquiries into the state of 
health, the ability to work, and the means of such applicant; and he will have to report 
the result of such inquiries, in a prescribed form, to the Board of Guardians, at their 
next meeting. Under ordinary circumstances, the amount of relief to be granted in 
each case will be fixed by the Board of Guardian? exclusively; altliougli the Relieving 
Officer, in accordance with the orders of the Guardians, will have to supply the weekly allow- 
ances to all persons on the relief list, within his district. There is, however, one exception 
to his being wholly dependent on an order of the Board of Guardians in reference to the 
amount of relief which he supplies. This one exception is, when a case of necessity arises 
which is both urgent and sudden; and in such a case, he may give provisional relief on his 
own responsibility until the next ordinary meeting of the Board of Guardians, and no 
longer. This relief may be supplied either hy an order of admbsion to the Workhouse or 
Fever Hospital of the Union, provided there is room therein respectively, and by conveying, 
if necessary, any destitute poor person to one of those establishments ; or by affordin® 
such poor person immediate and temporary relief in food, lodging, medicine, or medicail 
attendance. 

As the duties above-mentioned involve the entrusting, to a certain extent, sums of money 
weekly to a Relieving Officer, he will have further, to keep a separate and full account 
of all monies received and disbursed by him, and likewise of all articles received and 
given out by him for the relief of the destitute poor in his district. He will have to 
balance such account weekly, and to present the same to the clerk for his inspection 
and authentication before every ordinary meeting of the Board of Guardians, and to the 
Board of Guardians at such meeting for their approval. He will likewise have to perform 
other duties subordinate to the above, which will hereafter be specified in a general order. 

2. With regard to the qualifications of a Relieving Officer, the Commissioners have to 

observe, that no one ought to be appointed unless he is able to keep accounts, and iinles.s he 
engages to reside in the district for wtiich he is appointed to act, devoting his whole time to the 
performance of the duties of his office, without following any trade or profession, or entering 
into any service. . . 

3. The amount of salary which should be granted to each Relieving Officer will 
vary in different parts of Ireland according to local circumstances and the laboriousness 
of tlie duties which may have to be performed. Considering, however, the great importance 
of securing the services of efficient individuals, the Commissioners think that the salary 
should in no case (except under peculiar circumstances) be less than 351. a-year ; while in 
some instances, especially in large towns, a salary of even double that amount will not be 

4. In regard to the number of Relieving Officers in each U nion, the Commissioners 
think that it will be found, in practice, impossible to establish a general rule; and tho 
Commissioners bad intended to await from their Assistant Commissioners, a Report on the

Poor Law Com- arrangements which, after consultation with the respective Boards of Guardians, might be 
missioners’ Insiruc- Jeemed desirable for each Union. The early period, however, at which the operations 
Orders°*^ Genwal ^nder the Temporary Relief Act are to be brought to a close, renders it absolutely 

' necessary that there should be no fui-ther delay in advertising for candidates for the office of 

Relieving Officer. Under these circumstances, the Commissioners make the following 
suggestions in reference to the advertisements ; although such advertisements are not to be 
considered absolutely binding as to the course which the Guardians will pursue on the day of 
election. 

1. Ill Unions under the Temporary Relief Act, Relieving Officers may be advertised for in 
the proportion of one to each relief district. 

2. In Unions or electoral divisions not under the Temporary Relief Act, Relieving Officers 
may be advertised for in the proportion of one to a population of about 12,000. 

In conclusion, the Commissioners have to remark, that next to the essential point of 
collecting a sufficient amount of Poor Rates, the success of the new Irish Poor Law will mainly 
depend on the fitness of the individuals whom the Guardians select as Relieving Officers. And 
the Commissioners cannot impress too strongly upon Guardians the paramount importance of 
their resisting all private canvassings and solicitations, and of their keeping themselves 
unfettered, so that on the day of election they may he influenced in making the appointments, 
solely by the comparative merits of the rival candidates.

Arthur Moore, Chief CleTh

GENERA!. ORDER of the POOR LAW COMMISSIONERS for Regulating the 
ADMINISTRATION of OUT-DOOR RELIEF : — issued to each Union in Ireland. 

To the Guardians of the Poor of the several Unions named in the Schedule hereunto 
annexed, and the Officers of such Unions; to the Clerk or Clerks to the Justices of the 
Petty Sessions, held for the Division or Divisions in which the Townlands comprised 
within the said Unions are situate ; and to ail others whom it may concern. 

Whereas it is expedient to regulate the administration of the Relief of the Poor in the Unions 
named in the Schedule to this Order annexed, under the proviaons of an Act passed in the 
Tenih Year of the Heign of Her present Majesty, entitled “ An .4et to make further provision 
for the Relief of the Destitute Poor in Ireland,” and of the other Acts in foj'ce. for the Relief of 
the Destitute Poor in Ireland : 

We, tlie Poor Law Commissioners, in pursuance of tlie authorities vested in us by the said 
Acts, do hereby make the following Order, Rules, and Regulations, for the direction and 
coutroiil of the adraiuistration of Relief under the said Acts, in the Unions comprised in the 
said Schedule : 

Appointment of Relieving Officer. 

Art. I. — ^The Guardians of each of the Unions in the said Schedule, shall appoint so many 
Relieving Officers as the Poor Law Commissioners shall, from time to time, require or approve 
as the proper number of Relieving Officers for such Union, at such salaries as the said Com- 
missioners shall, from time to time, fix or approve; and shall assign to each Helieviiicr Officer, 
so appointed, such Electoral Division or Divisions, or parts thereof as the said Commissioners 
shall, from time to time, direct or approve. 

Art. II. — Tlie appointment of Relieving Officers shall be made in conformity with the rules 
prescribing the mode of appointment of Officers, which are contained in Articles 28 and 29 of 
the General Order of the Poor Law Commissioners, bearing dale the 5th day of June, in 
the year 1844, regulating the proceedings of Guardians, and the duties of Union Officers in 
Ireland. 

Qualification of Relieving Office7S. 

Art. III.-^The qualification of a Relieving Officer shall be as follows ; that is to say — 

No person shall be appointed a Relieving Officer who is engaged in a retail trade of any kind, nor 
who will not devote himself entirely to the duties of the office. 

No person shall be appointed a Relieving Officer who shall not have reached the age of Twenty- 
one years- 

No person shall be appointed a Relieving Officer who cannot read and write and keep accounts. 

No person shall be appointed a Relieving Officer who will not agree to give one month’s notice 
previously to resigning the office, or to forfeit one month’s amount of salary, to be deducted from 
the amount of salary due at the time of resignation. 

Security to be given by Relieving Officers. 

Art. IV. — The Board of Guardians shall take such security from every person appointed a 
Relieving Officer, as the Poor Law Commissioners shall approve, in conformity with the pro- 
visiops contained in Articles 3y and 39 of the above-recited General Order ; and the said 
provisions shall be alike applicable to Relieving Officers as to other Officers of Unions in 
Ireland.

Payment of Salaries of Relieving Officers. 

Art. V. — The payment of the Salaries of Relieving Officers shall be made in conformity 
with the provisions of Article 37 of the above-recited General Order; and the said provisions 
shall be alike applicable to Relieving Officers as to other Officers of Unions in Ireland.

Continuance in Office attd Suspension of Relieving Officers^ Supply of Vacancies. 

Art. VI. — ^The continuance in office of Relieving Officers, their suspension from office, and 
the filling up of every vacancy in the office, shall be conformable to the provisions contained in 
Articles 40, 41, 42, and 45 of the above-recited General Order ; and the said provisions shall 
be alike applicable to Relieving Officers as to other officers of Unions in Ireland. 



Duties of Relieving Officers. 

Art. VII. — The duties of every Believing Officer shall be : 

No. 1. To attend all ordinary meetings of the Board of Guardians, and to attend all other 
meetings when summoned by the Clerk. 

No. 2. To attend at all such places in his district, at such times of the day, and on such days in 
the week, as the Board of Guardians shall, from time to time, direct, for the purpose of dispensing 
relief, and of receiving applications for relief. 

No. 3. To receive all applications for relief made to him within his district, and forthwith to 
examine into the circumstances of every case, by visiting the home of the applicant, and by making 
all necessary inquiries into the state ot health, the ability to work, and the previous earnings and 
other means of such applicant, and to report the result of such inquiries, in the prescribed Form, 
entitled “ The Application and Report Book,” to the Board of Guardians at their next ordinary 
meeting. 

No. 4. Tn every case of sudden and urgent necessity, to afford such provisional relief to the 
destitute person as shall be requisite in the manner provided by law, that is to say, either by an 
order of admission to the Workhouse or Fever Hospital of the Union, provided there be room therein 
respectively, and by conveying any destitute poor person thereto, if necessary; or by affording such 
poor person immediate and temporary relief in food, lodging, medicine, or medical attendance, 
until the nest ordinary meeting of the Board of Guardians. 

No. 5. To report to the Board of Guardians at their next ordinary meeting all cases in which he 
shall have given provisional relief, and the nature and cost of the relief so afforded, in the pre- 
scribed Form, entitled “ The Application and. Report Book,” and to take the directions of the 
Board of Guardians regarding any further relief to be afforded in every case so reported. 

No. 6. Duly and punctually to dispense the weekly allowances of poor persons belonging to his 
district, and to relieve all poor persons within his district as directed by the Board of Guardians, 
and authorized by the signature and initials of the Chairman of the Meeting, in the columns pro- 
vided for the purpose in the prescribed Form, entitled ** The Application and Report Book.” 

No. 1. To keep a separate, full, and true account of all sums and 'articles dispensed by him for 
or on account of the relief of each poor person in the District for which be shall be appointed to 
act, in the prescribed Form, entitled " The Out-doot Relief List.” 

No. S. To keep a separate, fuU, and true account of all sums or articles received by him from 
the Board of Guardians, and expended or dispensed by him on the account of each Electoral Divi- 
sion in his District, or the Union at large, as the case may be, in the prescribed Form, entitled the 
“ Weekly Receipt and Expenditure Book,” and to balance the same weekly. 

No. 9. To present the prescribed Books of Accounts, severally entitled “ The Out-door Rdief 
List” and “ Weekly Receipt and Expenditure Book,” to the clerk for his inspection and authen- 
tication before every ordinary meeting of the Board of Guardians, and to the Board of Guardians 
at such meeting. 

No. 10. In no case to take credit in his Accounts, or enter as paid or given, any money or other 
articles which shall not have been paid or given previously to the taking of such credit, or the 
making of such entry. 

No. II. To make out at the end of each half-jear, list of all persons relieved at the charge of each 
electoral division, or the Union at large, in his district, in the Form prescribed for that purpose, 
entitled “ List of Destitute Persons relieved out of the Workhouse and to post, or cause to be 
posted, copies of the same in such public places as the Board of Guardians shall direct. 

No. 12. To submit to the Auditor of the Union all his books, accounts, and vouchers, at such 
place and time, and in such manner as may be required by the regulations of the Poor Law Com- 
missioners in force at the time. 

No. 13. To observe and execute all lawful orders and directions of the Board of Guardians 
applicable to his office. 



Further Duties of the Clerk of the Union. 

Art. VIII.— The Clerk of the Union shall perform the following duties in additon to those 
assigned to him in Article 47 of the General Order above recited : 

No. 1. He shall keep and punctually enter up the Out-door Relief Register, in the form herein 
prescribed. 

No. 2. Previously to every weekly meeting of the Guardians, he shall examine the Out-door 
Relief Listand “ Weekly Receipt and Expenditure Book” of each Relieving Officer in the Union, 
and authenticate, by his initials, the correctness of the same, if found to be correct.

Further Proceedings of the Board of Guardians in the Administration of Relief 

Art. IX. — The Guardians of tlie Union shall at each weekly meeting proceed as follows :

the d.ecision of the Board shall be forthwith recorded in the said book, to be authorized, if legal, by 
the signature or initials of tbe chairman of the meeting, in the columns respectively provided for 
the purpose. 

No. 2. They shall examine the several hooks of the Relieving Officers, and see that they are 
regularly authenticated, as hereinbefore is provided, by the clerk of the Union. 

No. 3. They shall examine, approve, and correct, if necessary, the “ Out-door Relief Register 
and the “ Out-door Relief Register,” when so approved, shall be signed by the chairman of the 
meeting, and countersigned by the clerk. 

No. 4. They shall direct such cheques to be drawn on the Treasurer, and such orders to be made 
on^'^'iesmen or other contractors, in favour of the Relieving Officers, as, after examination of their 
‘ Weekly Receipt and Expenditure Books,” and in reference to the balances standing at foot of those 
accounts, shall appear to he necessary to provide the Relieving Officers with the means of affording 
relief to the destitute persons in their several districts j and every such cheque or order shall be 
signed by the chairman of the meeting, and two Guardians, and countersigned by the cleric.

Circular as to Qualifications of Relieving Officers. 

Poor Laic Commission Office, 

Sir, Duhlin, August 

In reference to the approaching elections of Relieving Officers, the Commissioners have to 
state, that objections have been raised to the disqualification imposed by the Commissioners for 
that office, of persons exercising a retail trade. The Commissioners, therefore, deem it right to 
state the reasons on irhich that disqualification is founded, and to point out at the same time 
the description of individuals whom it would be desirable to select as Relieving Officers. 

In the first place, there is no doubt that the duties of a Relieving Officer, if properly per- 
formed, will take up the whole of one individual’s time. Now, if any one holding that situation 
were permitted, notivithstanding, to keep a shop, this would be a coustant temptation to him to 
neglect his public duties for the sake of his private interests. 

In the next place, a Relieving Officer will be supposed to be a person of considerable influence 
in his district, inasmuch as the views taken by the Guardians of the cases of applicants for relief 
will be believed to depend to a considerable extent on his representations. Hence an unscru- 
pulous Relieving Officer who kept a shop would be able by indirect means to obtain customers 
amongst the poorer classes ; even in the case of a thoroughly honest individual, customers might, 
without any effort on his part, be attracted to his shop, under the idea that they would thus 
conciliate his favour ; and although it might sometimes happen that considerations of this kind 
would really have no influence on any party, there would almost always be some handle for 
unpleasant suspicions, which it is better to prevent by timely precaution, than merely to devise 
a remedy for them when they have once arisen. 

With regard to the description of persons who are best adapted for the duties of Relieving 
Officers, the Commissioners desire to draw especial attention to individuals who woidd be denied 
eligible candidates for the police force. The main point to be looked to is intelligence in be- 
coming thoroughly acquainted with the circumstances of each applicant for relief ; and tliis 
again would imply considerable activity in order to obtain trustworthy informaiion from various 
sources. But neither intelligence nor activity alone would render any one a good Relieving 
Officer ; be ought also to possess firmness of mind, so as to be enabled in the discharge of his 
duty to resist intimidation, from whatever quarter it might come, and in whatever form it might 
present itself.

Circular as to the Admjnistr.ation of Out-door Relief. 

Poor Law Commission Office, Dublin, 

Sir, \‘ith August, ikif . 

The Poor Law Commissioners deem it right to address tire Board of Guardians on 
some points which will arise in carrying into effect the General Order of the Commissioners, 
dated the 2nd instant. 

In commencing their operations under tire 10th Viet., c. 31, the Guardians will bear in mind, 
the state of the law, as pointed out to them in the Commissioners’ Circular of the 1st ultimo. 

The Commissioners again enumerate the several classes of destitute persons who can legally 
receive relief out of the workhouse under the first section of the Act; tliat is to say — 

1. Destitute persons who are permanently disabled from labour by reason of old age, iofirmity, or 
bodily or mental defect. 

2. Destitute poor persons who, being disabled from labour by reason of severe sickness or serious 
accident, are thereby deprived of the means of earning a subsistence for themselves and their fami- 
lies, whom they are liable by law to maintain. 

3. Destitute poor widows having two or more legitimate children dependent on them. 

These are the only classes who can at present receive Out-door Relief of any kind from the 
Board of Guardians; and it is to the mode of procedure in bringing all such cases of dratitution 
on the Out-door Relief Books, and in dispensing to them the relief which may be requisite iu 
each case, that the Commissioners have now to call the attention of the Guardians. 

In Article VII. , No. 2, of the General Order, the Relieving Officer is directed to attend at 
such places in his district, at such times of the day, and on such days of the week as the Board 
of Guardians shall, from time to time direct, for the purpose of dispensing relief, and of receiving 
applicafiorfs for relief. 

To enable the Relieving Officer to perform this duty, the. Guardians will at once furnish each 
Relieving Officer with a set of books of account, as prescribed iu the Genera! Order. 

Secondly, They will fix the place or places in his district, at which they deem it necessary 
for the Relieving bfficer to attend in each week, for the purposes above stated ; and a proper 
station or room must be provided at the expense of the Union, for the use of the Relieving 
Officer at every point of his district, at which he shall be required so to attend. 

Tliirdlv, The Guardians will have to consider and determine the amount of cash or other 
means of relief which it may be necessary to place at the disposal of the Relieving Officer each 
week, in reference to the exigencies of his district. 

With regard to the last point, the Commissioners believe that the number of destitute persons 
falling within the three classes above specified, will be found to be a very limited portion of the 
population in each Relieving Officer’s district. The Relief Lists used under the Temporary 
Act will, as announced by the Relief Commissioners on the 31st ultimo, be pla.ced at the dis- 
posal of the Board of Guardians and their officers, and those lists may afford material assistance 
as to the names and number of the persons belonging to the three classes in question, but should 
by no means be permitted to supersede other means of inquiry, least of all such as must be made 
into every case by the Relieving Officer in person. 

The attention of the Guardians will be at once directed to the best course to be pursued, in 
dispensing relief to these three classes of destitute persons out of the workhouse. Under existing 
circumstances it appears most desirable, that the present accommodation in the workhouse 
should, as a general rule, he reserved for the relief of such able-bodied persons, not falling 
within the first section of the Extension Act, as may be deemed to be destitute ; and the Com- 
missioners are prepared to approve (for the present) the discharge of persons from the work-

house, -who may fall within any of the three classes specified in Section I., and who may be 
deemed properly and sufficienlly prodded for by a weekly allowance out of the workliouse, so 
lor^ as the causes of their destitution shall continue to exist. 

The question of relieving these classes in money or in kind must next receive attention. T,^ie 
statute, in prescribing food as the only mode of Out-door Relief to other classes, does not make 
the same restriction in regard to the three classes in Section I. 

The Commissioners think that the proved advantages of relieving in food, especially cooked 
food, are applicable to all classes of the destitute, but they deem it, on the whole, inexpedient to 
require that course to be pursued, under the present circumstances, with regard to the classes 
relievable out of the workhouse under Section I. Those classes, as already stated, are limited 
in extent, and the cases they include are of a nature easy to discriminate, and the relief, there- 
fore, in whatever form administered, is less liable to abuse and imposition than in other cases. 
For the present, therefore, and until the administrative arrangements are more matured, the 
Commissioners do not object to allowances of money being made to the destitute of these classes, 
where the Guardians may not be prepared to dispense relief to them in cooked food. 

The relief of destitute persons not falling within the three classes specified in Section I., must 
be conducted entirely by admission to the workhouse, until an order of tlie Poor Law Commis- 
sioners be issued, under the provisions of Section II. 

This order can only be issued by the Commissioners after it shall have been made to appear 
to them that adequate relief cannot be afforded to the last-mentioned classes of destitute persons 
by admission to the workhouse, either by reason of want of room, or by reason of the prevalence 
of infectious disease in the workhouse or workliouses of the Union; and wherever the Guar- 
dians consider that either of these contingencies have arisen, it is necessary that they should so 
express themselves in a representation of the facts to the Commissioners. 

Advantage having been taken of the present season as a fitting season to discontinue, in many 
Unions, the relief recently afforded, in food, to a great portion of the labouring population, and 
thus to throw them on their own resources, the Commissioners are reluctant, except on clear and 
distinct recorded grounds, to give effect to that provision of the 10 Viet., c. 31, which authorizes 
Boards of Guardians in Ireland, to give relief in food out of the workhouse to able-bodied persons, 
and other persons not included in the classes specified in the first section of that Statute.

Further Circol.\r as to the Administration of Relief under 10 VicT., c. 31. 

I^oor Laic Commission Office, Dublin, 

Sir, 26tA August, 1847. 

The Poor Law Commissioners propose to offer a few suggestions in reference to those 
Unions in which the Guardians are convinced that it will become necessary for them, unless 
they adopt precautioary measures, to grant Out-door Relief to able-bodied men during the 
approaching autumn. When the operations under the Temporary Relief Act are terminated 
on the 12th September, the Poor Rates throughout the whole of Ireland will be liable for the 
relief of a mass of apparent destitution which, in some districts, may prove wholly unmanageable, 
unless the Guardians have definite ideas of the precise evils which are most to be dreaded, and 
of the best way iu which those evils can be counteracted or mitigated. The Commissioners 
deem it right, therefore, to make generally known the views which they themselves entertain on 
this important subject. 

The Commissioners think that the evil which is most to be guarded against is the necessity 
of granting Out-door Relief to able-bodied men; and that the main point for the Guardians to 
keep steadily in view is, to make their workhouse as extensively available as possible for the 
rebef of this class. 

On the difiRculty of preventing abuses in granting Out-door Relief to able-bodied men, the 
Commissioners do not intend to dilate. The experience and observations of Guardians as to 
what has taken place under the I.abour Rate Act, and the Temporary Relief Act, will probably 
have convinced them that although such relief may be administered with the utmost ability and 
most upright intentions, it is liable to many abuses. During the past year, indeed, it has been 
absolutely necessary for the preservation of human life, but still it is a matter of notoriety, that 
numerous persons have bad a share of the public alms, who ought to have subsisted on their 
own resources. 

On the other hand, very extensive experience has proved that relief may be granted to able- 
bodied men in a well regulated workliouse, without entailing the certainty of any very serious 
evils. Speaking generally, such relief combines the two important advantages — 1st, that those 
who are really destitute will accept it ; and 2ndly, that those who are not really destitute will 
not accept it. And this may be illustrated without insisisting on the decisive experience of 
England, by referring to what has occurred in Ireland, in connexion with the distress of the past 
year. 

Daring last winter and spring, the workhouses in Ireland were so lull that they contained 
more inmates than they were originally built to accommodate, and in some Unions it became 
frequently the painful duty of Guardians to reject, from want of room, some of the applicants 
for admission. This shows that relief in a workhouse will be accepted when severe distress 
exists in a population. 

On the other hand, the effect of a workhouse, in bringing to light imposition, has been mani- 
fested in a remarkable manner within the last fortnight, in North Dublin Union. During the 
week ended Saturday, the 14th instant, there were above 20,000 persons on the Relief Lists of

The Commissioners do not anticipate that the results of pursuing a similar couree in the 
South and West of Ireland will be equally striking with what has occurred in North Dublin 
Union, but still the same principles of relief to able-bodied men will be found universally applic- 
able ; and it may be confidently expected that wherever those principles are acted on, the 
results will not differ in kind, but only in degree. 

In order, therefore, to carry out those principles, the Commissioners make the following 
recommendations in reference to those Unions wherein the Guardians are of opinion that it 
will become necessaiy for them to grant Out-door Relief to able-bodied men after the 12th of 
September, if the present mode of administermg relief is not previously altered. 

1st. To grant Ont-door allowances to destitute persons permanently disabled from labour. — The 
Commissioners think that such allowances should he sufficient in amount to prevent the necessity of 
begging. 

2nd. To grant similar allowances to widows with two or more legitimate children. The effect 
of this course will be, to place at the disposal of the Guardians, accommodation for the children of 
able-bodied men in the children’s wards. 

3rd. If the above measures are insufficient, to remove all the school children of the workhouse 
with the Schoolmaster and Schoolmistress, to a separate and distinct establishment, — such an 
arrangement, if made permanent, would he attended with numerous moral advantages to the 
children ; and no one measure would place at the disposal of the Guardians so much additional 
workhouse accommodation with such liltle inconvenience. 

4th. To hire a house or houses for the reception of poor persons affected with fever or other 
dangerous contagious disease, and to make use of such houses for the reception and medical treat- 
ment of such poor persons, in preference to the workhouse Fever wards. — This measure would be 
attended with the double advantage of giving additional workhouse room to the Guardians, and of 
diminishing, at the same time, the risk of infection to paupers in the workhouse. And it is to be 
observed, that an Order for authorizing Out-door Relief to able-bodied men, under the second sec- 
tion of the Irish Relief Extension Act may become requisite on account of fever or other infectious 
disease in the •workhouse. 

If, notwithstanding all these four expedients, it is still found necessary to grant Out-door Relief 
in any Union to able-bodied men, this would appear to the Commissioners an indication that 
the workhouse accommodation of the Union was insufficient ; and the Commissioners would 
willingly co-operate with the Guardians in enlarging the present workhouse, as far as is prac- 
ticable, or in the erection of a new workhouse. 

With regard to raising the requisite funds for this purpose, the Commissioners are not autho- 
rized 10 hold out any nope of their being able to obtain a loan for the Guardians from the 
Exchequer Bill Loan Commissioners. The Guardians, however, might borrow the money from 
any Company, or from private individuals, under the 35th and 90tb sections of the Irisfi Poor 
Relief Act, and they might charge the principal and interest on the Poor Rates, provided that 
they repaid the principal by annual instalments of not less than one-twentieth of the sum bor- 
rowed.

Further Circular as to the Support of the Tempor.ary Fever Hospitals 
and Dispensaries. 

Poor Law Commission Offee, Dublin, 

Sir, Qth October, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for the Relief of the Poor in Ireland 
desire me again to call the attention of Boards of Guardians to the provisions of the 14tli and 
15th sections of the Fever Act, 10 Vic., cap. 22, in reference to the temporary hospitals or 
dispensaries provided under auy order issued by the Relief Commissioners on certificates of 
the Board of Health. As the maintenance of those temporary hospitals or dispensaries will, 
henceforward, depend solely on the Poor Rates, the Commissioners deem it right to call 
earnestly on Boards of Guardians to direct their special attention to providing Finance Com- 
mittees with funds for this purpose, in the manner pointed out in the Commissioners’ letter of 
the 20th ultimo. 

The number of inmates in those establishments is at present about 13,000; and it appears 
to the Commissioners that the condition of those individuals has the strongest claims on the 
sympathy and solicitude of Boards of Guardians. The fever patients belong chiefly to the 
most destitute portion of the population, while their weakness and helplessness prevent them 
from obtruding tlieir distress on public notice in the same way as destitute persons in good 
health. The Commissioners, appeal, therefore, to tbe feelings of compassion, honour, and duty, 
in the Guardians throughout Ireland, not to allow the inmates of the temporaiy fever hospitals 
to languisli iu unrelieved suffering, through the want of funds for supplying tiieni with the 
nourishment and care which their condition demands. 

Similar considerations require tliat the doors of these establishments should not be shut 
against new applicants. It is a matter of notoriety, that without them tliere is not sulBcient 
hospital accommodation in Ireland; and the effect of closing them would be, to prevent tlie 
separation of tlie sick from tlie healthy, and to render it necessary that fever patients, if they 
received medical attendance at all, should be treated in their own dwellings, which are too often 
over crowded, ill ventilated, and dirty. The Commissioners have the authority of the Board 
of Health for saying, that the result would probably be, a continued and increasing generation 
of malignant typhus fever, a tainted atmosphere, and a wide spreading of the contagion over 
the whole country. 

The Commissioners have to add, that mere motive of self-interest, without regard to higher 
considerations, render it advisable to make ample provision for the separation and cure of fever 
patients. Although fevCT may commence its ravages amongst the poorer classes, it scarcely ever 
fails, ultimately, to visit the rich; and it is to be observed, that the mortality amongst rich 
persons affected with fever in Ireland, is nearly ten times as great as amongst the poor under 
similar circumstances. Indeed, melaucholjr instances will readily be called to mind by Guar- 
dians of highly valuable members of society, amongst the upper classes, whose career of 
usefulness has been cut short by fever, during the present year. Now, it cannot be doubted, 
that in the majority of cases the individuals adverted to, caught fever from infection diffused 
by the poor. — Hence, expenses incurred for the cure of destitute fever patients may be regarded 
to a certain extent, as a kind of life insurance to tbe rich who are in health. 

In conelurion, the Commissioners have to express the hope, that Guardians will jealously 
co-operate with the Relief Committees in carrying out the arrangements under the Temporary 
Relief Act, and that no material embarrassments will be allowed to arise from tlie circum- 
stance that Relief Committees and Boards of Guardians are not cemstituted precisely iu the 
same manner. 

The difficulties and dangers of the present period are so grear, that they can be onlv 
adequately met by the harmonious action of all; and it would be in the highest degree ilis- 
creditable to the country, if fever patients were not properly taken care ot', on aeoount of 
jealousies or misunderstandings between Relief Committees and Boards of Guardians.

Tee Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland, 
desire to draw the attention of the Board of Guardians to the necessity and importance of 
promptly bringing under review the subject of their contracts for provisions and other supplies, 
and the present state of their stocks of bedding and clothing, so as to be prepared in due time 
for any accession to the number of inmates which the present circumstances of the Union 
render probable. 

The Commissioners urgently desire and call upon the Guardians, in making such prepara- 
tions, to base their estimates on the a^umpiion that the whole accommodation which the 
workhouse affords will be placed in requisition. 

The experience of the past year has, in numerous instances, shown the serious results which 
arise from the Guardians undeitaking to relieve in the workhouse destitute persons for whom 
they are not prepared with supplies of clothing and bedding. Tlie Poor Law Commissioners, 
however, called the special attention of Boards of Guardians to the subject last year, before the 
distress commenced, and the Commissioners deem it their duty to bring the subject again under 
the notice of Boards of Guardians, at the present time.

CiRcuLAn to Boards of Guardians, with General Order, as to the Collection of Poor 
Rates. 

Poor Laic Commission Office, Duhlin, 

Sir, Octolicr 26, lb4/. 

The Coinmissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland, send 
herewith a General Order under seal, containing regulations which provide for a more frequent 
examination of the accounts of the collectors of Poor Rates than that wiiich has heretofore pre- 
Tailed in many Unions in Ireland. 

A further object of the order is to facilitate the examination of these accounts by the clerk 
of the Union, by the introduction of an additional book of account, in a very simple form, en- 
titled the “ Collector’s Rate-receipt Abstract.” 

Under the system established by this order, a collector is bound to issue a receipt for every 
sum received for Poor Rates : to issue no receipts but those contained in a Receipt Check Book, 
previously numbered and initialed by the clerk ; and to return to the clerk all the counterparts 
or blocks from which such receipts have been detached. 

In the next place, the collector is required to account, weekly, for everj' sum for wliich he 
has issued a receipt, to cast up those sums weekly, and to balance the totals weekly with the 
lodgments which he has made with the treasurer. 

The clerk is required to examine each collector’s accounts once, at least, in every fortnight ; 
and if the Board of Guardians shall require it, once in every week. 

In examining the collectors’ accounts, the clerk is required to see that every receipt deiachcd 
from a block or counterpart is accounted for, and that the sum appearing an the counterpart 
has been entered as paid. The clerk will also compare the iveekly totals with the treasurer’s 
receipts for lodgments, and authenticate the correctness of the balances. This duty of the clerk, 
although it is prescribed in the General Order of the 5th June, 1844, has not been, as the Com- 
missioners believe, duly carried out in all Unions, partly through the absence of such a form of 
account as is now prescribed, in which the contents of the block receipts are brought together 
and cast up by the collector, whereby nothing is left to the clerk but to compare entries and 
ascertain their correctness, as well as the accuracy of the totals. Such a system has for some 
time existed in several Unions, through the medium of a book of account similar to that 
called the “ Rate-receipt Abstract.” 

The Commissioners trust that the Board of Guardians will give their prompt and earnest 
attention to so important a point as the establishment of an effective system of accountability 
on the part of the collectors, and require exactness and punctuality from the clerk in the p‘r- 
formance of this part of his duty. If special assistance he at any time required for the per- 
formance of the clerk’s duties, the Commis>ioners wish that this portion of them should at all 
times be done exclusively by the clerk himself, and not by any assistant or deputy, except in 
the necessary absence of the clerk through sickness. 

The Commissioners are satisfied that the Board of Guardians may themselves exert a most 
important influence in securing due accountability in the collectors, by giving their attention, as 
a Board, for a short time each week or fortnight, as the case may be, to the examination of 
these accounts, or by entrusting that duty to one or more Committees. If the clerk performs 
his duty in conformity with the present order, the Guardians will, by inspection of the weekly 
balance sheets, be enabled, with a very slight expenditure of time and trouble, to exercise an 
effectual control over the proceedings of the collectors. 

Another influence, equally important, may he e.xerted by the Board of Guardians, or by a 
Poor Rate Committee, iu causing the names of individual defaulters of Poor Rates to be 
brought before them from time to time, in order that, where the collectors appear to be inac- 
tive, or to be under any influence either of fear or favour, specific directions may be given to 
them, and they may at once he placed under the alternative of doing their duty or losing their 
office. 

The attention of the inspector of the Union has been especially called to this subject by the 
Commissioners ; and he has been directed to give his personal attendance and assistance m the 
Guardians, or any Committee of the Guardians, when engaged in supervising the collection of 
the rates, as frequently as his other avocations will permit. 

I have, &c.. 

To the Clerk to the Guardians W. Stanlet, Secretary,

The powers of a Collector of Poor Rates are provided in the following Statutes : 

1. The '<3rd Section of the Irish Poor Relief Act, 1 and 2 Vic., c, 56, and the provisions of the 

Grand Jury Act there referred to, 6 and 7 Wm. IV., c. 116, Sections 152 and 153. give to collectors 
of Poor Rates — ® 

A power of immediate distress on the premises rated, after demand and refusal of the Rate ; 

A power, if the collector prefers, of laying complaint before a justice, after six days’ notice, and 
non-payment of the rate ; 

And a power of proceeding by civil bill for any sum not exceeding £50. 

2. The 78th Section of the Irish Poor Relief Act contains a further power, independent of those 
above stated, of proceeding by distress, as for recovery of rent, under which mode of distress not only the 
goods of the Rate-payer, but those of any other person found on the premises, may be taken. This 
power, _ however, is not available until two months after the rate has been made ; and the advantage 
attending it, of taking a stranger’s goods, if found on the premises, has been since extended to a distress 
made for Poor Rate, under the Grand Jury Act, by the 6th Section of the Irish Poor Law Amendment 
Act, 6 and 7 Vic., c. 92, which provides — 

_ “ That in all cases in wliich (under the Poor Law Acts) it is made lawful to levy any money by 
distress and sale of the goods of any person, all goods and chattels, to whomsoever the same may 
belong, found on any premises in respect of whicTi any person is or shall be rated as the occu- 
pier, or as occupier of which he is liable to pay the rate, shall be liable to be distrained and sold, 
as if they were the goods and chattels of such person.” 

Two legal questions of great and general importance have arisen under these statutes : — 

_ Firstly, — Whether a collector of Poor Rate can distrain under the Grand Jury Act, by virtue of 
bis own warrant from the Guardians, before the expiration of tw-o months from the making of the 
rate ? 

The Law Officers of the Croicn have all now concurred in opinion, that such distress may be 
made before the expiration of two months, that is to say, immediately after piillication of the Rates, 
and after demand of the Rale and refusal of payment. 

Secondly, — It has been asked whether under the 6th section of 6th and 7th Vic., c. 92, goods already 
seized by the landlord for rent, but remaining on the premises rated, can be distrained b^ the collector 
of Poor Rates ? 

The Law Officers of the Crown have advised that such Goods after being bond fide seised by the 
landlord, are in the custody of the law, and cannot be distrained for Poor Rates. 

3. The above provisions relate to the enforcement of Poor Rates from occupiers only of rated 
hereditaments. 

The proceedings to be taken for recovery of rates assessed on immediate lessors of tenements, at or 
uuder £4 or £8, as the case may be, are provided in the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th sections of the Irish Poor 
Law Amendment Act, 6th and 7th Vic., c. 92.

CiRcuL.\R to Relieving Officers, as to their Duties. 

Poor Laxo Commiasioxi, Dublin, 

Sir, November 10, 1847. 

The Commi^ioners for administering the Laws for the Relief of the Poor in Ireland 
enclose for your use a copy of their General Order of the 2nd August, 1847, for regulating 
the administatiou of relief under tlie Acts now in force for the relief of the Destitute Poor in 
Ireland. 

Article VII. of that Order prescribes the ^‘Duties of Relieving Officers;" and to this 
article the Commissioners call your especial attention. It is satisfactory to the Commis- 
sioners that 3 |ou should thus receive directly from themselves an official intimation of the duties 
which you will be expected to discharge j and they earnestly impress upon you the necessity 
of conforming yourself, in every particular, to the regulations which have been framed for your 
guidance and couti-ol. 

Tlie serions responsibilities of the office which you have undertaken should alone suffice to 
convince you of the prudence as well as propriety of your adiiering closely to the rules pre- 
scribed ; for by so doing, and not otherwise, will your conduct escape censure on any occasion 
on which it may appear that the benevolent purposes of the Irish Relief Acts have in any 
respect failed of their accomplishment. 

For example : should the funds necessary for the out-door relief of the poor not be provided, 
this is no reason why you should relax in the performance of such of your duties as you can, 
under the circumstances mentioned, perform. On the contrary, it will be your interest as well 
as your duty to use increased vigilance and exertion, lest on inquiry being made into the causes 
of mismanagement, any part thereof should be traced to your want of attention to your duties. 
You should, in such a case, not fail to receive -applications for relief at the times and places 
appointed by the Guardians, inquire into the circumstances of the applicants, record the facts of 
each case in the books provided for that purpose, and bring the whole under the cognizance of 
the Board of Guardians, whose duty it is to order or refuse relief, and to supply you with the 
necessary funds for dispensing relief. By such a course you will not only avoid censure, but 
will have done every thing w-ithio your province to remedy the defect of funds, by showing, in 
the proper quarter, the necessity which may e.xist for providing them. 

The Commissioners now call your especial attention to a most important section of the 
statute under which your appointment has been made j and in order to ensure your ac- 
quaintance with the e.xact terms of that provision, they proceed to quote it from the statute, 
word for word. 

It runs as follows : — 

“ Sec. VII. And be it enacted, That every Relieving Officer so appointed ns aforesaid, shall 
have power to give provisional relief in any case of sudden and urgent necessity, either by an 
order of admission to the Workhouse or Fever Hospital of the Union, provided there be room' 
therein respectively, and by conveying any destitute poor person thereto if necessary, or by afford- 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 29 

ing Euch poor person immediate and temporary relief in food, lodging, medicine, or medical 
attendance, until the next Ordinary Meeting of the Board of Guardians, at tvliich meeting he shall 
report the case, and the nature and cost of relief so afforded, in such form and manner as the Poor 
Lair Commissioners shall prescribe, and after such report, shall give no further relief, otherwise 
than by direction of the Board of Guardians, in the case so reported; and the Guardians of the 
Union shall furaish the Relieving OfEcers with the necessary funds for affording relief in manner 
aforesaid, and for the relief of those destitute poor persons to whom relief shall be granted by the 
Board of Guardians, at such times, and in such manner as the Poor Law Commissioners shall 
determine and direct.” 

On a judicious exercise of your powers under this section will depend, in a great measure, 
the success of your proceedings. It was not intended that you should, in the exercise of this 
power, undertake, on your own responsibility, an extensive system of relief wltiiout direction or 
control on the part of the Board of Guardians. Should yon do so, and should you thereby fall 
into a system of indiscriminately relieving all applicants, you will be adopting an extreme 
course which will expose you to ovenvhelming claims, to much consequent embarrassment, and 
probably, to ultimate confusion and failure. 

On tlie other hand, you oiight, from a sense of humanity as well as official responsibility, to 
be easily accessible, and keenly alive to the existence of actual suffering from destitution : and 
the funds which may be applied by you, under your provisional power, to the relief of real dis- 
tress, and the prevention of fatal consequences from privation, will be rendered of the higliast 
value in a public sense, by the certainty of their having been well bestowed. Should any case 
of sudden and urgent necessity be brought to your knowledge, and fail to receive attention or 
relief, and evil consequences be the result of such failure, official inquiry into the facts will invari- 
ably follow, and you will be required to show that the failure of due relief was not owing to your 
neglect, or to abide the consequences of your conduct. 

The Commissioners doubt not that you will appreciate the full difficulty and delicacy of the 
functions which you have to discharge, and they trust, by the exercise of humanity, juclgment, 
impartiality, and vigilant attention to your duty, the administration of relief will be properly 
conducted in your district, so far as your office is concerned, and that neither imposture will be 
successfully practised by the applicants lor relief, nor that the really destitute will fail to receive 
the relief which has been provided for them by law. 

I am, &c.. 

To each Relieving Officer. . Stanlev, Secretary.

salaries to be given to each of the said officers.

Ireland, do hereby onJerand direct that the number of Relieving Officers to be appointed in the 
said Union shall be four. 

And we do hereby define the limits of the several districts of the Relieving Officers so to be 
appointed, as follows, that is to say : — 

1. The first district shall consist of the electoral divisions of Moylougb, BallynakilJ, Rillian, 
Killeroran, and Killasolan, and shall be called the Moylough district.

gerril, Ballymacward, Kiiaan, and Taghmaconnell, and shall be called the Taghmacoonell district. 

3. The third district shall consist of the electoral divisions of Aughrim, Ballinasloe, Creagh, 
Cloontoosfceit, and Moore, and shall be called the Creagh district. 

4. The fourth district shall consist of the electoral divisions of Kiltormer, Abbeyconnican, 
Killimer, ELilquain, Eyrecourt, and Clonfert, and shall be called the Clonfert district

to the several relieving officers to be appointed sm aforesaid, namely, —

INSTRUCTIONS to POOR LAW INSPECTORS. 

CmctiL.AR to the Ordinary Poor Law Inspectors. 

No. 560— M /47. 

Poor Law Commission Office, Dublin, 

SrR, October 2%, 1847. 

The Comrnissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland 
enclose, for your information, a copy of a General Order issued by them, to provide for a 
more frequent and more effective examination of the coUectoi-s’ accounts, by the clerk of the 
Union. 

The Commissioners enclose also a copy of a circular letter accompanying the order, and 
addressed to each Board of Guardians in Ireland. 

The Commbsioners trust that these regulations will have the effect of securing due aecount- 
ahility on the part of the collectors of Poor Rates, and a i-egular and certain knowledge by the 
Commissioners and Boards of Guardians of the progress of the collection, and of the lodg- 
ments made from time to time on account of each electoral division. 

The regulations, however, in the order, are confined to the above purposes, and do not 
directly relate to the very important object of ensuring, on the part of the collectors, assiduity 
and vigour in soliciting and enforcing payment of the rates by individual rate-payers without 
fear or favour. 

You will perceive that the Commissioners have addressed the Guardians on this, latter point, 
urging them to undertake, either by themselves as a Board, or by the appointment of one or 
more Committees, a regular and efficient control over the collection of the rates. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 



33 



It is, however, chiefly to an effective supervision, by yourself, cf this part of the duties of the 
Board of Guardians, tlie Clerks, and the Poor Rate collectors, respectively, that the Commis- 
sioners trust for ensurinff that degree of activity and vijrour in the collection of the Poor Rates 
in Ireland, which the Commissioners are expected by Her Majesty’s Government, in the present 
exigencies of this country, to enfoace. 

The Commissioners deem it right, therefore, to point out to you two ways by which it 
appears to them the supen'ision of the inspector may be brought to bear with much effect on 
the collection of the rates, although in doing so the Commissioners may, perhaps, be suggesting 
to you what may have already been a part of your previous practice as an inspector. 

in the first place, the Commissioners would wish you, in everj' case in which you may deem 
any extraordinary exertions to be required, to induce the Guardians to have constantly brought 
before tiiem the names of individual defaulters of Poor Rates, in order that any fear or par- 
tiality influencing the collector may be exposed, and that specific directions may be given to 
him which will leave him no alternative but to do his duty or to lose his office. Such pro- 
ceeding would, perhaps, be more effective if a certain limited number of the defaulters, com- 
mencing with tho&3 rated at high amounts in each division, were brought forwar<l at one time, 
rather than a list of all who have not paid their rates ; and this course might Ije repeated suc- 
cessivel 3 ‘, until the names of all defaulters should come before the Guardians. The Commis- 
sioners think that vou can, with the gieatest advantage on such occasions, take a prominent 
part in suggesting'directions to the collectors, as well as in organizing an arrangement by which 
the Board of Guardians, or a Committee may be led effectually to govern the collection of the 
rates. 

Secondly, the Commissioners request that you will see that a regular system of accounting 
on the part of the collector is carried out, through the agency of the clerk ot the Union, in con- 
formity with the provisions of the present order. Vour personal attendance may be necessary, 
in some cases, to establish this system of accounting in the first instance; and the Commis- 
sioners trust that you well omit no opportunity of ascertaining whether the duties prescribed 
for the several officers, in the order, are duly and punctually discharged by them. 

In any Union in which the Guardians may, with the Commissioners’ consent, provide the 
clerk with assistance to discharge his increased duties, the Commissioners propose to ijisist that 
the important task of examining and checking the collectors’ accounts shall be performed by 
the clerk in person, and not entrusted to any assistant or deputy. 

I have the honour to be. Sir, 

Your obedient setrant. 

To each Poor Laic Inspector W. Stanley, Secretary, 

in charge of a District of Unions.

CiRCUL.vR to Tempor.arv Poor Law Inspectors for particular Unions. 

TVfo, 552 M 47. Poor Late Commission Office, Dublin, 

October '26, ]S-i7. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for the Relief of the 
Poor in Ireland, to acquaint you, that it having been deemed advisable that some of those who 
have acquired experience in carrying out the relief operations during the present year, should be 
appointed Temporary Poor Law Inspectors in some of the Unions in the south, and west, and 
north-west of Ireland, the Commissioners have been pleased to appoint you a Temporary Poor 
Law Inspector in Union. , j. -n 

Althouo’h that Union will still remain included within the district of one of the ordinary Poor 
Law Insiiectors, it is the intention of the Commissioners that you should, notwithstanding, 
discbar<^e in it all tire duties of an Inspector, which were formerly within the province of 
Assistant Poor Law Commissioners. Thus, the Commissioners wish that you should attend 
the weekly meetings of the Board of Guardians as often as is compatible with your other 
official enoao^meuts, and that you sliould regularly inspect the Union Workhouse. Still there 
are certain duties which are become at the present time of such paramount importance that the 
Commissioners are desirous of directing your especial attention towai'ds them as l«ing the 
points in which the effectual workmg of the Irish Poor Law during the next winter will essen- 
tially depend. ‘ , , , ,• e .u 

L The first point is the collection of the Poor Rates, and as the whole machinery ot the 
Poor Laws will be inoperative unless funds are obtained for the relief of the destitute, the 
Commbskmers are anxious that you should, in the first instMce. direct all your energiw to 
securintr the performance of this duty by the Boardof Guardians and the collectors. In© 
Commissicaiers believe that if the Guardians and collectors make a determined use of their 
undoubted powers, if the Guardians set a good example by paying the rates which are due 
from themselves, and if thev uiiftiDcbingly, without favour or affection, institute legal proceedi^s 
against immediate lessors and all others who are in arrear, there will not be any insuperable 
difficulty in the collection of the rates. • r , • j 

It is 'however, not impossible that in some few instances attempts, either tacit or av owed, 
to resist the payment of rates may be made, and in such cases you will not fail to assist the
