2. Next in importance to the collection of the Poor Hates, comes the due administration of 
them on sound principles, and on this head the Commissioners refer yon to their accompanying 
circular of the 26th of last August, as containing a detailed explanation of the line of action which 
they recommend to Boards of Guardians. The Commissioners attach much importance to the 
views contained in that circular, and they request you to use all your efforts to ensure their 
adoption. It will be observed that the main point is to make the workhouse as extensively 
available as possible for the relief of the able-bodied men, and that great efforts and sacrifices 
should be made for the attainment of this object. In the firet place, the destitute impotent 
poor, and destitute widows with two or more legitimate children, should receive out -door allow- 
ances. Secondly, the workhouse children of both sexes should be removed to a separate and 
distinct establishment ; and, thirdly, provision should be made for fever patients elsewhere than 
on the workhouse premises. By the combination of all these measures the Commissioners 
believe that the existing workhouses would, in some Unions, be found sufficient for the relief of 
able-bodied men. 

If, however, this should not be the case in your Union, the Commissioners will readily co- 
operate with the Guardians in endeavouring to procure additional workhouse accommodation. 
On this head the Commissioners request that you will impress on the Guardians in the strongest 
possible manner that they have ample powers to hire and fit up a building as a workhouse in 
any part of the Union, and that, under ordinary circumstances, it will be in the highest degree 
pernicious to the interest of the rate-payers to grant out-door relief to able-bodied men. In 
fact, the Commissioners regad with apprehension the possible necessity of issuing an order 
authorizing such relief; and they consider such an oi-der as an expedient which can only be 
entertained in case all other resources shall have failed. 

3. Lastly, the Commissioners request that you will take care that the relieving officers 
perform their duties properly, according to Article VII. of the Out-door Relief Order, a copy 
of which is herewith enclosed. It is to be remembered that relieving officers ar-e a class of 
functionaries hitherto unknown in Ireland, and that much will depend on the efficiency and 
trustworthiness of the individuals who have been appointed by the Guardians. The Commis- 
sioners are desirous that you should exercise the utmost vigilance over those officers, that you 
should give your support and encouragement to those amongst them who deserve it, and that 
you should make a special report to the Commissioners respecting those whom you deem 
incompetent or otherwise unfit for the situation. With regard to their accounts, you will per- 
ceive ffiat is the duty of the clerk of the Union to examine them weekly, and the Commissioners 
rely on your seeing that this duty is performed by him with that regularity and. efficiency which 
are necessary for the protection of the rate-payers. 

The Commissioners have only to add, that it is their wish that you should make a special 
report to them every week on the state of your Union, on the day after the weekly meetin® of 
the Board of Guardians; and if at any time any point of difficulty occurs to you in°the 
administration of the Poor Laws, you should communicate with this office without delay, and 
you may depend on receiving from the Commissioners an early answer.

APPLICATIONS for ALTERATION of ELECTORAL DIVISIONS so as to com- 
prise the whole of a particular Estate, exclusively, in one or more Division or Divisions of 
a Union. 

The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians op Newcastle Union. 

Poor Law Commission OMce, Dublin, 

Sir, November 15, 1M7. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland, have 
had under their consideration the memorial of the trustees of the estates of the Earl of Devon, 
in which the memorialists request, that the electoral divisions in which the estates of tlie Earl 
of Devon are situated in Newcastle Union, may be so altered as to comprise the whole of such 
estates^ exclusively, in one or more electoral district or districts. The Comrnis§ior)ei-s have 
also had under consideration various documents, in which the propriety of acceding to the 
request of the memorialists has been pressed upon them fay Captain Kennedy, the agent for 
those estates, together with numerous letters, in which other proprietors in Newcastle Union 
have expressed their own opinion respectively on the same subject. 

The Commissioners have given much consideration to the request of the memorialists j not 
only on account of the magnitude of the interests which would be immediately affected by the 

S -oposed alteration of the electoral divisions in Newcastle Union, but likewise on account of 
e great general importance of the principle which such an alteration would involve, and of 
the long train of practical consequences which would necessarily result from it in every part of 
Ireland. That principle, when fully stated, is no less than this: that estates of landed pro-' 
prietors should become an area of taxation for poor-law purposes. Por it is fully admitted, 
that if the principle is sanctioned in reference . to. the estates of the Earl of Devon, it must, in 
fairness, be extended to the estates of other landed proprietors in Newcastle Union; and it is 
obvious that the principle, if admitted in Newcastle Union, could not be restricted by the Com-' 
missioners to that Union alone ; hut that they would be eventually called upon to extend its 
application fairly and impartially, by remodelling, in reference to it, the electoral divisions in 
all the Irish Unions. 

The question, therefore, which the Commissioneis now have to determine is, whether they 
are prepared to act on the principle of making the estates of landed proprietors an area of 
taxation for poor law purposes? and, after the closest consideration which the Commissioners- 
have been able to bestow on the subject, they have arrived at the conclusion, that, even sup- 
posing that the principle were in itself both practicable and expedient (on neither of which 
points do the Commissioners propose to express any opinion on the present occasion), it would 
be improper for them, as a purely administrative body, to act on that principle, unless it pre- 
viously received the deliberate sanction of the Legislature. 

The grounds on which the Commissioners have arrived at this conclusion are the following : — , 
The principle of making estates an area of taxation does not seem to have been adopted by 
the Legislature in any part of the United Kingdom. Omitting notice of towns, cities, and 
boroughs, and the penalty which maybe inflicted on townlands in Ireland for malicious inju- 
ries, it will be found, on examination, that the area of taxation in Ireland consists of pai’ishes, 
baronies, electoral divisions, or unions ; in England and Wales, of parishes, hundreds, town- 
shiiis, unions, ridings, or counties ; and in Scotland, of parishes or counties. It sometimes 
indeed happens, that, owing to circumstances, the boundaries of an estate are identical with 
the boundaries of a parish or an electoral division ; but still the Commissioners believe it to be 
undeniable that the making an estate, as such, an area of taxation, b a principle wholly unknown' 
to the law. 

Now, the Commissioners are precluded from supposing that this silence of the law on the 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 



37 



subject has arisen either from indifference or from the idea not having presented itself to the 
mind of the Legislature. It is a matter of notoriety, that the principle of taxation by estates 
has, in one forni or another, been freqtiently advocated, as one means of remedying the calami- 
ties which have been occasioned by the failures of the potato crop during the last two years; 
and at the period when tlie Irish Relief Extension Act was under discussion durin® the last 
session, the principle could not have escaped the notice eitlier of Government or of Parlia- 
ment. The Commissioners, therefore, feel justified in assuming that Parliament may be 
regarded either as having virtually’ rejected the principle, or, at anv rate, as haviiio- arrived at 
the conclusion, tiiat its immediate adoption was not desirable. 

The Commissioners are fortified in this view of the question by the consideration that, even 
assuming the principle to be in itself practicable and expedient, its adoption would produce 
obvious inconveniences and injustice, unless accompanied by further alterations in the* law of 
rating, and of chargeability on electoral divisions. For example, it ia evident that one of the 
immediate effects, as the law at present stands, would be, in many instances, to cause the 
pulling down of cottages, to give a stimulus to clearances from estates, and to throw an undue 
and overwhelming burden on certain localities, such as small towns or large rillages in which, 
owing to the great number of proprietors, there would be no systematic unity of action to 
prevent the influx of ejected tenants and of persons bordering on pauperism. *The fact that 
such localities would become unduly taxed in the present state of the law is fully conceded; 
and in order to obviate the palpable injury which would be inflicted on them, it 'is proposed 
that when their poor rates exceed a certain amount, the balance required for the relief of their 
destitution should be levied either as a Union or a national rate. But without entering on the 
question of whether a Union rate or a national rate in such cases would or would not be expe- 
dient, it is evident that no such rate could be made without an alteration of the law, and with- 
out admitting principles of taxation for poor law purposes, different from those sanctioned by 
Parliament in any part of the United Kingdom. 

Under these circumstances, the Commissiorters are of opinion, that they would not be justified, 
as an administrative body, in introducing the principle of making estates an area for taxation, 
to which, in point of fact, the proposition now before them is confined. They think that the 
principle, if adopted at all, should previously receive the sanction of the Legislature ; that the 
carrying it out would be unjust and oppressive to particular localities, unless accompanied by 
alterations in the existing laws; and they therefore feel bound to decline complying with the 
request of the memorialists respecting the estates of the Earl of Devon in Newca’stle Union.

The Poor Latr Commissioners have the lionour to state, for the iuforma- Westport Union,

With regard to the assertion contained in the resolution of the Board of 
Guardians, reflecting a supposed statement of Mr. Otway, the Commissioners 
desire to state that, as the Board is now dissolved, the Commissioners cannot 
carry the matter any further, but they w'ish nevertheless to place on record 
their disbelief that Mr. Otway ever made such a statement. 

The Commissioners are led to this conclusion not only by their well-founded 
reliance on the correctness of Mr. Otway’s statements, and by the internal 
improbability of what is imputed to him, but likewise by a remarkable instance 
of inaccuracy of assertion respecting Mr. Otway in the identical Board of Guar- 
dians which has now been dissolved. 

The Westport Boai'd of Guardians, at a meeting on the 14th of April, in a 
resolution in which they expressed indignation against the Commissioners for not 
having sent a loan to the Guardians for the support of the workhouse, ventured 
to assert that Mr. Otway, as far back as the 17th March, 1847, had promised 
the Board, that having struck a rate upon the Union excessively large in amount, 

CDnsideruig the circumstances of the rate-payers, he would take care such loan 
would be granted. The Commissioners on that occasion, as on the present.

Mr. Otwat to the Poor Law Commissioners: Au^st 4, 1847. 

In reply to your letters of the 21st and 30th ultinao. Nos. 20,766, and 22,447, I have 
the honour to state that I directed the clerk of the Union, in person, on the 1st instant, to 
inform the Guardians that I would attend the Board of Guardians on this day, and to request 
their attendance to meet me. I arrived at Westport this morning, from Swineford, at half-past 
12 o’clock, and on proceeding to the workhouse, I met the master and cierk on the road, who 
informed me that there was to be no meeting of the Board of Guardians, owing to the assizes 
at Castlebar, and that the clerk had written to me, to Castlebar, to that effect, "and that they 
were then proceeding to try and get, up and down.through the town, on credit from the shop- 
keepers, what food would support the inmates of the workhouse for the ensuing week. The clerk 
also informed me that Lord Sligo had called at the workhouse, and hearing that there were no 
Guardians preseut, or likely to attend, drove away. 

Now, Gentlemen, I cannot but consider the non-attendance, even to form a Board, on this 
day, considering all the circumstances of the case, as one of the most striking instances of dere- 
liction of duty, on the part of Guardians, at a fearful cri.sis, that has yet come under my notice. 
The Guardians were aware at their last meeting, that there were no funds to provide for the 
maintenance of the inmates, and that food for the previous week or two had been supplied 
through the bounty of Lord Sligo ; and yet no steps were then taken to provide funds or food 
(and the clerk had to beg for it from the shopkeepers and merchants of the town); and this day 
they were requested to attend and meet me, knowing, as they did, the critical position of the Union, 
and that 540 human beings (and 106 of those sick in fever, and other diseases) were to be fed^ 
yet no meeting took place, on the e.\cuseofthe assizes at Castlebar. Now the judges are not to 
arrive at Castlebar until to-morrow, and the grand jury were not sworn in until 3 o’clock this 
day; there are only, comparatively speaking, a few of the guardians who are required to 
attend at the grand jury, and there are three Guardians living in the town, (besides Lord Sligo, 
who did attend,) who had nothing to do with the grand jury, viz., Mr. Bland, Mr. Graham, and 
Dr. Bourke. 

Considering these circumstances, together with ihe past state and management of this Union, by 
the Board of Guardians, as can be learned from the official papers and my former reports, I am 
led to the conclusion that this is a case that requires the exercise of the Commissioners’ powers, 
under the 18th section of 10 Viet., chap. 31, and that it would be injurious to the working of 
the law, and to the interest of the ratepayers of the Union, as well to the destitute poor, if the 
Board of Guardians were allowed to continue to manage the affairs of the Union, especially at 
a time when the carrying into beneficial operation of the Poor Law Extension Act, requires 
the energy of intelligent, zealous, and heartily co-opevatiug administrators. Even if the pre- 
sent Board of Guardians struck sufficient rates, I cannot anticipate, judging from the past, that 
they would fake the necessary steps to collect them, or to carryout the Poor Relief Acts, 
according to tlie benevolent intentions of the Legislature.

The Poor Law CoMMissiONRRs to the Bo.ahd of Go.a.rdians : August 10, 1S4/. 

The Poor Law Commissionere have received the minutes of the Guardians of Westport 
Union of the 4th instant, whereby it appears that no meeting of the Guardians took place on 
that day, the Marquis of Sligo having been the only Guardian who attended at the Board 
room on that occasion. 

'fhe Commissioners have also before them, a report from their Assistant Commissioner, Mr. 
Otway, who informs them that he attended at the Board-room of the Guardians, on tlie 4th 
instant, and was disappointed in not finding a sulBcient meeting of the Guardians, having given 
notice to the clerk on tlie 1st instant, of his intention to be present. Mr. Otway further reports 
that he found the clerk and master endeavouring to obtain on credit in the town what food 
would support the inmates of the ensuing week. 

Considering the extremely critical state of the Westjiort Union, at the present time, the Com- 
missioners cannot but regard the non-attendance of Guardians to form a Board on the 4th 
August, as a great default on the part of those Guardians through whose absence a meeting 
of tfie Board failed to take place. The Guardians were aware at tiieir previous meeting, that 
there were no funds to provide for the maintenance of the inmates, and that food for some days 
previously had been provided only by the bounty of the Marquis of Sligo, yet the Guardians on 
this occasion failed to meet and face the difficulties of their position. 

On the 26th ultimo, the Commissioners addre^ed the Guardians on the subject of certain 
rates, which they proposed to make, amounting only to 3187., on seven out of ten electoral 
dinsions of the Union, at a time when their liabilities were known to exceed 26S07., and 
urgently requested the Guardians not to add to the present embarrassments of the Union, by 
signing rates so inadequate to its present wants and requirements. 

In reply to that letter the Guardians have stated their surprise at its contents, having, as 
they'say, deferred making a general rale of 2^. 6c7. in the pound, (equivalent nearly to 50007.), 
on the 'representation of Mr. Otway, the Assistant Commissioner, who requested that this rate 
should be deferred until October next. 

Of the truth of this statement the Commissioners have received Mr. Otway’s unequivocal 
denial; and the Commissioners certainly think it most improbable that Mr. Otway should 
recommend the step adverted to, having on all occasions expressed to the Commissioners 
bis opinion of the urgent necessity of ample rates being promptly made in the Westport Union, 
and having reported the exertions whicli he used to induce the Guaixlians to make sjich rates. 

After due consideration of the present state of the Union, the past proceixlings of the Guar- 
dians, and the correspondence which has lately passed on the subject, the Commissioners deem 
it incumbent on them to dissolve tlie Board of Guardians of Westport Union, on the ground 
that, through the default of the Guardians, the duties of the Board of Guardians have not been 
effectively discharged according to the intention of the Acts in force for the relief of the desti- 
tute poor in Ireland. 

A copy of the order of dissolution is enclosed herewith, and this order will be followed in 
due course by the appointment of paid officers, to carry into execution the duties of the Board 
of Guardians. 



Order dissoloing the Board of Guardians. 

To the Guardians of the Poor of the W^estport Union, to the Clerk of the said Union, 
and to all persons whom it may concern. 

Whereas by an order duly signed and sealed, bearing date the Thirteenth day of July, One 
thousand eight hundred and forty, the Poor Law Commissioners did, in pursuance of the pro- 
visions of an Act passed in the second year of the reign of Her present Majesty Queen 
Victoria, intituled " An Act for the more effectual Relief of the Destitute Poor in Ireland,” 
order and declare, that on the Twentieth day of July then instant the townlands and places 
therein mentioned should be, and thenceforth remain, united for the relief of the destitute poor, 
by the name of the Westport Union, and that a Board of Guardians of said Uniem should be 
constituted according to the provisions of the said Act : 

And whereas a Board of Guardians of said Union has been constituted accordingly : 

And whereas, through the default of the Guardians, the duties of the Board of Guardians 
of the said Union have not been duly and effectually discharged according to the intention of 
the said recited Act, and of the other Acts in force for the relief of the destitute poor in Ireland, 
now therefore I, Edward Turner Boyd Twisleton, one of the Poor Law Commissioners required 
by one of Her Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State to act in Ireland, for the purpose of 
carrying into execution the provisions of the said Acts, and now acting therein, do hereby, in 
exercise of the powers of the said Acts vested in lue in this behalf, declare the said Board of 
Guardians to he dissolved, and the said Board is hereby dissolved accordingly. 

Given undermyhand and seal, this Tench day of August^ in the year of our Lord One 
thousand eight hundred and forty-seven. 

(L. S.) ^E. T. B. Twisletok.

On our arrival we found that the collection of the rates had been confided Baiiinrobe. 
to one individual, Robert Bowen, Esq., a magistrate of the county IMayo, and as 
we were informed, frequently acting as grand juror. There was a considerable 
amount of rates due, and some time previous to our arrival the collector had 
made an attempt to enforce payment from about dO defaulters, by means of the 
magistrate’s Court of Petty Sessions, but failed in consequence of the Rate 
Books, which were produced as evidence, being found, as the Bench considered, 
defective, from part of the forms not having boon filled up with the dates, and 
also no dates being entered in the collectors’ warrants. We cannot let pass the 
mention of these most strange omissions of inserting the dates in these books 
without expressing a belief that they must have resulted from design, as per- 
sons at all accustomed to the duties of office must have observed the defective- 
ness of a document not having a date. However, a case has been submitted to 
the law officer of the Crown, and an answer received from him that the omis- 
sion of the date did not invalidate the document, if parole evidence could be 
had of the signing of the books and the declaration of the rate. We are not 
at present in a position to give you information as to the amount of rate col- 
lected by Mr. Bowen, and the arrears due by defaulters, as the books have been 
in the hands of Mr. Finlay, a gentleman sent down from the Poor Law Com- 
mission office to examine and report on this subject, and also on the state of 
the other books of the Union. Judging of Mr. Bowen’s efficiency for collecting 
by a cursory view of his books, we should be led to consider him a most 
useful officer, for they appear to be well filled up with entries of rates received, 
but Mr. Finlay’s inquiry must, after all, be the test on Avhicli to form an 
opinion. 

With respect to the general state of the Union, we feel justified in saying 
that Ave fear the great majority of all classes have experienced a sad and tr} ing 
reverse by the calamity of the last year, and that it will require a long series 
of prosperous harvests to restore the people to anything like their former re- 
ported condition. 

It is difficult for persons circumstanced as we are, to forai a decided opinion 
of the former state of this couni ry as contrasted with its present ; but it is appa- 
rent that it may be looked upon as having been for some time in what might 
be called a state of transition. Lands Avere let m large tracts to a number of 
persons aaIio lived in villages, and who in a great measure held in common, or 
were, at least, jointly subject to the proprietor’s claims, — a system by Avhich the 
property of the industrious man became subject to the debts of the idle and 
laz}'. As the evils of such a mode of management became apparent, the pro- 
prietors seem to have in many parts dispersed the villages, and given to each 
family or man a separate holding, in the majority of cases of small extent ; and 
thus a great part of the country became divided into small holdings, Avhich 
have been again sub-divided into smaller to meet the exigencies of the holders, 
arising sometimes from giving a settlement to younger members on their 
marriages, or from the necessity of acquiring means to pay debts by a sale of 
I^art of the lands. When a country, sub-divided in this manner, without a 
middle class of yeomanry who might from their condition be able to encounter 
a difficulty, Avas visited by a great calamity, its population was immediately 
prostrated, the claims of the landlord were but partially discharged, and as the 
necessity for acquiring the means of purchasing food continued to preSwS, the 
cattle, horses, sheep, pigs, and even the fowl, were brought to market and sold 
for whatever they Avould bring, and hence the almost utter deficiency of stock 
on the smaller holdings is apparent to the commonest observer. This system 
of almost universal small holdings is also prejudicial to the labour market. 

Every holder of a small tenement cultivates his own land, and requires no 
assistance beyond his own family, and AA-hen his crops are sown, there is no one 
to give him a day’s work : his neighbour is in the same predicament with him- 
self, and the domains of the gentry are few and far between. The very low 
price of labour here is the natural result, for even in the busy time of harvest 
the reaper receives, in general, no more than Sd. or lOr/. per day without food, 
when, in Leinster, they Avould receive from 2s. to 3^, ; and this will account for 
the multitudes of labourers who leave this country to reap the earlier harvests

— Except from report, we cannot give an opinion of the extent of laud under 

cultivation, as compared with former years. In this way we have learned that 
probably it is not so great; many fields and. patches that might have been ad- 
vantageously sown, are left bare ; and this is the more to be lamented, as there 
appears to be a most promising crop of wheat, barley, and oats. The small 
breadth of potatoes sown look well, and wthout any appearance of disease ; and 
an attempt, to a great extent, has been made to grow turnips ; but, from igno- 
rance of the proper management, this crop by lio means promises well, aJthougli 
were they even now properly thinned out, and the land hoed and cleaned, much 
food would be derived from them. The harvest as to time will be about an 
average of seasons ; already some wheat and barley has been cut, and another 
week or ten days will likely see a large breadth secured. 

As to the disposition of the labouring classes to find employment for them- 
selves, an observer must arrive at rather an anomalous conclusion. Experience 
proves that large numbers of both men and women yearly migrate to other 
lands to seek employment, and endure much hardship and privation in order to 
accumulate a small hoard with which they return to their families, and yet at 
home the same individuals do not exhibit the same energy of character, neglect- 
ing many advantageous employments on their own gardens, in cleaning, weed- 
ing, and cultivating the land ; and this at a time when the Government has 
been generously and lavishly supplying all their W’ants as to food. On Thurs- 
day moniing last, on a journey of 20 miles from Westport to Ballinrobe, be- 
tween the hours of 7 and 11, we did not remark a single individual in the 
fields, and only a few drawing turf from the bogs. Aud 'yesterday, between, 
Ballinrobe and Castlebar, except in one or two meadow fields, we made the 
same observation. If they had the disposition to work even for themselves, 
supplied as they are and have been, there is abundant opportunity; but we fear 
the disposition of the peasantry for honest labour and employment has been 
deeply and injuriously affected. We are often asked if there will be any Public 
Works, and to those we are convinced the people would fly with avidity, as 
there they would receive as much as their usual rate of wages, and be able to 
loiter away the time in pretended labour. 

Finally, we beg to assure you that no exertions have been or shall be wanting 
on our parts to meet your views in pressing forward the collecting of rates in the 
Unions under our charge. You are aware of the position in which the matter 
stood in Ballinrobe, and that, until operations over which we could scarcely 
exercise any control shall have been brought to completion, no commencement 
can be made; but when all these obstacles shall have been surmounted, our 
most strenuous efforts shall be made for the fulfilment of your views, and to 
justify the confident reliance you express of our using every exertion to place 
the finances of the Unions oil a satisfactory foundation. 

On looking over this Report, we find that we have omitted any notice of your 
inq^uiry as to the state in which we found the workhouses. 

Baijinrohe. In Ballinrobe we soon ascertained that the master, schoolmaster, and porter 

were persons wholly inefficient to fulfil the duties of their offices. The master 
was unable to establish any classification of the inmates, or maintain the disci- 
pline so essential to the order and regularity of a large establishment : the paupers 
appear to have gone in and out of the house, without the form of an admission 
or discharge. On taking a census of the inmates, about 150 individuals were 
found whose names did not appear on either the admission book or register, 
aud consequently there were no means of charging their previous support to 
the proper electoral divisions. In some of the books to be kept by the master, 
no entries had been made for nearly six months ; and, on further examination, 
he acknowledged that he could not keep accounts, aud that anything in that 
way was done by his son, a boy of 14 or 15 years of age'. He had no inventory 
of any articles in his possession, nor could he account for much tin-ware aid 
clothes lately purchased. The house was all through dirty ; the walls black 
with dust ; no tubs or buckets in the dormitories to receive the contents of the 
utensils, from which, of course, the atmosphere of those rooms must have been 
dangerously polluted ; the yards were overgrown with weeds, and the grounds 
around the house in a most neglected state. We have endeavoured to redress 
all these things, and hope soon to have them in respectable order.

Messrs. Lecky, Thom.^, and Carey, Vice-Guardians, to the Poor Law 
Commissioners : — August 27, 1847. 

In continuation of our Report of the 2 1st instant, which we had the 
honour to forward to you from Castlebar, we have to state that the greater part 
of that Report relating to the state of the Ballinrobe Union, the extent of land 
under cultivation at present, as compared with former years, the state of for- 
wardness of the harvest, and the disposition of the labouring classes to find w’ork 
for themselves, is all equally applicable to Castlebar, with, however, this difference : 
that the general quality of the land in the Ballinrobe Union is much superior to 
that of Castlebar, and that of both superior to Westport ; and there is also a 
greater appearance of advancement and improvement in those parts of the Bal- 
linrobe Union which we have visited, than can be traced in either of the others. 

As yet, there is but little progress made in the harvest work, although much 
of the wheat appears to be quite fit for the sickle ; and in the Ballinrobe Union, 
and indeed wherever sown, this crop promises to yield abundantly. The 
workhouse in Castlebar, as to its cleanliness and order, w’e found in a much 
better state than that of Ballinrobe, and 'Westport better than either ; but the 
grounds of all were disgraceful, being overgrown with thistles, docks, rag-weed, 
and every species of dirt which neglect and carelessness could encourage. 

The master of Castlebar house liad been but lately appointed to the situation, 
and did not appear to feel the power or authority with which he was invested ; 
and this, added to want of energy of character, militated mucli against the proper 
maintenance of discipline. We have endeavoured to stimulate him to more 
lively exertion, and with apparent success; andw^ere it probable that the man 
could make himself acquainted with the routine of keeping his books, he would, 
in our opinion, become a moderately useful officer. He is evidently anxious to 
make himself useful, but one thing we have to fear, that he is not sufficiently 
watchful to prevent the inmates quitting the premises and wandering to the 
town. Should our suspicions be confirmed on this x^oint, we intend formally 
reporting him for neglect: we have frequently remonstrated with him about it. 
Ill all these establishments there has been an utter want of implements for men 
to work with, w’hich has afforded some excuse for the land not being tilled, 
but it does not justify the allowing such a crop of tall w'eeds as disfigured the 
grounds, and which miglit have been pulled. We are thus minute on these 
points, as such observations convey means of knowing the characters of this 
class of officers, as well as affording a knowledge of the condition of the pre- 
mises tliemselves. 

We were glad to find the ivorkhonse of Westport comparatively clean and 
orderly, and a striking disxiosition in the master to fulfil his duties. He appears 
remarkably intelligent and zealous, and, considering the adverse circumstances 
with which he has had to contend, has liis house in a very good state ; and 
had the proper supplies of implements and necessaries been afforded him, we 
are convinced no fault would have to be found with his charge. 

On the subject of the required estimate of the numbers which hereafter may 
require relief in these Unions, we find it impossible to arrive at any safe conclu- 
sion. We have no sufficient data to proceed on. For the last year the Public 
Works, and latterly the distribution of food, in various ways tended to keep off 
the x>ressure from the w'orkhouses ; as those capable of doing any labour, would 
prefer being abroad to aceex^ting the shelter to be afforded there ; and at this 
season, the harvest labour, and many employments the country may afford, 
will very probably keep the tide of applications for admission at a low standard 
until the winter sets in ; but should no extraneous means of emx>loyment arise, 
and provisions become enhanced in value, we much fear there will be after 
Christmas a considerable change in the case. The common food o£ the iieople 
will, ere very long, be quite consumed : as it is, since the striking off of such 
numbers from the Relief Lists, a great inroad has been made on the small 
breadth of potatoes sown. The only information the inspecting officers could 
afford us, was founded on their lists of those not having more than one rood 
of land (and of returns of those the Government are already in possession) ; but 
the numbers are so overwhelming, amounting in some Unions to 20,000, that 
all calculation was set at defiance from this source. However, those gentlemen 
are now preparing lists of the residue at present on their books, which it is 
probable will afford a clearer view of the numbers of the actually destitute.

There are at present no rate collectors in the Union of Castlebar. Two 
brothers, of the name of O’Malley, who held the office, having been dismissed 
by you before our arrival. There appears to l^e an arrear of about 700^., which 
has been carried into a new set of books, in addition to a rate of 3^. in the 
pound, apportioned to the liabilities of the several electoral divisions. 

Advertisements have been inserted in the two local newspapers, calling for 
tendei-s for the collection of these rates, but the only one received for the whole 
Union was at 3s. M. in the pound, which we rejected ; and the man since 
made an offer, verbally, of collecting for 2s. 9d., which we also rejected. 
We have refrained from advertising a second time, lest it should throw discredit 
on the Union ; and should be very glad to have your advice on this point, 
now that the books are almost ready to be handed to the collectors. 

In Westport, we found that the late Board had pursued the strange course of 
striking a large rate on part of the Union, which they hoped would prove pro- 
ductive, and leaving the rest, which constituted the great bulk of the rural dis- 
tricts, almost burdenless. The consequence was, that no provision was made to 
pay off the liabilities of the Union, amounting to nearly 3000/., or for the heavy 
wants of the house. We have prepared an estimate, on which to found a rate, 
u'liich will amount in the total to nearly 7000/. It is probable a considerable 
part of this may not be collected at present, l)ut enongh may be got to satisfy 
in part the pressing claims of creditors and keep the house open. 

There is much of the Union of Westport which we have visited in almost a 
totally rmproductive state : for instance, the electoral division of Achill and 
Ballycroy, and part of the electoral division of Newport. At present, the 
pressure from those parts is not heavy, nor is the population of the two former 
large ; but should no employment be found whereby wages may be earned, 
the population of these two divisions must either depend upon the workhouse or 
perish. Two of our numljer who visited these localities, did not see as much 
crops on the land as would feed the people for a month.

As you have desired that we should report to you from time to time on. 
fl.11 matters relating to the affairs of the Unions under our charge, we resume

It is pleasant to be able to say that our three workhouses are improving in 
order and cleanliness. There ajipears to be a great degree of zeal and efficiency 
on the part of the officei*s, and a determination to exercise a more stringent 
discipline in the management of the inmates. Our Minutes will have shown, 
you that as yet there has not been much pressure for admission manifested ; 
and although from the wan countenances and wasted figures of most of the 
applicants, considerable distress may be supposed to pervade the country, still 
there is such an inherent dislike to the confinement, restraint, and order ol a 
well-regulated workhouse, that except from dire necessity the bulk of the 
adult population will not seek a refuge in it There is doubtless a general 
wish to quarter the women and children on the rates, by representing such as 
widows and orphans, or deserted wives ; but a careful examination generally 
discovers the deceit, and latterly there have been but few attempts at fraud in 
this way. When the relieving officers come to discharge their duties, we hope 
much of this kind of scheming will he put an end to, and many of our diffi- 
culties lessened. You will also have perceived from the Minutes, that in the 
Castlebar and Wtesti)ort houses fever has nearly disappeared, whilst in that of 
Ballinrobe it is almost as rife as when we arrived : happily it is of a mild cha- 
racter, and rarely ends in death.

manner in which the affairs of the Union had been managed, those parties were 
now able to walk about and laugh at all responsibility. \Ve said such informa- 
tion was valuable, and should be attended to. Sir Richard said he should feel 
happy at being allowed occasionally to visit us, which we told him would afford 
us satisfaction, and he took his departure. 

The last subject of Sir Richard’s communication we think so important as to 
deserve your consideration, whetlier an appointment should be made to exa- 
mine the books of the Union. On inquiring from the officers of the house, wc 
learned that of the first rate of lOcZ. in the pound over the whole Union, much 
remained unpaid, and that when the Board of Guardians were about to strike 
the next rate, of I6cl, they proposed to bum the last rate-books and begin over 
again ; that tliere were large arrears due, but it would be difficult to unravel the 
mystery, as the collectoi*s would refuse to give information. 

"iVe request you will take into your consideration, whether we ought not to 
give the collectors of the new rate directions to make tlieir lodgments with the 
treasurer in the names of the Vice-Guardians. There are such a number of 
outstanding cheques, and to such large amount, that all tire first collections would 
be absorbed in discharging those liabilities, and the present difficulties in 
maintaining the houses be continued for an indefinite time ; and probably many 
claims would be paid wdiich might require to be closely examined. 

We are sorry to have to inform you, that great loss has been sustained by the 
ravages of the storm of Wednesday and Thursday last on the standing croirs. 

Either from ignorant prejudice or inertness, the farmers left their crops of 
wheat and oats uncut long after the proper time, and w'hen caught by the high 
winds, w’hich prevailed on those days, much grain was shaken out of the ear 
and consequently lost. There is still a large breadth of corn remaining uncut 
through the county Mayo, and also much that has not yet come to maturity.

hands that the books have been in, I fear that I have been duped.

The Poor Law Commissioners to the Vice-Gi-audians of Ballinrode U.nion: 
— October 1, 184/. 

With reference to the letter addressed to Mr. Bowen on the 22nd ultimo, 
a copy of which has lieen transmitted lor your information, the Commissioners 
desire me to forward to you herewith a copy of a letter v\ Inch they liave received 
troni Mr. Bowen, dated the 25th ultimo, containing the explanation which he 
has to offer of the circumstance of Iiis having omitted to lodge in the hands of 
the Union treasurer a sum of 720/. 6s. lOIs/., which he had collected. 

"U ith regard to Mr. Bowen’s statement, — unconsciousness that so large a sum 
as that referred to had been collected without being paid into the hands of the 
L’nion treasurer, and his doubts upon the point, — it appears to the Commissioners 
that there could be uo doubt as to the amount collected, the books showing it, 
and that 3Ir. Bowen ought not, therefore, to have doubted his owing so much 
as it ap]->ears that he does. 

Mr. Bowen does not, however, refuse to be accountable for this debt ; but he 
declares his inability to pay it, aud tenders, as security for payment hereafter, 
liis note of hand at 91 days, and the poundage on the new rate if appointed 
collector. 

As a security, his note of hand is not more available than hispersonal liability, 
otherwise than as barring plea in case of law proceedings for recovery ; and it is 
to be kept in view that he can only jiay the amount out of the produce of the 
new rate. 

It therefore appears almost a certain consequence of such arrangement that he 
would become as much in debt under the new rate as he is at present; but in 
that case there would be a new bond, with responsible sureties ; even that, how- 
ever, is not certain ; while it is obvious that the course proposed, of allowing 
Mr. Bowen to collect the new rate, is a compromise of principle, in admitting a 
collector who has detained the public money for his own uses, contrary to law, 
to be placed in a position that would enable him to detain more money, with a 
view of answering the necessities arising from the proposed stoppage of his 
official allowance. 

For these reasons it would be advisable that the Vice-Guardians should obtain 
the services of a collector in the room of Mr. Bowen, and have tlie necessary 
steps taken to recover the money which lie has detained. The Commissioners 
will also feel bound to issue a sealed order for his removal, imless some strong 
grounds be stated to justify a departure from this usual course in such cases. 

The Commissioners request that they may be informed when the new rates 
will be signed on each of the Unions under your superintendence.

and his prosi^ects as to his future employment as a rate-collector ; and after a 
good deal of consideration, -we deem it right to inform you of our present 
opinions. 

Mr. Bowen freely admits his responsibility for the amount of balance which 
appears to the debit of his cash account with the late Board of Guardians ; 
and he states that in his letter to you he offers his bills, or to allorv his poundage 
from the forthcoming rate to be stopped, for the purpose of liquidating it. The 
former, we fear, are of small value, as it seems the general opinion that his debts 
are large, aud his property encumbered to the full. His second offer might be 
deserving of some consideration, were it in his power to give ample security 
to us, for the faithful discharge of the duties of his office. That we consider as 
the material feature of the case. With two good and solvent securities, joined 
with himself for 3000/., and a stringent and watchful supervision of his collec- 
tion as it progressed, and not allowing money to any considerable amount to re- 
main, save from week to week, in his hands, we see no reason to fear that the 
balance due by him to the Union would not be secured, and the present rates 
collected and properly lodged. But can he obtain such security ? The general 
opinion is in the negative ; and it might probably be the simplest course at once 
to ascertain this point, as in case of his not being able to satisfy us clearly and 
sufficiently, there must he the strongest and most insuperable objections to allow 
of his being engaged. There can be no doubt of Mr. Bowen’s activity and 
energy in promptly making his collection ; but these qualities, good in them- 
selves, would be of little value, were they to be accompanied by any possible risk 
of the forthcoming of the money about to be collected : aud we feel com- 
pelled to the persuasion that, viewing the whole circumstances of the case, 
nothing could justify his being allowed to continue in so responsible an office, 
but a satisfactory expectation of saving to the funds of the Union so large a 
sum as that due by him. 

Looking to the possibility of Mr. Bowen’s failing in the essential qualifi- 
cation to which we have alluded, and your being satisfied to risk the sub- 
sequent repayment of his debt, it is well that you should understand that there 
is every reason to conclude that a respectable substitute can be found at hand. 
Yesterday evening, Mr. Walsh, a cess collector for the barony of Kilmaiue, 
waited on us, at our Board-room, and said, that having heairi that Mr. 
Bowen would not be engaged again as a rate collector, he had come to offer 
his services for his own barony, which embraced one half of the Union. 
We told him it was not possible at present to entertain his proposition, inas- 
much as a negociatiou was pending between Mr. Bowen and the Commissioners; 
but that should the result of that uegociation leave us at liberty, we thought the 
course most likely to be adopted was that of writing to the different barony cess 
collectors of the Union, and in this way he would come to be iufonned of the 
issue. We asked him in case of his being offered the collection of the whole 
Union, would he take it ; he said he would. On inquiry, we have learned that 
Mr. Walsh is a very respectable man, of considerable wealth, and in partnership 
with a Mr. Fair, in collecting the county cess of the barony of Kilmaine, and 
can give undoubted security to any amount.

views of the position in which tliat gentleman stands, as a defaulter ^of the

Referring to our letter of the same date, in which we recognize a strong coin- 
cidence of sentiment with you on this important subject, we cannot but approve

to the course to be pursued in such dismissal, we have no reasons to offer why 
the usual mode should not be observed as in similar cases of delinquency. 

In the letter above alluded to, we informed you of an offer made to us by 
Mr. Thomas Walsh, of Garristown, near Hollymoimt, to become the collector. 
On subsequent inquiry we have heard much to the advantage of this gentlcmau ; 
his connections are highly respectable ; he is punctual in his dealings, of indus- 
trious habits, and independent in property and position. Immediately on 
receipt of your letter we wrote to him, requesting his attendance on the Board 
on Thursday next, and that he would be pleased to give us a written proposal, 
for collecting the rates of the Union, also stating the terms on which he would 
collect them; and the names of two sufficient securities. We judged it best for 
the public service to be thus prompt, as were we to wait a call on and reply 
from the other cess collectors of the Union, — one, we under.stand, living in the 
County Galway, — ^much valuable time would have escaped. We are sadly 
annoyed that tliis has been so much the case already ; but the position of these 
Unions, with respect to the new rate has been peculiarly adverse ; in almost 
every department confusion has existed ; old hands were obliged to be dis- 
missed, and new ones called in ; time consumed in arranging with you on the 
proper amount of rate to be struck ; and other circumstances which have com- 
pelled a protraction of the affairs, greatly to be lamented. But we now hope 
those hindrances have been happily surmounted : to-morrow, at an adjourned 
meeting of the Board here, we propose signing the books, and appointing our 
collector for Castlebar, and only await the arrival of the new form of bonds, 
and having them comjdeted to put the collection, in operation. 

In Ballinrobe, we expect the bool^ will be in readiness on the next Board 
day, and the foregoing statement respecting Mr, Walsh informs you of the 
position of that Union in this respect. In Westport, we expect four of the 
books will be ready on next Board day, but their other means are not so pro- 
mising. No collectors are willing to undertake the duty, altliough some have 
been pressed to the engagement ; however, we hope our advertisement in the 
Dublin Advertiser and the local newqiapers, may produce some success. 

You will perceive by the Minutes of last week’s proceedings, that a great in- 
crease has taken place in the number of applications for admission to all tlie 
houses; nearly 200 each in Westport and Ballinrobe, and 100 here. In

Castlebar, October 18, 1847. 

W E have the honour to inform you, tliat on coming to sign the rate-books 
of this Union on Saturday, some errors iu the calculations were discovered,, 
which required that they shbuld be more carefully examined, which is x>ro- 
ceediiig, and having adjourned our Board to 10 o’clock this morning we intend

answer to the usual queries, aud hope to have your sanction by to-morrow’s 
post. 

The i>ressure for admission here was not so severe as at Ballinrobe, yet still 
there were 68 taken in, and most of them in a wretched suffering state, their 
countenances pale and cadaverous, and their persons wasted almost to skeletons, 
evidently corroborating the common rumour, that great numbers of the 
peasantry have been latterly living solely on turnips, and these being now 
nearly exhausted, they are forced to the workhouse by hunger. In Castlebar 
the workhouse has beeu constructed to accommodate 700, consequently there 
will be 130 vacancies for the admissions of next Board, calculating on the 
general average of discharges and deaths. 

In some few instances we have sanctioned the relieving officers giving 2 a 6d. 
or 3-s. a week to families afflicted with lever, where the sufferers were not in a 
conditiou to be removed to the workhouse ; and we were prompted to this from 
a persuasion that it would be more advantageous with our present limited ac- 
commodation for such j)atients to keep them in their own cabins at a light 
expense, than bring them to the workhouse while under the disease, and thus 
probably spread it through the crowded inmates there. With this -^vasting 
malady spreading thi'ough all parts of the Union, it is most distressing and 
lamentable to have to reflect that there is not one fever hosj^ital in its wide 
extent, or auj" available place of refuge to be obtained where the houseless or 
impoverished sufferer from fever could be accommodated and provided for. 

Should you be of ox>inion that Mr. Wilkinson’s suggestion ought to be acted 
on, of postponing the building of the fever ward until the spring of next year, 
we -would strongly advise that the second half of the wooden shed on tJie 
■^vorkhouse premises should be immediately constructed, and the wooden roofs 
of both be covered with some material capable of keeping out the rain, wliich 
the half now finished camiot do in its jn'esent state.

JMessrs. Lecky and Thomas, Vice-Guardians, to the Poor Law Co-mmissioners ; 

October 26, 1847. 

Having experienced a most painful day on Saturday, in being obliged to 
remain for many houi-s listening to the clamorous and pitii'ul applications for 
admission from a wretched mass of human miserj% to the number of 200, which 
were congregated about the door of the workhouse, but which tlie position we 
were placed in, debarred us from relieving, we came to the determination of 
deputing one of our colleagues to- give you a statement of what occurred, and of 
the perilous prosjK'cts of this country for the future. 

Had we on Saturday even a prospect of obtaining a sufficiency of shirts and 
shifts for the creatures whose filthy condition rendered them doubly dangerou , 
we might have yielded to our feelings of commiseration, and liave admitted 
tlie most urgent cases : but the stock of those articles in our possession was 
barely sufficient jbr the use of those already in the house, and our advertise- 
ment for supplies appeared to be treated with scorn, as not one tender was sent 
in : this, and the protest of the medical officer, whose zeal and attention to his 
-duties we have every reason to be satisfied with, compelled us unwillingly to 
shut the doors. However, we now hope to be in a better position lor next 
Saturday. Yesterday we waited on the Rev. Mr. Stoney, who has a consider- 
able number of poor persons employed in manufacturing frieze and linen, and 
having represented our need to him, we obtained a considerable quantity of 
those goods from him, and liave put every female- tliat could be spare<l from 
the uecessary business of the house, to make inside garments lor the number we 
may deem it prudent to admit ; but even this wiU be but small allevkition, 
-compared with the quantum of destitution in the Union, and which must burst 
upon us as the winter approaches. 

We are happy at being able to inform you that we have fairfy got our new 
collector afloat at last ; he signed his bond ost Saturday, and yestei^ay we gave 
him his collecting books, and one receipt book for each division, and the blank 
filled up with the name of the electoral division for which the receipt was in- 
tended, and gave him the strongest injunctions to commeiiee his operations in 
the electoral division of Castlebar, and to look in the first instance most urgently 
to the great and wealthy. We tliink l\Ir. Malley will prove an honest and 
spirited officer, who will IcHward our views and the interests of the Union to the 
'itmost of his iiower.

looked to when funds came in, their confidence was restored, and tliey again

in the article of fuel ; no contract could be effected for a supply except for 
ready money, and yesterday we had to advance a sum of money to the master 
to keep the boilers going. 

We adjourned the Board to Monday next, for the double purpose of signing 
the rate-boolis, and meeting some gentlemen to form a committee to assist the 
fishermen of the coasts and islands, in the prosecution of their calling. We 
have had an offer of a loan of money from the Society of Friends in^Dublin 
for this purpose, and having consulted Lord Sligo and some influential persons 
in Westport, a few individuals have agreed to meet on that day, and endeavour 
to bring the matter to bear. The prospects of the fishery are most promisinf’-, 
hut the fishermen have neither boats nor nets ; a small outlay on those neces- 
saries would do a vast deal of service. From 10/. 10^. to 12/. would be ample 
to furnish a boat and oars and nets sufficient to employ six fishermen, who 
may, in one night, catch the value of the entire outlay. We liave strong 
expectations of being able to stimulate some persons in this adventure to rouse 
the people to endeavours for self-support.

stopped by the Vice-Guardians on the objections stated. ’ 

I am now in your hands, and shall remain here (although incurring expense) for your 
turtber orders and directions. o i j

Dr. Dempster, Temporary Inspector of Ballinrobe Union, to the Poor Law 
Commissioners : — November 27, 1847. 

On the 22nd instant I visited Kilmain and Shrule districts, relative 
to the schools in those places, and to ascertain whether a bakery could be 
properly established. . . . 

I also went to Claremorris on the 23rd, for similar purposes, like-wise to \osit 
and inspect the temporary fever hospital there. I regret to say, that ^ere 
appears much apathy in regard to the hospital, and that it will not be fit to 
receive patients for some time. , t. ■ ^ -l 

I also took with me the clerk of the Union, to w itness Mr. Brannick, the 
poor-rate collector for the division of Claremorris and Ballindine, sign his 
bond, which, I beg to state, is perfected and in the possession of the clerk of 

the Union. , •, n • i • 

On the 24th I visited the temporary hospital at the iNeale, which is not 
yet ready for the reception of patients, but in progi-ess of repair. I fear much 
that it will prove insufficient for the purpose, bemg only fitting up for 20 
beds. , „ 

I then proceeded to Gong, Clonbur, and Maune, to ascertain the state ot the 
people in these localities, and the number of schools, with the children attend- 
ing, &c., for the information of Count Strzelecki, to whom I hope early next 
week to send the required return : great difficulties exist, as Dr. M‘Hale, the 
Homan Catholic Archbishop, discountenances the national system of education 
in his diocese. , , j- • 

I regret to report that the destitution of the people in all diese districts is 
very great, the sole food they have to live upon being turnips, and, when 
these are exhausted, there will be no other resource but tbe workhouse or out- 
door relief, the time for which will now rapidly approach: and, referring to 
your letter of the 6th instant, enclosing a copy of a letter from Count Strzelecki Page 35. 
relating to the conditions on which assistance may be given by the British Relief 
Association in certain Unions, I beg to say that, upon the most mature con- 
sideration, I am of opinion that the most prudent plan will he to erect a bakery 
sufficiently large in the town of Ballinrobe to supply certain localities ; and 
another at Doon, near Drumsnave, the residence of Captain Blake, to supply 
the division of Ross and jiart of Ballingholla, he being a gentleman in whom I 
can place the most implicit reliance, and who already is favourably Imown to 
the British Association for his philanthropy and untiring exertions m the cause 

of the unfortunate sufferers in his locdity. * 

I have consulted Mr. Lecky and the other paid Guardians on this subject, 
who perfectly agree with me in these views, and by whose knowledge and expe- 
rience of this Union I have been principally guided ; and as we have all the 
same interests in view, the relief of the destitute, I hope by our umted exertions 
to carry out the benevolent intentions of the Government and the Association 
with economy and efficiency.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Dr. Dempster, Temporary Inspectoi- of 
Ballinrobe Union ; — November 30, 1847. 



I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland to acknowledge the receipt of your report of the 
27th instant relating to the Ballinrobe Union ; and I am to request that, in 
making arrangements for out-door relief in the Union, you will keep in view 
that the funds which may hereafter be placed at the disposal of the paid 
Guardians by Count Strzelecki must be brought into the Union accounts as 
loans, and administered as other Union funds by the Guardians’ officers ; and, 
therefore, that, however valuable the co-operation of the local gentry may be, 
they cannot be made the administrators of relief, which must in every case be 
ordered by the Guardians and be distributed by their relieving officers, no 
matter whence the funds shall l)e derived. 



Swine ford U nion. Sicineford Union. 

Captain Broughton, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners. 

Swineford, Mayo, November 17, 1847. 

I HAVE to inform the Poor Law Commissioners of my arrival at this 
place on Monday night. I attended yesterday (Ikiesday) a meeting of the 
Board of Guardians held at the Union workhouse. The attendance was not by 
any means large, three Guardians only being present, and the chairman absent. 

From what I have been able to gather, I should not consider the circumstances 
of this Union so desperate as may have been represented. The valuation of the 
Union amounts to 45,966^. ; the liabilities, as I am informed, to about 6000^. 
There appears to be no resistance to the rates \ but, from the circumstances of 
property in the district, a difficulty exists in the collection, a considerable 
portion being in Chancery. 

The town is infested with beggars ; it appears there is no magistrate residing 
within two miles of it, and hence a difficulty in carrying out the Vagrant law. 
I drew the attention of the Guardians to this fact, but no one seemed inclined 
to take the initiative in remedying this evil. I have tliis clay seen the police 
officer, who has promised to do what he may be able in putting the law into 
force. 

The workhouse, which was built for 700, has at present only 500 inmates ; 
hence 200 vacancies remain. The internal arrangements appear very orderly, 
and beautifully clean ; but the yards and courts are in a very unfinished state, - 
and require levelling, forming, &c. This was accounted for by there having 
been so few able-bodied paupers in the house. 

There were two cases of families in fever, utterly helpless, residing at a dis- 
tance ; the fever hospital is not finished, and the house not full ; were they to 
be relieved as out-door patients ? The doctor was requested to visit them, and 
the relieving officer desired to furnish them with support. 

The ^oimt of rate paid in yesterday was 711 Is. 9d. ; this appears the only 
money in hand ; there remains to be collected about 2763/. 

The objects applying for relief were wretched in appearance, but I am bound 
to say, at the market held yesterday, whereat about 2000 persons were collected 
from all roimd the neighbourhood, their appearance was highly respectable ; 
indeed the women were rather overdressed, and no indication of want was to 
be observed amongst them.

in November 1845, a general order of the Court of Chancery vrus made, that in swineford Union 

all cases in n-hich the landlord instead of the occupier, is rateable for holdings 

comprised in properties under the management of that Court, the Receiver,

It appears that no fever hospital has been established under the Board of 
Health in the Swineford Union ; and it would be desirable that the attention 
of the Relief Committee for the district in question should be dra^vn to the case.

Relief Extension Act, the relieving officer can only provide relief provisionally, 
under the 7th section; but ordinary relief, in cases of destitution by sickness, 
may be afforded under the 1st section of the Act. 



Captain Broughton, Insj)ector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : —

I YESTERDAY again visited the workhouse and new' fever hospital in pro- 
gress of erection in connexion with the workhouse. 

The state of the house yesterday w'as 62 able-bodied men, of whom S w’ere in 
hospital; 94 able-bodied women, of whom 22 were in hosjatal; 137 male and 
150 female children, 19 infants, 15 infirm men, and IS infirm women; there

No work, at least very trifling, can at present be given to the able-bodied for

for the purchase of 200 hammers, 20 wheelbarrows, 12 hand barrows, 20 
spades, 20 shovels, and 2 sledge hammers. It would be very desirable that 
these should be at once provided. 

I adverted in my former report to the state of the yards and out premises. 
At present tlie workhouse is unenclosed, the road totally unformed, the draii^ 
incomplete, and the whole in a mess, affording great employment during the 
ensuing season if tools could be made available. The interior arrangements 
appear complete, with the exception of the want of tables and forms in the 
dining-hall, and some stretchers in the dormitories. 

It does not appear in this Lluion, that a Fever Committee was ever formed 
under the Temporary Act ; notwithstanding sheds have been built in rear ol‘ the 
hospital. 

I have to draw the attention of the Poor Law' Commissioners to the 
state of the burial-ground for the paupers who die in the worlihouse ; this is on 
tlie premises, and in an old gravel pit, open and unlevelled, and altogether in a 
most indecent and unchristian-like state.

Poor Law Commission Office, Duhlin, 

Sir, July 20, 1847. 

The Poor Law Commissioners have the honour to forward herewith, for the informa- 
tion of the Lord Lieutenant, a copy of a report which they have received from Mr. Richard 
Bourke on the subject of the state of the Ballina Union, and the possibility of compelling the 
payment of the poor rate by the parties rated. 

The Commissioners desire at the same time to state that they are of opinion that the 
information given by Mr. Bourke in the report is important, but they do not intend in any 
degree to relax in their exertions to induce the Guardians to proceed vigorously in collecting 
the rates which they have lately made in the Union. 

The Commissioners enclose, for the information of his Excellency, a copy of a letter which 
they addressed to the Board of Guardians on the 17th instant.

Report from Mr. Richard Bourke, Assistant Poor Law Commissioner. 
Gentlemen, Ballina, July 15, 1847. 

My letter of the 12th instant has furnished you with the fullest information I could 
collect upon the condition of the Ballina workhouse, and I now proceed to report upon the 
second subject referred to me in your letter of the 9th instant, viz., the general state of this 
Union in reference to the possibility or probability of compelling the payment of poor rates. 

I have endeavoured since ray arrival here, both by personal observation and by communi- 
cation with many intelligent and trustworthy persons, to make myself acquainted with the 
circumstances peculiarly affecting this Union, and the result of my inquiries has been to 
satisfy me that any attempt at the present time to collect, even the moderate rate imposed by 
the Board of Guardians must end in disappointment. 

There are three classes of persons who pay poor rates. The landed proprietor — the occu- 
pier of land—and the owner or occupier of house-property. 

The landed proprietor generally throughout Ireland has this year become less able than on 
former occasions to pay his rate, in consequence of the small amount of rent received by him. 
But in this county he is under peculiar difficulties ; his property is infinitely subdivided, so 
much so, that by far the majority of occupiers appearing on the rate-books are valued tinder 
bl. per annum. This at all times throws a large portion of rate on the proprietor, which is at 
present increased by the number of tenements that have been abandoned by their occupiers. 
In some cases the farms have been vacated in sufficient time for the proprietor to take pos- 
session of the land and till it, but in the greater number they have been held until the time for 
sowing bad passed. The extent of arable land in this Union which has been left uncultivated, 
and producing nothing but weeds, cannot fail to excite the attention of every pei-son who visits 
this country. Thus the proprietor is this year liable to an amount of rate much heavier than 
usual, whilst his means of meeting it are reduced both by the non-payment of liis rents (which 
are generally 18 months or two years in arreav) and by the increased amount oi'tillage he has 
had to undertake in consequence of so much land having been deserted. 

With regard to the occupiers themselves, there are, I believe, many instances in which they 
are liable to pay their rates, but the difficulty which is at this moment felt in collecting the 
Grand Jury cesS leads me to believe tliat it would be impossible to levy this heavier tax. 
The barony collectors for Tyrawley and Grallen have both stated .to me that they find it almost 
impossible to collect the Grand Jury cess, and have found it necessary to employ a large force 
of police to assist and protect them in this duty. I do not, therefore, believe that it would now 
he possible to collect the poor rate from this class of payers. 

The owners and occupiers of house property in towns like Ballina, Killala, or Crossmolina 
would more likely discharge the amount of their rates on demand though even there much 
poverty exists among the small traders. But the amount to be expected from this source would 
be totally insufficient for the support of the poor in the workhouse even for one month. I have 
sought and obtained information upon the state of this Union from persons of various classes, 
and their opinions have all agreed in these points. Amongst those I have consulted I may men- 
tion the names of Colonel Knox Gore, lieutenant of the county of Sligo, a gentleman possessed 
of large landed property in this county ; Mr. Henry W. Knox, a magistrate ; Mr. Sims, agent 
to the Earl of Arran, who has large estates ; Mr. Joyner, the manager of the Provincial Bank j 
Mr. P. Kelly, an e.xtensive solicitor at Ballina ; Mr. James Knox, high constable of Tyrawley; 
and Mr. Oliver Jackson, high constable of Gallen, as well as several members of the Board 
of Guardians. Mr. Joyner appears to me to have in his capacity as banker good means of 
forming a sound judgment upon the financial condition of the Union, and he has given it as his 
opinion that the present resources of the principal rate-payers of the Union would not enable 
them at this moment to meet the demand that would be made upon them, if the rate now 
struck, were to be enforced. 

This rate is unusually high, being about twice the amount usually struck, and it may be 
right to add that the Guardians very unwillingly signed the collectors’ warrants, not because 
they were averse to trying the collection of the rate, but because (as they stated), the books 
were inaccurately prepared, and had been signed upon the express understanding, that 21 days, 
would be given for their correction. This feeling will further operate unfavourably on the col- 
lection of the rate.

August 12, 1847. 

I am directed by the Poor Law Commissioners to state, for your infor- 
mation, that your report of the 15th ultimo, relating to the prospect of the 
collection of the rate in the Ballina Union havmg been referred to Mr. Otway, 
Assistant Commissioner, the Commissioners have received Mr. Otway’s 
observations on the subject, in which he states that he thinks tliat the 
largest portion of the present rate could be at once collected if proper and 
active steps were taken by the Board of Guardians and collectors, and if 
the gentry and magistracy lent a ready and willing co-operation in the collec- 
tion of the rate and set the example of paying it tliemselves. 



The Poor Law Commissioners to the Clerk to the Guardians of the Ballina 
Union : — August 13, 1847. 

I am directed by the Poor Law Commissioners to acknowledge the 
receipt of your return, showing the state of the funds of the Balhna Union at 
the close of the month of July. 

The Commissioners perceive by the 13th column of the above retm-n, that 
none of the collectors attended at the close of the month of July for the 
examination of their accounts, and they do not appear to have attended 
at any time during that month. 

In reference thereto I am to request that you will bring the above matter 
under the consideration of the Board of Guardians at their next meeting. 

The Commissioners consider it most desirable that each of the collectors 
^ould attend regularly, at the close of every month, for the purpose of having 
his accounts examined by you ; and the Commissioners trust that the Guardians 
will take measures to secure their regular attendance at the close of every 
month in future. 

The Commissioners request that the several collectors may be called upon 
to furnish an explanation of the above neglect of the Commissioners' regu- 
lations. 

With respect to the present state of the collection, the Commissioners regret 
to find that no money was lodged during the month of July, although the 
warrants for the collection of 13,000/. were issued as early as the 12th July.

As regards the resjionsibility attached to tlie office of collector of poor rate, 
the Commissioners take this occasion to acquaint you that they deem it to be 
the duty of a collector to bring his collection to a close as siieedUy as possible ; 
and with this view they consider that he is bound to proceed to enforce the

in cases where payment lias been applied for without effect. The Commis- 
sioners, accordingly, feel called upon to take the most serious notice of collec- 
tors who may appear, upon investigation, to have suffered rates to remain 
unpaid for any length of time, without resorting to legal measures for the reco- 
very thereof: and any poundage due to such collectors should be withheld by 
the Guardians until their accomits be closed, and until it be seen whether any 
loss be incurred by their default. ^ 

As regards the collection within your district, the Commissioners trust that 
you will experience no difficulty in bringing it to a speedy close. 

The Commissioners enclose for your information and assistance, a copy of 
the Collector's Manual, which has been prepared by their authority, for the 
guidance of collectors.

As the rate to -which Mr. Otway refers has since the date of my report been 
put in collection, it is of but little importance now to speculate on its effect, 
which -will in a short time be shown beyond all doubt or q^uestion; but I may- 
add, that as far as now appeared, the result has justified my anticipations, as 
during the three weeks in which the collectors have been engaged, very little 
more than 100/. has been paid in. 

If all the co-operation alluded to by Mr. Otway could with confidence be 
expected, I might agree with him in the effect it would produce, but my opinion 
was mainly founded upon the belief that this co-operation could not be relied 
on, and experience has confirmed me in this opinion.

Memorial addr^sed to His Excellency the Lord Lieutexant by the Guar- 
dians of tlie Ballina Union, and referred to the Poor Law Commissioners. 

To His Excellency the Earl of Clarendon, Lord Lieutenant- 
General and General-Governor of Ireland. 

We, the Guardians of the Ballina Union, beg leave most rcspectfullv to 
lay before your Excellency the following facts, under the impression that when 
your Excellency is made fully a^vare of the exact situation of this unfortunate 
Union, the prayer of your Memorialists, on part of the rate-payers of the 
Union, may be acceded to. 

We take this opjiortuuity of declaring our gratitude for the public and 
private aid the population liave received during the last season of famine, ami 
we by no means repudiate repayment of all just demands on us the moment n c 
are in a position to do so. 

It is admitted by all authorities that the calamity entailed on this country by 
the failure of the potato crop fell Tvitli peculiar violence on the county 
of Mayo, and even in this afflicted country most heavily on the Ballina Union, 
the people having been, from various causes, entirely dependant for food on the 
potato. 

Immediately on the first pressure of famine, and before any means of 
external aid could be had, the starving people rushed to the workhouse, 
and though the Ltnion was (from the natural property of the district, as 
compared with its population,) in debt, yet rather than see human beings 
])erish, we not only admitted the full number the house was built to contain 
(1,200), but actually made use of extraordinary means to accommodate 
an increased number (up to 1,480). 

We were thus plunged into debt, and W'hen we looked round to seek 
for payment of rates, we saw that except the land actually occupied by 
persons of station, the rest had been either deserted by the better class of 
tenantry, who had, almost to a man, fled to America at the approach of the 
famine, carrying with them most of the capital of the counti*y, or was in 
the possession of persons unable to sow their grounds, except by assistance from 
some source. 

To collect a rate of 4^. Qd. or 4s. in the pound, which has lately been 
struck for in-door relief on some of the electoral divisions of this Union, would 
be at present perfectly impossible, and the attempt would lead to the most 
unhappy results, possibly inducing a resistance to a legal demand, which your 
Memorialists are most anxious to prevent. 

We, on part of the rate-payers, declare our willingness to meet all demands, 
when we recover somewhat the effects of the late calamity ; we, therefore, 
propose that no electoral division be called on at present for more than 2.?. Qd. 
in the pound, and we implore the Government to advance the balance, and add 
it by small instalments to the rates that will be struck from time to time. 

The Government, in the amended Bill they brought before Parliament last 
Session, proposed 2 a-. Qd. in the pound as the maximum that any electoral 
division should be called on to pay within the year, and surely now, when one- 
half the country is an uncultivated waste, it would be an act of confiscation to 
endeavour to enforce a rate of 4s. Qd. in the pound. 

Though the retrospect is most painful to us, yet we cannot in duty refrain 
from glancing at one circumstance alone, which proves undeniably the awful 
extent of calamity in this Union, — actually upwards of 1000 persons died 
within the workhouse in the space of a few months, and amongst them the 
physician and his wife. 

We, therefore, feel justly confident that your Excellency will see meet to 
extend the hand of indulgence to a district that has suffered so dreadfully from 
a visitation of the Almighty. 

And your Memorialists will pray. 

Signed on behalf of the Board, 

E. Howlet, J. P. and D. L., Chairman. 

BelleeJc Castle, Ballina.
