The Poor Law Commissioners to Mr. Atkinson : — October 1, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for the Relief of the 
Poor in Ireland have had under consideration your letter of the 21st ultimo, 
addressed to the Under Secretary for Ireland, requesting to be informed 
whether it is the intention of his Excellency the Lord Lieutenant to reduce the 
rate of 4s. 6</. in the pound in Ballina electoral division to 3s. in the pomid, in 
reference to the annoimcement on the part of Government, that they will not 
require that more than a rate of 3s. in the pound should be made previous to 
the 1st of January next in any electoral division. 

In rejily, the Commissioners are authoiiscd to state that the announcement of 
the Lords of the Treasuiy had reference to the repayment of advances from the 
Relief Commissioners, and it stated that no repayment would be required 
before the 1st January next, from any division in which a rate equal to or 
exceeding 3s. in the pound was levied for the purpose of defraying the 
expenditure under the Irish Poor Relief Acts. 

The rates in Ballina Union were made for ordinary expenditure, and having 
been made, no power exists to reduce the amount, even if it were desirable. 

The Commissioners ftnd, by minutes of proceedings of the Board of 
Guardians of the 27th ultimo, that it was resolved, that owing to the extreme 
pressure of the rates on the rate-payers, the collectors should accept 3s. in the 
pound on account of rates exceeding 3s. in the pound. 

The Commissioners are not prepared to mterfere with this arrangement, if it 
should be shown that more money may ultimately be collected in this manner 
than by attempting to collect at once a rate of 4.s. 6d in the pound.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Mr. Richard Bourke, Poor Law Inspector :

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, to transmit herewith a letter received from a 
collector of poor-rate in Ballina Union, with reierence to a resolution of the 
Board of Guardians of the Union, directing the collectors to accept 3^. in the 
pound in those divisions in -which the rates exceed that amount. 

In reference thereto, the Commissioners desire to state that they arc not 
disposed to sanction the collection of 3s. in the pound, in the divisions in 
question. 

Such an arrangement might apply to a class of rate-payers, hut the wealthy 
should be compelled to pay the entire amount. 

In the few instances in which such an arrangement has been permitted to be 
carried out, the rate had been made eitlier u-holly or in part for the repayment 
of advances from Government. But the rates in Ballina Union were made 
wliolly for ordinary expenditure, and are not more than sufficient for the 
puiposo. 

As regards the ability of the rate-payers to pay the rates, it appears to the 
Commissioners, that the accompanying letter of Mr. M'Andrew, the collector 
for the highest-rated division, and who must be supposed to l^e intimately 
acquainted with the means of the rate-payers, is strongly corroborative ol‘ the 
views expressed hj Mr. Otway. Poor Law Inspector, on the 8th August last, 
that the largest portion of the present rate could be at once collected, if jiroj^er 
and active steps were taken by the Board of Guardians and collectors. 

Mr. Phelan, Poor Law Inspector, in an official report of the 30th August,

■were even ex-officio Guardians, -who had never paid any rate, and who then .

rates had Ijeeii taken against them. 

Under these circmnstances, the Commissioners apprehend that decisive 
measures must he adopted to counteract any obsti-uctiou which may be offered, 
either directly or indirectly, to the due collection of the rates.

The PooE Law Commissioners to Mr. Corcoran, Collector of Poor Rate : — 
October 13, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 
9th instant, stating that the rate of poundage in the divisions of Ballina Union, 
for which you are a collector, is 2^. 6c/. in the pound, and inquiring whether 
you are justified in taking part payment from tlie gentlemen who have already 
refused paying the entire rate in full. 

In reply, I am directed to acquaint you, that you are not justified in accept- 
ing part payment of the rate in question. Your warrant empowers you to 
demand and levy the full amount of rate ; and it is your duty to proceed to 
obtain the entire rates by the means which the law places at your command ; 
and the Commissioners request that you will not fail to fulfil the promise 
contained in your letter, viz., to do all in your power to enforce the payment 
of the rate by all parties who are able to pay.

ins^t, upon the subject of the rates nowin progress of collection in the Ballina 
Union, directing me personally to examine the collectors’ books and ascertain 
the names of all parties possessing means of payment, whether magistrates,

communicate the information on sheets inclosed for the purpose, together with 
a statement of the amount due by each party, particularly sjjecifying the

tion of the jn’oceedings of the Guardians, particularly with reference to tlie 
present rates, I consider that they have adopted such measures as the circum- 
stances of the Uuiou rendered it imperative upon them to take, in order to 
administer the affairs efficiently and to the best of their ability. 

In pursuance of these instructions, I procured the attendance of all the 
collectors during my late visit to Ballina, and entered upon the inqui)y ; hut 
finding, as I advanced, very considerable difficulty in carrying out your wishes, I 
detejmined alter some hours of labour, to furnish you with the result as far as I 
had gone, and submit for your consideration whether your object would not 
be better attained by calling on the different collectors to supply retuims of all 
rates remaining uncollected, according to the circular alluded to at p. 3/9 of 
the Compendium (Ed. 1846), which would contain all the mateiials necessary 
for such a statement as you require. The first difficulty I found was in distin- 
guishing the parties “ wlio possessed means of payment” from those who did 
not: but iwesuming that this might be determined by selecting those of the 
highest standing and consideration in the district, I was then met by the 
further difficulty that about -l ^ths of the rate and arrears remain still to be 
collected, that the amount is scattered over 12 thick volumes, and tliat the 
tenements in resjject of which these persons are chargeable as immediate lessors 
are so very numerous, that to extract them from the collectors’ books would 
occupy many days and amount to nothing more than a transcription of the 
greater poi-tion of their contents. Under those circumstances, I have thought it 
best, for the present, to forward such particulars as (with tlie assistance of the 
collectors) I obtained during the examination already made (and which are 
accordingly enclosed), and shall now proceed to offer sucli general obsei vations 
as appear to me applicable to the object you have in view, holding myself 
in readiness (if you so desire it) to return to Ballina at an early period, and 
make out a more complete return in the mamier you have already pointed out. 

Tliere is^ no doubt whatever that, up to the present time, scarcely any advance 
has been made in the collection of these rates, the total amount being 13,869/., 
and the amount paid in from the 2nd August, -when the first lodgement was 
made, being only 868/ It is equally certain that large sums of money are still 
due on account of this rate by persons of the highest consideration and position 
in the county of Mayo, both in respect to land occu 2 ued by themselves and 
that for which tliey are liable to rates as immediate lessors. As to their ability 
to 2 >ay the amount so due, I feel it my duty to state, for your information, my 
opinion at some length, and to lay fully’’ before you the reasons upon which it 
is founded. 

The charge now imposed upon this class of persons is heavier than upon any 
former occasion, not only by reason of the higher poundage, but from their 
having Iiecome chargeable as immediate lessoi's for a vast number of lioldings 
deserted by the occupiers, who have died or emigrated and left the land wholly 
imcultivatcd, whilst the proprietors’ means of meeting this augmented charge 
has been diminished by the almost complete suspension of payment of rents. 
I believe that, until the haiwest came in and the autumn fairs commenced, the 
large majority of resident gentry in the Ballina Uuiou had not tlie means of 
paying these rates ; and I further believe that, to pay the full amount at this 
moment, they would be comi)elled to sell grain and cattle at a most ruinous 
sacrifice. At the meeting of Guardians on Monday, gentlemen of jiroperty and 
worth (whose names I do not consider it improper to mention), such 'as Colonel 
Knox Gore, Mr. Vaughan Jackson, Mr. Paget, Mr. H. Knox, and others, openly 
declared, in most emphatic terms, that it would be completely impossible for 
them at the present time to jirovide money for the liquidation of the entire 
amount of their rates. In tlie same manner, Air. Ormsby, agent to Colonel 
Wingfield, and Messrs. Stewart and Kincaid, also land-agents for persons of 
property in the county, have stated that they are at present without funds to 
jiay the rates ; and that, •nhereas in former years they nave at this time held in 
their hands large balances to the credit of their emjiloyers, they are themselves 
now considerably in advance. 

I feel further bomid to declare my opinion, that there is no indisposition on 
the part of the gentry to pay the rates ; that it is only now that they are

becoming in cii-cumstances to discharge them ; and that if, whilst all due vigour 
and strictness are employed in collecting, some concession could be made in the 
mode of receiving payment, a tolerably good collection may be expected. If a 
contrary course be adopted, I cannot conceal from you my conviction that much 
difficulty will be experienced, much expense incurred, and in the end no better 
result obtained. The Ballina Union is, undoubtedly, the poorest of those under 
my charge, where so numerous a resident proprietary is to be found. It is not 
a part of my duty to inquire into the circumstances which have made it so ; 
but close observation and inquiry into its present position have removed all 
doubt of the fact from ray mind. It is felt in every class of society ; affects 
every branch of ti’ade aud industry ; and is to be traced in every house and 
establishment in the district. 

I have stated thus fully my views, because they differ from the opinions of 
others, to which, as appears by your letter of the 2nd instant, you are disposed 
to attach more weight than to mine. I confess that I felt at first some disti’ust 
of my own judgment when opposed to that of Mr. Otway, but further observa* 
tion has confirmed my first impression; and I can only account for Mr. Otway’s 
opinion by supposing that he judges from the position of matters in former 
years, when he was in charge of the Union. As to Mr. McAndrew’s informa- 
tion, I caimot think he possesses by any means such good opportunities of 
judging of the persons whose affairs are now under discussion as I do ; and, 
moreover, I do not consider his evidence as totally uninfluenced by motives of 
interest, as (not to mention other reasons) the collecting of rates by instalments 
would impose upon him a considerable increase of trouble. Neither do I think 
that Mr. Phelan’s short visit to Ballina can be presumed to have afforded him 
the means of forming an independent judgment upon a question of magnitude 
lilie the present 

With these views of the circumstances of the Union, I recommended the 
resolution to he sanctioned which authorised a collection of the rates by instal- 
ments of 3^. in the pound, when the poundage exceeded that sum. In accord- 
ance with this recommendation, you expressed your assent to the resolution, but 
on receipt of a remonstrance from Mr. M‘Andrew, you rescinded this assent, 
and addressed a circular to each of the collectors desiring them to collect the 
entire rate. The Guardians, to whom all the circumstances are known, feel 
aggrieved at this greater show of confidence in his assertion than in theirs, and 
are most anxious for eveiy inquiry as to the relative truth of both statements. 
It appears to me, however, that it would tend to no good result now to insti- 
tute any such inquiry. Your decision has been pronounced and must now be 
left to the collector to carry out ; aud whatever the inconvenience may be 
to the rate-payers, I cannot see how any interference can now usefully take 
place. 

It only remains for me to reply to that portion of your letter referring to 
the line of conduct pursued by the Guardians in regal’d to the collection of the 
rates. Upon this point I have no hesitation in stating that, in my opinion, the 
Guardians have completely failed in their duty in this respect. The rate-books 
were not signed until many months after the amounts were fixed upon ; and not 
until nearly one month after the signature of the warrants, was any lodgment 
made beyond a mere trifle ; and yet I can find no resolution on the Minutes 
condemning this delay. Since the first lodgment on the 2nd August the 
amounts paid in have been very small ; and yet, with the exception of one 
general resolution calling on all rate-payers to discharge their obligations, I do 
not see any record of exertions on the part of the Guardians to accelerate 
the collection, nor have they (with some few exceptions) shown by their own 
example any readiness to comply with the terms of their resolution. I find 
that the clerk did not examine any of the rate-books on the first Board day in 
this month, and further I find that up to this day not one of the collectors 
have perfected their bonds. 

At the meeting of the Board of Guardians on Monday I addressed the 
members present at some length on these subjects, and urged them in the 
strongest possible maimer to adopt a more vigorous coin’se in future ; • and I 
not fail to see that the officers of the Union vrill, in future, perform the duties 
connected with this branch of the law, as well as others, with more exactness 
than they now appear to devote to them.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Mr. Richard Bourke, Inspector: — 
October 23, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, to acknowledge the receipt of your report on the 
subject of the rates now in progress of collection in Ballina Union. 

The Commissioners have had under mature consideration the contents of 
your Report 

The Commissioners regret to find, in the extracts from the collectors books, 
the names of so many parties of rank and consideration among the number of 
the defaulters for poor-rates, after four mouths from the signing of the rates. 

The Commissioners still more deeply regret the nature of the avowed causes 
for non-payment of the rates in many of these cases, — namely, the positive want 
of funds, and the impossibility of their at once ^tisfying the demands of the 
collectors without selling grain and cattle at a ruinous sacrifice. ^ 

Looking, nevertheless, to the present financial state of the Ballina Umon, and 
the necessity of the destitute poor being maintained from the poor-rates, the 
Commissioners deem it their duty to declare that no consid.erations of the nature 
urged in your report, justify, in their opinion, any delay in the enforcement of

rates due from tlie owners of landed property in the Union ; and they request 
that in your future communications with the Guardians and the collectors, you 
will proceed, in accordance with this view, to press on the immediate collection 
of the rates from all parties who remain in possession of available property, of 
whatever description, wdiatever may be the consequences to such parties. 

Should the Guardians continue to neglect their duty in reference to so im- 
portant a point as the collection of the rates, the Commissioners will feel 
obliged to consider their own responsibility under section 18 of the Relief Ex- 
tension Act. 

The Commissioners approve of your intention to see that the officers do their 
duty in this respect. 



Extracts from Guardians’ Minutes : — October 25, 1847. 

Resolved, on the recommendation of the Inspector, — That the list of 
defaulters now handed in by Mr. Kirkwood, one of our collectors, be forwarded 
to our solicitor, with a view to proceedings being taken against them in the 
superior Courts during next term ; and the Poor Law Commissioners he applied 
to for permission accordingly. 

Resolved , — That the remaining rate-collectors be desired to furnish us, against 
next Board-day, with a return of all persons owing rates in their several 
districts, where the amount equals or exceeds 20Z. ; and that our solicitor do 
attend here on the same day to receive our orders conceming them. 



The Poor Law Commissioners to the Guardians of the Ballina Union: — 
November 6, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor 
in Ireland have had under consideration the minutes of proceedings of the 
Board of Guardians of Ballina Union of the 25th ultimo ; and with rei'erence to 
the resolution relative to the list of defaulters against whom it is proposed 
proceedings should be taken in the superior Courts, I am directed to state, that 
the Commissioners recommend that separate lists should be prepared, so as to 
separate the immediate lessors resident in Mayo and Sligo ii’om those elsewhere, 
and again, those resident in other parts of Ireland from those in England or 
abroad ; as in the first cases it may be advisable to proceed primarily, ^ the 
law allows, by serving the 15 days’ notice ; and in the cases of persons resident 
out of Ireland, it is to be apprehended that no proceeding in the- superior 
Courts of Dublin would be available ; so that any costs incurred by proceedings 
against inaccessible parties would necessarily have to be paid by the Guardians. 



The Poor Law Commissioners to Mr. R. Hamilton, Temporary Inspector for 
Belmullet District : — November 9, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland to request that you will examine upon oath the 
collector of poor-rates of the Belmullet district, in order to obtain from him 
the names of the immediate lessors who have not paid their rates, and the 
arrears due from each respectively. 

I am at the same time to request that you will ascertain from the collector 
whether he has made application to all or any, and if any, which, of such 
immediate lessors, and what answer or answers he may have obtained from all 
or any of them, and otherwise to take the evidence of the collector as to any 
real or supposed difficulties connected with the collection of the rates in h4 
district. 

I am further to state that the Commissioners deem it a matter of serious 
importence that the maintenance of the destitute poor of Belmullet should not 
be unjustly thrown upon the benevolence of others unconnected with the 
locality, while rates remain unpaid by those who possess property in the district ; 
and the Gonunissioners accordingly request that you will make a searching

Lieutenant Hamilton, Temporary Inspector of Ballina Union, to the Poor 
Law Commissioners: — November 10, 1847. 



I HAVE visited the poor-house frequently siuce my arrival, and endea- 
voured, as far as possible, to make myself thoroughly acquainted witli the 
state of affairs both in and out of the house. 

With respect to the interior economy of the house, it does not appear to me 
to be nearly so satisfactory as other poor-houses which I have been in in Ireland ; 
but at the same time there are many allowances to be made, such as the dreadful 
mortality which occurred in the house during the past year, the want of either 
funds or credit to do more than actually feed the inmates, in consequence of 
which, in addition to there being a great want of clothing and bedding, that 
now in use is not in good condition 5 there does not appear to have been a 
visiting Committee for some months. I was informed by the master that the 
infirmary has not been visited by the Guardians for a considerable time. I 
found in it some cases, which appeared much in want of nourishment; there 
were three children which had suffei’ed from dysentery, very little remov^ 
from skeletons ; I never saw sucli dreadful objects in my life. Dr. Devlin 
stated to me that he was afraid to order them any extra diet, in consequence of 
having been found fault with by some of the Guardians on former occasions. I 
desired Dr. Devlin to order such nourishment and stimulants as he considered 
necessary, and not on any account to allow a person to perish for the want of 
proper medical treatment. I shall bring this subject to the notice of the 
Guardians on the next day of meeting. IVIr. Knox, one of the Guardians, who 
visited the infirmary to-day, was greatly shocked at the appearance of some of 
the patients. Ten cases of fever have broken out in the house during the pi^t 
week. They were at once removed to the fever hospital, in which there is still 
some available accommodation. Temporary fever sheds have been recently 
erected in rear of the iufinnary ; they have never been occupied, are not water- 
proof, and appear to have been very badly constructed. 

Although there are at present only 1000 persons in the house, which is con- 
structed for 1200, the medical officer declares that any increase of numbers 
will lead to a repetition of last year’s disease and mortality. 

You will have seen by the minutes of last Monday’s proceedings, that the 
Guardians are about to increase the accommodation in the house for able- 
bodied, by hiring a store or large building, and removing thereto in the first 
instance, the school children, together with the schoolmaster and mistress. 
They have likewise authorised the purchase of 500 sets of bedding and clothing, 
and some improvements in the way of ventilation; all of which are most 



necessary steps. , , , . •. t xi. 

The Board day has been altered to Friday, with the view of enabling the 
Guardians to give more time to the affairs of the Union. 

The rates are coming in gradually ; the Guardians have ordered the clerk to 
comply with the directions relative to making separate lists of defaulters m. 
Ireland, England, and abroad. . . „ 

There appears to be an evident determination on the part of a m^onty ot 
the Guardians, if possible, to throw the district of Erris on its own resource ; 
one of them, Mr. Jones, declared that the people in his neighbourho^ would 
not pay a farthing of their rates, if the Erris people are to be support^. 

I am afraid that the well-disposed members of the Board of Guardians, such 
men as Colonel Jackson, Mr. Symes, Mr. Knox. &c., will have not only a ma^ 
of destitution to provide for before long, but that their difficulties will be much 
increased by the opposition of other members. I wish that it were in my power 
to state that I anticipate that self-exertion and co-operation among all classes, 
which alone can effectually meet the coming calamity, and prevent staiaation. 
Many gentlemen have done their duty', audwill do it again ; but there are many 
who hOTe done nothing. When I mention that 65,000 rations were distributed 
daily in this Union, exclnsive of Erris. during the month of September, you 
may suppose that there was yery little thought for the future among its dis- 
tributors.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Lieutenant Hamilton : — 
November 12, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor 
in Ireland have Jiad under their consideration your report of the lOtli instant, 
which they have this day received, relating to the state of the Ballina Union 
and your ins23ections of the workhouse. 

With regard to the first j^art of your report, in which you refer to the state 
of some children in the w'orkhouse, for whom proper diet has not been pro- 
vided, the Commissioners request that you will sec that the medical officer 
exercises the power given to him with respect to the diet of sick paupers by 
Articles 18 and 66 of the Workhouse Regulations. 

With resi^ect to the distress which exists in the Erris district of the Union, 
and to the observations in your report on tire disposition of the Board of 
Guardians as to that district, the Commissioners request that the attention of 
the Board of Guardians may, at the next meeting, be drawn to the state of the 
collection of the rates in the Erris electoral divisions, with a view to the 
adoption of active measures immediately for enforcing the rates wherever 
unpaid, and recoverable ; and the Guardians should in the mean time provide 
for the relief of destitute persons, as the law directs, charging the amount of 
ex23enses so incurred to the proper electoral divisions, to be levied in the usual 
course. 

The Guardians must be well aware that it is not lawful or necessary to defer 
the relief of the paupers of any electoral division, until sufficient rates for the 
puiq^ose are actually collected from that division ; and the Commissioners have 
learned with tlie deepest regret that the Guardians have in some instances 
refused relief to destitute persons in Erris because rates had not been collected 
there. 

The responsibility of relieving the destitute in that district rests solely with 
the Board of Guardians of Ballina Union, and the Guardians cannot directly 
or indirectly divest themselves of that responsibility. 



Lieutenant Hamilton, Temporary Inspector of Ballina Union, to the Poor 
Law Commissioners: — November 13, 1847. 

I AGAIN attended a meeting of the Board of Guardians of this Union, 
yesterday. 

I drew the attention of the Guardians to the illegality of their resolution 
“ refusing admittance into the workhouse to the Erris paupers .” After a great 
deal of opposition on the part of Mr. Jones, the remaining Guardians unani- 
mously agreed " that so long as there shall be room in the workhouse, relief 
shall be afforded therein to destitute persons from Erris.” 

I have communicated this resolution to Mr. Hamilton, Temporary Poor Law 
Inspector, at Belmullet, for his guidance. 

I likewise drew the attention of the Guardians to the following subjects, viz 

The appointment of visiting Committee. 

The state of the infirmary. 

The diet, both in the infirmary and infirmary wai*ds. 

Tile want of medicines, which the medical officer states that he applied 
for several times. 

The medical officer’s report. 

You will see by the minutes of the day’s proceedings, that the Guardians have 
taken steps to remedy tliese several matters. 

I lastly brought the subject of the collection of the rates before the Board, 
and especially the fact of the large amount of rates due by some of the 
Guardians themselves, whose names I read out. I urged as strongly as I could 
the necessity of losing no further time in taking more active measures. 

I cannot offer an opinion about Erris ; but I think that in the remainder of 
the Union, the collectors will be able to collect alarge amoimt of rates, without 
being obliged to resort to very extreme measures. 

There is no time, however, to be lost. The Commissioners may rely upon 
my taldng every step in my power to assist the collectors.

Mr. R. Hamilton, Temporary Inspector at Belmullet, to the Poon Law 
Commissioners. — Notember 10, 1847. 

I ARRIVED here last night, having attended the meeting of the Board of Ems district. 
Guardians at Ballina on Monday. 

The Guardians passed a resolution ai^pointing a Committee for Erris, under 
the 6th Section of the Act 10 Vic. cap. 31. and a sum of 140/. remitted to the 
credit of that district by the late Inspector at Belmullet, was voted should be 
placed at the disposal of this Committee, in order to afford relief to those 
unfortunate creatures 'who had been refused admittance to the Union work- 
house last week, and some of whom had died of want on their return to Erris. 

However, as all these applicants w^ere able-bodied, and as the Commissioners 
had not made any order for giving out-door relief to tliis class in Erris, I de- 
clined expending this money until I received further instructions. 

The Guardians likewise expressed a wish, that a house should be taken in 
Erris for the reception of paupers from the electoral divisions of Belmullet 
and Binghamstown, and placed under the management of the Committee ; but 
as theyalso stated “ that not one fartliing of the rates collected from the other 
“ electoral divisions of Ballina Union should be applied to the support of the 
“ Erris poor,” and as Erris never has hitherto been able to take care of its own 
poor, I do not think it likely it will be aide to do so now, when all classes are 
either staiwing, or next door to it. It is quite evident that the Guardians are 
determined to do all in their power to make Erris a distinct district from the 
rest of the Union, and throw the entire responsibility of meeting the awful 
distress at present existing there on any person but themselves. Under these 
circumstances, I beg you will have the goodness to inform me, with as little 
delay as possible, what course the Commissioners would recommend my 
adopting. 

I have directed the relieving officers to make out lists of those persons who 
are entitled by the Act of Parliament to receive out-door relief; and I hope to 
be able to report on the state of my district at the end of the week.

gjp Dublin, November 11, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland have 
had before them Minutes of Proceedings of the Board of Guardians of Ballina Union on the 
8th instant • and in reference thereto, I am directed to state that the Commissioners deeply 
re<^ret to observe, that, during the meeting of the Board tipwards of 400 persons were waiting 
for admission, many of whom appeared to be in great destitution, but none were admitted, the 
Guardians having only appointed a Committee to purchase clothing and bedding. 

The Commissioners cannot but feel that in a season of so much distress the Guardians have 
failed in due precaution, by not having clothing and bedding in readiness for the number of 
paupers which they are at liberty to receive into the worhhouse ; and the pommissionei's trust, 
that at the next meeting some course may be adopted which shall be within the law, to provide 
for the relief of such dtstitute pei-sons as cannot be longer denied it with safety. 

With reference to the Guardians’ resolution relative to the appointment of a Committee to 
provide for the relief of the poor in the district of Erris, the Commissioners direct me to state, 
that this Committee cannot do more than receive applications and report on them to the Board 
of Guardians, with whom it rests to order relief, and which should not be given (e.xcept in cases 
of emergency, as the Act provides), until ordered by the Board of Guardians. 

The Commissioners must further observe, that it was not a proper course to place 140Z. at 
the disposal of the Committee ; but that a small sum might have been issued to the Relieving 
OfScei'S for cases of emergency, and the nece^ary provision should be made for dispensing out- 
door relief to the classes specified in the 1st Section of the Act 10 Viet. cap. 31, so as to be in 
readiness for affording such relief as might be ordered by the Board after due inquiry. 

The Commissionei-s approve of the course proposed for providing in-door relief in Erris, as 
they cannot consent (except as the law provides, and under circumstances of actual necessity), 
to the out-door relief of the able-bodied classes, or of any other classes than tliose specified in 
the 1st Section of the Extension Act.

The Commissioners request that the Guardians will proceed without delay 
to have payment of the rates enforced by all the parties in arrcar ; and they 
recommend for the consideration of the Guardians the expediency of employ- 
ing a solicitor in the cases in which it will be necessary to adopt legal pro- 
ceedings. 

Such immediate lessors as reside in either county iu which the Union is 
situate, should be served with 15 days’ notice, in pursuance of the 2nd Section 
of the Irish Poor Relief Amendment Act, and on non-payment of the rate, 
should then be summoned before the magistrates, by which course there can 
be a distress on the property of the party rated. 

If this course is not deemed expedient in any particular case, proceedings 
may be taken by means of civil bill in the court of proper jurisdiction, which 
is that of the assistant barrister of the county in which the landlord resides. 

In cases in which the immediate lessor has not a residence in either of the 
counties in which the Union is comprised, but in some other part of Ireland, 
the Commissioners on receiving the application of the Guardians, w'ill he pre- 
pared to give tlieir consent to proceedings being taken in the superior Courts of 
Record in Dublin. 



R. Hamilton, Temporary Inspector at Belmullet, to the Poor Law 
Commissioners: — Novemher 13, 1847. 

During the past week, I have visited every portion of my district except 
the extreme western part of Belmullet electoral division ; and I regret to state, 
that distress, — indeed judging by the appearance of the people, I may say 
starvation, — appears nearly general throughout it, but more particularly in the 
electoral division of Binghamsto^vn, where the poor really are iu a sad state, 
their only food bad turnips, and their supply of them limited ; many have nothing 
to subsist on but the roots of weeds. The relieving olficer-has several hundreds 
on his books ; but the poor people are afraid to venture a second time to 
Ballina, the distance being nearly 40 miles. The British Association having 
placed a small quantity of provisions at my disposal, I have given out some 
of it in this district through the medium of the clergymen, in order to prevent 
deatli from starvation, but have confined the relief principally to destitute 
females and cliildreu under a certain age. There are seven established schools 
in this electoral division; and I hope to have 1000 children on Monday next 
receiving their daily rations in these establishments. There is no proprietor or 
person of any respectability who takes the least interest in the welfare of the 
unfortunate poor in this district. 

Although Belmullet division is much distressed, still I do not think it can 
be as bad as Binghamstown, because I hardly went through a village in it I did 
not see a dog in every house, and I am quite certain when they can keep a dog 
they cannot be starving. The feeding of the children at established schools 
^vill likewise succeed in tliK division, and I shall have rations issued at several 
on Monday. 

I shall report, from time to time, on the state of this district, which I have 
no doubt will require aid from other sources before long beside the rates.

Mr. R. Hamilton, Temporary Inspector at Belmullet, to the Poor Law- 
Commissioners : — November 22, 1847. 

During the past week I brought all applications for relief in this district 
before the Committee of Guardians, and reported to the Board on each case, 
distino-uishiug those classes named in the 1st section of the Act 10 Viet., cap. 31 ; 
aud the Guardians at their meeting on Friday last passed a resolution autho- 
vizin"- out-door relief in Erris to those classes. They likewise stated that by

pauf)ers, and for the preseut will check urgent distress. 

I brought the subject of taking a house in Erris, for the reception of paupers, 
under the notice of the Board ; but they seemed to be of opimon that if they 
would have to pay for it, they should prefer taking additional accommodation 
in BalUna; and on this point I think they are right, because I do not consider 
tlie Guardians for these two electoral divisions would undertake the manage-

much afraid it would not be managed in such a manner as wo^d meet the

provide in-door accommodation for paupers in Erris, I shall do all m my

I have not heard of any deaths from starvation; but I have no doubt many 
will talve place before long, and it will not be within the power of the Boor 
Law to prevent it, as some of the most distressed in this district are precluded, 
by law from obtaining relief, owing to their being in the occupation of more than 
a quarter of an acre of land, and they seem deteiinmed, if possible, to hold on 
hvtlieiv spot of land, in the vain hope that Government iviU l^oth feed them and

the same want of energy appears to exist among all classes at this moment 
Wore, I certainly think they must be allowed to feel the degraded state

Fever has made its appearance in this town again ; and I reget to say my 
seiwant, whom I brought down with me, is very ill with it, I found the 
greatest difficulty in getting any person to ^ow him to remain m their house, 
and the nearest fever hosiiital to this is in Ballina.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Mr. R. Hamilton, Inspector at Belmullet: — 
Noveinher 24, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor 
in Ireland have had under their consideration your report of the 22nd instant 
relating to the district of Erris, in the Ballina Union ; and with reference to the 
wisli of the Board of Guardians (to which you advert) to provide additional 
w’orkhouse accommodation at Ballina for applicants for relief from Erris in 
preference to providing accommodation in that district, I am directed to state 
that the Commissionei-s consider that temporary workhouse accommodation in 
Erris managed hy proper officers, and more particulaidy while a Temporary 
Poor Law Inspector is at Belmullet, nmuld he advantageous to the rate-payers 
as well as to the really destitute poor. It is apprehended that during the 
winter the long journey to Ballina might in some cases be attended with great 
hardship ; and should it not be possible on any occasion to provide for the 
applicants by admitting them to the workhouse at Ballina, much suffering or 
difficulty would follow. 

With respect to the management of such an establishment, the Commissioners 
are of opinion that competent and trustworthy pci-sons should be appointed as 
master and matron, and that, if necessary, a schoolmaster and schoolmistress 
should be appointed. 

As regards the hoiie which you state to be entertained by many of the poorer 
farmers that Government will advance funds for the support of the inhabitants, 
and for the cultivation of their farms, I am to state that care should be taken, 
as much as possible, to disabuse these poor people of such an impression. The 
Commissioners at the same time request that you will make sncli requisite 
inquiries as may enable yon to state, of your owii knowledge, that there are 
many farmers whose holdings are of an extent to require hired labourers (which 
you can learn from the rate-books of the divisions), and that such farmers, or 
any considerable number of them, are believed, on reasonable grounds, to possess 
means of giving employment necessary for the proper use of the lands occupied. 

The Commissioners will communicate with the Central Board of Health 
with respect to the prevalence of fever in the district. 



Lieutenant Hamilton, Temporary Inspector of Ballina Union, to the Poor Law 
Commissioners: — November 22, 1847. 

I HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt, this day, of your 
letter of the 20th instant, in which you request me to furnish a specific 
report on the state of the population in my district of this Union. 1 beg to 
acquaint you, for the Commissioners’ information, that I hope to be able, before 
mauy days, to complete a tour of my district, which comprises nearly 340,000 
acres. 1 liave hitherto chiefly directed my attention to the state of the work- 
house, with a view of endeavouring to provide accommodation in it for all 
applicants, being convinced by experience, that the workhouse test is the only 
index of actual destitution. 

I have carefully avoided either doing or sayiug anything, that might en- 
comage the supposition that the British Association will assist the Guardians 
mider any circumstances j because I am satisfied, that all local exertion would 
become paralysed. I have, therefore, as far as time would admit, made my own 
observations and judged for myself as to the general appearance of the people ; 
the state of the haggards, &c. I have been agreeably surprised, in both respects. 
At the same time, some of the small holdern of land, (whose land was either 
uncropped or badly cultivated,) persons resident in towns and villages, squatters, 
and hnbitual beggars, are in a very deplorable state. They generally refuse 
to go to the woidchous^ allow their children to starve, or bring them, to the 
workhouse when their cases are hopeless. 

I am of opmion, that, at present> such cases are the exceptions, and that they 
are not suffiei^tly numerous as to be beyond relief, or to cause any alarm to 
the Guardians, provided that the latter will cordially co-operate with the Com- 
missioners in carrying out the suggestions contained in their letter of the 26th 
of August last. 

The greatest difficulty, I apprehend, will be to provide for the number of 
able-bodied persons who are in a state of destitution in the district of Erris.

Lieut. PIamilton, Temporary Inspector of Ballina Phiioii, to the Poor Law

I ATTENDED the usual Weekly meeting of the Board of Guardians of

Captain Gilbert, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners: — 
November 3, 1847. 

In conformity with your instructions, I have inspected the workhouse of 
this Union, and attended yesterday the meeting of the Board of Guardians, 
having previously given orders to the collectors and relieving officers to attaid 
also. 

The poor-honse I found extremely clean and well regulated, but containing 
more people than it was originally intended to hold. Several paupers went 
out, and a considerable number were admitted. There are now about 50 
paupers more than the complement. 

Orders were given to send out 13 infimi old men and ISO widows and 
children to receive out-door relief, in order to make room for able-bodied men 
who have made applications to be admitted. 

TJiere is a large building, an old charter-house, which , has for some months 
been occupied as a temporary fever hospital. It was proposed yesterday that 
the patients, being now few in number, should be removed to the county hos- 
pital, and the house made available for as many oiphan cliildreii as it would 
contain. There are at present 360 in the poor-house, and the charter-house 
will hold about one-half. It is about half a mile from the poor-house, sur- 
rounded by a good wall ; and if sheds were erected in the yard, or an addition 
made to the house, the whole of the orphans could he removed to make room 
for able-bodied paupers. 

There are between 40o and 500 children, besides the orphans, in the poor- 
house; and I strongly recommend that some temporary buildings or sheds 
should be erected within the walls of the poor-house to contain the whole of 
the children. 

The present heavy debt, being nearly 10,000Z., almost precludes the possi- 
bility of erecting any new buildings without the co-opei-ation and entire assist- 
ance of the Commissioner. 

With regard to the collecting of the rates, I found them progressing in some 
districts, and in others not at all. The collectors themselves seem, for the most 
part, a bad class of persons for that duty, and will require constant attention, 
and some, I make no doubt, immediate dismissal. 

There have been lodged within the last week, in the treasurer’s hands, only 
650^. I have threatened iffie collectors with dismissal, unless they show more 
activity and willingness to perform their duty. 

I trust you will take into your consideration the very great advantages tliat 
would he derived if the poor-house could he in any way enlarged for the 
accommodation of the children ; by which means, I think, at least for the pre- 
sent, much out-door relief will not be required.

Poor Law Commission Office, Lublin, 

Sir, November 20, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland, have 
had under consideration the resolution in which the Board of Guardians of Sligo Union at a 
meeting on tlie 16th instant, recommending proceedings to he taken in the superior courts for 
rate due by a Mr. Burrows, in consequence of his activity in getting up opposition to payment 
of the poor-rates ; also against various rale-payers in consequence of the difficulty reported by 
Mr. Harloe Phibbs, to be met by him in obt^ning orders against such parties as have been 
■summoned before the magistrates. 

The Commissioners beg to refer the Board of Guardians to the 78th section of the Act 
1 and 2 Vic. cap. 56, and 2nd section of the Act 6 and 7 Vic. cap. 92, by which it will be 
observed that proceedings in the superior courts can only be taken for recovery of rate due by 
immediate lessors for tenements in respect of which they are rated instead of the occupiers. 
It will be also observed that the law likewise enables the Guardians to proceed against such 
lessors if resident in the county in which the Union is situate, either summarily or fifteen days’ 
notice, or by civil bill ; in consequence of the option thus given to the Guardians, it would not 
be safe to proceed in the superior courts against any lessors who can be reached by the sum- 
mary process or by civil bill, as being opposed to a rule of the superior courts, except on very 
special grounds ; and it would in any event be competent to the defendant to pay only the 
costs of the civil bill process. 

The Commissioners will be prepared to authorize proceedings in the superior courts against 
any immediate lessors not resident in the county Sligo, but in some other part of Ireland, and 
who may not pay rates due by him on proper notice. 

The original papers, transmitted with the copy of Mr. Phihb’s report, are now returned. 

I have, &c. 

The Clerk to the Guardians of the W. Stanley, Secretary.

I have to report that the result has been highly satisfactory and beneficial. 

I annex a report from the clerh, which I have got printed, and^ forward 
a dozen copies, in case any application should be made tor information from 

the Unions. , , . , i t n 

At Rathkoale, the Indian meal is mixed with what is termed whole flour, 
that is, wheat ground and tlie bran not separated. At Tipperary, the mixture 
of Indial meal and whole flour is also practised. At Kilmallock, the Indian 
corn meal is used alone. In these Unions, as at Limerick, the work is per- 
formed by the females generally, from 16 to 20 years of age, with one or two 
steady, elderly women, to teach them the proper mode of making the meal 
into cakes. 

It may be observed, this bread does not come to more than the tormer price 
of potatoes. The usual allowance for dinner, being from 3^ to 4 lbs., if 3i lbs. 
and the potatoes 4cf. per stone, the expense was Ic^., the bread cost less than 
the Id. 

The health of the inmates appears more satisfactory, considering the very 
awful epidemic consequent upon the state in which many of the inmates were 
received into the workhouse.

Indian-Com Meal Bread. 

I HAVE the honour to report the particulare regarding hot plates in tEs workhouse, for 
baking bread. 

Hot plates (made of metal) 18 feet long, 3 feet 2 inches wide, and 1 inch thick, erected in 
Mill-house, to the back of the kitchen Sues, which Sues are found to answer to the kitchen and 
bakehouse. 

Cost of erection, including all expenses, about 21Z. 10s. 

The plates were in use here about 18 months, and required but very little repair j they were 
well set with large fire-blocks. 

The bread is made of Indian-corn meal, by the female paupers, like griddle-cake ; there is 
nothing mixed with the meal, save a little hot water to work it up ; the baking employs 14 
paupers daily. 

The allowance of meal made into bread for dinner is : — 

Men . . . .12 ounces. 

Women . • . 8 ,, 

Children . . . 8 , , including luncheon. 

The bread for men is made into cakes of 24 ozs., of H lb. ; for women and children, into 
cakes of 16 ozs. or 1 Ih. Immediately after the cake is worked up. and before placing it in 
the plate, it is partly cut into two even parts, so that each inmate receives their quantity by 
itself. 

The numbers in the workhouse supplied yesterday for dinner wdth Indian corn meal bread 
were — 

284 Men. 

476 Women. 

680 Children. 



1440 

The Guardians do not allow this bread for the sick, aged, and infirm, or children undet 5 
years. 

The plates are capable of baking for 2000 daily, but, at present, we do not require for more 
than 1440. 

The contract price for Indian-com meal is 9Z. 125. 6/f. per ton, or a small fraction more 
than Irf, per lb. • . . j i lu p 

Twelve ounces of good Indian-com meal properly baked on this plan, will produce 1 lb. of 
bread, at a cost, including fuel and salt, of less tban Id. per lb. 

The contract for bread, at present, is 7d. for the 4 lb. loaf.

Observations of 8th November of Mr. D’Arcy, Temporary Inspector, on 
Dr. Barclay Sheil’s Letter of the 4th November, 1847 (the paper having 
been referred to him). 

Much difficulty pr^ents itself in regard to the fever hospital. The 
Guardians refuse to sux)ply funds as it is not placed under their control ; and 
it would appear they are justified iu doing so by sec. 5 of Act 9 Vic., c. 6, and 
which is not repealed by any part of the Act 10 Vic., c. 22. There is another 
point upon which I think the Guardians justified in remonstrating, viz., that it 
is, or has been, only an electoral division hospital ; if it were made an Uniem 
hospital, and that attached to the workhouse, cleared of its inmates, it would 
render signal service as affording so much more room and additional workhouse 
accommodation, so necessary as a test for able-bodied. The Guardians state, 
and with truth, that the Union is almost bankrupt, and deprecate any expense 
that can be avoided. They struck cheerfully the rat^, winch appear to he re- 
quired to meet their liabilities and the wants of the Union,' yesterday ; and at 
such a time I think it judicious to avoid any pressure that can be avoided, and

any part of the 10 Vic., c. 22. 

In reference to this point I am directed by the Commissioners to state, that, 
upon a careful examination of the 9 Vic., c. 6, you will find that the 5th section 
relates only to hospitals and dispensaries procured by the Guardians under the 
4th section, and the hospital in question was not procured by the Guardians, 
but was established under the 3rd section of the 10 Vic., c. 22, the 5th section 
of which moreover provides that hospitals or dispensaries procured by the 
Relief Committees, or by any Board of Guardians under the first recited Ac^ 
shall be managed by such Relief Committee. 

The Commissioners desire further to observe, that it is expressly stated in the 
preamble to the 10 Vic., c. 22, that the provisions of the Act on which the 
present Fever Act is founded can be more effectually carried out by the Relief 
Committees than by the Board of Guardians ; and it is to he remarked that the 
elected and ex-ojficio Guardians resident in the electoral divisions concerned are 
members of the Relief Committee. 

The Commissioners enclose, for your information, a copy of a letter which 
they recently received from the Board of Health on the subject, and they 
request that you will, at the next meeting of the Board, endeavour, by every 
means in your power, to have the fever hospital continued, in accordance with 
the provisions of the law. under the management of the Relief Committee. 

The Commissiouers -will address a separate letter to you in regard to the 
appointment of relieving officers.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Mr. D’Arcy: — November 11, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 
9th instant, reporting on the condition of the workhouse of Ballyshannon 
Union, and requesting instructions on certain matters connected ■with the 
Union. 

The Commissioners approve oi the steps which you have taken for having 
the paupers employed, and improving the state of the workhouse ; and they 
■will consult their arcliitect on the subject of the drainage when the report 
which you state the master is to present on next Board-day comes before them. 

With reference to your observations, that "some money might be made of 
the industiy of the paupers,” the Commissioners deem it right to point out, 
that although the employment of paupers of all classes in the workhouse is a 
matter of the utmost importance, such employment ought not to be undertaken 
as a source of profit to the Union ; and any manufacture introduced into the 
workhouse for the purpose of employing the inmates should, as far as possible, 
be limited to articles required for use and consumption in the workhouse, and 
should not be carried on for diqiosal by sale in the neighbourhood, lest, by 
such competition, the general market for such articles of manufacture be inter- 
fered ■withj prices lowered, and the wages of some portion of the labouring 
classes depreciated, and individuals thrown out of employment. The Commis- 
sioners will add that there has been considerable experience in England as to 



Printe'd image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 



99 



the result of attempting to make pauper labour a source of profit to Unions, 
and that such attempts have so often been unsuccessful that it is now a settled 
maxim of Poor Law j)ractice to abstain from repeating them. 

As regards the system of proceeding by summons before the justices to 
enforce the payment of poor rate, I am to state that the collector is not bound 
to adopt that mode of proceeding if it appears more expedient to distrain at 
once under the authority of his own warrant. There are diiferent modes of 
proceeding for the recovery of poor rates; and the most advisable mode of 
proceeding in any particular case must be determined by reference to the cir- 
cumstances of such case. 

As regards the apprehended difficulty in the collection, the collector should 
make a full statement of the case to the magistrates of the district ; and the 
Commissioners have no doubt that every protection that may be needed will 
be afforded. 

With reference to your inq^uiry as to what course you should adopt if the 
Guardians persist in refusing to raise the salaries of their officers in accordance 
with the order of the Commissioners, or whether such refusal will necessarily 
involve their dismissal, I am to state that such refusal does not necessarily 
involve the dissolution of the Board ; but the Commissioners have, after a long 
correqjondence with the Board of Guardians, deemed it right to apply to the 
Court of Queen’s Bench for a mandamus to enforce obedience to their order. 
The Commissioners were most reluctant to take this step, but as the Guardians 
persisted in their refusal to pay what the Commissioners considered very 
moderate salaries for the duties required to be performed, the Commissioners, 
after repeated attempts to convince the Guardians of the justice and propriety 
of increasing the salaries, and of the superior economy, in the long run, of 
allowing adequate salaries, and thus securing the services of efficient officem, 
felt that they had no other course open to them. 

The salary which the Commissioners have fixed for the clerk (who is 
reported both by the inspector and the auditor to he a most efficient officer), is 
hut 40^. a-year, and the Guardians decline to pay more than 25Z. The salaries 
fixed by the Commissionem for the other officers whose salaries are in question 
are as follow, viz., matron, 20Z. ; schoolmaster, 201. ", schoolmistress, \5L; and 
porter, 10/. The salaries proposed by the Guardians for these officers are — 
matron, 15/. ; schoolmaster, 8/. ; schoolmistress, 8/. ; porter, 6/. 

The salaries as fixed by the Commissioners are all below the aver£^e amount 
of such salaries, as paid in other Unions having workhouses of the same size as 
that at Ballyshannon ; and the total annual difference between the salaries, as 
fixed by the Commissioners and as proposed by the Guardians, is only 43/. 

As regards the relieving officers’ districts, you are at liberty to state to the 
Guardians that the Commissioners have no objection to remodel such districts 
according to any reasonable plan that may be proposed to them by the 
Guardians, provided the number of districts is not increased. 

The Commissioner would have preferred that the Guardians would, in the 
first instance, have arranged the districts, and submitted them to the Commis- 
sioners for approval ; but as the Guardians, who at one time refused to appoint 
any relieving officers at all, afterwards determined, and persisted in the deter- 
mination to appoint 10 (a number which the Commissioners, with whom alone 
the legal power to determine the number of relieving officers in an Union rests, 
felt the circumstances of the Union neither warranted nor required), they issued 
the order fixing the number of relieving officers, and defining their districts ; 
that appearing to be the only mode of bringing the question at issue (viz., the 
number of officers to be appointed), to a conclusion. 

The Commissioners entirely approve the proposal to permit the aged and 
infirm to leave the workhouse, and to receive a small weekly allowance (either 
in money or food), as this step will place additional workhouse accommodation 
at the disposal of the Guardians for the relief of the able-bodied ; but you will 
not fail to point out to the Guardians that the adoption of this step renders the 
immediate appointment of relieving officers more essentially necessary than 
ever.

Copy of a Letter addressed to the Catholic Clergy. 

Rev. Sir, Ballyshannon, No'cember 11, 1847. 

ixAKE the liberly of writing to you, on a point of great importance, and one in 
which I am sure you are interested, and which your co-operatiou and advice would materially 
assist in leading to a successful issue. 

The support of the destitute persoas of this country, must, in future, be pi-orided for by 
means of rates, to be levied under the Poor Law, and upon the amount to which they are made 
available will depend the relief of the poor of each Union. 

My view in thus addressing you, is to solicit your aid to that benevolent object by pointing 
out to your congregation, that it is but an act of'chaiity and justice, of those whom Providence 
has phieed in more" coiuibrtable circumstances, to pay this cheerfully for the support of their 
poorer brethren, and that delay or obstruction will produce the deepest misery to them. 

Relying upon your good offices, I have tlie honour to be. Rev, Sir, 

Your very obedient Servant, 

John S. D’Arct, 

Poor Law Inspector. 

I see the greater necessity to use every means to induce a favourable view of 
the law amongst the people, as hitherto they have been used to so low rates. 

Now, in this division, the last rate was sixpence, the new three shillings. 

Friday last, as I reported to the Commissioners I purposed to do, I went to 
Derrygo'nelly, eighteen miles, to attend the petty sessions ; on my arrival I 
found neither the collector nor magistrate arrived. I examined the criminal 
book, and there found the charge exactly as detailed in Fauy’s letter, but to 
my great surprise when the Court assembled, I found that the summons, 
althoiio-h filled, had not been signed ; I remained to get it signed, and the case 
now stends for the 26th instant, when I propose again attending. On Thursday 
next I propose being at Belleck Petty Sessions, to induce the magistrates to 
tyrant assistance to a collector, who has already obtained warrants, but fears to 
proceed to sale under them, having been threatened ; and he is prepared to 
swear, that he believes his life would be in danger, did he proceed to levy 
them without force. 

My own previous observation has confirmed me in the opinion tliat I can in. 
no better way promote the main object for which I have been sent here than 
by attending every sessions at which any rate case may be likely to be before 
the bench, as my presence will be more or less a stimulus to proper exertion, 
both to the collector and magistrates. 

Within the fortnight w^hich has elapsed since my arrival, 106/. has been 
collected, although so much does not appear on the minutes, as a portion of it 
was paid whilst the Board of Guardians was occupied on Saturday, but it will

Johnson to propose a resolution last Saturday that the collectors securities 
shall be proceeded against if all be not paid next Friday ; but this I do not

then think the wiser course is to proceed with the new rate, as but about 200/. 
of the old rate will be outstanding, and a good deal of it could in no way be 
made available, even did we delay longer. I hope the new rate-books wiU be 
ready for signature next Board-day, as I directed the clerk to employ two 
additional hands ; and in consequence we shall have them complete withm the 
fortnight.

Mr. D’Arcy, Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners: — November 22, 1847. 

^ HAVE the honour to report what occurred at the meeting of the Board 
of Guardians of this Union, which took place on Saturday the 20th instant. 

I had hoped that the rate books should have been signed that day, but some 
of the arrears not having been taken in, they will not be complete for signature 
till next Board day. 

The collectors were in attendance, and three of them showed great reluctance 
to undertake the new collection, stating they had been warned by their friends 
not to attempt it, for that lives would be lost in the collection ; and to 
impress the Guardians with the disturbed state the country was in, instanced 
the murder of Mr. Hassard, a crime hitherto unknowm in Fermanagh. All the 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 103 

collectors, witliout exception, stated that if the assistance of police tras not 
afforded them in the wild districts, and where violence might be apprehended, _H ' 
they would under no circumstances be concerned in it. 

There is a feeling of general insecurity abroad, some of the ex-<>jfficio Guar- 
dians left the Board-room early, not wishing to be out after dark ; Captain 
Johnston mentioned a report that he was shot had been very general in Sligo ; 
and that it was ominous, as there were frequent instances where murders liave 
been committed of such rumours preceding them ; Mr. Dickson stated to me 
that as he drove into the town, one man remarked to another, alluding to him, 

“ that is the man who is not afraid to drive alone,” which showed that the minds 
of the people were occupied with such subjects; and he warned me not to be 
out late, as the people were already aware that I was urging the collection of 
the rate. 

I state these circumstances, not that I personally have the slightest fear, and 
am ready, if directed to do so, to accompany the collectors in the performance 
of their duty ; but I do so for the purpose of impressing on the Commissioners 
the necessity in the commencement of the collection of the new rate, that an 
order should be issued to the magistrates, where collectors have reason to 
apprehend the slightest violence, to direct police to accompany them. The 
success, or the contrary, the first week will determine whether or not rates 
shall be made available. If the people see a demonstration of force they will 
sti’ike at once, and pay, as far as they are able ; but on the contrary, should a 
collector and his assistant be foiled in the first attempt, it will embolden them, 
and a general resistance will be the consequence. 

I do not put these views lightly or inconsiderately forward. I have a perfect 
and intimate knowledge of the peasantry and their habits ; I am convinced of 
the sound policy of the course I take the liberty of bringing before the notice 
of your Board ; there is no populace more easily excited by the most remote 
possibility of being able successfully to resist the law, and none more easily 
held in check, if a determination to enforce it with a strong hand is 
exhibited. 

Tlie Guardians in some cases spoke of reducing the amount of poundage on 
the collection of the next rate, as it would be so much larger than the last, and 
in others expected it would be done for the same sum, viz., sixpence in the 
pound ; my opinion is, in no case should less than a shilling in the pound be 
offered ; if the contraiy course is pursued, we shall be sure to lose the services 
of the present collectors, and at such a period, when more than ordinary 
difficulty is to be apprehended, this would be most injurious, as no man 
unacquainted with the rate-payers and divisions could possibly be as effective 
as they would. 

I produced the estimates for support of the Temporary Fever Hospital, and 
the Guardians only wait a reply whether the Union at large is liable for its 
support to supply funds. 



The Poor Law Commissioners to Mr. D’Arcy: — November 25, 1S47. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 
22nd instant, reporting theproceedings of the Ballyshannon Board of Guardians 
at their meeting on the 20th instant 

In reference to your observations as to the attempted intimidation of the 
collectors, and your suggestions that an order should be issued to the magis- 
trates, where collectors have reason to apprehend violence, to direct police to 
accompany them, I am to state that the proper course for collectors to pursue 
if they have valid reasons for apprehending personal violence in the discharge 
of their duty, is to swear informations to that effect before a magistrate. Thus 
is the course usually adopted through Ireland, and it has generally been found 
effectual. If any magistrate does not grant efficient support to the collectors, 
this would be a ground for special complaint to his Excellency ; hut the Com- 
missioners could not, with propriety, request his Excellency to order the 
magistrates to do what it is their boimden duty to do without any such order. 
The Commissioners deem it desirable that you should urge each collector who 
you have reason to believe would be justified in doing so, to swear an infor- 
mation accordingly ; and then, if any magistrate refuses him assistance, the

Donegal, November 6, 1847. 

I ARRIVED in this Union on the 3rd instant. The following morning 
I inspected the workhouse ; I was satisfied with the good order of the esta-

Letterkenny for the purpose of conferring with Mr. Otway, Assistant Poor 
Law Commissioner, previous to the meeting of the Board of Guardians ; as he 
did not visit that place, I returned here again yesterday evening.

nature of my appointment; and I am happy to state they manifested a readi- 
ness to co-operate in carrying into effect the instructions of the Commissioners. 

With reference to the collection of the rates, considerable progress is making. 
On the 29th ultimo there were 283^. in the hands of the treasurer. Since then 
about 2001 has been collected ; and legal proceedings were directed to be 
instituted immediately against the wealthiest defaulter, and notice given to the 
five highest rate-payers amon^ the defaulters in each electoral division, that, in 
case their rates are not paid by the 13th instant, legal steps will be taken to 
enforce them. 

The outstanding debts of the wmrkhouse amount to upwards of 800^. 

Relieving officers have not yet entered upon their duties, the Guardians 
objecting to be at the expense of their salaries mitil the number of inmates in 
the workhouse increases.

I have this week been using my exertions towards seeing their regulations 
placed upon a proper footing, particularly with regard to the internal condition 
of the state and discipline of the workhouse, and urging the collectors to per- 
form their duties. 

With reference to the collectors, it is very necessary that compulsory mea- 
sures should be resorted to with them, as the Guardians have not urged them 
to a strict discharge of their duties ; they are disposed to take their leisure ; 
they were all summoned to attend early this morning for the purpose of 
examining their books, but only two thought proper to attend ; had the notice 
been strictly legal, I would have caused the absent ones to be fined ; in future 
they are ordered to attend at the Board-room on each Friday to report their 
proceedings. 

The 1st January has been fixed for closing the collectors’ books. 

There are still many destitute persons in the Union, but they retain a pre- 
judice against entering the workhouse ; as also people suffering from fever 
decline being taken to the fever-shed, 

The numbers in the workhouse being only 200, the relieving officers are not 
yet permitted to enter upon their duties. 

I have induced the Visiting Committee to resume their duties, which is essenr 
tial for the internal economy of the workhouse.

Milford Union. 

Mr. Horsley, Temporary Inspector, totlie Poor Law Commissioners: — 
November 16, 1847. 

I ATTENDED the meeting of the Milford Board of Guardians yesterday ; 
it was but thinly attended, only three Guardians being present. The rate- 
collectors were in attendance and exhibited their books, from which it appeared 
the arrears at present owing amount to 1 13/^ an inconsiderable sum, when the 
heavy rates which had been struck over the Union and the severe pressure of 
the times are taken into account. 

New rate and collectors’ books have been prepared and a fresh rate declared, 
which, if collected, would realize a sum of 3177/. The poundage on the 
several electoral divisions varies from Is. to 3.v. 

From all I can learn, a good feeling prevails among the rate-payers generally, 
and they have every disposition to pay to the utmost of their ability the new 
rates imposed upon them. 

The nothern portion of the Union (comprising five electoral divisions) is a 
wretchedly poor and populous district, and the amount which the rate-payers 
therein will be in a condition to pay wdll, I fear, lie altogether insufficient to 
meet the requirements of the impending destitution. Some extraneous assistance 
will, therefore, have to be afforded to the district. 

Mr. Otway, Poor Law Inspector, attended at Milford wmrkhouse yesterday, 
and gave me the benefit of his valuable advice and experience. He pointed out 
to me the matters which he thought should engage my first and best attention, 
in commencing my duties as Temporary Inspector of the Union. 

There has lately been a change among the officers of the workhouse, and the 
new clerk and master are only beginning to learn how to discharge correctly 
the duties attaching to their respective offices. 



Mr. Horsley, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 
Nove77iber 22, 1847. 

I ATTENDED the meeting of the Board of Guardians this day ; eight 
Guardians were present. . 

On Thursday last I inspected the house, and regret to say, I foundit ni avery 
slovenly condition. There was a most offensive smell in every part of it, dor- 
mitories and day rooms, especially in the dormitories. The floors were not 
properly cleansed, and it \vas but too apparent that the necessities of nature 
were performed without due regard beiiig had to decency and cleanliness. The 
straw in the beds (furnished by contract) appeared to be old and musty. _ Ven- 
tilation seemed to be imperfect. Much might be effected by keeping the windows 
of the dormitories open throughout the day-time. 

The house, moreover, is badly found in clothing and all requisite utensils. 
Judging from the general state of the house, it would appear that the Visiting 
Committee have hitherto neglected their peculiar province. 

I brought all these matters under the notice of the Board, and shouted them 
how neeessary it was to enforce on the inmates the observance of cleanliness 
and decency, both as regarded their health and morals ; and I also impressed 
on the master the necessity of his estabtishing his authority at the outset, and 
tliat although it was his duty to be kind and humane in his treatment of tlie 
paupers, it was also his duty to act with firmness and decision in all mattei-s 

affecting the order and discipline of the house. 

I shall endeavour, with the assistance of the Board, (which I am sure will 
be cheerfully given,) to bring the house into a better state than it is in at 

^^With the admissions to-day, the house now contains within six of the number 
of inmates for which it was originally constructed; and out-door rebel will, m 
all probability, have to be provided for on next Board day. The relieving 

officers are in possession of their books. ^ 

The cottier class are in a miserable condition. There is litue or no employ- 
ment for them, and for the last few weeks they have been subsisting almost 
entirelv on the turnips raised in their small gardens. This low and watery diet 
is, in fact, telling on their health and strength. Fever and dysentery are rife 
among them.

Lowtherstown Union : — Dissolution of the Board of Guardians. 

The Poor Law Commissioners to Sir Denis Le Marchant: — 
November 1, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland to transmit, for the information of Secretaiy Sir 
George Grey, a copy of the correspondence bet\veen the Commissioners and 
the Lowtherstown Board of Guardians, which terminated in the dissolution of 
the Board by the Commissioners, and in the appointment of paid officers under 
the 18th section of the Irish Poor Relief Extension Act. The Commissioners 
likewise transmit a copy of a protest against the dissolution, signed by indivi- 
duals who had been previously Guardians of the Union. 

The Commissioners deem it unnecessary to advert to that protest, as far as 
it relates to the dissolution of the Board of Guardians, because, although it 
contains strong expressions of feeling, it leaves the reasonings wholly untouched, 
by which the Commissioners pointed out to the Guardians that they had been 
guilty of a breach of faith. 

With regard to two other points alluded in the protest, although they are 
altogether irrelevant to the grounds on which the Board of Guardians was 
dissolved, the Commissioners desire to make the following observations : — 

1st. In reference to the raising the chaplains’ salaries, the Commissioners 
Imve to state, that the fixing their amount is exclusively witliiii the province of 
the Commissioners. The amount of increase was merely from 25/. to 30/. 
a-year , and appeared to the Commissioners to be proper in itself, and equitable 
lu reference to the salaries in other Unions. The Commissioners were much 
surprised that the increase should have been seriously objected to, and much 
more that an attempt should have been made to convert it into a grievance. 

-nd. The master and matron were guilty of gross and culpable neglect of 
duty, as is shown in the accompanying report of Mr. Phelan, the medical 
inspector, imd they were accordingly removed from their office. The Com- 
missioners had previously offered to them the alternative of resignation, of 
which they declined to avail themselves, in consequence, as they have since 
contessed, of the instigation of others, and contrary to their own judgment.

The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians. Lowtherstown

Poor Laio Commission Office, Dublin, 

Sir. August Z\ , . 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for the Relief of the 
Poor in Ireland, to state that they have had under consideration the resolution of the Board 
of Guardians of Lowtherstown Union of the 25th instant, in which they state that they are of 
opinion that the general rate of lOd. iii the pound resolved on by them is the highest sum 
which it is necessary and advisable to strike. 

In reference to that resolution, the Commissioners desire to state that the proposed rate of 
lOri. in the pound appears to the Commissioners insufficient for even the ordinary purposes of 
the workhouse. It may be true that the present number in the workhouse may be only 26S, 
and the out-door relief may almost entirely have ceased; but the Commissioners think that 
the continuance of this state of things cannot be calculated on, and that die least estimate on 
which the Guardians can base their calculation consistently with prudence, ouglit to be founded 
on the assumption that the wliole accommodation which the workhouse affords will be placed 
in requisition during a considerable period, commencing from the termination of han'est. The 
Commissioners think that the omission of the Guardians to act last year on the Commissioners’ 

Circular of the 10th September, 1846, in which the Commissioners urgently advised and called 
upon the Guardians to base their estimates on a somewhat similar assumption, is one of the 
main causes why the finances of so many unions have fallen into a state of embarrassment and 
confusion ; and the Commissioners warn the Lowtherstown Board of Guardians not to make a 
similar mistake at the present time. 

The rate of only lOrf. in the pound is open, however, to the still greater objection, that it 
makes no provision for the repayment of advances under the temporary Relief Act. The Cora- 
missioners have received from the Relief Commissioners the following statement, showing the 
amount in the pound for each division of the sums required by them in repayment of the 
advances made to each division of Lowtherstown Union : —
