The Commissioners deem it right, therefore, that the Guardians should make provision in 
their next rate for the repayment of the whole of the above sums ; and the Commissioners now 
call upon the Guardians to make such provision accordingly, in addition to a provision for the 
purposes of the ordinary Poor Law, based upon the assumption that the whole accommodation 
which the workhouse affords, will be placed in requisition during a considerable period, com- 
mencing from the termination of the harvest. 

At the same time the Commissioners wish it to be distinctly vinderstood that they do not 
require of the Guardians that their next rate in any division of their Union should exceed 3s. in 
the pound for all purposes ; and that, although the Commissioners require provision to be 
made for the repayment of advances under the Temporary Relief Act, it is intended that 
the produce of the collection should be applied in the first instance to paying the other debts 
of the Union, and defraying the expenses of the ordinary Poor Laws. 

The Commissioners regard it as of the highest importance that the Guardians should keep 
faitli in repaying the advances which have been made to them by Her Majesty’s Government ; 
and if the Guardians do not make provision for such repayment, the Commissioners will deem 
it their duty to exercise their powers under the 18th section of the Irish Poor Relief Extension 
Act.

I a M directed by the Commissioners for administering the laws for Relief of the Poor in 
Ireland to state that they have had under consideration the resolution of the Lowtherstown- 
Board of Guardians of the 8th instant, in which the Guardians decline to make provision in 
their next rate for repayment of the whole of the adi'ances under the Temporary Relief Act, 
and merely offer to strike and levy immediately a rate equivalent to the sixth of the money 
advanced, with a promise to repay the remainder in five yearly instalments. ^ 

The Commissioners deeply regret the course which the Guardians have thought fit to pursue 
on this occasion, as it involves a distinct breach of faith in reference to the conditions on which 
alone the Guardians received pecuniary assistance from Her Majesty’s Government during 
the last five months. ® 



The Guardians would have received no loan fi-om Government unless they had resolved to 
make a rate for repayment, and unless the Inspector had certified that, to the best of his belief 
the Guardians were proceeding with all possible despatch to make and levy such rate. That 
the Guarchans, therefore, having received money on these terms, and having expended it 
should now decline to act in accordance with their solemn moral obligations, and should merely 
offer to pay their debts by six yearly instalments, appears to the Commissioners inconsistent 
with that honesty m pecuniary traosactions whicli ought to he one of the leading priuciplcs both 
or individuals and of public bodies. 

The unreasonableness of the Guardians in the line of conduct which they have adonted is 
aggravated by the consideration that the amount of rate which the Guardians were required to 
make for repavtnent of the advances under the Temporary Relief Act did not in any electoral 
division exceed Is. lOrf. in the pound, and in one division was as low as M. in the pound : and 
if their own estimate of lOrf. in the pound for ordinary expenses was correct, they would not 
have been under the necessity of making a higher rate than 2s. &d. in the pound for all purposes 
in any electoral dmsion, wlule in one division it would have been sufficient for theni to Wve 
made a rate of Is. 7cl. in the pound. 

Under fhese circumstances, the Commissioners feel that they have no other alternative than 
to exercise their powers under the 18th section of the Irish Relief Extension Act, and they

tainecl, on putting quesfions to the women in charge of the cell, were then only affected with

appeared lo be dangerously ill; but a woman jay on the floor, with a little straw under her, as 
-scarcely to cover it, respecting whose case I made inquiry. I then learned that she was drop- 
sical, and further affected with dysentery; on going to examine her, the foetorfrom her person 
was such as almost to compel me to desist. I, however, examined her, and found her nearly 
pulseless. To ascertain the cause of the foetor 1 turned up the bed-clothes, and found the bed 
and hed-clothes, I may say, flooded with the discharges from her bowels. I then sent ft>r the 
matron, exposed the woman so far as to show the condition in wliich she was, and asked her 
and the master how any pauper in their charge could be permitted to lie in that condition. 
The matron endeavoured to excuse herself, but her husband agreed that no excuse could be 
■offered. I told the matron that I purposely sent for her, disgusting as the scene was, that she 
should witness that which, were slie to exercise ordinary supervision, could not occur, and 
which should never take place, and I informed her that it is her duty to see that those in these 
idiot wards are equally taken care of as others, and that she and her husband must be held 
responsible for such very culpable neglect of duty. The master appeared lo be greatly shocked 
at this additional instance of the gross inattention of those placed in charge of the sick, and 
candidly, and I think honestly, declared that he could not, and would not, attempt to del'end 
himself or the matron. 

I pointed out to both that it is their duty to visit all parts of the institution daily, and to 
satisfy themselves, by tbeir own inspection, and not by the reports of others, that the paupers 
are everywhere kept as they should be. It is evident that hitherto this has not been the case 
here, or if it be, that the supervision has been carelessly performed. 

Oil inquiry of the acting medical officer what medical treatment he was adopting for lliis 
wretched patient, I ascertained that for some days there was none, not even any particular 
attention to diet, and no stimulus given, so as to make an effort to relieve her. I advised that 
no time be lost in doing what was necessary for her, small as might be the chance of her 
recovery. I beg to add that, unless as a mere suggestion, I never advise any particular treat- 
ment for the sick. 

In this instance, however, I advised some wine or diluted spirits to be given, with such nu- 
tritious diet as the woman’s case required. A little pauper girl, more kind than the doctor or 
matron, was spoon-feeding her. I think it the best means of exemplifying the want of attention 
to the sick and the helpless in this bouse, and the want of capacity on the part of the acting 
medical officer to discharge the important duties which have been entrusted to him. 

In the inflrm female dormitory, I found a boy affected with general dropsy and greatly 
reduced ; half his body lay on a small quantity of straw, the other half was on the floor. I 
asked Mr. Martin what he was doing for him, when, as he appeared confused, I asked the 
nurse if the boy were latterly getting any medicine. Her reply was in the negative, but Mr. 
Martin said he gave her some powders lately for the patient, which, however, the nui-se denied. 
There beincr no prescription-books, the accuracy of either could not be tested; but I instance 
this second case on die matron’s side of the house as a proof that she has been overlooking her 
duty. This dormitory is one which peculiarly demands her watchfulness. The boy should not 
have been there, hut in the infirmary ; but as she permitted him to remain with a female rela- 
tive, and had daily opportunities of seeing him, it is evident that she was not sufficiently alive 
to the unfortunate state in which I found him, and in which he had been for some time. In 
•going through the several adult male and females, and boys and girls’ dormitories, I found the 
greater number occupied with persons who were sick, and others who were not, and who had not 
recentfy been. In all, 73 were in them, without any attention to classification; even boys of 
13 were in wards where girls slept. All those 73 were on sick diets, many, I suspect, who were 
not ill. Iq one ward a girl, ill of fever, was in bed with several others ; and in another, in 
•which women and girls ^pt, a boy of 1 5 was in bed, whom the master, four days before, desired 
to have removed to the infirmary. The boys were ill of fever. 

Under these circtimstances, and with a medical man evidently incapable of comprehending 
nny suggestioiB I might be disposed to offer, I thought it right to communicate witli the Board 
of Guardians. I annex a copy of my letter, and from the clerk’s to me. 

The amount of serious epidemic disease in this house is not considerable, and there is nothing 
in the site or sewerage to affect the health of the innmtes, or to render its sanitary condition 
bad. Defective superintendence appears to be the chief circun>stance to be complained of. I 
•will do the master the justice to observe of him that be appears anxious to regain character, 
which he dearly saw be had lost by the exposure bef(»e me, but I must look on him, and espe- 
cially on the matron, to have been very ne^igenL 

I am not aware if there be any qualified medical man residing in Low'therstown, who, in Dr. 
Beatty’s absence (who only left the day before my inspection), would take chaise of the house; 
hut I met a Dr. Nagle there, the gentleman that attended the Bantry workhouse after I in- 
spected it. He is now acting under the Board of Health in the Lowtherstown district. Possibly 
his services may be engaged for such time as the restoration of the medical officer’s health may 

require. oiin 

The admissions into the bouse since the 29th of September last, have amounted to 2110; 
the deaths to 432, or 20J per cent. The house diertary is defective, as no supper is given to 
any class, even to boys and girls under nine. The girls’ dietary, as marked, appears pretty 
£iir, hut I am informed that the ordinary drinks of me fever cases is butternulk, on which boil- 
ing water has been poured. 

Until a competent medical officer takes a charge of the sick, I fear that no beneficial change 
ts like to take place. Such a person could at once remedy many of the defects I allude lo.

Protest of late Guardians. 

We the members of the late Board of Guardians of tlie Lowtherstown Union, dissolved 
bv YOU in Aercise of the power vested in you by the Act 10 Vic., cap. 31, feel ourselves called 
upon to take notice of the arbitrary proceedings adopted by you towards tins Boai-d. 

First, with respect to the late increase in the Protestant and Homan Catholic chaplains sala- 
ries ■ aAin, in the dismissal of the master of the workhouse ; and, lastly, in tho dissolving of our 
Boal-d in a time of great distress. The Roman Catholic chaplain’s salary was raised by you 
without any reference to the Board as to the necessity of so doing. A resolution was passed 
by us deprecating such a proceeding. In the face of this resolution, you immediately increased 
the Protestant chaplain’s salary. You were communicated with on the last increase ; to that 
communication you did not deign to reply. On a report of one of your Assistant Commis- 
sioners, Dr. Phelan, without any reference to the Board, and without any investigation, you 
dismissed the master. Our Board remonstrated; of such remonstrance you_ took no notice. 
The conduct pursued by you on both these occasions may be legal, but certainly was neither 
courteous nor marked by that deference which, in our opinion, should be paid by Poor Law 
Commissioners to a Board of Guardians composed of the persons most deeply interested in the 
welhbeing of the Union. 

As to the dissolving of our Board, your assistant, Mr. Barron, has explained that you were 
coerced to do so by instructions received from the Lords of the Treasury as to payinent of 
advances under the Temporary Relief Act; but as the letter accompanying the dismissal, we 
must express our unanimous opinion that you have exceeded your duty, by presuming to wiite 
to any Board of Guardians your opinion of what moral obligations, and of what honesty or dis- 
honesty may consist in, and in doing so may have taken advantage of your official position to 
use language to a public Board which, in a private capacity, you dare not use to them as 
private individuals. 

Our Board are willing to leave to public opinion on which side the honesty or dishonesty 
may be — our offering to pay the advances in six half-yearly instalments, or the Government 
demanding it in one.

Mr. Lucas, Vice-Guardian, to tlie Poor Law Commissioners. 

Loxoiherstown, November 13, 1847- 

In accordance with the instructions contained in your letter of the 
1 1th inst., I beg leave to submit to your consideration the following observations 
relative to the general state of the LoYrtherstown Union, at the period when the 
administration of its affairs first devolved on Mr. Hopper and myself, and also 
on the condition of the Union at the present time. 

The attention of myself and colleague was first directed to the financial con- 
dition of the Union. We found that a debt of about 1200?. had been suffered to 
accumulate, while the necessary efforts had not been made to obtain the sums 
remaining uncollected. For example, the books of the collector who had 
undertaken to collect the first rate, struck 2nd April, 1 845, had not been closed ; 
that, in fact, there remained a balance unaccounted for, and in the payment of 
wMch we deemed it necessary to serve notice on the collector of our intention 
to take legal measures, if after the interval of time named in the notice the 
balance ^ould remain unpaid. This proved effectual, for the collector ulti- 
mately paid to the treasurer the amount of the balance due. 

With respect to the rates struck 3rd February, 1847, and then payable, we 
found that there remained a large arrear uncollected, and notwithstanding that 
directions were given to the collectors to use all possible efforts to collect the 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. Ill 

amounts due, on]7 a small portion Tras obtained, and in order to avoid delay in 
procuring funds, the remainder was added to the rates last struck, as arrears 
leviable I'rom the respective parties. It further appeared that much delay had 
arisen in the collection of the rates, from the collectors having called at the 
express orders of tire Board of Guardians, on the occupiers of tenements valued 
at and under Al., for payment of the rates, notwithstanding that the immediate 
lessors (the parties primarily liable under the Irish Poor Law Amendment Act), 
were resident within the Union. 

It may be necessary to add that the Union had ceased to possess any credit 
with its treasurer (the Ulster Bank), the cheques drawn by the late Board of 
Guardians having remained uncashed for a considerable time, and it was only 
on representations made by myself that the treasurer was induced to make fur- 
ther advances. 

As to the management of the workhouse, I beg to state that it would appear 
that the Board of Guardians had not exercised any of their functions in that 
respect. It would appear that a Visiting Committee had never been appointed, 
or, if appointed, had never acted, as the Visiting Committee’s Report Book did 
not on our arrival contain a single report of any insjjection having been made. 
The result of this neglect was but too plainly apparent in the dirty condition of 
the house, and the utter squalor and listle^ idleness of the whole of the inmates. 
On making our first inspection of the workhouse our attention was arrested by 
the very attenuated appearance of the inmates, especially the children, whose 
sunken cheeks and lustreless eyes plainly exhibited the exhaustion of the 
system. My colleague having been aware (officially) that fever had been pre- 
valent in Lowtherstown, inquired of the medical officer whether the children 
in the workhouse had become debilitated by that disease, to which he received 
the reply that the children had suffered piincipally from dysentery, the result of 
want, and of improper food ; in explanation he added, that his representations 
as to the necessity of an amended dietary had been disregarded, and the chil- 
dren could not be expected to be in good health unless they had sufficient 
food. 

The schools were no exception to the general inefficiency of the establish- 
ment, only two or three children in either school were able to read words of 
one syllable, which seemed to be the highest amount of knowledge obtained ; 
the larger portion of them barely knew the letters of the alphabet, and not 
one of them could write. The explanation offered by the teachers for this 
want of progress was that the Guardians had never furnished them with the 
necessary hooks. 

In explaining to the teachers that they would be expected to use every effort 
to teach the cliildren to read and write, the schoolmaster said that he would 
try, but “he was no great hand at writing ” on further examination it was 
proved that the schoolmaster possessed neither the kaowledge nor the mere 
physical ability necessary to his efficiency in the office he held. It appeared 
that the schoolmeister’s father had held office in the workhouse and had died 
therein, and the son had been elected by the Guardians from motives of cha- 
rity ; previous to his election he had been a gai’deiier, but in consequence of 
illness he was no longer able to do work as such. 

With regard to the books required by your order to be kept by the work- 
house-master, it was found that neither the clothing-books, the relief-lists, nor 
the inventory-book had been kept, and the register of paupers was incorrect. 
The result of this irregularity w’as that the stores had nearly all disappeared, 
and as no inventory appears to have been taken when the late master entered 
on his duties, it is difficult to say how far he w'as blameable for the deficiencies ; 
he had not been required to enter into any security for the due and faithful 
performance of his duties. I cannot say I had any confidence in him, as I 
found that he had kept several (four or five) of his children in the workhouse 
witli liim, I presume unsanctioned by the Guardians ; however that may be, it 
is next to certain, that illegal expense was thereby incurred by the Union, or in- 
justice done to the inmates of the workhouse, in the malappropriation of their food. 

I have also to remark that after his removal it was discovered that he had 
left behind liim one of his children, who was removed from the workhouse 
only after notice had been sent to Mr. Walsh of our intention to prosecute him 
for the desertion of his child.

243 paupers in the workhouse, and but 15 in the infirmary ; while the deaths 
have diminished from 10 in the former week to two in the latter. 

The children are quite changed in their appearance. Swings have been

Captain Wynne, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners: — 
November ^0, 1847- 

I HAVE the honour to state, for the information of the Commissioners, 
that, previously to recommending their sanction of the appointment of Messrs. 
Lynch and Peyton as collectors of poor rates, I considered it advisable to have 
an interview with those gentlemen, in order that I might clearly point out that 
course which it would be indispensable that they should adopt and pursue if 
they hoped to be continued in office, and to recommend them strongly not to 
proceed further towards perfecting their bonds, unless they were fully deter- 
mined to pursue that course steadily, perseveringly, and uncompromisingly. 

I have accordingly, in presence of the Board of Guardians, stated to them, 
that the rates must be collected on any terms, at any risk, and notwith- 
standing any difficulties or obstacles that may be thrown in the way. That 
they must put in force those powers with which the Act provides them, against 
all defaulters, irrespective of the rank or position of the parties, or of any other 
circumstance whatsoever. That it would be necessary at all times to be able to 
show that each rate-payer’s liability was paid in, or that some one of the 
remedies provided by the Acts was in progress against the defaulter, and that 
no excuse would be received for delays in collecting, Ijeyond what could he 
shown to be unavoidable from the nature of the case. That I should be pre- 
pared at all times to assist them with my advice, in case of difficulties arising, 
and by my personal attendance, whenever and wherever such might be likely to 
facilitate the execution of their duties. 

They have undertaken the office on these conditions, and I have reason to 
think are determined to use their best exertions. I also think them competent, 
and may therefore recommend the sanction of their appointment by the Com- 
missioners. 



Captain Wynne, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Cosimissioners : — 
November 27, 1847. 

This week my time has been entirely occupied between visiting the 
workhouse and such portions of the Union as I was enabled to reach ; in doing 
which I took occasion to call on such persons as I considered possessed local 
influence, explaining to them that the rates were now the sole source to which 
they could look for the relief of the multitudes of destitute, at present crowding 
the roads in every direction, and soliciting their countenance and support on 
behalf of the collectors. 

In most cases I received rather encouraging promises. 

I also availed myself of these opportunities of visiting the several schools 
situated in the localities through which I passed, and of obtaining such informa- 
tion as is required by the British Relief Association, to whom I this day for- 
warded a report. 

With respect to the workhouse, its condition would be highly discreditable 
to the master and the other officers immediately connected wi^ its manage- 
ment, but that almost all the requisites for keeping it in proper order are want- 
ing, and have been frequently applied for to the Guardians in vain. 

It is necessary to have three breakfasts and as many dinners, per day, in 
consequence of there being only one-third of the tins required, even for the com- 
paratively small number at present in the house. 

The urine-tubs are out of order, and ffist going to pieces, and cause great inr 
convenience. 

The rain comes in, in various directions ; and the pipes and cocks are so 
much out of order that the boilers overflow on a wet day, producing great incon- 
venience and disorder. 

In the grounds there is a field for the employment fully aud advan- 
tageously, of such of the paupers as are able to work, for a very long period, 
but no implements. _ 

The master is not, in my opinion, a man of orderly habits, but he seems 
zealous and anxious to improve ; and, certainly, he has not had a fair trial 
heretofore. 

I this day called the attention of the Guardians to the necessity that exists 
for immediately supplying implements for the execution of a w’ork, the further

Eeo-lect of which seriously threatens the health of the house. I allude to the

The Guardians plead want of funds ; and such is the state of their credit,

Boohs are also required; more than half the children being obliged to sit

particularly Mr. Lynch, who has advanced this day 100/., which he is to repay 
himself, and which will enable us to go on for some time. 

I understand the ex-collectors are using their influence to get up a systematic 
opposition ; and one is giving receipts for arrears from an old receipt-book, 
which he retained in his possession at the time of his dismissal. This man’s 
sureties are not to be found. 

We have posted notices that all future receipts will require the initials of the 
clerk ; but if he (the collector) ante-dates, we have no remedy but by a com- 
parison with his arrear sheets, which have been already found to be incorrect. 
I have had the attention of the police directed to this man. 

I anticipate very great pressure on the house the moment it is opened, wliich 
at present it cannot be said to be. In fact, the Poor Laws cannot be said to be 
in operation in this Union. 

There are now wandering about the Union about 1600 persons, most of whom 
have given up their houses and land, and are only waiting for admittance to the 
house, and indeed they appear fit and legitimate objects. The niimljers are 
stated to me much higher ; but in my calculation there arc no able-bodied, or 
any persons on whom the workhouse test would he likely to operate. 

We were enabled to admit a large number to-day, as will appear from the 
Minutes. 

Much inconvenience will arise from want of clothing for the adults. 

In conclusion, I must say the chairman appeared willing to adopt every 
suggestion of mine; nor was there any opposition on the part of the Guardians 
assembled this day. 

Several small bills were paid and credit considerably re-established, and pro- 
vision made for the wants of the ensuing week. 

Tradesmen were also directed to furnish estimates on Saturday next for the 
necessary repairs to be done to the house ; and implements have been ordered 
to employ the paupers to a certain extent. 

On the whole, I feel satisfied with the day’s proceedings. 



Captain Wynne, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 
NoveijAer SO, 1847. 

On my arrival here this day, I found that the arrangements of last 
Saturday had been upset by the resignation of the Messrs. Peyton and Lynch. 

As stated in my report of Saturday, the latter gentleman had advanced lOO/. 
to the Guardians, which enabled them to admit a large number of paupers to 
the workhouse, also to give checks, in liquidation of several small and urgent 
demands, and to provide for the workhouse expenditure for the current and 
ensuing weeks. 

In consequence of the murder of the late Rev. Mr. Lloyd (who was one of 
Mr. Lynch’s sureties), and the general alarm which the event has produced, he 
(Mr. Lynch) determined on declining entering further on the duties of his office, 
and early on Monday drew the money, which the treasurer unfortunately 
refused to enter to the account of the Guardians, it being, at the time of 
Mr. Lynch’s calling on Saturday, past banking hour. 

The consequence was that the Guardians’ checks were dishonoured on 
Monday, when presented for payment. 

This trar^action (I need scarcely add) has placed the workhouse establish- 
ment_ in a position of great difficulty, as on examination this day, I find there 
remains scarcely provision for three days’ consumption in the house, and by this 
last transaction the credit of the Guardians is in a worse position than before. 

With respect to the election of future collector, I think it right to state, that

from my own observation, and from the inq^uiries I have been able to make, I 
entertain no liopes of the Guardians being able to find, in the locality, men who 
will undertake the office on the conditions on which alone reasonable liopes of 
success might be entertained. I am still of opinion that the selection of 
Mr. Lynch was a good one, perhaps the best that could be made by the 
Guardians from amongst the candidates, as he possessed many local advantages 
over the others, and would have fewer difficulties to contend with, than perhaps 
any man in the Union ; but the last sad and atrocious murder has completely 
decided him and all others whose lot is permanently cast in this country, and 
on whom vengeance would undoubtedly fall at some future period, if not 
immediately. 

Under these circumstances, I would beg to suggest that four resolute men 
should be sent down from Dublin as collectors, and that I should receive the 
Commission of the Peace for Leitrim and Roscommon, to enable me to afford 
protection to them in vigorously carrying out the law'. 

It need not be expected that the local magistrates, who must continue to 
reside in this country, will act with that vigour which will be essential to 
success. 

The delay wdiich has already occurred from the resignation of the collectors 
has placed the establishment in a position from which I know not how to 
extricate it ; and therefore if the notice required previously to election could 
be dispensed with, little delay need take place, as the books are ready to place 
in the hands of any new ones that may be appointed. 

I have reason to believe that no opposition will be given to the election of 
any persons the Commissioners may send down. 

I am already aware that this proposal is open to the objection that it would 
take a portion of the responsibility off the Guardians, w'hich ought to be 
avoided as long as possible ; but I see no other course which promises suc- 
cess, and I shall become answ erable for the collection of the rates if it be 
adopted.

Captain Wynne to the Poor Law Commissioners : — December 2, 1847-

they had declined to enter on their duties (as stated in Mr. Clarke’s letter ot

I find Mr. Lynch has positively declined acting in the present state of the 
country, and has formally resigned, stating as his reason that, from all he has 
been able to learn in reference to his prospects of success, he would not be 
able to collect the rates, and that his personal safety would be seriously 

endangered. . , , . • i 

With respect to Mr. Peyton, he has also resigned, but expre^es anxiety to be 
allow'ed to retain office, but under such a relaxation of the original conations 
on which he accepted it as would render his acceptance far from degrable.

Mohill Union : — State of the Union, and Dissolution of the Board of Guardians. 

MohUi Union. Major Haliday, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 

November 5, 1847 * 

I HAVE the honour to report, for your information, that, in accordance 
with your order appointing me a temporary Poor Law Inspector for the 
Union of Mohill, I attended the regular meeting of the Board of Guardians 
at the workhouse of Mohill yesterday the 4th instant. 

Mr. Flanagan, the ordinary Inspector for the distnet, having been present, 
and having called the attention of the Board to the several instructions and 
orders recently issued with respect to the necessary preparation for out-door 
relief, and to the more effectual examination of the collectors’ accounts and 
rate-books ; I should not have thought it necessary to make any report, had Iris 
engagements permitted Iiim to do so ; as my want of experience, as yet in this 
service, and the short time I have been here, must render my information 
meagre and of little value. But as he is otherwise occupied, and your instruc- 
tions require a report, I shall present in a brief form my impression of the state 
of the Union. 

On Wednesday, the 3rd instant, following my arrival here, I visited and 
examined every part of the Mohill Union workhouse; and, in that visit, 
gathered more information then from the proceedings of the Board which was 
attended by but three of the lective Guardians, and two of the ex officios, (the 
chairman and Mr. Godley,) out of the whole number. 

It appears that the Union is in debt to the amount of 2500/., of which sum 
1200/. is due to the late contractor, who supplied the house with provisions 
during the past 12 months; that he has ceased to supply them, and that their 
credit is so low, that no one will now tender to do so. And, consequently, that 
for the last few weeks the inmates have been subsisted solely by the master, 
who purchases, from time to time, sufficient oatmeal and Indian meal to give 
the paupers daily two meals of porridge, which is the only food used, with the 
exception of a very small quantity of bread allowed for the hospital. 

The latter is nearly full of cases of fever and dysentery, the latter being 
especially prevalent among the children. 

The house is in a very lapidated condition. In the kitchen only one boiler 
is seiwiceable, and all the dormitories, day-rooms, school-rooms, and wards, are 
open to the weather, through a number of large square holes broken through 
Idle walls during the time that the house was ravaged by fever. No provision 
has been made for repairing these or inserting windows, and much of the gln ss 
IS broken. 

The school-rooms ai'e nearly useless, from cold, and from the absolute want 
of ordinary requisites; the schoolmaster has not even ink to write his report 
Tnth, and there is neither paper, pens, nor even printed letters to teach the 
alphabet, the substitute for the latter being one or two sheets torn out of a 
spelling-book ; the children look wretched and unhealthy. 

All the pumps being choked or useless, the paupers are necessarily em- 
ployed, several hours each day, in carrying water from a well in the public 
street near the workhouse, and from this cause, as well as the easy egress per- 
nutted.by the open holes in the room walls, and the lowness of the enclosure 
walls, it is manifestly impossible td maintaiia the proper discipline, — the sepa- 
ration of the sexes, or the confinement required by the rules for the manage- 
ment of workhouses.

AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 117 

The house may justly he designated as little better than a large shed, and it 
is liable to be absolutely closed any week, upon even a trifling diminution in 
the ammmt of rates now obtained weekly by the collector and paid into the 
treasurer. 

With respect to the rates, I find that there is an arrear of about 1600/. out- 
standmg of the rate struck previous to the last one of 3j. in the pound, which 
has been approved of by the Poor Law Commissioners ; and that of this the 
collector has hitherto been recovering only from 30/. to 40/. weekly, wdiich 
is barely sufficient to defray the current expenses of the house ; that of the 
new rate not a shilling has been yet obtained, nor are the rate-books even made 
up, these last having been delayed by the revision of the valuation of the 
Union, which is now in progress, and will not be completed before the end of 
this month ; that the two newly appointed collectors ha\*e therefore at present 
no power to proceed. 

Two relieving officers have been appointed, but no districts have yet been 
assigned to them, nor do they appear to exercise any functions. 

I cannot report that any effective measures were agreed upon, or even 
proposed by the Board yesterday, either to expedite the collection of the rates, 
or to provide for the contingency of out-door relief, or extend the accommoda- 
tion of the w'orkhouse, or repair the present defects. Indeed, as to all these 
atter points, several of the Guardians expressed their opinion that it was use- 
less to thiuk of them, when they might be shortly unable even to kecj) the 
house open, as it is now ; and out of a crowd of 40 or 50 applicants for admis- 
sion, then at the gate, they merely authorized the master to admit 15 of those 
whose cases appeared most urgent, the rest not being even inquired into. 

Although the admissions thus given increases the inmates to 700 (the number 
for which the workhouse was calculated), yet the greater proportion of these 
being women and children, there still remain in the house, unoccupied, two 
dormitories, which are reserved to meet the application of able-bodied men ; 
but from what I have already observed and heard of the condition of the j)oor, 
and the absence of any apparent prospect of employment being afforded during 
the winter, I am constrained to express my apprehension that there must be, 
ere long, a rush of applicants for relief on any terais, for which the Guardians 
are totally unprepared ; and that far from being able to maintain the shelter of 
the workhouse as a test for the able-bodied, they may be compelled to close it 
against even the classes they are at present imperatively bound to relieve. 

As the Guardians meet but one day in the week, and it is, I understand, often 
very difficult on those days to get together a sufficient number to form a Board, 
I feel at x>resent unable to devise any adequate means of impressing upon 
them the gravity of the present conjimction, and the urgent necessity for imme- 
diate exertion. 

On Wednesday next I shall meet the collector, and examine his books (he 
did not attend at all the last one), as he is at present occupied daily in the 
endeavour to recover the arrears of rate; and I may be enabled by Thursday, 
the Board day, to form a more mature opinion as to the possibility of carrying 
out the requirements of the law and your instructions through the instrumen- 
tality of the present Guardians.

tricts have yet been assigned to them, nor do they appear to exercise any 
function. The Commissioners do not find that any effective measures were 
agreed upon at the last meeting of the Guardians cither to expedite tlic collec- 
tion of the rates, or to provide for the contingency of out-door relief, or extend 
the accommodation of the workhouse, although Major Holiday rejxorts that 
out of a body of 40 or 50 applicants for admission then at the gate, the Guar- 
dians merely authorized the master to admit 15 of those whose cases appeared 
most urgent, the rest not being even inquired into. 

It seems that although the admission thus given, increased the inmates to 700 
(the number for which the workhouse was originally calculated) yet the greater 
proportion of these being women and children, there still remain in the house, 
unoccupied, two dormitories, which are reserved to meet the applications of 
able-bodied men, but from what he has already observed and heard of the 
condition of the poor, and the absence of any apparent prospect of employment 
l^iug afforded during the winter. Major Haliday expresses his apprehension, 
that there must be ere long a rush ol‘ applicants for relief on any terms, for 
which the Guardians are totally unprepared, and that far from being able to 
maintain the shelter of the workhouse as a test for the able-bodied, they may be 
compelled to close it against even the classes they are at present imperatively 
bound to relieve. 

Under these circumstances the Commissioners feel it necessary to request the 
most serious attention of the Board of Guardians to the state of things existing 
in Mohill Union, and desire to impress on them the importance of remedying 
the defects above represented, and of urging forward the collection of the rates 
by all the means in their power. 

The Commissionei^ request that the Guardians will forthwith require the 
collectors to proceed vigorously in the immediate collection of the outstanding 
arrears of the last rate, and to exercise all the powers -with which they are 
invested for this purpose.

Major Haliday to the Poor Law Commissioners : — November 12, 1847. 

I HAVE the honour to submit, for your information, the following report 
on the state of the Moliill Union, at the workhouse of which I yesterday 
attended the "weekly meeting of the Board of Guardians. 

It was with much difficulty, and only by the exertions of the master seeking 
for and inducing three of the Guardians to attend, that a quorum could be 
formed; and, but for this, the ordinary machinery for keeping open the house 
must have been stopped, as the master would not have had the means of pro- 
curing food for the inmates during the ensuing week. 

As none of the three Guardians present were accustomed to transacting the 
business of the Union (though all of them apparently persons of excellent inten- 
tions), the proceedings were confined to the mere routme necessary to authenti- 
cate the various books and accounts, to sanction the petty ^bursements of the 
past week, and furnish the master with the means of keeping the house open 
for another, and to receiving various applications and notices of intended legal 
proceedings against the Board for recovery of monies d.ue by them ; and I found 
it useless to attempt to impress upon them the import^t consideration sugges^ 
in your recent circulars, and your instructions respecting the duties of relieving 
officers, for carrying out of which they are absolutely destitute of funds.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Major Haliday:— 17, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, to acknowdedge the receipt of your reports of 1 1th 
and 12th instant, relating to Mohill Union. 

In regard to the small attendance of Guardians, and the difficulty of pro- 
curing the presence of a sufficient number to constitute a Board, I am to state 
that the Commissioners have directed a circular to be addressed to each mem- 
ber of the Board of Guardians, calling the attention of the Guardians to the 
state of the Union, and urging their attendance for the due performance of the 
duties of their office. A copy of the circular is enclosed herewith for your 
information. 

With respect to the collection of the rates, the Commissioners W'ish, in refer- 
ence to those cases in which arrears are due of rates upon properties for which 
receivers, &c., have been appointed under the Courts, that the attention of the 
Guardians and the collectors should lie called to the two circulars dated 
respectively 3rd December, 1845, and 15th June, 1846, (copies of which were 
sent to the Guardians at the time, and are herewith enclosed,) containing orders 
of the Courts of Chancery and Exchequer for payment of the poor rate in such 
cases, by the receiver, guardian, committee, or sequestrator, without further 
rule or order in that behalf, w'here such rates are due from the landlord ; and 
if after application to the receiver, whose notice should be specially drawn to 
the orders above referred to, the rate be not paid, it may be necessary that a 
special application should be made to the Court to enforce payment of the 
rate due. 

In regard to the case of the widow of an occupying tenant, now deceased, on 
whom the rate was originally made, I am to state that under section 71 of 
1st and 2nd Victoria, c. 56, the rate may, in all cases of default of payment by 
the person in occupation at the time the rate was made, be recovered from the 
person subsequently in occupation, by all the same ways and means as it might 
have been recovered from the person originally rated, if he had continued in 
occupation of the premises for which he w'as rated ; the magistrate is equally 
bound to issue a summons in the one case as in the other, and the collector may 
equally proceed on his own warrant in both cases. 

It appears to be of great importance that the revision of the valuation should 
be completed with the least possible delay ; and the Commissioners request 
that you will endeavour by every practicable means, to have this complete at 
the earliest possible periods, so that a new rate may then be made. 

Meanwhile the necessary estimates of the sums required to be levied may be 
prepared, so as to be in readiness for striking the rate as soon as practicable, 
and the rate can be made on any division, as soon as the valuation of such 
division is completed, and so from time to time, until a rate on the whole 
Union is completed.

Major Haliday, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners: — 
November 18, 1847. 

I HAVE the honour to submit to you the following report upon the state 
of this Union:— 

1 . The pressure of extreme want is making itself more visible in the emaciated 
appearance of the women and children who may be seen in the country roads, 
and of the applicants for admission (in increasing numbers) to the miserable 
workhouse. 

The Guardians having now come to the resolution not to admit any more at 
presen^ and possessing no funds to obtain additional accommodation or to enable 
the relieving officers to administer aid in food or money, the latter can no longer 
perform their duty, as directed in Article 7 of the General Order issued on the 
7th of August last, in any case of destitution, however urgent ; and the law is 
practically suspended, except within the walls of the workhouse, and in behalf 
of its present inmates. 

2. Fever is extremely prevalent in many districts of the Union, and so dis- 
heartened or reckless are the people, that I have been informed of a case where, 
within the last fortnight, the body of a woman who died of that disease was left 
in a ditch with merely some straw thrown over it, where the effluvia from the 
progress of decay attracted attention, and the collector of poor-rate, near whose 
residence it was found, was obliged to hire men to dig a hole to cover it. 

3. I attended this day the meeting of the Board of Guardians, where there 
was some delay and difficulty in getting together a quorum, your circular letter 
to the Guardians on the subject of attendance not having yet had time to produce 
effect. 

I did not fail to call the attention of the Board to the condition of the house, 
which continues in the same dilapidated state (and for the repairs of which no 
tenders wliatever have been put in) ; and more especially to the revolting state 
of filth in the yards adjoining and in rear of the hospital in consequence of the 
privies and cesspools being quite full and choked. • The master was directed to 
inquire for and if possible employ a person who had emptied them two or three 
years before ; but the Board, having no funds, were unable to take any steps for 
the repair of the house. 

I also brought again to their notice the highly alarming state of the Union, 
in consequence of this want of means, and the extreme importance of accelerating 
the collection of the rate. The collector was called before the Board and dis- 
tinctly informed that he must enforce it by every means in his power against all 
parties whatever. A list of immediate lessors, by whom such arrears were due, 
which had been at my desire prepared by the collector, was laid before the 
Board. 

The solicitor to the Board was also called, and desired to follow up the legal 
steps against such absentee lessors, whose agents have all been written to by him 
without effect, and also to apply to the respective Courts for special orders to 
those agents and receivers of rents under them who have not paid the arrears, 
and who have also been ^vritten to in vain. I had called the notice of the Board 
to the fact that their solicitor was himself a defaulter to a considerable amount 
both as an immediate lessor and as agent for several other parties, and it was 
stated that he would pay those amounts. 

The valuator was also called in, but it appeared that he has, as yet, completed 
but seven of the electoral divisions, and three others in part ; that he dud not 
expect to complete the whole before the end of the year. He was ordered to 
use all possible expedition, and the clerk was direct^ meantime to fill up the 
rate-books of the divisions now completed. 

As the balance remaining in the treasurer’s and collector’s hands, after 
paying certain small outstanding cheques, did not appear sufficient to defray 
tlie cost of subsistence for the present inmates of the house until tlie next Board 



Mobill Uoloa 



Page 9.

Mohill Union, the master was furnished with all the available funds to purchase food, and 

it was resolved meantime to advertise for contractors to supi^ly the house from 
week to week, to be paid out of the rates collected weekly ; and the Board also 
directed the master to reduce the ration of food to each of the inmates, and not 
to admit any more. About 50 applicants were at the gates, but only three 
orphan children sent in from a great distance, who it appeared but too probable 
must otherwise starve, were taken into the house. 

Although the Guardians, who formed the Board this day, appear thus to have 
done all that was possible for them in theii- collective capacity, it is evident that, 
in the present crisis, starvation to a lamentable extent may ensue. An extra- 
ordinary meeting of tlie Board is to be called, before the funds in the master’s 
hands are quite exhausted, and on the collection of the next few days depends the 
possibility ofmainbuning the inmates of the workhouse. 

With respect to the collection of rates,, I was present at the examination of the 
collector’s books, by the clerk yesterday, and continued my scrutiny into, the 
progress of the collection, I regret to say, with a less favourable result than. I had' 
hoped for. In two of tlie electoral divisions, where there is a heavy arrear, I find 
that the townlands are subdivided into very numerous small lote, the greater- 
number of the occupants of which, it appears from the collector’s- notes, are 
reduced to extreme poverty. In many tenements there' are only, women andi 
children whose husbands and fathers have left this country ; and among the. 
remainder, a general combination to resist payment defeats nearly all the colIectoi’’s 
efforts. Even those who have already been compelled to pay^ assist the- others' to 
evade it, by storing their crops' in their own Iiaggards, and some seizures that he 
has made are yet ineffectual, as he cannot hire a car to carry, away the distress, 
nor will any one, he avers,, risk employment in such service. Sufficient detei> 
mination may overcome some of these obstructions,, but it seems in vain to expect 
successful recovei-y of rates- in general, until such' occupiers be removed. It will 
be observed, that the total amount collected within the past week has been but. 
about 33Z. I caiuiot help adding that, although the orders of the Board of 
Guardians were, on this occasion, very explicit, I do not believe they will prove' 
effectuiil ; nor that the rates will be enforced with the requisite degree of vigour' 
and expedition, until both attorney and collectors be found who are totally 
unconnected with the country, and inaccessible to the numerous local influences 
and connexions of the neighbourhood. 

One of the relieving officers, lately appointed, sent in this day his resignation. 
No reason was assigned, but I conclude it was from finding that the office was in 
reality a mockery, and the duties impossible, without funds or. power of admission 
to the workhouse. 

It is scarcely necessary to add that no steps have been taken, nor, under the 
present circumstances, are likely to be thought of, for obtaining additional accom- 
modation, or making any provision whatever for out-door relief.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Mr. Redinqton : — November 23, 1847. 

I HAVE the honour to transmit, by direction of the Commissiouers for 
aiimiuistering tiie Lau's for Relief of the Poor in Irelaud, for the information of 
his Excellency the Lord Lieutenant, the accompanying copy of a report, which Page 133. 
the Commissioners have received from Major Haiiday, Temporary Inspector, 
relating to Mohill Union. 

From this report it appears that destitution prevails to a great extent in this 
Union, and shows every symptom of increasing ; that the Guardians have ordered 
the daily allowance of tlie inmates of the workhouse to be reduced, and no further 
admissions to be allowed ; that out of 50 applicants only three orphan children, 
sent from a great distance, and who, it appeared, would otherwise starve, were 
admitted into the workhouse, the rest being refused on account of the ini[>overished 
state of the finances of the Union ; the balance remaining to the credit of the 
Guardians not being sufficient to maintain the house for the ensuing %veek. 

Major Haiiday also reports that fever is prevalent in the Union, and that 
recklessness on the part of the peojxle as to the interment of those who die, 
exists to a great extent ; the body of a woman who died of fever having been 
left in a ditch with merely some straw to cover it. 

Major Haiiday states that one relieving officer has resigiied, giving no

Major Haliday states that he called the Guardians’ attention more especially 
to the revolting state of filth in the yards adjoining and in the rear of the 
hospital, in consequence of the privies and cesspools being quite full and 
clicked, and that the master was directed by the Guardians to inquire for, and 
if possible, to employ a person to empty them who had done so two or three 
years before ; but that the Board having no funds were unable to take -any 
steps for the repair of the house. 

The Commissioners have addressed a communication to Major Haliday, in 
reply to his report, in which they have stated that, lamentable as the condition 
of the destitute poor in the Union undoubtedly is, they are determined not to 
make any application to Government for pecuniary assistance to tlie Guardians 
to meet their current expenses for relief; that they were desirous that it 
should be generally understood in the Union that the responsibility of any 
deaths from starvation, if any such should unfortunately occur, would rest with 
the Guardians and the rate-payers, and that the poor-rates were the funds to 
which the destitute poor must look for relief. 

The Commissioners stated at the same time, however, that in consequence 
of the deplorable state of the workhouse, and as a mere matter of sanatory pre- 
caution, in order to prevent its becoming the centre of pestilence to the 
surrounding district, they had applied to his Excellency for a loan to the 
Guardians of 150/., in order that some of the most serious defects and evils 
pointed out in his report may be remedied. 

The Commissioners accordingly desire to submit the circumstances for the 
consideration of his Excellency the Lord Lieutenant, and to request that his 
Excellency be pleased to authorise a loan of 150/. being granted to the 
Guardians for the purpose referred to. I am at the same time to state, that if 
his Excellency shall be pleased to direct that the sum of 150/. be advanced to 
the Guardians, the Commisssioners will endeavour to have the loan repaid at 
the earliest possible period.

Mr. Deane, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 
November 2, 1847. 

I attended yesterday for the first time the weekly meeting of the Board 
of Guardians of this Union, which was held in. the court house of the town of 
Clifden, the members of that body having, for some time, discontinued their 
meetings at the workhouse, owing to the prevalence of fever therein. 

There was a full attendance of the elected Guardians at the Board, and I took 
occasion, in the first instance, to impress on the members present, the absolute 
importance and necessity of proceeding to the immediate collection of the 
rates. 

I explained to the collectors the nature of their duties, and urged them to 
the prompt and vigorous execution of the same. Of the four collectors, but 
two have as yet received the general warrants and rate-books for the collection 
of the recent rate. One collector is in fever, but, I understand, is in a fair 
way of recovering, and will be shortly able to resume his duties. The appoint- 
ment of relieving officers was yesterday postponed for a fortnight, the Guardians 
expressing a wish not to proceed to the election in the absence of the chairman, 
Mr. D’Arcy. I urged on them the importance of making their appointments 
w.ithout any further delay. 

The Guardians are beset -with applications from the dealers and tradesmen

of this town for the amount of their accounts for necessaries supplied to the 
workhouse. I find that there is but 19/. 9^. 2c?. in the hands of the treasurer of

The collectors have about 80/- unlodged, which they allege they find a

The Commissioners are aware that Galway is 50 miles distant from Clifden.

The Guardians are very desirous to ascertain whether the Commissioners

The debts due by the Guardians in the immediate neighbourhood, and in the 
town of Clifden, are about 260/. ; this sum is due among 40 creditors, who are 
taldng every advantage of the necessities of the Board, and are charging at an 
exorbitant rate for the goods they supply. 

I inspected the workhouse to-day. I regret to report that its internal state 
is in a very unsatisfactory condition. Fever is raging among its inmates, and, 
I fear, imtil accommodation be supplied for fever patients apart from the work- 
house, neither cleanliness, order, or regidarity, can be insured. As I have 
stated before, the Guardians do not meet at the workhouse, and the conduct of 
the establishment has not therefore been subject for some time past to that 
careful inspection so necessary for its proper management. 

I occupied myself, during a portion of this day, in driving about the electoral 
division of Clifden. I was accompanied by one of the Board of Guardians 
(Mr. Maher), an extremely intelligent person, w'ho was formerly in the Coast 
Guard service. I was enabled to obtain much local information from him. I 
regret to state, from the close observation of the extensive district I passed 
through, that the most abject poverty and distress appear to exist. 

But a very small amount of agriciiltural produce can be seen, and the reck- 
less improvidence of last year, in the non-cultivation of the land, is painfully 
observable, 

I hope, in a few days, to be enabled to furnish the Commissioners with a 
detailed report of my inspection of the state of the Union generally *, the short 
time that has elapsed since my arrival here has not permitted me to obtain 
much more information than I have now the honour to submit. 

I beg leave to accompany this report with a letter which I have received 
from the medical attendant of the workhouse in reference to the increase of 
fever therein.

Mr. Bodkin, Medical Officer of Workhouse, to Mr. Deane : — November % 1847. 

As the workhouse is now completely filled, there being over 300 paupers in it, and as 
there are forty-fire patients in the hospital just now labouring under typhus fever, I would 
most earnestly impress upon you the great and paramount necessity for providing a tempera^ 
fever hospital, in order that all those labouring under contagious disease may be entirely 
separated from those that are in health, and thereby, if possible, prevent the inevitable spre^ 
of contagion among a community so densely crowded together, numbers of whom, I apprehend, 
are predisposed to take the disease upon the slightest occasion, their constitutions being so 
roduetd, and their vital energies and spirits so much depressed, by starvation and wretched- 
ness.

The result of last week’s collection placed the Guardians in a position to

Letter from Dr. R. X Morgan to the Central Bo.\rd of Health, transmitted 
to the Poor Law Commissionei-s on November 10, 1847. 

Gentlemen, Clifden, November 3, 1847. 

I HAVE, according to your suggestion, laid before the Clifden Board of 
Guardians your letter to me, and the enclosed circular, relative to their sup- 
plying funds for the continuance of the Ballindoon Fever Hospital. 

Their first reply was, that their pecuniary embarrassments were such that 
they could not afford me any assistance. However, on my pressing them 
again and again, and assuring them that I myself would not trouble them for 
some time for my own salary, they reluctantly granted me a mere trifle, viz., 
5/. only, for an entire foiinight : that sum, I need scarcely remark, will go a 
very short way in meeting all expenses during that period; the number of 
patients must be very limited indeed, unless the Board will be so kind as to 
afford me an additional sum in the way of assistance. Allow me, gentlemen, 
to add, that the hospital is as much req^uired in this locality this very moment 
as it was three months ago, for fever is, in many places, even on the increase. 
Your reply, advice, and assistance in this matter would very much oblige 

Yours, &c., 

The Central Board of Health, Robert John Morgan, M.D. 

Dublin.

Mr. Deane, Temporary Inspector, to*1;he Poor Law Commissioners : — 
November 16, 1847. 

I attended the weekly meeting of the Board of Guardians yesterday. 
There was a full attendance, in consequence of the election for relieving 
oflScers having been definitely fixed for the 15th. 

I had to encounter every possible attempt by some of the Guardians to post- 
pone the appointment of these o£B.cers; but after much waste of time and useless 
discussion, I at last succeeded in forcing the election. 

Fifteen candidate sent in wiutten applications, and four were elected. 

The Guardians have consented in writing to borrow the sum of 200/. for the 
erection of a temporary fever hospital. Fever is extremely prevalent, and I 
iTOuld agairi respectfully state to the Commissioners that it is in vain for me to 
effect ^ything like permanent reform in the workhouse until separate accom- 
modation be provided for fever patients. 

There is a building (now almost in ruins) near the town, and which was built, 
as I understand, for a school, that might be converted into an hospital. The 
National Board of Education has, I believe, some control in reference to this 
building, and, with the permission of the Commissioners, I might seek informa- 
tion upon the subject from the secretaries. 

The immediate appointment of a local treasurer for the Union would be of 
me greatest importance, and I can recommend with safety that Dr. Suffield, of 
Clifden, should be entiusted with the duties of that office. He has consented 
to perform them, I believe, at some personal inconvenience. 

The last week’s collection, owing to two of the collectors being in fever, was 
unavoidably small. The Clifden collector is giving me much satisfaction in the 
discljarge of his duties. He collected 60/. 10#. during the week. I have felt it 
n^essi^y to state that the public service cannot be delayed much longer, and 
that other collectors must be appointed, should they not he enabled to resume 
their duties. 

The Roundstone collector is likely to be enabled to attend on Monday next, 
which day is ^ed for the purpose of signing the warrants for the new rate for 
the electoral divisions of Ballindon and Roundstone.

AND STATE OF THE UNIONS. IN IRELAND. 131 

Since my last report I have been constantly occupied in travelling through 
the Uniou, and my attention, during the past week, has been more particularly 
directed to the state of the schools in the district, owing to the communication I 
received from the Count Strzelecki, with respect to the relief about to be ex- 
tended to children, &c. 

Having felt it my duty to visit every school in the Uniou, I made a tour of 
inspection, and, it is with much regret, I inform the Commissioners that there 
exists the most lamentable and culpable neglect of education in this extensive 
district. In the electoral division of Renvyle, containing a population of over 
7000, 1 found hut two schools ; in one there were 47 scholars, male and female, 
in another, none on that day, and, as I was informed, the average attendance 
12 1 In Clifden electoral division, two of the schools are unoccupied, and the 
houses are in wretched repair. The schoolmaster of the Cluggan School 
is, and has been, receiving his salary for some time, for which he is giving no 
consideration, there being no scholars to teach. 

In another locality (Ballinafad), I went into the school-house, and at 12 
o’clock in the day, found no one at the school. In fact, save at Roundstone, 
where the monks have, by the benevolence of the Society of Friends, been 
enabled to feed the children at the school, I may say, that there is no regular 
attendance at any of the schools. ^ n . t i* i .-l i. 

The condition of the children is truly distressmg, but I feel that a great 
amount of injury will be effected in this Union, if gratuitous relief be given 
without getting some return, in labour, for it. I have written very fully to 
the Count Strzelecki on this subject, and I have strongly urged the value and 
importance of diverting auy available fund for the purpose of clothmg the 
children, into as many channels of industrial relief as practicable, and with tins 
view I have forwarded him a proposition for employing the people m maufa(> 
turin’o- frieze and flannel for the children that shall attend the schools. It would 
afford me much pleasure to put this plan into practical operation. 

That there is in some districts of the Union great distress, is beyond all doubt ; 
but I believe that the existing law’ for the relief of the poor will go far to meet 
it I shall be very slow to certify that the » extent of the distress really exceeds 
all the power of relief.” for I am satisfied that another season of gratuities 
would tiid to the worst results. Of the mischiefs it has effected, in this district, 
many can bear testimony to ; but at an investigation held before the magistrates 
on lit Saturday and the Monday following, in the courthouse at Chldeu, there 
was evidence given of the clearest kmd, criminating mdividuals for robbing and 
selling meal belonging to a Relief Committe^ The parties charged are held to 
bail to take their trial at the next sessions. There ai;e oRier oases that will also 
come to light, which, I understand, are likely to exhibit fraud to a very great 
eXt The investigation will, I trust, lead to the punishment of the parties 
charged, which would necessarily he productive of much good.

I ATTENDED the Weekly meeting of the Board of Guardians this day. 

It affords me much gratification to state tliat a:i imp/i’oved spirit is obsorvaljle 
at the Board, and that the Guardians are practically evincing a desire to 
su])port me in tlie execution of my duties. 

The Commissioners will perceive from the Minutes that the Board are 
gradually paying off their liabilities. The ruinous prices ^vhich they have been 
charged heretoibre renders it absolutely necessary to alter the system ; and tlie 
provisions, &c., are now jiurchased for ready money, which wiU make a con- 
siderable difference in the e.xpenditure. 

The workhouse at present is quite full. Numbers of applicants seek admis- 
sion, but it is deemed prudent not to overcrowd the house in its present state. 

Fever and dysentery still rage, both in the workhouse and the tJiiion ; but 
the establishment of the Temporary Fever Hospital v.-ill conduce most mate- 
rially to check the sjiread of these diseases. 

I have already communicated with the Commissioners in reference to tlie 
site for the hosiiital. 1 cannot too strongly recommend to tlie consi(leration of 
the Board the propriety of sanctioning the hospitr.l beuig established in a build- 
ing in every respect so eligible. Anticipating, however, that there may be some 
difficulties with the Commissioners of National Education on this matter, I 
have suggested to the Board of Guardians to api>oint a Committee for the pur- 
pose of choosing a site for the wooden building. This suggestion has been 
attended to, as will appear from the Minutes. 

The new rate-book for Roundstone electoral division was signed to-day, 
Lyder the collector, having resumed his duties. 

Flynn, the collector of Ballindoon, was also in attendance ; and the Guardians 
have told him that unless he makes a hotter progress in the collection ol the 
rate he is to be dismissed at the next meeting. 

The collector for Renvyle electoral division is still in fever. A new collector 
will be appointed in his place should he be imable to attend on Monday next. 
It is hut right to state that he is a very deserving officer, and has done his duty 
strictly heretofore. . . 

The collector for Clifden electoral division is giving me great satisfac tion ; 
and the Board of Guardians liave increased the rate ol liis poundage in couse- 
queuce of liis exertions. , ^ ... 

Dr. Suffield was appointed local treasurer at this day s meeting ; he is a 
gentleman in whom the Board has every confidence. 

The medical officer for the Temporary Fever Hospital has not been yet

have occupied myself, as the Commissioners are already awi^e, m makmg 
inquiries as to sites for the Fever Hospital, and also in investigating the qualifi- 
cations, &c., of the individuals appointed Relieving Officers. I arn, therefore, 
unable to continue to offer observations as to the state of distress m the more

The Count Strzelecki has requested me to confer with Mr. Lynch, the

Clifden Union. Xhc PooE Law COMMISSIONERS to Mr. Deane, Temporary Inspector: 

Novemher 26, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland to aclcnowledge the receipt of your i cport of the 
22nd instant, relating to the Clifden Union ; and in reference to the mode in 
which supplies are procured by the Board of Guardians ibr the maintenance 
of the workhouse, I am to request your attention to the 17th article of the 
General Regulations of the Commissioners, which directs that supplies of pro- 
visions and necessaries for the workhouse should be procured by contract 
tenders for the supply of such articles having been previously advertised for. * 

The Commissioners think it expedient that this course should not be departed 
from, except in pursuance of the proviso contained in the 22 nd article of the 
Regulations. 

As regards the number of persons seeking admission to the workhouse, the 
Commissioners recommend that steps should be taken by the Guardians for 
providing additional accommodation. The Guardians should make an entire 
revision of the inmates of the workhouse generally, with a view of dischargiuo- 
those who are not fit objects for sucli relief, or to whom out-door relief mio-ht 
properly be given under section 1 of 10 Vic., c. 31, and of making the work- 
house available to as great an extent as possible for the relief of the able-bodied 
applicants. 

The Commissioners also recommend that the Guardians should closely scru- 
tinize the cases of the children in the workhouse, with a view of ascertaining 
whether there are any receiving relief therein whose parents are not in the 
workhouse, or are at work out of the house; the relief of children without 
their parents, who are bound to maintain them, being at variance with the pro- 
visions of the Irish Poor Relief Acts, and likely to be attended with great 
abuse. ° 

With reference to the collection of the poor-rates, the Commissioners trust 
tJiat the continued attention of the Guardians will be directed to this important 
matter. ^

The Poor Law Commissionehs to the Boaud of Guardians 
Novemher% 1847. 

Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in 
Ireland, have had under consideration the resolution of the Board of Guar- 
dians of Galway Union, of the 27th ultimo, to the effect, that a rate should be 
struck on the several electoral divisions of the Union, which added to the 
present current rate, would amount to 35 . in the pound on the Poor Law 
valuation. 

considering the accompanying instructions from the Lords Commissioners 
01 Her Majesty’s Treasury, the Commissioners are of opinion, that the course 
proposed by the Guardians, in reference to Galway electoral division, does 
not satisfy the requirements of those instructions. 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 135 

The rate which the Guardians are now about to make, ought to amount to 
3s. in the pound, including the arrears of the old rate. The course which the 
Guardians actually propose, is, that the rate in Galway division should amount 
to 3s. in the pound, including the original amount of the old rate, and the 
effect is, that the rate which the Guardians now proceed to levy, would not 
exceed altogether 2s. Sjc?. in the pound, being Is. additional rate, and Is. 
for arrears. 

The Commissioners therefore request the Guardians to alter their rate in 
Galway electoral division, so that the new rate, including the arrears of the 
old rate, should amount to 3s. in the pound. 



Extract from Minutes of the Board of Gu.\rdians : — November 3, 1 847. 

Present, in the Chair. Robert Bodkin. Fifteen other Guardians present. 

Read a letter from the Poor Law Commissioner, requesting the Guardians 
to change the rate in the Galway electoral division, so that, including the 
arreai’s, it should amount to 3s. in the pound instead of 2s. 

Resolved, That the Galway rate-books being now completed at Is. in the 
pound, and as any increase in the poundage would require the preparation of 
new books, we are unanimously of opinion, that such a delay would not only 
much embarrass, but perhaps completely obstruct the collection of tlie rate; we 
therefore earnestly request the Poor Law Commissioners to allow us to postpone 
the additional 5|rf. now required, untd the striking of the next rate. 



Captain Hell-ird, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners: — 
November 4, 1847. 

With reference to your letter of the 2nd instant, addressed to the clerk 
of this Union, calling upon the Guardians to add an additional sum of 5|d. in 
the pound upon the rate lately struck for the electoral division of the county 
of the tovm of Galway, I have the honour to acquaint yon that the books for 
the 3s. rate struck on the 27th ultimo being nearly complete for proceeding 
with the collection thereof, the Guardians, at their meeting yesterday, resolved 
to add the sum in question to their next rate, in order that the collection of 
the 3s. rate, now so far progi’essed with, should not be retarded by waiting for 
a supply of other books, which appears to me so reasonable, that I cannot but 
fully concur with them, and submit their resolution for your favourable con- 
sideration. 



The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians: — 
November 9, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for the Relief of the 
Poor in Ireland direct me to state, in reference to the resolution of the Board 
of Guardians of Galway Union of the 3rd instant, requesting the Commis- 
sioners to allow the Guardians to postpone the required addition of 5%d. to the

Captain Hellard to the Poor Law Commissioners: — November 12, 1S47. Galway Union. 

^ In reporting upon the state of the Union, I do myself the honour to 
aeq^uahit you, with reference to the workhouse, that until the paupers are 
properly supplied with clothing, it is quite impossible to have that order and 
regularity w'hich it is my particular wish to see observed in this establisliment ; 
nor can anything like regular occupation for the inmates be established until 
they are classified and placed in divisions under a proper superintendence of 
ward-masters and steady men selected for this liighly important duty ; this 
system once regulated, I hope to see something like labour obtained within 
the waUs. On Tuesday the house contained 1081 paupers, and upon my close 
inspection of every part of it yesterday, and looking over the books, it appeared 
154 had been admitted on the following day, thus leaving a total numljer of 
1235 now accommodated. The Guardians are using their best endeavours to 
obtain separate accommodation for the children, and removing the whole of the 
sick to the adjoining premises at their lodge, and they appear altogether avei*se 
to any out-door relief even for the aged. 

The Union generally will, I fear, be found in a, very distressed state as the 
season closes, more particularly in the county of the town, as nimibers are daily 
arriving from the rural districts, and taking up their abode under the impression 
that large public works are to be commenced. 



The Poor Law Commissio.neks to Cap>tain Hellard : — November 13, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland to acknowledge the receipt of your report of 12th 
instant, relating to the state of the Galway Union ; and in reference thereto, I 
am to request that you will press on the Board of Guardians the necessity for 
providing an ample supply of additional clothing and bedding without delay. 

I am at the same time to observe that the Commissioners concur with the 
Guardians in the sound policy of providing means of limiting relief to the 
workhouse as far as practicable, consistently with the healthy condition of the 
nmates.

County of the Town of Galway,! The information of Patrick Martin, of Upper Dangan, in 
to viit. /the parish of Hahoon,iothe county of the town of Galway, who

from my custody, at said place, by William Conneely, of Ballybane More, and Keane, the

more, of Rahalin aforesaid, who were aided and assisted by several other persons unknown to

that on same day I seized about 50 sheep on the lands of Ballybritt, in said county, for poor

sequence of the violence and resistance offered to myself and my assistant, by Patt Connor and 
Timothy Connor, both of Ballybritt aforesaid. That said Patt Connor then and there struck me 
violently with a stone on the back, from the effects of which I still feel extremely unwell. My 
assistant, James Toole, was also struck and knocked down by the said Patt Connor. Saith, 
that in different districts of the county of the town of Galway, I have, within the last week or 
ten days, and even on said day, made seizures for poor rate, and that in every instance the 
greatest resistance and violence were exhibited towards me, so much so,' that in no case could I 
succeed in collecting the rate, or removing the distress. That this violence and resistance were 
not confined to one or two localities, but were general throughout the rural parts of the said 
county of the town of Galway, both east and west; and I now swear that it is my firm con- 
viction and belief that no person can with safety to his life, even attempt the collection of said 
mte, much less to collect it, unless such person shall have the protection of a suffioient military 
or police force; and I make this information from personal observations of the violence and 
determination manifested generally, by the country people, against the payment of the poor 
rate, moi'e particularly within the last week or ten days.

of causes, which have arisen from the house having been first opened by order 
of the Commissioners before any funds had been collected for its support, and 
by the neglect of the Commissioners to enforce upon the Board of Guardians 
in each of the years subsequent to its opening the laying on and collection of 
rates sufficient for its maintenance, and from the difficulty which has lately 
existed in the collection of the rates by the extreme distress of the country. 

That your memorialists, as individuals, cannot charge themselves with having 
been parties to this neglect, and they trust that your Excellency will he iileased 
to depute some persons to examine into the present state and past management 
of the workhouse.
