The Poor L.\w Commissioners to Mr. Redington: — August 24, 1847. 

The Poor Law Commissioners have had under their consideration the 
memorial which the Guardians of Scariff Union have forwarded to his Excel- 
lency the Lord Lieutenant, setting forth the embarrassments of the Union, and 
making a statement of the causes of those embarrassments ; and in compliance 
v/ith Uie request of his Excellency, the Commissioners have to report as 
follows on the statements contained in the memorial of the Guardians : — 

The finances of Scariff Union are undoubtedly in a very unsatisfactory state 5 
the net annual value of the Union is 44,609/., the population is 53,568, and the 
debts of the Board of Guardians on the 1 st of last July were 5004/. 

The real cause of the financial difficulties of the Union is that the Board of 
Guardians, whose special duty it is to make and collect rates, have neglected 
to make and collect rates of a sufficient amount. 

The causes assigned by the Guardians are, 1st, that the worldioi^e was 
opened by order of the Poor Law Commissioners before any funds had. been 
collected ; 2ndly, that the Commissioners neglected to enforce upon the 
Guardians the collecting of sufficient rates ; and 3rdly, the difficulty which 
has lately existed in the collection of rates, from the distress of the country. 

In regard to these cai^es, the Commissioners desire to observe, that the two 
first only are contained in the copy of the memorial which is contained in the 
Guardians’ Minutes, and on looking at the original (which the Commissioners 
herewith return), it will be seen that the statement respecting the distress of 
the country is in a different handwriting from the rest of the memorial, and 
was manifestly an afterthought. In fact, the Commissioners do not feel sure 
that it was not inserted in the document after all the signatures had been 
attached to it 

With regard to the assertion respecting the opening of the workhouse, the 
Commissioners have to make the following statement : — 

The workhouse of the Union was opened as far back as in the month of May 
1842, that is to say,, more than five years ago. Now, from tlie introduction of 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit

141- 



Irish Poor Law to the present time, the average annual rate of collection has 
been only 7\d. per pound, and the highest rate ever made on the Union has not 
exceeded the small amomit of I 5 . Zd. in the pound, although on one occasion,, 
in one electoral division, there was a rate of I 5 . per pound. But as the 
Guardians previously to the late distress could at any time, by a moderate- 
increase of the poundage, have relieved themselves from their debts, it seems, 
unreasonable to endeavour to attach importance to the supposed premature 
opening of the workhouse in 1842. 

The Commissioners will add that, on referring to the documents in this office 
of the period adverted to, the Commissioners find that tlie workhouse was. 
declared fit for the reception of paupers on the 1st of October, 1841, and that the 
first rate of 5d in the pound was made on the 8th of February, 1842. As the 
workhouse was not open for the reception of paupers till three months after- 
wards (namely, the 1 1th of May in the same year), it appears to have been the 
fault of the Guardians if they had not by that time adequate funds in their 
treasurer’s hands. The Commissioners are not certain what were the precise 
views of the Commissioners in 1842 ; but it is not improbable that the Commis- 
sioners thought that if the workhouse was not to he opened till the Guardians 
had funds, the opening of the workhouse might be inconveniently postponed to 
a distant day. 

With regard to the second cause assigned for the financial difficulties of the 
Union (namely, that the Commissioners neglected to enforce upon the Guardips 
sufficient rates), the Commissioners have to observe that the duty of making 
and collecting rates, and of appointing rate collectors, is vested by law exclusively 
in the Guardians, and not in the Commissioners ; and that the Guardians cannot 
ill any way shift from themselves their responsibility in thk respect. 

Sti'il the Commissioners have not been altogether inattentive to^the financial 
circumstances of Scariff Union ; and they proceed to show that the present em- 
barrassments are mainly owing to the omission of the Guardians to collect 
i*at 03 during the last 17 months *, and the Guardians certainly cannot complain, 
with truth, that the Commissioners have neglected to urge them during that 
period to collect rates. 

From the annexed tabular statement marked A, it will be seen that on the 
25tli of March, 1846, the total excess of expenditure over income in Scariff 
Union, from the commencement of the Union, was only 4.0U, while the receipts 
during- the half-year ended on that day exceeded the expenditure by 439Z.' 
There was nothing, therefore, in the state of the Union funds to call for parti- 
cular remark at that time. The Guardians had only to persevere during the 
following half-year in the course which they had pursued during the previous 
half-year, and the Union would be out of debt. 

During the following half-year, however, the Guardians omitted to collect 
a sufficient amount of rates ; and their expenditure exceeded their receipts by 
1034/., so that their total excess of expenditure over the receipts amounted 

to 1435/. , ~ •ivTT • 

Now in the course of this half-year, the Commissioners sent to bcaxitt Unio^ 
as well as to other Unions in Ireland, a copy of the subjoined circular, and if the 
Guardians had simply acted upon the contents of that document (B.), and had 
vigorously collected the rates, they might, without material difficulty, have 
extricated themselves from all their embarrassments. 

Since the date of that circular the Commissioners have had frequent commu- 
nications -with the Guardians, respecting the collection of the rat^, by letter, 
and the Commissioners transmit herewith a copy of their correspondence with 
the Guardians on the subject (C.). In fact the Commissioners: are unable to 
point out what more they could have reasonably done, unless they had dissolved 

the Board of Guardians. , ^ . 1 t. 

This is an extreme measure, to which the Commissioners always have 
recourse with reluctance ; but still the Commissioners do not feel certain that it 

will not become necessary in Scariff Union. . r. tt • 

With respect to the statement respecting distress m_ Scariff Union, Wie 
Commissioners do not deny its existence during the last 17 months ; and ti^ 
undoubtedly has rendered the collection oi the rates more difficult than would 
otherwise have been the case. Still the Commissioners have to observe that 
distress appears likewise to have existed m the adjoining Umon of Ennis , and 
yet in Ennis Union on the 1st ultimo the net amount of money remaining to 



Scariff Union.'

Soariff Union, the credit of the Ennis Guardians, after deducting their liabilities, was no less 
than 625/., while, at the same time, the debts of the Scariff Union, after de-

Again, during the seven past months of the present year, the Ennis Guardians

duty has been neglected by the Scariff Board of Guardians.

Poor Law Commission Offko, Dublin, 

SiR» _ September 10, 184S. 

Advertino to the information received from the Board of Guardians regarding the 
state of the potato crop in the Scariff Union, I am directed by the Poor Law Commissioners 
to express their deep regret that the report of the Guardians is to so great an extent 
unfavourable. 

The Commissioners anticipate, in consequence hereof, a great increase of poverty and dis- 
tress among the labouring population of the Union, and it is their earnest wish that those 
means of affording relief which the law has placed at the disposal of the Guardians should be 
made available to the utmost practicable extent. 

They recommend, therefore, that the Guardians should promptly bring under review the 
subject of their contracts for provisions and other supplies, the present state of their stocks of 
bedding and clothing, and the general state of their finances, so as to be prepared in due time 
for any accession to the number of inmates which the present circumstances of the Union 
render probable. 

In making such preparations, the Commissioners urgently advise and call upon the 
Guardians to base the estimates for their financial and other arrangements on the assumption 
that the whole accommodation which the workhouse affords will be placed in requisition, during 
a considerable period, commencing from the close of the present autumn. The means of relief 
placed at the disposal of the Guardians being limited, it will be a source of satisfaction hei-e- 
after, both to the pnblic and to the Guardians themselves, if nothing be left undone to make 
the utmost use of those means, so far as they may be found necessary; especially in the relief 
of the prraary objects of the Irish Poor Law — aged^ infirm, or otherwise disabled persons, to 
whose relief the recent measures of Parliament, enacted for the employment of labour, apply 
only in an indirect manner, and who may, therefore, be expected to form the class most liable 
to destitution, in consequence of the present calamity. 

What number of inmates may be safely and properly accommodated in each department of

Gentlemen, Scariff Union, November 19, 1846. 

I AM directed hy the Board of Guardians of this Union, at their meeting held on the 
] 7th instant, to call your attention to the slate of this workhouse with regard to supplies for the 
numerous inmates now receiving relief within its walls. 

I beg leave to state that no oatmeal can be purchased in this part of the country; or, if it 
were within their reach, there are no available funds to purchase it. At this moment we have 
741 paupers in the workhouse, and our stock of oatmeal will be consumed before 10 days 
expire. The Guardians are anxious to carry out the law to it.s fullest extent, and are desirous 
of being informed how they will proceed to raise funds to continue relief. Unless some means 
are devised by the Commi^ioners, the house must be closed, and the unfortunate paupers 
thrown on the world. In the present state of society, such an alternative must be shocking to 
contemplate. I fear it must be realized, unless your interposition meets such an emergency. 

I have, &c., 

The Poor Law Commissioners, Martin Hennesst, Clerk.

Extkact from Guardians’ Minutes ; — January 19, 1847. 

To the Poor Law Commissioners. 

Gentlemen, 

The financial embarrassments of the Scariff Union are such, that we are under the ne- 
cessity of applying to you for your sanction to allow interest to the Provincial Bank on such 
sums as they may be disposed to advance to us on the credit of the Union, the Government 
having refused to lend money on the security of the j-ates, and the auditor having refused to 
allow interest to be charged in the accounts. 

The Board of Guardians are deprived of all means of providing food and necessaries for the 
inmates, and of making such arrangements as are requisite for carrying on the business of the 
House. The Commissioners must be aware that cheques to a very large amount are in circu- 
lation, and as many of those may have been lodged with tlie treasurer of the Provincial Bank, 
as secuiities for advances of money, the Bank would apply the first receipts from the collectors 
to {the liquidation of those cheques ; and that thus tlie Guardians might, for a long time, bo 
deprived of any means of meeting the current esenses of the establishment, unless some 
general arrangements can be made to relieve our embarrassments. Tn fact, at this very 
moment, there is no meal in the House to supply a breakfast to the inmates on to-morrow 
morning, and the gentleman who has hitherto supplied the. house has just left the Board-room, 
declaring that he would not supply any more meal, until he had been paid the debt now due 
to him. 

Hoping for an early and favourable answer, 

We have, &c. 

The Guardians of the Scariff Union. 



Poor Law Commission Office, Duhliii, 
January 22, 1847. 

The Poor Law Commissioners have had before them the letter of the Board of Guar- 
dians, of the Scariff Union, on the 19th instant, relative to the pecuniary embarrassments of 
the Union, and requesting the Commissioners to sanction the allowance of interest on such 
sums as the Pro^ncial Bank may be disposed to advance on the credit of the Union funds. 

The Commissioners are deeply concerned at.the destitution prevailing in the ScariflT Union, 
and at its pecuniary difficulties ; but they trust the Guardians will use all their exertions to 
provide for the present emergency. If a personal guarantee be given to the treasurer for the 
payment of interest for money advanced, he will probably make a loan to the Guardians, beino- 
ce^n that the loan will be repaid to him, as all the Union funds pass through his hands. * 
The guarantee for interest only would not involve any great personal liability. The interest 
for 10007., even for a year, at 57. per cent., would not be more than 507. ; and the Commis- 
sioners presume that a considerable amount of rate will have been collected before so large a 
sum as 10007. can have been required for the clothing and maintenance of the paupers. 

The payment from the poor-rates, of interest for money borrowed to defray the current 
^penses of the Union, is undoubtedly illegal ; but the Commissioners desire to suggest to the 
Board of Guardians, whether the comparatively trifling sum required for interest to the 
treasurer for a temporary loan might not be raised by private subscription. 

To the CU of the Omrdians, A. Mooee, Chief aerk.

I BEG to inform you that I waited yesterday on Mr. Menzies, Manager of the Provincial 
JBank at Ennis, fo speak to him relative to an advance of money at iiifei'est to meet the exi- 
•geiicies of the Scariff Poor Law Union, and his reply was that there should bey?rst a positive 
.sanction of the loan and interest from the Poor Law Commissioners, and then he would lay 
the application before the Directors of the Bank.’* This would occupy so much time that I fear 
it puts the matter out of the question, as there are no provisions available for the workhouse, 
except what will suffice for two or three days, and even those had to be procured by the 
Guardians on their individual credit, so the house must close, and I must add, that had you in 
your letter of the 22nd instant, given a direct sanction to our borrowing the money, instead of 
offering uncalled-for and ridiculous suggestions relative to our subscribing from our private 
resotn'ces to meet the wants of a public institution, this state of things might have been obviated. 
There are now in the worlchouse near 250 persons, who, from sickness, decrepitude, old age, or 
infancy, are totally unable to provide for memselvea, and the result of iinhousing them now 
will, 1 fear, be their immediate death, which must positively bo followed by a searching Par- 
liamentaiy inquiry. If you are disposed even at' this late period to do what you ought to have 
done ten days ago, namely, to give a positive sanction to oiir borrowing the money, please to 
direct your reply to me, directed to the Scariff Workhouse, where I will receive it on Tuesday.

Poor Law Commission Office, Dublin, 

Sir, February 1, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Poor Law Commissioners to acknowledge the receipt of your 
letter of the 31st. ultimo, relative to an advance of money at interest to meet the exigencies of 
the Scariff Poor Law Union, in which you state that you fear the sanction which the treasurer 
requires before advancing the required loan would occupy so much time that it puts the matter 
out of the question, as there are no provisions available for the workhouse except what will 
suffice for two or three days, and that, consequently, the house must close; and you add, that, 
had the Commissioners in their letter ofthe 22nd ultimo given a direct sanction to the Guardians 
borrowing the money, instead of offering uncalled for and ridiculous suggestions relative to the 
Guardians subscribing from their private resources to meet thewants of a public establishment, 
this state of things might have been obviated ; and, after intimating your opinion that immediate 
death must result to a large number of paupers should they be now turned out of the workhouse, 
and that this must positively be followed by a searching Parliamentary inquiry, you conclude 
by requesting that, if the Commissioners were disposed even at this late period to do what they 
ought to have done 10 days ago, namely, to give a positive sanction to borrowing the money, 
they will direct their reply to you at the workhouse. 

In reply, I am directed by the Commissioners to state that your letter is written under a 
misapprehension of the powers which have been conferred on the Commissioners by the Irish 
Poor Relief Acts. To charge on the poor-rates interest for money borrowed to defray the ciiiTeat 
expenses of the Union is illegal, and the point is not one on which the Commissioners have a 
discretionary power. 

Under these circumstances, the Commissioners, being desirous of aiding the Guardians in 
their embarrassments, suggested a mode in which they might extricate themselves from those 
embarrassments by a comparatively trifling exertion on the part of those possessed of property 
in the Union ; and the Commissioners regret that the suggestion was not received in the same 
spirit that it was offered, even although tliere was an unwillingness to act upon it 

I’hc Commissioners have instructed their Assistant Commissioner to report on the specific 
class of rote-payers who are in arrear in Scariff Union ; but they deem it right to remind }’ou 
that the Board of Guardians possess as ample powers for collecting rates as are possessed by 
any body in the State for tlie collection of any rate or tax an^he Commissioners can only 
advise the Guardians to make energetic use of those powers, and to push vigorously forward 
the collection of the new rate. 

1 have, &c., 

J. P. Molony, Esq., A. Moore, Chief Clerk. 

Chairman ofthe Board of Guardians,

Letter to the Goaedians, with reference to the Rates proposed on the 9th September, 1847. 

Poor ioio Commission Off.ee, DuhUn, 

gjj{ SoiMmher 15, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland, 
direct me to acknowledge the return furnished by you on the I4lh instant, showing the par- 
ticulars of the rates which the Guardians o!' Scarift Union have passed a resolution to levy 
for the purposes of ordinary expenditure and the Temporary Relief Act, conjointly, by which it 
appeal's that the proposed rates would exceed 3j. in the pound in most of tiic electoral 
divisions. 

With reference, thereto, the Commissionei-s direct me to state, that in consequence of a 
communication from the Lords Commissioners of Her Majestv’s Treasury, they deem them- 
selves authorised not to require the Guardians to strike a liigner rate than 3 j. in the pound 
before the 1st January next, in any electoral division in which the sum required for ordinary 
expenditure alone would not exceed that sum. 

The Commissioners have further to state; that their Lordships being strongly impressed 
with the importance of giving every practicable aid to the Guardians of the poor in the execu- 
tion of the duties, which have devolved upon them under the permanent Poor Law system, as 
amended by the lOih Viet., cap. 31, are pleased to determine, that no repayment of advances 
made under the Temporary Relief Act (10 Viet., cap. 7) shall be demaucled before the 1st 
of Japuary next, from any electoral division, in which a rate eqvial to or exceeding 3s. in the 
pound, is levied before that period for the purpose of defraying the current expenditure of the 
permanent Poor Law, and that in those electoral divisions in which tlie rate to be levied for that 
purpose before the 1st January next, is less than 3s. in the pound, repayment shall be de- 
manded only to the extent of the difference between the amount required for tlie current 
expenses of the permanent Poor Law and the sum which a rate of 3s. in the pound in such 
electoral division, would produce. 

In making the above announcement, the Commissioners, in order to prevent any misappre- 
hension, desire distinctly to state that the poor-rate will remain liable for the repayment of the 
advances undei’ tlie Temporai-y Relief Act, if the Guardians do not make the requisite repay- 
ment from the next rate, or from the following rates, supposing that tlie rates levied are required 
for the ordinaiy expenditure. 

With reference to the above announcement, the Commissioners recommend the Guardians to 
reconsider the amount of rate necessary to be levied for ordinary expenditure alone. It appears 
that the debts of the Guardians on the 1st instant amounted to more than 2^. 6<Z. in the pound 
on the entire Union. 

The Commissioners do not consider, therefore, that a rate of less than 3«. 4d. in the pound, 
including the sum of lOrf. in the pound, already in the books, would suffice for the immediate 
purposes of the Guardians. 

It will be necessary, however, that the rate required should be apportioned on the several 
electoral divisions, according to the 6'2nd section of the Irish Poor Relief Act, and the Com- 
missioners request that they may be informed of the amount of rate proposed to bo levied off 
each electoral division, as soon as the Guardians have reconsidered the question. 

The Commissioners trust that by adopting a suitable scale of rates, and having them put in 
collection promptly, the Guardians will be enabled to retrieve the credit of llio Union. 

I have, &c.. 

The Clerk to the Guardians, A. Moose, Chief Clerk.

Letter to the Guardians with reference to the Resolutions of September 30. 

Poor Law Commission Ofke, Dublin, 

Sir, . ‘ October ‘1, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland have 
had under serious consideration minutes of the proceedings of the Board of Guardians of Scariff 
Union on the 30th ultimo, from which it appears that the Guardians have resolved as 
follows : — 

1st. That the arrears due on the rate struck ou-the 8th September, 1846, and 19lh January, 
1847, be Immediately collected, according to the old valuation. 

2nd. That Mr. Molony, of Kiltanon, Mr. Molony, ofCragg, and Mr. Purcell, of Banroe, be 
requested to institute a comparison between the Ordnance valuation of the townlands, in the 
county of Galway, which forms part of the Union, and the valuation of same townlands, as 
■made by Mr. Wilson, and also to investigate the principles upon which Mr. Wilson has made 
his valuation ; and 

3rd. That the same three Guardians be deemed a Finance Committee hr respect of endea- 
vouring to effect some beneficial arrangement with the creditors of the Union that will admitof 
a portion of the rate being applied to the support of the poor of the Union. 

With reference to these Resolutions, the Commissioners have to remark as follows 
1st. The proposal to collect the arrears of rates made on the 8th September, 1846, and 
19th January, 1847, as it implies practically the postponement of the immediate preparatton 
and levy of a new and sufficient rate, is one which the Commissioners cannot sanction. The 
rate of the 19th January last is onlylOrf. in the pound, whilst the debts of the Guardians to 

contractors and others exceed the sum of 2s. 6tl. in the pound. . i, i 

2nd. The proposal to appoint three Guardians to compare the recent valuaUon with the 
Ordnance valuation, and to investigate the principles upon which it was made, is one which, 
under different circumstances, might be open to no reasonable objection ; but if the prcparatien 
of a new rate should bo held in abeyance, until the proposal was earned out, the consequenc^ 
might be— 1st. Great suffering on the part of many destitute persons in_ the Union, whose sole 
dependence the law has placed on the poor rates ; and 2nd., an indefinite postponement or the 
payment of many heavy debts contracted for the past support of the poor. i. c • i 

3rd The proposal that a Finance Committee should endeavour to effect some beneficial 
arran.^ement with the creditors of the Union that will admit of a portion of *e rate being 
applie“d to the support of the poor of the Union would, as the Commissioners believe, only give 
T^e to a reasonable and fixed determination on the part of the creditors to insist on immediate 
payment of their claims, if they saw that the Guardians were not exercising the powers vested 

in them of levying sufficient rates to defray their expenses. _ , r* • • v v «= 

Upon a careful review of all the circumstances of Scariff Unio^ ffie Coraniissioners believe 
that the postponement of the making immediately a new and sufficient rate in the Unwm, m 
accordance with their repeated requests, would inevitably give rise to the evils now adverted to, 

and would be otherwise seriously detrimental to the interests ot Scanfi Union. ^ 

Accordingly, the Commissioners feel themselves called upon now to announce to the Gu^^^ 

dians, that if at their next meeting final measures be not adopted for putting a 
rate in preparation, the Commissioners will have to consider the 

appointing paid officers in the Union_ to discharge the primary duty of levying rates for the 
supDort of the destitute poor of the Union.

The Clerk oftke Chardiem,

Extract from Mwotes of GnAEDiAUs of Scariff Union, Octoljer 5, 1847. 

The Committee to whom it waa referred on Thursday tot to examine the valuatjon 
madehy Mr, Wilson, and also to endeavour to effect some benehcial arrangement with the 



Scariff Union.

152 PAPERS RELATING TO THE RELIEF OF DISTRESS, 

creditors of the Union that will admit of a portion of the rate heiiig applied to the support of 
the poor of the Union, beg leave to report as follows ; — 

In respect to the valuation, the members of the Committee, attended by Mr. Wilson, 

sat for some hours at Tulla on Friday, and at Kiilaloe on Saturday, to hear any objections tlrat 
might be tendered to them by parties who objected to the valuation ; and it appeared to them, 
although there might be some few cases where Mr. Wilson had over-rated houses, yet in tlie 
his valuation had been conducted on just principles, and ought to be supported by the 
Guardians. 

The Committee were confirmed in this opinion by the gratifying fact that several persons in 
Kiilaloe expi-essed themselves perfectly satisfied with the valuation of ihcir respective tenements. 
There were, however, three cases in Tulla, and one in Kiilaloe, which Mr. Wilson agreed in 
opinion with the Committee might be reduced. 

The Committee are not sufficiently instructed as to the principles upon which the Ordnance 
valuation has been made to offer any decided opinions as to how far it affords a fair criterion 
by which to judge of the correctness of Mr. Wilson’s valuation ; but if they are rightly informed, 
the two valuations proceed upon different principles, the one taking for its basis the intrinsic 
value of the soil, depending on its nature and quality, the other contemplating the fair letting 
value to a solvent tenant, depending on the state of improvement, the locality, and other 
advantageous circumstances. The Ordnance valuation does not include houses under 5Z. in 
value, whereas the valuation for Poor Law rating includes them. This latter circumstance will 
account for a difference of about six per cent, between the Ordnance valuation of the townlands, 
in the county of Galway, which are included in the Scariff Poor Law Union, and the valuation 
made by Mr. Wilson of the same townlands. 

In conclusion of that subject, your Committee strongly recommend the Board of Guardians 
to sanction Mr. Wilson’s valuation. 

In respect to the financial position of the Union, the Board must be aware of the extreme 
difficulties of the case, and there is no suggestion which your Committee can offer that may not 
be open to serious objections. But the question is, in what way the Board of Guardians may 
be enabled to carry out the enactments of the law, which gives to the poor a right of relief 
allowing to the fullest extent the claims of the creditors of the Union, it is still to be remem- 
bered that the poor may also bo regarded as having equally valid claims. The difficulty of 
the case is enhanced by the ‘fact of the Guardians having given cheques to parties who had 
claims on them which have become negotiable securities ; and in one case, judgment has been 
obtained, and followed up by a writ, which placed the furniture of the workhouse under the 
dominion of the sheriff of the county, your Committee find, on inquiry, that cheques to the 
amount of 639Z. 10s. 2d. are held by the manager of the provincial bank, who is treasurer of 
the Union, on account of the parties to whom they belong, although the bank in question has 
no manner of claim on them, still when any payments are made to the treasurer of the Union, 
he may consider himself under the obligation of seeing that their cheques are liquidated in 
preference to any others, and if so, he might receive others, preventing the application of any 
funds to the support of the poor, until the whole debt had been extinguished. 

It appears to your Committee that there is a necessity imposed upon the Guardians, of 
addressing a letter to the manager of the provincial bank, forbidding him to pay any of tlie now 
outstanding cheques of the Guardians of the Scariff Union, and at the same time putting upon

The Commissioners for administering tlie Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland have 
had under consideration the resolution of the Board of Guardians of Scariff Union ofilic 12th 
instant, in which it is stated that the Guardians had no other object in proposing to levy the 
lOd. rate made in January last, and the arrears of the preceding rate at onco under the old 
valuation, and the new rate in the ensuing month of November under the noiv vabiation, than 
of putting the collection of the rate, to which very serious objections were urged, on the valuation 
of Mr. Wilson ; and the Commissioners are urgently requested to inform the clerk iiow he is 
to proMtd, with as little delay as possible, as (here is not one day’s provision in the bouse, and 
it is only kept open by the private security of some of the Guardians. 

In reference to tlie above resolution, the Commissioners desire to state, that they c.Tpeodingly 
regret the perilous position in which the workhouse inmates are placed, owing to the delay in 
putting a sufficient rate in course of collection. 

Witii reference to the request of the Guardians, that (he Commissioners will instruct the 
clerk how he is to proceed, the Commissioners have to state, that there does not appear to be 
any difficulty in the way of a rate being made in the usual and proper manner. 

Tlie rate-book contains a column for arrears of former rate, into which column the actual 
sums ill arrear ouglit to be brought forward; and in the case of Scariff Union, these arrears 
would be the actual sums in arrear on the rate of 19th January last, and the preceding rate of 
September, 1846. The clerk would simply have to add the two items together, and enter them 
ill the now rate books, as arreare of fornipr rate, in the proper column for arrears. 

The total riite, (insisting of the new rate, and tlie arrears would tlien be canned out in the 
total column ; and, after the arrears have been entered, the clerk should sign a further certilicale, 
and the Guardians a further allowance of the rate, in the usual form. 

Under the distressing circumstances in which the Union is placed, owing to the cmbai-rass- 
ments of the Guardians, the Commissioners consider that the Guardians ought to lose no time 
in applying to tlie proper completion of the rate and collecting books whatever assistance they 
might require iu addition to the services of the clerk.

Poor Law Commission Offca, DuMin, 

Sir, October 25, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for the Relief of the Poor in Ireland 
have had under consideration the minutes of the proceedings of the Board of Guardians of 
Scariff Union on the I9th instant, from which it appears that the Guai*dians did not act upon 
the suggestion of the Commissioners, to carryforward to the new rate the arrears of tiie old rate, 
but resolved that the warrants should be handed to the collector, in order that the coilecticm of 
the rates which the Commissioners deem illegal and objectionable should be commenced 
forthwith. 

The Commissioners have considered the course taken by the Guardians on this occasion, in 
connexion with the fact that, owing to the omission of the Guardians to collect a sufficient 
amount of rates, the Union is now above 6000/. in debt ; and in order to prevent the Union from 
being involved in still further embarrassments, the Commissioners have deemed it advisable 
to discharge the present Board of Guardians from the duty of administering relief to the 
destitute in Scariff Union. 

Accordingly, the Commissioners transmit herewith a sealed order for the dissolution of the 
Scariff Board of Guardians ; and the Commissioners will proceed without delay to appoint 
paid officers under the 18th section of the Irish Relief Extension Act. 

Ill taking this step, the Commissioners are strongly sensible of the great difficulties with 
which the paid officers will have to contend : and it is with considerable reluctance that the 
Commissioners withdraw the administration of the laws for relief of the poor from the hands of

I HAVE the lionoiir to report my arrival here on the 9th of November.

I thought it desirable to take the earliest ox)portunity of suggesting the re- 
moval of the children from the poor-house to some other locality *, and I am 
happy to say, tliat the Guardians mianimously agreed with me in the expediency 
of this proceeding, in anticipation of its absolute necessity. 

The cursory examination I have made of the workhouse is unsatisfactory ; in- 
discipline and irregularity certainly extet. I will endeavour to rectify this by 
making frequent visits, which the Guardians desire of me. The master is inert, 
^ind, I tear, too old to learn those habits of order and regularity necessary to the 
government and well-being of a large body. I will, however, give him a fair 
ar.d iMitient trial. . 

The Guardians have also authorized me to make a scrutiny of the whole 
liouse, with a view to removing those classes who can legally be relieved out 



of doors. . . T \ 

I cannot doubt that the northern part of the Union (Kilmurry m particular) 
is in so bad a state that it can hardly be exaggerated ; 6000 “ notices to quit ” have 
been served in the Union I « . . j 

I have seen and heard enough to satisfy me that want of activity and energy 
may be justly alleged against both Guardians and collectors. I will at an ea.rly 
pieriod visit the districts, and encourage the collectors to overcome tlie diffi- 
culties they have to contend with. _ i 

A great mistalce has lieeii committed in the late issue of the warrant for col- 
lectimi. A month earlier would have been a great matter, before the crops were 
swept by landlords or realized by tenants. ‘ 

In some localities, small-pox is raging and fever to great extart ; the deaths 
in the workhouse amoimted to 21 last week. The contractor for coffins is unpaid, 
and threatens to “stop the supplies.” • * e 

The hospital adjoins' the workhouse, and I hope, with the assistance oi the 
medical officer, to prevail on the Guardians to remove it to some more fitting 
localify : this fact, however, accounts for the house being as yet uiicrowded. 
Popular terror attributes all deaths in the house to fever, and Ae proximity ot 
the house to the hospital deters many from seeking that refuge they would 
otherwise apply for. 

No out-door relief has yet been given to any cl^s. r- _

The Poor Law Commissiokeks to Captain Kennedy, Temporary Inspector :

In reference to your inquiry as to the mode of admimstering out-door 
relief, I am to state, that the Commissioners have not officially expressed any 
conclusive opinion, as to whether relief to the impotent poor and to other 
parties authorized to receive out-door relief under the 1st Section of the lush

XiirusTi Union, poor Relief Extension Act, should he given in money or food. They have 
left this question open to the discretion of the Boards of Guardians, as is the 
case in England and Wales, where such reliel' in some Unions is partly in 
cash and psu-tiy in food; and in some Unions, especially in Lanc^ashire and in 
the north of England, is for the most part wholly in money. 

The Commissioners have no doubt that relief in food is on the whole far less 
attractive to the recipient than relief in money ; Imt, on the other hand, M'itk 
respect to the classes entitled to permanent relief under tlic 1st Section, the 
Commissioners doubt whether food alone, especially during the winter months, 
would relieve all their wants, or whether the present inmates of workhouses 
could reasonably be required to leave those establishments, if their out-door 
allowances were to consist merely of food. 

The Commissioners deem it proper to add that, although relief in money is 
more attractive to the recipients than relief in ibod, the Commissioners do not 
feel confident but that the dispensers of relief are disposed to be more lavish 
in giving rations than they would be in giving money, especially if the money 
is raised by local rates. 

Under these circumstances, considering that the advantages and disadvantages 
in granting relief, either in money or food, to the impotent poor, are, to a 
certain extent, balanced, the Commissioners think that the views of the Board 
of Guardians on the question may be consulted, inasmuch as something may 
depend on the peculiarities of the district comprised in each Union. At any 
rate the Commissioners do not wish to lay down any positive rule on the 
subject, and they will readily give you their support in either of the two courses 
which you may prefer ; it being at the same time understood that something 
more than mere food, as an out-door allowance, must, under any circumstiinces, 
be given to the impotent poor who are at present inmates of Kilrush work- 
house. 



Captain Kennedy to the Poon Law Commissioners: — November 18, 1847. 

I ATTENDED the weekly meeting of the Guardians yestei’day, and Ijog to 
refer to the minutes for their proceedings. 

The admissions to the workhouse amounted to nearly 200. Such a tangled 
mass of poverty, filth, and disease, as the applicants presented, I have never 
seen. Numbers in all stages of fever and small-pox mingling indiscriminately 
■with the crowd, and all clamouring lor admission. I had them separated as 
quickly as possible. Their misery and utter helplessness baffles dcscrii^ion. 
The parents of a large family often disj>laying hardly the sagacity of an animal. 
It was really an a])palling sight. The Chairman and Guardians present, 
regardless of personal danger, examined and admitted them to the house or 
hospital. I was in the house from 11 o’clock a,m. till 6i o’clock p.m., and 
returned to my lodgings covered with vermin ! 

Paper could not convey a description of the horrors and misery concen- 
trated among those 200 persons ; yet all of a description to be remedied or 
mitigated by the exercise of common energy and intelligence. 

I need not recapitulate the numerous and culpable irregularities I have 
found to exist in the house, and which I have undertaken to correct by daily 
visits. How the house has so long escaped general infection I am at a loss to 
conceive. On the last visiting day I found a side-gate open, and free access lor 
the friends of fever patients to pass to and from the hospital ! I rei>rimanded 
the master severely, and procured an order to forbid it for the future. By 
daily attendance, I have put the general discipline, cleanliness, and regularity 
of the house on a better footing. Much, however, remains to be done, and 
which I hope soon to accomplish, with the support and assistance of the 
Guardians, which they cheerfully afford me. 

The Guardians are now less desponding, and, of course, more efficient. 

The house is now overcrowded, but contains a great number of those classes 
relievable out of doors, but who could not be turned out till provision was 
made for them, and winch is only now being done at my earnest request. 
Want of funds is alleged as the cause of delay. These arrangements com-

Rathkeale Union : — Out-door Relief. 

Tlie Clerk of the Guardians to the Poor Law Commissioners. 

Sir, llathkeah, October 2Q, 1847. 

In reference to my lettei* of ycsterdaj', stating that an attack had been 
made on the n-oridunise )jy a large molj, which had put a stop to the proceed- 
ings of the Board on Monday, the 18th instant, I beg to send you the following 
detailed report of occurrences: — 

For some days previously it liad been rnmoured that a large number of 
able-bodied labourers were to assemble at the workhouse at the meeting of the 
Board on Monday, and to demand instant admission, which, from their num- 
bers, it would lie impossible to grant, or else immediate out-door relief. On 
Sunday last notices were posted on most of the cliapels in the part of the Union, 
and in those portions bordering on the Shannon, calling on the people to 
assemljle on the Ibllowing day, proceed to the vvorkliousc, and demand their 
rights. On Sunday night straw was lighted in the same districts, this being a 
common mode of giving a general signal ; and on Monday morning the people 
were gathered by the sounding of horns in the villages situated in the above 
localities. An-aiigements had been previously made lor the junction of the 
several parties at a point where two roads meet, about hall' a mile from the 
W'orkhouse. Up to near 12 o’clock on Monday the mim])er ol' persons coming 
in by the western roarl was not much greater than might have been expected, 
q^uarter sessions being then going on at Rathkeale ; Imt about 12 a large crowd 
was observed to be collected at the point above referred to ; and soon after, 
these liaviug been joined by other parties, the entire body came towards the 
v/orkhouse. On observing their approach, I gave directions to the oflicers to 
locli and bolt all the entrance doors, and on no account to admit any stranger 
into the premises. _ This direction was immediately attended to ; and by the 
time the crowd arrived at the house, all the doors and gate;! were secured. Up 
to this time but two or three Guardians had attended ; and as tlio crou’d was 
becoming very noisy,' they were in doubt what course to adopt. Sevcu-al of the 
ex-officio and elected Guardians, how'ever, now came in, having, as I liclicve, 
heard at the Court-house ol the proceedings, and two of the cx-offic:io Guardians 
addressed the crowd at the door at considerable length. The Board then pro- 
ceeded to business, it being about one o’clock; but the crowd still continuing 
noisy and excited, and liaving commenced shouting and blowing horns, it was 
agreed that they should be requested to select 10 or 12 of their number to 
come before the Board as a deputation, in order that they might be distinctly 
informed what the powers and intentions of the Guardians really were. Accord- 
ingly, about a dozen persons were chosen by the crowd ; and on these coming 
into the Board-room, the Guardians explained to them their powers under the 
amended Poor Law, and cxpi’essed their determination to carry out those 
powers to the utmost extent, regardless of expense, and also to memorialise the 
Government to grant relief in the shape of labour by completing some of the 
imfinished works in the Union. This appeared to satisfy the greater portion of 
the deputation, who departed. The crowd was now considerably reduced, a 
peat number liaving gone into Rathkeale. The Board again proceeded to 
busings ; but in a short time the crowd retumed from the town, blowing horns, 
shouting, and ivith greater appearance of excitement than before, it being 
evident that several of them were under the influence of liquor. A rush was 
soon made at the front door, which was forced open, and the entrance-hall was 
completely filled by the crowd, who then, notwithstanding the efforts of the 
porter and relieving officers to arrest their progress, forced their way into the 
Board-room by breaking open the door, and about 60 of them entered, driving 
b^ore them the relieving oflicers and a number of applicants for admission, 
who wp'e on the stairs, and thus completely filling the apartment. The crowd 
altogether now amounted to over 3000 persons, a great portion of whom w’^ere 
young able-bodied men ; and while those outside continued shouting and blow- 
mg horns, the party which had got into the Board-room commenced shouting, 
leaping, whirling their sticks, and striking the table, several of them being 
dearly ^cited by whiskey. At last, however, through the exertions of the 
Roman Catholic curates of this parish, who were then in the room, the crowd 
was persuaded to leave the Board-room, Shortly after they departed, the mob

proceeded to force their way into the interior of the workhouse; aud after Rathkeaie Union, 
some delay, owing to the interference of the above-mentioned clergymen, they 
succeeded in breaking open the door leading from the entrance-hall to the main 
building. 

They proceeded at once to the master’s hall door, and with a volley of stones 
demolished the glass with which half the door is fitted up. They then 
attempted to force the door open, but did not succeed, it being defended by the 
master tailor, and one of the paupers, who kept it securely closed, although 
repeatedly struck at with sticks from outside. Being foiled at this j>oint, they 
broke open the wicket leading into the girls’ yard, and by forcing out one of the

and from thence into the girls’ school-room, frightening the childrf*n dreadfully. 

Here they were again delayed by the door leading from the school-room to the 
master’s apartments ; but after some time this was also broken open, and the 
mob, rushing through, proceeded to the master’s kitcheu, where one of them 
took up the tongs for the purpose of compelling those belonging to the house 
who were present, including the matron, to open the provision store. The 
efforts of the clergymen here, as w’ell as at the other places, delayed their pro- 
ceedings, and the stores were eventually saved. 

In the mean time a number of the mob got in over the walls of the women’s 
yard, and opened the gate by breaking the lock, letting m a large body of their 
comrades, and an attack was instantly made on the door from that yard to the 
dining-hall. This door was defended by the assistant master and some of the 
paupei-s ; and although very mucli battered with stones ajid spades found in the 
yard, it withstood the efforts of the assailants. 

While tilings ivere in this state, it being then about half-past o’clock, a 
party of ten dragoons and an officer came down the avenue, aud proceeded to 
deal’ away that portion of the crowd which still remained at the front en- 
trance. While in the act of doing so, a desperate attack w^as made upon them 
with stones, by which the officer and two of the men were severely hurt. The 
dragoons, from the confined situation and the nature of the ground, were unable 
to act with any effect, and were completely exposed to the mol), who stoned 
them from behmd the ditches, until a party of infantry, and about eight or ten 
policemen came down, who shortly alter their arrival dispersed the crowd ; 
wliich however immediately collected again at the entrance gate, where they 
remained till dusk, the military also remaining near them, a small party of 
police having been placed in the workhouse, from wlience they departed about 
11 o’clock. One of the mob received a bayonet wound, which the medical 
oflficer of the workhouse into which the man was brought, considers to be 
dangerous. The case of this man exemplifies the manner in which the crowd 
was collected. He was at work digging potatoes on ftlonday morning, when 
the mob came upon him and forced him away against his will. 

At about 1 o’clock the master, being apprehensive for the stores, sent a person 
to inform the authorities at Rathkeale of the state of affairs; and again, about 
an hour afterwards; but no protection arrived till about half-past 3. 

The persons breaking into the house appeared to have two objects ; one was 
to plunder the stores, the other to execute summary vengeance on the master 
and assistant master, who have been lately instrumental in punisliing parties in 
and out of the workhouse for theft. The most violent expressions were made 
use of by the mob against these two officers. 

From the confusion which existed, very littlebusiness was done by the Board ; 
and when the attack was made on the military, all proceedings were imme- 
diately suspended, and the greater number of the Guai’dians departed when the 
mob was cleared away. I could not, in consequence, get the proceedings regu- 
larly finished that evening, and have appointed this day for competing tlie 
proceedings, if I can procure the attendance of a sufficient number of Guardians. 

However, in order that the occurrence might not operate mjunously to the 
really destitute, I advised the officers, after the mob was dispereed, to admit 
provisionally all who appeared to be proper objects for relief ; and m pursuance 
of this arrangement, 99 persons were admitted, including about 20 who had 
been admitted by the Board. ^ i t, v 

It is but justice to the officers of the house to state that they acted all through 
with the utmost coolness aud determination. They kept the doors f^tened, 
notwithstanding the most violent threats against them. The master tailor also

The Cleek of the Guardians to the Poor Law Commissioners: — 
October 28, 1847. 

At the meeting of the Board of Guardians of Rathkeale Union, held on 
Monday the 25th instant, and continued by adjournment until yesterday the 
27th instant, it having been reported to the Board that the County Inspector of 
Constabulary had attended at the workhouse on Friday last for the purpose 
of making arrangements for the prevention of outrage thereat, and had strongly 
recommended that a small party of police should be placed in the premises to 
guard against any sudden or unexpected attacks, and that such party, consisting 
of six men and a constable, had been accordingly placed in the male probationary 
ward (for a long time past imoccupied), on Sunday night, where they still 
remained ; the Board approved of the arrangement, and, as the apartment in 
which they were placed was not at present required, the Board considered it 
would be desirable, for the protection of the officers, and to guard against any 
sudden outbreak, that tliey should continue there for some time longer ; and in 
order to enable them to prepare their food without communicating with any 
other part of the building, it was ordered that the stove in the room above- 
mentioned should be removed, the five-place opened, and a grate put therein ; 
also that two small sashes should he placed in the side ventilators.

The Poor Law Commissioners to the Clerk of the Guardians; 

November 6, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the La^vs for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland to acknowledge the reccixit of your letter of the 
3rd instant, reporting the resolution of the Board of Guardians of Rathkeale 
tJnioii on the 2nd instant, in which they request the Commissioners to issue a 
sealed order to enable the Board to commence the system of out-door relief to 
able-bodied labourers, unemployed, and holding no land, and express their 
belief that the able-bodied labourers can thus be supported on much cheaper 
terms than by resorting to the power of taking additional houses lor the use of 
the poor. 

In reference thereto, I am directed by the Commissioners to state that they 
would not feel justified in issuing a sealed order authorizing out-relief, under 
the second section of the Irish Relief Extension Act, until the Guardians had, 
as far as was practicable, had recourse to the various measures pointed out in. 
the Commissioners’ circular of the 26th of August. 

The Commissioners obseiwe, however, that the Guardians have not fully 
adopted any of those measures, and the Commissionei's are not even assured that 
the Guardians have given out-door allowances under the 1st section of the Act 
to all those who might legally receive it, and who would he fit objects for .such 
relief. 

In reference to the supposed superior economy of out-door relief for able- 
bo^ed men, in comparison with relief in the workhouse, the Commissioners 
desire to state that there has been ample experience elsewhere as to the com- 
parative economy of the two systems, and that it is contrary to recorded facts to 
suppose that out-door relief is on the whole cheaper. The fallacy consists in 
loolcing merely to the expense in any one individual case relieved, without con- 
sidering whether the niunber of individuals relieved would be equally great 
under a system of in-door relief. 

It is true that if in a particular week any individual pauper must absolutely 
be relieved, and the weekly cost of maintaining him out of the workhouse is 
only it would be cheaper for the one week to gi'ant him out-door relief 
than to maintain liim in the workhouse for I 5 . 7\d. On the other hand it is to 
be remembered, that relief in a workhouse is not generally an object of desire, 
and is not attractive, so that it would be an understatement to assert that 500 
persons would be anxious to receive out-door allowances for every 50 who 
would be anxious to receive relief in a workhouse. Now the Commissioners 
believe that the Guardians will, in making the calculation, find that 500 ten- 
pences amount altogether to far more than 50 sums of Is, 7^d. The Commis- 
sioners will ad(h that paupers in a workhouse will usually be found more 
desirous to obtain private employment than is the case with paupera receiving 
out-door rations j and it is indeed notorious that during tlie late relief operations, 
there was a difficulty in some parts of Ireland in inducing paupers receiving 
rations to work for private individuals. Hence it may be confidently asserted 
that the effect of out-door relief is to retain able-bodied paupers longer on the 
list than if they were relieved in the workhouse, and thus the mere cost of 
rnamtenance during any one week becomes secondary to the question^ of which 
of the two systems has a greater tendency to infuse habits of self-reliance and 
uidustiy , and to produce efforts to obtain employment in peisons who are in the 
receipt of relief.

hall’, contending with the chairman for out-door relief, and did not leave the 
Board-room till dusk, when, in consequence of the aljsence of the Guardians,

I have made an airangement with the Relieving Officers to meet me at the

sufficient number of Guardians to form a Board, I will have their books 
examined.

The Poor Law Commissioners to each of the Ex-Officio and Elective 
Guardians of the Union, and to Mr. PIancock, Inspector : — November 13, 
1847. 

I am directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for the 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, to state that they have received, with much 
concern and surprise, a document signed by twenty-four Guai*dians of Rath- 
keale Union, tendering the resignation of their office. 

In reference to tliat document, the Commissioners desire to state that they 
do not admit the power of Guardians to divest themselves of the responsibility 
which has been imposed upon them by the Legislature; and the duty of 
administering relief to the destitute in Rathkeale Union still rests with the 
ex-officio and elected Guardians. 

As much suffering will necessarily be experienced if the destitute poor in 
Rathkeale Union remain unrelieved, the Commissioners request your attendance 
at the next Board meeting, and they will afford to you every support and 
assistance in their power in carrying out the existing laws for the relief of the 
poor, in accordance with the intentions of the Legislature. 

At the same time the Commissioners forward to you a copy of their 
Circular, of the 26th August last, and of their instructions to the Temporary 
Poor Law Inspectors, as embodying the views which the Co mm issioners 
entertain of the course which ought to be adopted by Boards of Guardians at 
the present crisis.

The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians : — 

November 18, 1847. 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for the 
ReUef of the Poor in Ireland to state that they have had under consideration 
the resolution passed by the Rathkeale Board of Guardians on the 9tli mstmt, 
in which the Guardians again request the Commissioners to issue a sealed order, 
authorizing out-door relief to able-bodied men in Rathkeale Union. 

In reference to that resolution the Commissioners desire to call the attention 
of the Guardians to the Commissioners’ Circulai* of the 26th August last, and to jg^ 33 ^ 
the Commissioners’ Instructions to the Temporary Poor Law Inspectors, a copy 
of which is forwarded herewith for the inlbrmation of the Board ot Guardians ; 
and the Commissioners have already sent a copy of both these documents to 
each individual Guardian of the Union, as embodying the views winch the 
Commissioners entertain oi'the course which ought to be adopted by Boards oi 
Guardians at the present crisis. . 

It will be seen that the Commissioners will not enteriam a proposition lor 
authorizing out-door relief to able-bodied men until all other resources have 
failed. From the Minutes, however, of the Rathkeale Board of Gnardiaus oi 
the 9th instant, it appeared that the Guardians declined to take measures either 
for granting out-door allowances to paupers in the workhouse under the lirst 
section of the Irish Relief Extension Act, or for obtaining additional wori^house 
accommodation, although both these expedients were pomtedly brought under 
their notice. „ . . 

Under those circumstances the Commissioners were of opmion that they 
would not be justified in complying with the request to issue an out-door reliel 
order in Rathkeale Union, unless they were prepared to abandon ^e safeguards 
which had been devised by the wisdom of the Legislature for distmguishmg 
real from fictitious distress, and for thus preserving rate-payers from the burden 
of a taxation which might be otherwise too heavy for them to bear. 

For the same reasons the Commissioners stiU decline at the present moment 
to issue an order authorizing out-door relief to able-bodied men m la i 'e e 
Union. They call upon the Guardians, in the first instance, to revise the list ol 
paupers in the workhouse, and to grant reasonable out-door allowances to such 
of them as are permanently disabled from labour by reason of old age, iniirmi y, 
or bodily or mental defect, and to those who are destitute poor \ndows having 
two or more legitimate children dependent upon them. The Commissioners 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




166 PAPERS RELATING TO THE RELIEF OF DISTRESS, 

Rithkeale Union, further call upon the Guardians to use every exei'tion to ohtaij! additional work- 
house accommodation ; and more especially to procure a separate buildino- to 
which they may remove all the workhouse children. If the Guardians wili at 
once act upon these two suggestions, and will then offer relief in the workhouse 
to all destitute able-bodied male apfdicants, the Commissioners trust tliat there 
will be no reason why the Guardians should again at the present period apply 
for an order under the second section of the Irish Relief Extension Act. ’ 
At any rate the Commissioners desire to impress upon the Guardians the 
ruinous effects which must necessarily result from, yielding to menaces and 
combinations amongst lawless able-bodied labourers, and attempting to orant 
them out-door relief before the necessity for it really arises. The expense to 
the Union of such relief would ultimately become intolerable ; and there is no 
class of persons on whom as a system it would inflict deeper and more irre- 
parable injury than on the labouring classes themselves. The Commi.ssioners 
therefore, rely upon the Guardians warding off this evil from the Union, by 
the exhibition of timely energy, discretion, and firmness.

No. 2. — ]\Ir. O’Brien to the Poor Law Commissioners. 

Cahermoyle, RathJeeale, 

September 14, 1847. 

I THINK it right to apprise you that a very large number of ablc-hodied 
labourers applied for admission to the Newcastle workhouse this day, and the 
number of those who liave signified their intention to enter before next Board- 
day, under the authority for provisional admission, vested in the master, is so 
great,^ that il such intention be fulfilled, we shall be under the necessity of 
applying immediately for permission to grant out-door relief to the able-bodied 
as well as to the infirm poor. Under these circumstances, 1 think it desirable 
that our Board should be furnished with suggestions as to the best mode of 
deahng with the applications which will probably be made for relief within a 
very short time, by several hundreds, perhaps by several thousands, of able- 
bodied labourers, unable to find employment, who, with their families, must 
starve unless supported either in or out of the house. The collection of the 
rate proceeds very slowly, in consequence of the consolidation of the very 
heavy rate required to pay the ration advances with the rate necessary to carry 
mto effect the ordinaiy law. Much indisposition to pay it has also been created 
by the circumstance that the rate in an adjoining Union has been limited to 3^. 
in the pound ; whereas, in our Union, rates as high as 4:s. I Itf. have been im- 
posed upon some electoral divisions. Believing that an attempt to persevere in 
the collection of any rate exceeding 3^. in the pound would throw this district 
mto confusion, I have taken upon myself the responsibility of advising our 
Board to authorise the collectors to receive 3^. per pound on account, in all 
electoral divisions in which the rate exceeds that sum, leaving repayments of the 
temporary relief advances to be dealt with hereafter, upon whatever principle 
shall be applied to other parts of the kingdom. With this limitation, I hope 
that the Guardians will he able to succeed in causing the rate to be collected.

No. 4. — Mr. O’Brien to the Poor Law Commissioners. 

Cahermoyle, Raikkeale, 

October 6, 1847. 

The workhouse at Newcastle is now quite full. The additional building 
engaged for temporary occupation is also overcrowded. The Reports of the 
Relieving Officers convince me that the number of able-bodied poor in imme- 
diate want of relief, will amount to several thousand persons. No change of 
arrangements, therefore, will enable us to apply the workhouse as a test. Under 
these circumstances it is desirable that the Guardians should be informed as to 
the views of the Poor Law Commissioners with respect to the best mode of 
relieving the able-bodied ; and being anxious to give effect to the Poor Law in 
the manner most beneficial to the county, I take the liberty to ask, — 

Whether the Guardians will be at liberty to employ the able-bodied poor 
udio are relieved by rations, in completing the works commenced by the Board 
of Works in this Union, almost all of wliich have been left unfinished. 

Also, whether -we are at liberty to give rations to those who may be able to 
obtain employment occasionally, but not sufficient to maintain their families. 

p,S. — ^This letter has not been written by direction of the Board, but in order 
that I may be enabled to offer advice to the Guardians at their next meeting.

Newcastle iJuinn. malving of auy other roads, should not be raised at the present moment. If the

2ndly. The Commissioners are anxious strictly to prohibit and i)roveut the 
granting relief on account of the insufficiency of their wages to persons occa- 
sionally employed during the week. 

It appeal's to the Commissioners that there is no rule of greater importance 
in the administration of out-relief to able-bodied men than that they should be 
maintained either wholly by their employer or wholly by the Board of 
Guardians ; and that the strongest line should thus be drawn between relief 
and wages. 

In the event of out-door relief to the able-liodied becoming necessary in New- 
castle Union, the Commissioners would feel great satisfaction if they could 
obtain your support in maintaining this rule unimpaired.

and it has been, by yonr Board, left an entiredead letter for thc.se three months. In vain, do we 
send up our cries and our groans and our humble supplications before you. In vain, do we 
describe, in the strongest terms we can command, our dreadful, our unprecedented evils and 
woes. You have other matters to engage your attention, you are shooting on the mountains; 
you are engageil on your journeys for business or pleasure ; you are enjoying all the luxurious 
plenty of your rank and station whilst wo are perisliing, whilst the faces, dear to us, are turned 
green, almost as the wretched vegetable wliich constitute o\ir sole and unnatural nourishment. 
Can we bring ourselves to believe, that persons, in your high rank and station, have conspired 
agaiiist the laws and against the lives of the poor and the helpless. To defeat a minister who 
seems to feel for the wants of the Irish poor; to defeat a Government that we will in future 
call the Poor Man’s Government may be a triumph; But to achieve this triumph, you will 
have to stalk over tlie emaciated bodies, the skeleton corpses of the aged, the palsied, the 
decrepid, of tlie widow and the orphan whom you have cons%ned to slow death, by your 
refusal to carry out the law made to save them from famine and pestilence. The soldiers of 
the ruthless Ireton drove the Irish of his day to fee<l on grass, the lips of the dead were coloured 
green from the food on which they tried in vain to live. We are not reduced to cat grass, 
you have only reduced us to eat cabbage, a diet to which you wotild never dream of reducing 
your days. 

Gentlemen, we are not the fools you think us ; we see the plan (at least we think so) of 
the great and powerful, by the severe and stem exaction of rents. They endeavour to make 
the payment of the rate by the former an impossibility. You yourselves neither pay your own 
rates iior take any effectual means to get them collected from others, and in spite of your fair 
profe.ssions, wo see that you are ns you have ever been, utterly indifferent to the well being of 
those, by whose toil and labour the ground is i*end«rod fruitful, and ycni, yourselves, supplied 
with those multiplied luxuries, of whicii you have not rerfenehed a single one. ^ But we, alas, 
are perishing in the midst of those harvests which we assisted but a few weeks since in reaping 
and gathering in. , ir i 1 1 i 

Gentlemen, we have heard some cf yon profess your sympathy lor us. lour heart bleeds 
for us, you say. You wwp over our miseries : we will not presume to say that these are 
crocodile tears. Let the sympathising gentleman but pay the rate on his demesne and grazing 
lands : this will be to obey the law ; he will no longer seem to defraud the aged poor, the 
widow, and the orphan. Do. gentlemen, give— what the law commands you to giwj— hare 
support to the thoroughly destitute, and it will be more to the purpose than a world of sighs or 
an ocean of tears. Af'ain, some among you say, “ I will pay my rates when this lord and that 
baronet or (he other member of Parliament shall have paid his.” In our humble walk we 
have been taught, we ought not to wait for the example of others to fulfil our honest obligations. 
Your rates, gentlemen, are not your own: they belong to those to whom the law assigns 
them ; and we cannot reconcile it with our notions of common honesty for you to spend on dogs 
and horses, and pianos, on beef and mutton, and wines and liqueurs, what ought to be paid to 
enable (he feeble old man to add a few ounces of Indian meal to his disgusting mess of green 
cabbage. It may be, gentlemen, you care as little for our good opinion as you do for our 
welfare. Many of the great in Ireland are with yon ; and if lords and earls approve of your 
proceedings, you can afford to make little of the sad complaint and just remonstrances of the

of the best description it amounts to as much in the pound as the occupiers share of t^he poor- 
rate amounts to. This cess is collected with little or no difficulty. Nobody doubts but it 
would be collect ed if it were 50 per cent, more than it is. But if the great refused to pay their 
own county rate, if they took every opportunity by open assertion and covert insinuation to dis- 
parage counly charges as unjust in principle, illegal, and not recoverable by law. they would

No. 14. — Mr. Hancock to the Poor Law Commissioners: — Octohei' 16, 1847. 

I HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your communication 
of yesterday s date, requesting to he informed “ whether I am satisfied 
“ that no suitable building can be procured in the Union to be used as an 
“ additional workhouse for the reception of the boys and girls, or any other 
“ class of imnates!’' 

I pressed the Guardians very strongly on Tuesday, and instanced the case of 
Roscrea; where a house capable of containing 200 boys, was obtained four miles 
from the workhouse, hut the Guardians coidd not point out any place. The 
Chairman stated that it was very unfortunate that Captain Kennedy, the agent 
to the Devon estates, was not at home, as he might have been enabled to poin 
out some house. The temporary house in Newcastle, is by no means a satis- 
factory one for the pui'pose at present used, namely, for women and children, 
and there would be no room for schools at all. 

As far as my inquiries went, I was not able to hear of any house suitable for 
the purpose, which could be had. 

Caplin Kennedy returned home on Friday night, and it is probable the 
Guardians will avail themselves of his advice aud assistance upon the next 
Board day.

No. 17 The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians : — < 

October 18, 1847. 

Adverting to the resolution passed by the Board of Guardians of New- See No. s in this 
castle Union on the 5th instant, requesting the Commissioners -to issue their p- 
order authorising and empowering the Guardians to administer relief out of 
the workhouse, I am directed by the Commissioners for administering the 
Laws for Relief of the Poor in Ireland, to state that they have been in com- 
munication with their inspector, Mr., Hancock, on the subject, especially with 
reference to the question whether additional workhouse accommodation could 
not be provided in the Union ; and the Commissioners have instructed Mr 
Hancock to ascertain by further inquiry whether some suitable building may 
not be found for an additional workhouse. 

Meantime, the Coromissioners would earnestly press upon the Board of 
Guardians the great importance of endeavouring by every means in their 
power to provide sufficient and suitable workhouse accommodation for the 
able-bodied. The Commissioners observe, by the Report of the Committee 
appointed to investigate the cases of those already in the workhouse, that the

Of whom, were ready to leave the house . . . .117

only for whom workhouse accommodation is required, and even those 36 
would leave, on being allowed a week to provide themselves with shelter 
outside. It further appears that there are 120 boys in the house, for whose 
accommodation, it is hoped, other premises might be obtained, and thus vacan- 
cies for 273 would be created in the workhouse, besides such further room as 
might be obtained by a narrow scrutiny of the cases of the 18 married women, 
who, with their children (50 in mimber), are stated to be in the worlchouse, 
their husbands being outside or having deserted them. 

Under these circumstances, the Commissioners trust that the Guardians may 
be enabled to continue the administration of relief to the destitute \vithout 
resorting to the provisions of the 2nd section of the Irish Relief Extension Act. 
The Commissioners desire, at the same time, to state that they do not consider 
themselves in a situation to issue an order under that section until they are 
satisfied that every means of procuring additional workhouse accommodation 
has been tried and found imav^ing. 

The Commissioners have observed by the Guardians’ Minutes of the 12th 
instant, that the Guardians have passed a resolution that the Relieving Officers 
be authorised provisionally for one week to distribute rations to such of the 
able-bodied poor as the Guardians of the several electoral divisions shall deem 
to require immediate relief ; and the Commissioners therefore deem it their 
duty to point out that the course pursued by the Guardians in this respect, in 
anticipation of an order of the Commissioners under the 2nd section, is not in 
accordance with tlie provisions of the Irish Poor Relief Extension Act. 



No. 18.— Minutes of Proceedings of Board of Guardians \~Odoher 23, 1847. 

At a meeting of the Guardians of Newcastle Union, held at the Board- 
room of the workhouse, on Saturday the 2.3rd day of October. 1847, called 
in compliance with the lOth article of the General Order of the Poor Law 
Commissioners, for regulating the meetings and proceedings of Boards of 
.Guardians. Present, Captain Kennedy, Thomas Locke, and James Wigmore. 

Captain Kennedy, was called to the Chair. 

_ Having taken into consideration the urgent necessity, and impending starva- 
tion of numbers of able-bodied as well as impotent poor in this Union, together 
with the fact, that the poor house is quite full, as well as the additional accom- 
modation ill the town of Newcastle, wliich has been placed at the disposal of 
the Guardians, for the reception of paupers. 

Resolved , — That the Relieving Officers of the several electoral divisions, be 
immediately directed to issue, with the least possible delay, the regulated 
allowance of meal, for one week, to indigent families, upon their respective 
lists, able-bodied as well as impotent.

No. 20. — Mr. M'Mullen to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 

October 30, 1847. 

I HAVE the honour to report that on the 26th instant I examined the 
houses taken by the Board of Guardians for temporary accommodation. At 
present there are two houses occupied, both of which are in the town, but not 
near each other. In one of these houses there are 51 women, but I think from 
30 to 35 are as many as should be put in it; it is not at all suitable for the 
purpose, and in so dilapidated a state, that it cannot be properly repaired ; it 
was formerly the relief depot. The other house, in which there are 120 to 
130 boys, I do not think could safely contain more than 100 ; it is not at all 
suitable for the purpose, and it wiU be absolutely necessary to take the garden 
in the rear for airing ground. As this house is taken by the month only, it 
would not be desirable to make any outlay in alteration or improvement 
of it. At the Guardians’ request I looked at the old Court-house, which would 
give good accommodation for about 35 persons. I am not aware of any 
other houses in the neighbourhood, nor do I think there are any suitable for 
this purpose. 



No. 21. — The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians: -svith 

Order authorising Out-door Relief to the Able-bodied : — November 1, 1847- 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland to transmit to you herewith an order authorizing 
out-door relief in Newcastle Union under the 2nd section of the Irish Relief 
Extension Act for the period of two months from the date of the order. 

The Guardians will observe that no relief under this order can be legally 
given to persons in employment ; that such relief must be in food only, and 
that no able-bodied man should receive relief except in return for work. 

With regard to the nature of the work which should be offered to able- 
bodied men, the Commissioners desire to call attention to their letter of the 
8th ultimo (addressed to W. S. O’Brien, Esq., the Chaiiman of the Union), as 
containing their deliberate opinions on this subject. 

It will be seen that the Commissionei-s recommend the setting able-bodied 
men to stone-brealdng by task work as a condition of relief, and as much will 
depend on the knowledge, firmness, and discretion of those- who may be 
appointed to superintend the stone-breaking, the Commissioners cannot too 
strongly urge the Guardians to be peculiarly careful in permitting themselves 
to be influenced by no other considerations than those of personal fitness in 
selecting candidates for that highly important office. 

The Commissioners will take this opportunity of observing that in specifying 
the period of eight hours at least in the day. during which every able-bodied 
pauper should be required to work, they have made allowance for the present 
season of the year, and for the possible circumstance that some of the able- 
bodied paupers may come to the stone-breaking from a considerable distance. 
It is not, however, by any means intended to prevent the Guardians from 
requiring work during a still longer period of time. The period of eight hours 
is in fact merely the mwimum space of time in the day during which every 
able-bodied pauper should give the value of his labour to the Union.
