In conclusion the Commissioners desire to remind the Guardians that the 
accompanying order is merely temporary, and that they should in the mean- 
while use every possil^le exertion to obtain separate workhouse accommodation 
for the pauper children, in order that the existing workhouse may be made 
av£ulable almost exclusively for the relief of able-bodied men. 



No. 22. — Copy op Order. 

To the Guardians of the Poor of the Newcastle Union ; To the 
Clerk and other Officers of the said Union, and to all other persons 
whom it may concern. 

Whereas it has been shown to our satisfaction, that, by reason of the 
want of room in the workhouse of the said Union, adequate relief cannot be 
afforded therein to destitute poor persons not being persons permanently 
disabled, or destitute poor persons disabled by sickness or accident, or destitute 
poor widows having two or more legitimate children dependent on them, and 
it is expedient to authorize and empower the Guardians of the said Union to 
adu^ster relief out of the workhouse to sucli destitute poor persons, for a 
limited time as hereinafter mentioned. 

Now therefore, we, the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, do hereby authorize and empower the said 
Guardians to administer relief out of the workhouse, in food, to destitute poor 
persons not being persons permanently disabled from labour by reason of old 
^e, infirmity, or bodily or mental defect, and not being persons disabled from 
labour by reason of severe sickness or serious accident, and thereby deprived 
of the means of earning a subsistence for themselves and their families, whom 
they are liable by law to maintain, and not being poor widows having two or 
more legitimate children dependent on them, for two months next ensuing 
after the date of this order. 

And we do hereby make the following rules and regulations as to the 
granting, ordering, and giving of relief to all persons who shall be relieved by 

the said Guardians, under the authority of this order, that is to say : 

1. Ei-eiy person relieved under the authority of this order shall be relieved in food only, 
and such food shall, as far as is practicable, be cooked food. 

Every able-bodied male person relieved under the authority of this order shall, so far 
as IS practicable, be set to perform a task of work during eight hours at least ofevorv 
day for which he receives such relief. 

3. No able-bodied person who shall be in employment, nor any part of his or her familv, 
shall receive relief as a destitute pei'son under the authority of this order. 

And for the more effectual administration oi‘ relief under this order, we do 
hereby authorize and direct the Guardians oi‘ the said Union to appoint so 
many relieving officers as shall be found sufficient from time to time, to 
supermtend the labour of such persons as shall be set to work, in pursuance of 
the regulations in this order contained, and otherwise to assist in the admi- 
shaU t under this order, as the Guardians, subject to our approval, 

Sealed with our Seal, this first day of Novembei’, in the year of our 
Lord one thousand eight hundred and forty-seven. 

. E. T. B. Twisleton. 

T. N. Redington.

dated Newcastle, November 17, 1847. 

I HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter, dated 
12th instant, directing my attention to a passage marked “ A,” m a letter 
received from the clerk of the Guardians of the Rathkeale Union, viz., “ Some 
“ of the Guardians stated that the proceedings in the adjoining Union of New-

“ requiring that the same system should be adopted in the Rathkeale Union, 
“ and directing me to proceed, with the least possible delay, to Newcastle, to 

examine into the allegations adverted to, and to inquire to what extent the 
“ Commissioners’ order of the 1st instant, authorizing out-door relief to the 
“ able-bodied under certain conditions, is carried out according to its real intent 
“ and spirit.” 

I have the honour to report that I attended the meeting of the Guardians 
held here yesterday, being the first Board day after the receipt of your letter. 

The order issued by your Board on the 1st instant, authorizing out-door 
relief to the able-bodied, under certain conditions, has not been acted on in any 
case, nor does it appear to have had the effect of producing any test of labour 
to the recipients of relief. The amount of relief has been given in precisely 
the same manner before as subsequent to the issuing of that order. The relief 
was given previously in food — that is, in raw Indian meal — and that system 
has been continued since. 

-The accounts of the relieving officers are in a vbry unsatisfactory state ; 
many of the books have never been initialed by the chairman ; and, on bringing 
the matter before the Guardians, it was openly admitted that the time taken 
up in discussions upon the policy- of the law, and its mode of administra- 
tion, had not left time for the details of the relieving officers’ hooks. I sug- 
gested that the Guardians should do as had been done in other Umons, adjourn 
from day to day, fixing particular relieving officers to attend, so as to have the 
books carefully examined and duly authenticated. This course has been 
adopted, and to-day the Guardians met and proceeded to examine the Ballin- 
garry electoral division relieving o-fficers’ books. -BaUingarry electoral divi- 
sion adjoins the Unions of Rathkeale and Kilmallock, and it was in the first- 
mentioned electoral division the meetings were held, presided over by James 
Meehan, the resolutions adopted at 'which were forwarded to the Guardians of 
the Newcastle Union, and the Rev. Archdeacon Fitzgerald, tl^ pari^ priest, 
addressed a letter to the chaiiman, Wilham. Smith 0 Brien, Esq. Copies of 
these documents I have already transmitted ; and it being admitted generally 
by the Guardiarw, that the meeting so held, and the letter so addressed, was

I annex a return show'ing that from that date, namely, from the week ending 
16th October to the week ending 6th November, 14,564 persons over nine 
years of age, and Q872 persons under the age of nine, received 50 tons of Indian 
meal, of the value of 650/. 

It appeared, however, upon the examination of the books to-day, that the 
books of the relieving officer had not been initialed by any of the chairmen 
presiding at the meetings of the Guardians, that no order signed by the chair- 
man or Guardians had been issued to the contractor, but a list had been 
furnished by the relieving officer to the contractor, who delivered the quantities 
to the persons in these lists. It does not appear that there was any check upon 
the relieving officer or contractor, both having unlimited power to do as they 
pleased. The relieving officer stated he had regularly attended the meetings 
of the Guardians, but could not get his books checked off, the pressure of other 
business was so great, and that the Guardians contented themselves with giving 
verbal directions to him. It is needless to say the out-door relief list was not 
made up, nor was there a single entry from the electoral division of Ballingarry 
in the out-door relief register. There was not a single entry in the relieving 
officer’s receipt and expenditure book. ° 

The value of the electoral division of Ballingarry is 1 6,8 1 5/. Ratos to upwards 
of 3,000/. have been made, but only 234/. has been paid in. The balance against 
the electoral division on the 29th September was 370/. 19 a-. lO^c/., so that 
Ballingarry electoral division is stiU in debt to the Union, altliough meal to the 
amount of 6507. has been distributed in four weeks, which, if continued at the 
same rate, would amount to 8,450/., or 10s. to the pound in the year. 

It is admitted by many Guardians that the resolution of the 5th October, to 
grant out-door relief provisionally for one week was hasty and ill-judged, and 
has led to the embarrassment of the Union. When once the order was given 
by the Guardians they lost all power or control over their own acts.

culties of the present position of the Union.

No. 25.— The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians : — 
November 22, 1847- 

I AM directed by the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, to state, that on the 12th instant, they instructed 
their Inspector, Mr. Hancock, to inquire and report to thein, wlicther tlie 
Commissioners’ order, of the 1st instant, authorizing out-door relief to the able- 
bodied, under certain conditions, was carried out according to its real extent 
and sihrit. 

The Commissioners have since received a report, dated 17th instant, from 
Mr. Hancock, in which he states that the order adverted to, has not been acted 
on in any case, and that it does not appear to have had the efi'ect of producing 
any test of labour to the recipients of relief. Mr. Hancock I'urther reports that 
the accounts of the relieving officers are in a very unsati-sfactory state ; that 
many of the books have never been initialed by the chairman, and that on 
bringing the matter before the Guardians, it was admitted that the time talcen 
up in discussions upon the policy of the law, and its mode of administration, 
had not left time for the details of the relieving officers’ books. 

Mr. Hancock states, however, that the Guardians, at his suggestion, agreed 
to adjourn from day to day, fixing particular relieving officers to attend, so as 
to have the books carefully examined and duly authenticated. 

In pursuance of that suggestion it appears that the Guardians met on the 
1 7th instant, and proceeded to examine the Ballingarry electoral division re- 
lieving officer’s books, and Mr. Hancock gives a detail of the facts connected 
with the administration of relief in that division. 

It appears that on the 5th October last, a proposal was accepted to supply 
that electoral division with Indian meal, at the rate of 13/. per ton, and liy a 
return from the relieving officer, which Mr. Hancock has forwarded to the 
Commissioners, it appears that from that date to the 6th instant, 14, .564 jicrsons 
over nine years of age, and 2372 persons under the age of nine, received 50 tons 
of Indian meal, value 650/', yet on examination of the books of the relieving 
officer, it was found that they had not been initialed by any of the chairmen 
presiding at the meetings of the Guardians ; that no order signed by tlie chair- 
man of Guardians had been issued to the contractor, but that a list had been 
furnished by the relieving officer to the contractor, who delivered the quanti- 
ties to the persons in the lists. 

Mr. Hancock further states, that it does not appear that there was any check 
upon the relieving officer or contractor, and that both had unlimited power to 
do as they please ; that the relieving officer stated he had regularly attended 
the meetings of the Guardians, but could not get books checked off, the pressure 
of other business was so great, and that the Guardians contented themselves 
with giving verbal directions to him. 

The out-door relief list was not made up, nor was tlicre a single entry from 
the electoral division of Ballingarry in the out-door relief register, and there 
was not a single entry in the relieving officer’s receipt and expenditure book. 

On a review of the above facts, the Commissioners are of opinion that there 
has been a great dereliction of duty on the part of the Ne\^’’castle Board of 
Guardians, and that they and the relieving officers have in many instances ex- 
pended the funds of the Union in an unauthorized and illegal maimer. The Com- 
missioners liave accordingly forwarded to the auditor a copy of Mr. Hancock’s 
Report, and they liave instructed the auditor rigidly to disallow in the accounts 
all sums expended for relief which shall not have been given in accordance 
with the Irish Poor Relief Acts, and with the Commissioners’ regulations. It 
is further the settled intention of the Commissioners, that every individual or 
individuals debited by the auditor with the sums disallowed by him shall be 
proceeded against under the 28th section of the Irish Relief Extension Act, and 
shall become responsilile for the money of the rate-payers, which he or they 
may have expended contrary to law. 

The Comraissiouevs will likewise cause strict inquiry to be made into the 
manner in which the relieving officers have discharged their functions. 

Having made these remarks, the Commissioners now call upon the Newcastle 
Board of Guardians to take immediate steps for administering relief in future, 
in conformity with the Commissioners’ General Order of the 2nd of August

last and witK the Commissioiiei’s’ order of the 1st instant, to Newcastle Union, Keycastle Union.

Commissioners, The Guardians therefore now occupy a peculiarly important 
and responsible situation, and it will be in the highest degree unsatislactory, 
and even discreditable to them, if they prove themselves une<iual to cope with 
the difficulties which surround them ; and if they now precipitate the Union 
into a course of unauthorized expenditure, the effects will be almost equally 
disastrous to every class in the Union, whether consisting of proprietors, occu- 
piers, or labourers.

Lieut. Hotham, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners:— 

November 5, 1847. 

I ATTENDED the meeting of the Board of Guardians of the above-named 

and Ventry were allowed by all the Guardians to he 
in a deplorable state, and so much so, that it was asserted that any further 
delay in affording relief might be productive of the most serious consequences. 

At the- same time it was allowed by all the Guardians that no dependence 

whatever could be placed on the books of the relie^ng officers. 

Thus the Board was x>laced in the situation of being compeUed either to

Tralee Union.

188 PAPERS RELATING TO THE RELIEF OF DISTRESS, 

delay the relief until the books had been completely remodelled and oxamiucd 
or else to commence giving relief while they were of opinion that the really 
distressed might not be those who received it. ^ 

Under these circumstances, and placing no faith on the boolis ol‘ the re- 
lieving officers, they determined to make the workhouse the test of destitution 
in all cases, by removing tire first two classes mentioned in Circular, No. 433, 
M/47, and_ receiving into the house all applicants, whether able-bodied or 
infirm, retaining the able-lrodied in the house, and granting, after a -throe weeks’ 
residence in the house, out-door reliel' to those who proved to be of the first 
two classes before mentioned. 

But in effecting this an olwious difficulty arose ; many of the present inmates 
have resided in the house so long, that they have actually no house to return 
to, and scarcely clothes to put on. 

. On this it was proposed on the one hand, that besides their ration of meal they 
should receive one halfpenny per diem for each adult, and one fartliiug per 
diem for each child to enable them to supply themselves witli clothes and 
shelter. 

On the other hand, it was argued that giving money was dangerous, and that 
the finances of the Union could not bear even that small allowance. 

It w'as finally resolved tliat a temporary pecuniary allowance should be given 
to those at present in the house who should be ordered to q;uit it, but that this 
should not be extended to any future comers. 

The day's proceedings were interrupted by a tumultuous assembly, chiefly 
from tlic town of Tralee, bearing a black flag with words in white on it, “ Flag 
of Distress,” who making tlieir w'ay to the workhouse broke open the gates of 
the enclosure, but committed no fui-ther violence ; the military and police were 
immediately sent for, and on their arrival the ringleaders were arrested without 
any resistance, and the mob dispersed ; and, as usual in such cases, those com- 
posing the mob were far from being in a distressed state. 

The Commissioners will perceive from the above report that our real diffi- 
culty arises from the inexperience or inefficiency of the relieving officers, 
upon whom the Board of Guardians are not disposed to place the sliglitcst 
dependence. Every allowance should, however, be made for them ; succeeding 
to a low administration of relief, they arc placed in a most difficult position ; 
everybody who received relief under the former system thinks him.self much 
aggrieved if his name is not returned under this ; thus the relieving officers are 
overwhelmed with applications, whilst it must be confessed that the shades of 
Irish jJoverty are so nicely defined as to require a very careful and experienced 
observer to know where the correct line should be drawn. 



Lieut. Hotham to the Poor Law Cohmisssioners. 

Tralee, NoMemher 10, 1847. 

I ATTENDED the meeting of the Board of Guardians held yesterday. 

I had previously determined that it would be my duty to recommend the 
Board to apply to the Poor Law Commissioners to talce advantage of the 6th 
section, Act 10 Vic., cap. 31, and divide themselves into District Committees. 
1 his the Board, without mucli deliberation, determined upon. 

The duties of the relieving officers were then brought forward by me. 

The Board had previously given their directions only to enter such names 
down in their application for relief book as appeared to them to Ise proper sub- 
jects for relief; but such instructions appeared to me not only to be directly 
contrary to your orders wherein it is specified that all ajjplicatioiis must be 
entered, but also calculated to throw a very heavy responsibility on the 
relieving officers, which they were not fitted by their previous habits or rank 
in life to bear. 

I therefore maintained that it was the duty of the relieving officers to enter 
all applications down, referring tlie applicants in every case, where it was prac- 
ticable, to the Guardians themselves to be rejected or allowed, and that it was 
the duty of the Guardians to investigate and decide upon each separate case, to 
enable them to do which the 6th section of Extended Poor Law was passed. 

The Board, after a lengthened discussion, unanimously adopted these views, 
and recorded them in their resolutions.

I 1-i.iVE the honour of informing you tliat, on inspecting the Kanturk 
•\vorkhousc, I Ibimd it to contain 1351 paupers; 582 of these were admitted 
in the week ended the 30th ultimo, every one of which was sent into the dor- 
mitories in their own clothes, there being none in the master’s hands to give 
them. 

You have it on the Guardians’ minutes, that, in the week ended the 13th

those 335 went out on tlie promise of getting out-door relief. They comprised 
33 aged and infirm men, 7S women chiefly widows, 98 boys, 111 girls, and

The dormitory accommodation of the house, including a shed in each of the

clean and in good condition, far better than could be expected under the 
circumstances ; but no attention to them can keep paupers so crowded in good 
health. On going through the adult male yard I was surprised by an immense 
number of able-bodied men, many of them fine atliletic fellows from 30 to 50 
year’s old, but a large proportion from 18 or 20 to 30. Some had tolerable 
clothing, but generally their attire was very wretched. They were clamorous 
for better food, and for obtaining it outside; and 1 shoirld much apprehend 
that they may be easily excited to such acts as the master rvill be unable to 
repress, although I find he is of a different opinion. I am assured that they 
entered the house from having no employment merely. I should state that the • 
number of this class is 468, — 400 at least of 'which are of the description above 
alluded to. They present a reckless appearance — ready, I should fear, lor any 
foolish but mischievous acts. I may perhaps be mistaken m this opinion, bih 
I feel it right to express it. I reasoned with them, and, for the moment, with 
some effect on them ; but I doulit the pei-maneucy of any impression now made 
in that way. _ j i 

I next inspected a tan-yard and store w’hich have been rented by the 
Guardians for female paupers. It contains 371 women, giids, and children, 
and some, but not many, boys. The day-room for all these is only 78 by 19, 
and 7^ feet high. There is a sufficiency of windows at one side, but none at 
the other. On my entrance it was crowded with a dense mass of th^e paupers 
in the greatest state of confusion and disorder ; and as the space is so inade- 
quate, and all in their own wretched garments, many filthy and many very 
scanty, the foetor and uncomfoi*tableness 'ivas most distressing. 

I should add that this day-room is boarded, hut that the boards are placed 
over tan-pits from which the water was baled out. These pits are mft hollow, 
and may naturally be supposed to be moist, possibly to gradually have water 
accumulated in them. Of course, even if there was no overcrowding, this 
must l 3 e deemed a very unfit place for the paupers. Altogether it )s very 
objectionable. w icn

It is sufficient to state that the dormitoiy accommodation of tins store does

Mr. Crawford, Inspector, to the Poor Law Comwissionkrs: — 
JSovemher 2, 1847. 

I HAVE the honour to inform you that on this day I attciiidod a meeting 
of the Board of Guardians at Kanturk. 

Tlie difficulties in which the Guardians are placed have become so great 
that they came mianimously to a resolution tendering their resignation as a 
Board. 

I do not think any other course can be adopted than forthwith to dissolve 
the Board, and appoint paid officers to manage the affairs ol'tho Union. 

The Guardians have got themselves involved in difficulties of no common 
kind; tliey have filled their poorliouse to such an extent as to make it a matter 
of certainty that pestilence will break out among its crowded inmates, being in 
number nearly 500 above that limited by the order of tlie Commissiontivs. 

The tendency to disease is much aggravated by the inmates being nearly 
altogether dressed in their own clothes, the Guardians not having sufficient 
clothing for so large a number of inmates. 

I find that the relieving officers have been giving out-door roliel’, without first 
having had their books initialled by the chairman, or their accounts revised ; 
and I fear tliat the greatest abuse is taking place in this q^uartcr from the 
Guardians’ continued neglect of checking their acf'ounts. 

The expenditure of the Union under this system is now amounting to upwards 
of 400/. per week, the effect of which will, in a short time, l)c to plunge the 
Union in inextricable debt. 

I consider the present Board as completely incompetent to grapjdc with the 
difficulties in which they are placed, and • I must repeat the expression of my 
opinion that it is absolutely necessary that the Board sliould, in compliance 
with their wishes, be at once dissolved, and paid officers appointed in their 
place. 



The Poor Law Commissioners to the Clerk of the Kanturk Union : — 
Novemher 8, 1847. 

I AM directed l3y the Commissioners for administering the Laws for the 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland to state that they have had under considm’ation 
the resolutions jiassed by the Board of Guardians of Kanturk Union on Tuesday, 
the 2nd instant, to the effect tliat the Board tender their resignation to the 
Commissioners, and req^uest them to appoint paid Guardians, as they find they 
cannot perform their duties from the difficulty of workuig the iirescnt Act in 
their Union. 

In reference to that resolution, the Commissioners desire to state that they 
do not consider it competent for any Board of Guardians to resign their office, 
and to relieve themselves, by their own act, of the responsibilities and duties 
which have been imposed on them by the Legislature. The Commissioners, 
therefore, would by no means consent to dissolve the present Board of 
Guardians merely because the Guardians had tendered their resignation, and 
had expressed a wish that paid officers should be appointed to manage the 
affairs of Kanturk Union. 

Still there are certain circumstances connected with the past conduct of the 
Kanturk Board of Guardians which lead the Commissioners to tlic conclusion 
that the Guardians have failed duly and effectually to discharge their duties ; 
and on this account the Commissioners have decided to issue an order for the 
formal dissolution of the Board. 

The Commissioners received on the 2nd instant a report from their Inspector, 
Mr. Crawford, in which he states that the Guardians have filled the workhouse 
to such an extent as to make it a matter of certainty that pestilence will break 
out among its crowded inmates, being in number nearly 500 above' that limited 
by the order of the Commissionere.

Mr. Crawford further states that the relieving officers have been giving out-

Mr. Crawford further states that the expenditure of the Union now amounts, 
under this system, to upwards of 400/. j)er week. 

The Commissioners have received a report from their Inspector, Mr. Phelan, 
from which it appears that, on his recent inspection of the workhouse, he found 
that it contained 1851 paiipei’s, 582 of these having been admitted in the week 
ended the 30th ult., eveiy one of whom Mr. Phelan states were sent into the 
dormitories in their own clothes, the master having none in Ms possesion to 
give them. 

Mr. Phelan stat^ that the dormitory accommodation of the house, including 
the shed in each of the idiot yards, and also the idiots’ cells, day-rooms, and 
dormitories, is not sufficient for more than 910; and that 1474 having been 
placed in these apartments, several of the dormitories are greatly overcrowded. 

Mr. Phelan states that he inspected a tan-yard and store, which have been 
rented by the Guardians for the accommodation of female paupers, containing 
371 women, girls, and clrildren, and some, but not many, boys ; that the day- 
room for all these is only 78 by 19 feet in length, and 7^ feet in height; that 
there is a sufficiency of windows at one side, but none at the other ; that on 
Mr. Phelan’s entrance it was crowded with a dense mass of these paupers in the 
greatest state of confusion and disorder, and, as the space is so inadequate, and 
all are in their own wretched garments, the fostor was most distressing. _ 

Mr. Phelan finally states tliat the dormitory accommodation of this store 
does not exceed 150, and that he cannot doubt that, from the insalubrity and 
overcrowding of the place, disease mil arise, and must rapidly extend among 
these paupers. Such, in fact, appears to he already the case, as the paupers 
were only five days in the store, and Mr. Plielan found that 11 cases of fever

eight two days before. 

On a consideration of all the facts stated in these Reports, the Commissioners 
are of opinion that there has been a serious default of duty on the part of the 
Kantiivk Board of Guardians. The Commissioners accordingly tr^smit here- 
with an order for the dissolution of the Board, under the provisions of tire 
18th section of the Irish Relief Extension Act; and they will proceed, with 
the least possible delay, to appoint paid officers to administer relief to the 
destitute according to the intentions of the Legislature.

Lieut.-Col. Claiuce, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 
Noveniher 5, 1847. 

I HAVE the honour to report to you that I arrived here on the 3lst ultimo, 
and immediately proceeded to put myself in communication with the ex-officio 
Guardians. 

I afterwards made a most minute inspection of the workhouse, wMch I foimd 
perfectly clean, but in a lamentable state of deficiency of every requisite. 
Paupers three or four in a bed, for want of straw to fill tbe bed-ticks, and that 
in use not having been changed since the house was opened in October, 1846. 
Broken glass throughout the basement story, and not even the necessary imple- 
ments for cleansing the premises. As is always the case in a builffing diverted 
from its original purpose, many inconveniences exist, to remedy which a greater 
expense is incuiTed than if a suitable building had been erected in an eligible 
site, which is not here the case, it being neaidy four miles from the town, and 
consequently a most exorbitant addition is made to all contracts on account of 
carriage. j • t. 

I yesterday attended the ordinary meeting of the Board of Guardians; there 
was a tolerably full attendance, hut only one ex-officio Guardian w^ present. 
After the preliminary business I produced my commission and appointment to 
the Union, and explained at considerable length what was expected from the

country. I impressed most strongly that the first step was to obtain funds, by 
putting the rate of 3^. in the pound (for wliich a resolutio3i had been passed), in 
immediate course of collection ; but it appeared that the collectors had not per- 
fected their securities. The Guardians entered into tlic consideration of the

I explained to tlie collectors that upon their exertions in a great measure 
depended the weliare of the country, aJid that they should perform 
their duty with the strictest impartiality; that they should not commence their 
collection with the lowest class of rate-payers, but with the immediate lessors, 
and their own nearest relations and friends, and thus convince the poorer classes 
that the law was eq^xtally applicable to the rich as to themselve.s ; moreover, as 
the majority of them were rate-payers, I should expect the first receipt in their 
cheq^ue Ijooks to be from themselves, as an example. 

A lengthened discussion took place as to the mode of relief that should be 
adopted, some of the Guardians strenuously insisting that the workhouse should 
be reserved lor the aged, impotent, and orphans, and that the out-door relief 
should be given to the able-bodied. I urged every argument suggested by my 
experience against this proposition, and succeeded in inducing them to abandon 
the idea ; and in order to afford additional accommodation, it was resolved to 
sulimit for your approval that the sick should be removed to the district Fever 
Hospital (in which there is abundant space) under the care of their own medical 
officer ; this would give room for 100 additional inmates. It ivas also resolved 
to solicit you to increase the number of 400, stated in the order of the 23rd 
March of the present year, to 500, and I perfectly concur in oi>iniou with the 
Guardians tliat this might be done without inconveniently crowding the liouse, 
as two temporary sheds have been erected as fcivor hospitals, w'hich are not 
required for that purpose; and I would propose that the day-rooms within the 
building should be converted into dormitories, and one-half of oacli of the 
sheds used as day-rooms, and the other half appropriated to a jnu'posc I shall 
introduce hereafter. 

The number of children in the house is about 225. I have made every 
inquiry as to the possibility of finding premises to lodge them elsewhere, but I 
fear it is impracticable. Blany of these belong to parents who are not inmates, 
they having been taken in during the last spring, in order (as the Guar<lians 
say) to enable the fatlrer to support the remainder of the lamily on his inade- 
quate wages. It is very difficult to shake the strong prejudice that exists on this 
point, which is so false in priucijffe. Again, there are many illegitimate 
children in the house whose fathers are well known. I have directed a list of 
all such to be prepared, and the Guardians will, I believe, compel the fathers 
to repay the expenses that have been incurred, and to support them for the 
future : but even with the additional accommodation proposed, and the dimi- 
nution in tins class, I consider that out-door relief to the able-bodied will 
become an imperious necessity. I shall be very unwilling to have recourse to 
this measure, and nothing short of the most positive conviction that it cannot be 
avoided will induce me to recommend its adoption : and in the mean time I 
would request your instruction, whether labom- should be exacted for the relief 
so afforded. 

The distress for want of money is extreme, and the credit of the establish- 
ment at so low an ebb, that it is almost impossible to induce parties to furnish 
supplies, and every advantage is taken of their necessities by demanding a large 
per centage above the market price for every article. Bread (even for the sick) 
canuot be procured. The Guardians informed me that Mr. Crawford had 
upon several occasions procured them advances, and expressed a hope that I 
would do the same. I assured them that I had the desire to serve them in 
every possible way, but that I had no reason to believe that such a request 
could be acceded to, and that before asking the question I must be thoroughly 
convinced that every practicable effort was being made by themselves. At the 
same time, if there be any available funds at your disposal, I would respectfully 
recommend that a small sum should be advanced until the rate is in course of 
collection, particularly to provide proper diet for the hospital patients.

Some allusion was made to applying for a paid Board of Guardians. 1 CahircLvcen Umoii.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Lieut-Colonel Clarke 
November 16, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in 
Ireland have again had before them your report of the 5th instant, relating to 
the Cahirciveen Union, together with the observations of Mr. Crawford, Poor 
Law Inspector, on the matters to which you refer. 

With respect to the state of the workhouse, Mr. Crawford informs the Com- 
missioners that he represented to the Guardians strongly when he last visited 
the house the necessity of obtaining straw for bedding, and of having the 
windows mended, and that orders were given that both of these matters should 
be attended to. The Commissioners request that you will be so good as to ' 
press the subject again on the consideration of the Guardians at their text 
meeting, if the deficiencies complained of have not already been remedied. 

The Commissioners await Mr. Phelan’s report, as to an alteration of the order 
which at present restricts the number to be admitted into the workhouse to 
400 ; but they desire me in the mean time to state that Mr. Crawford concurs 
in your views as to the probability that 500 can be accommodated in the house 
without danger to health, and arrangements may at once be made for the re- 
ception of that number. ^ 

As regards the statement made to you with respect to the number 01 children 
in the workhouse, Mr. Crawford states that the Guardians never, so far as he 
was aware, acted upon the principle of admitting parts of families. lu all cases 
where such admissions have taken place, the parent liable according to the 53rd 
section of the Irish Poor Relief Act, for the support of such inmates, should be 
required to support them, or to join his family in the workhouse, ^ should be 
proceeded against in pursuance of the provisions of the 10th and 11th Vict, 
cap. 84. It is to be observed that the mothers and not the fathei-s 01 illegiti- 
mate children are liable by law for the maintenance of such children, and that 
until the Guardians shall have declared any relief aflbrded in the workhouse 
to be by way of loan in pursuance of the 55tli section of the Irish Pool Reiiet 
Act and the 23rd article of the General Regulations, the Guardians cannot take 
legal proceedings for the recovery of the cost of such relief. 

With respect to the means of providing for the maintenance of the workhouse 
inmates, and affording relief to the destitute poor in the Union. I am to stete 
that there are no funds at the Commissioners’ disposal for this purpose, and that 
the funds of the British Association will in no case be advanced untd it sbail be 
shown that due exertions have been made to make and collect adequate rates 
in the Union.

Lieut-Colonel Clarke, Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 
November 11, 1847. 

I THIS day attended the ordinary meeting of the Board of Guardians. 
It was expected that the collectors would have had the rate-hooks comidcted, 
so as to enable the Guardians to sign the wai’rants lor collection ; but such was 
not the case, and the meeting was adjourned until Monday next, ivlicii I hope 
to be able to communicate to you that this very necessary preliminary has been 
effected, as it is impossible to make any arrangements until funds shall be 
procured. 

I find that the collection of the last rate has been satisfactory ; and, after 
allowing for poundage to collectors, and for parties against whom it would be 
useless to proceed, a very small sum (probably not exceeding 30/. for the wliole 
Union) will be in arrear. The Union treasurer not having sent in his book in 
time for the meeting, prevents my stating the sum that has been collected 
during the past M'eek, but it is generally understood that the principal dolaulters 
have paid. 

I explained to the Guardians that it was hopeless to expect assistance from 
any quarter unless the greatest exertions should be made by themselves ; and 
they one and all assured me tliat they would work with me most cordially. 
Mr. James O’Connell, who is an extensive proprietor in the Union, is about to 
call a general meeting of the proprietary. His views are very satislactory, and 
I hope his influence may induce othei^ to adopt them. He fully admits the 
absolute necessity of maldng every sacrifice to meet the present rate ; and pro- 
poses tha.t the landlords should immediately pay their own proportion, and ad- 
vance that for their tenants, which they would have the right to deduct from the 
next gale of rent, and repudiates altogether the idea of taking money on account 
of arrears, and thus evading the rate, unless it be over and above the current 
gale. I much wish the same liberal spirit was more prevalent. 

No measure has given more universal satisfaction than that of giving food 
ai^ clothing to the children of destitute parents attending the existing schools, 
which will, I believe, do more to soften down religious animosities than any 
1 ^^^ could have been devised. I am in communication with the clergy 
of both persuasions throughout the Union on this subject, ajid to-morrow com- 
mence a tour of inspection in order to ascertain the extent of school accommo- 
dation in each electoral division, and shall, in a few days, be prepared to make 
a full report to the Count Strzelecki,

Lieut-Colonel Clarke, Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 
November 17, 1847. 

The rate-hooks and warrants were signed for four electoral divisions, 
when it was found that the clerk had neglected to provide the necessary forms of 
notice, which wdll cause a further delay in the collection. I cautioned him in 
strong terms on his want of forethought, and on some neglect of orders, which 
I hope may not occur again. 

The warrant for Valencia cannot be signed until the rate on the slate mines 
shall be revised, which I have directed in accordance with your instructions. 

I lind great irregularity has prevailed in giving cheques on the Union trea- 
surer in anticipation of funds, and thus a favoured i'ew of the creditor obtain 
an advantage over the general body ; and a gi-eat hardship is inflicted on the 
collectors, who are obliged to pay in the full amount of their collection, and 
have no chance of receiving theii* pomidage mitil all outstanding cheques 
shall be paid. These at the present moment amount to upwards of 400/. I 
shall endeavour to have a resolution passed to-morrow to put a stop to this 
practice, and at the same time to fix the first meeting in each month as the 
only day for giving cheques, which will prevent advantage being taken of a 
thin meetiug to favour particular parties so frequently as it is done at present. 

With regard to increased accommodation within the house, Mr. Phelan is of 
opinion that with the sheds it will contain 532, being 32 beyond the number I 
stated, and he has, I presume, reported to that effect. He has also certified 
that the sheds are substantially built. Having had some experience in that 
description of building, I can state them to be in perfect accordance with the 
plans and specifications of your architect.

having this defect remedied at present. 

A difficulty arises respecting the occupation of. sheds, wliichisthat of render- 
ing them weather-proof. There is no tradesman who will give the Guardians 
credit for the requisite materials ; and before they can touch- one pemiy of tlie 
current rate, upwards of 1 lOOZ. must be coUected to meet outstanding cheques. 
With every possible exertion, this will require several weeks •, and, in the mean 
time, valuable room, so much required, is left unavailable. 

I have a return before me of the children now in the workhouse, which 
shows 93, whose parents are also there ; 69 oi*phans and deserted children ; 
and 30 who have been admitted without their parents. I shall bring the subject 
before the Board on Thursday. 

I have had the honour to submit my ideas respecting the measures of the 
British Relief Association to the Count Strzelecki ; and I am happy to say they 
are in perfect accordance witli his own. I am using the utmost exertions for 
bringing them into immediate operation.

The Poor Law Commissioners to Lieut-Col. Clarke i—iVeyemier 26,1847.

presume that the hardships were foreseen hy the legislature, and 
on the whole, a less evil than the permitting any one to receive reliet irompoor

The Commissioners take this opportunity of observing, that an individual 
holding more than a quai'ter of an acre of land, cannot legally receive reiiei,. 
either in a workhouse or out of a workhouse, from the poor-rates.

Cahirciveen Union, able-bodied; a rush is made for admittance to the 'vvorkhonse by persons who 
have no intention of remaining. I was made aware that siicli would be the 
case yesterday, and having made a very minute examination, accompanied by 
Dr. Berry, of the extent of accomodation, I agi’eed in opinion with him, that it 
would be advisable to admit as many as possible ; accordingly 71 applicants 
were received, making the total number within the house 460, and, as I antici- 
pated, many, finding that all deemed eligible obtained admission, went away ; 
and it is reported to me, that six of those received, discharged themselves this 
morning. 

Taking the circumstances of the Union into serious consideration, I am of 
opinion that it would be hopeless to expect that the 3^. rate, now in course of 
collection, will be very productive. The heavy amount of debt, that must be 
discharged, will absorb the greater part, if not the whole, of this collection ; 
and I much doubt the capability of the country to meet another rate for a 
considerable time to come; with this in view, it may probably bo expedient to 
make the relief intended by the British Association available for the impotent. 
I perceive that the number of persons of that class, not possessing land, who 
received relief, on the 4th July, amounted to 1225. I think many persons are 
included iu that number to whom the term is not strictly applicble; but 
assuming it is coi-rect, they might be fed from the soup-kitchens I am establish- 
ing for the schools ; but in addition to these, there will be a great mass of des- 
titution to provide for. The total number of persons, not holding land, who 
received relief on the 4th July was 10,340. The deduction, I calculate upon, 
is 3000 children attending schools, 1225 impotent persons, 600 in the work- 
house, and 1000, representing 200 labourers employed in drainage, and leaving 
4515. I excluded from the calculation all persons holding land, as there 
appears little disposition to surrender ; indeed, there is more activity disjilayed 
in collecting manure and cultivation than I have ever before seen at this period 
of the year. In. some parts of the Union, ejectments on a large scale will be 
carried into effect, but this may probably be met by a greater extent of employ- 
ment than I have calculated ; but I am of opinion that 4500 persons beyond 
the extent of relief I have proposed, and the capabilities of the country to pro- 
vide for, will recjuii’e food. To organize a plan for relieving tliis number will 
require much consideration, particularly with regard to the nature and extent 
of labour to be executed and as to the management ; but I would recommend, 
ill the strongest possible terms, that funds should not be entrusted to local 
Committees, as under the Temporary Relief Act.

Colonel Clarke, Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 
Novemler 27, 1847- , 

I HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 25th 
instant, enclosing a further statement of the Rev. Eugene O Sullivan, relating 
to the distress existing in the electoral division of Killorglin. In my weekly 
report of the 26th instant, I mentioned that I had received a letter from the 
reverend gentleman, on the same subject, which I transmit herewith, with a 
copy of my reply, and his answer thereto ; and I beg to refer to that repoit, as 
to the steps adopted by the Guardians. 

It appears to me the object is to force the Guardians to commence the system 
of out-door relief, which they have determined against so long as in-door ac- 
commodation can be provided. I have no doubt that there is a considerable 
extent of destitution, but do not tliink it greater than in other electoral divi- 
sions. That part of Killorglin attached to this Union is not the poorest of 
the division. And when I recollect the tenns of Captain Stewart s report, and 
the assurance of Mr. James O’Connell (whose information and veracity may 
be depended upon), that Killorglin has received greater assistance in propor- 
tion to its real wants, than any other electoral divisions, I cannot but suppose 
the reverend gentleman’s statement is somewhat highly coloured. 

I have reason to believe that on tlie next Board day an attempt will be made 
from Killorglin to swamp the accommodation in the workhouse, of which I 
have apprised the Guardians, in order that they may be prepared. And I 
warned the relieving officer, that if he hired conveyances for persons who were 
able to walk, or gave provisional relief to those not entitled to it, the responsi- 
bility would rest upon himself.

Sir, Killorglin, November 22, 1847- 

In the Killorglin electoral division of the Cahircivecn Union the most appalling desti- 
tution prevails. NoSiing whatsoever has been done to relieve the blind, the maimed, the 
widows, and orphans, the infirm from old age and from sickness, though, by law, they are

my opinion, before relief can reach them some must die fi-om stai-vation; at present they are 
mere spectres. 

Prom the information which you have communicated to the Poor Law Commissioners it 
strikes me, that you are of opinion that no distress prevails in this electoral division, and you 
have arrived at this conclusion, from the fact, that no applications have been made for 
admittance into the workhouse since the Temporary Relief Act expired; now, the reason why 
applications for admittance have not been made, by persons from this district, was, because it 
was generally believed, on the best authority, that the workhouse was full. Even if there was 
room for a great many in it, the impotent classes could not avail themselves of it. A journey 
of nearly 30 miles could not be accomplished by persons who are wasted away by age, famine, 
and sickness. I respectfully implore of you to adopt some means to save the people from 
certain death.

SiRj Killorglin, November 24, 1847. 

I HAVE the lionour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of yesterday's date, and 
i-egret to state that it is perfectly unsatisfactory. Before the arrangetnents you contemplate 
are complete, many will be in their grave, and I envy not the position of those who have

Guardians were compelled to give out-door relief to the impotent class. What I stated was, 
that that class comprising, as it does, the crippled, , the blind, the infirm, tlie widows and 
orphans, are legally entitled to out-door relief. If this class is not legally entitled to relief, 
the Guardians of the Killarney Unions are acting illegally in giving relief to them. Not a 
very likely thing ! The Poor Law Commissioners, in their Instructions to Relieving Officers, 
evklently’contemplate giving out-door relief to the above class. Therefore, sustained by such 
authorities, I am right in slating that they are entitled to relief. You concur with me with 
regard to the inconvenient extent of the Union. But why is not this remedied ? You also 
state that, under the 4th article of Regulations for Relieving Officers, provision has been made 
for the conveyance of sick and infirm persons. Why has not that provision been carried into

visilod this electoral division, because, of course, he has received no instructions to do so.

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor 
in Ireland, have had under consideration your report of the 27th instant, 
relating to the distress alleged to exist in the Killorglin division of the Cahir- 
civeen Union, and enclosing your correspondence on the subject with the Rev. 
Eugene O’Sullivan. 

In reference thereto, I am directed to state that the Commissioners recom- 
mend you to advise the Guardians at their next meeting, if there should be a 
large number of able-bodied applicants, at once to clear the house of such per- 
sons as may be fit to remove, and can be legally relieved out of doors, under the

of the able-bodied applicants as may appear to be admissible, and be the most 
destitute ; after which, if unable to deal with all the cases, it would be 
advisable to adjourn for a few days, and send the relieving officers to investi- 
gate the cases remaining, by the local intiuiries which they are the proper 
persons to make.

Extract from Minutes of the Guardians of September 7, being a Letter in 
reply to a communication of the Union Inspector. 

In reply to your inquiries with respect to the steps this Board have taken 
for the collection of the rate required by the Relief Commissioners for out-dooi* 
relief in this Union, we beg to inform you that ou^the 29th of Juno last we 
struck a rate of 3 j. in the pound, being the amount required by the Commis- 
sioners for that purpose, and advertised for collectors, but no one offered ; we 
requested the Poor Law Commissioners to send down persons for the purpose ; 
they however directed us again to advertise, which we did, and after several 
attempts, and the loss of some time, one pci*son offered for four of the electoral 
divisions of the Union, and we appointed him, and to remove any difficulty fixed 
his security at 500/, although the amount of his collection would be nearly 
4000/., and we had hitherto always required security for the full amount, The 
person appointed was unalile however to get security for that small amount, thc^ 
impossibility of collecting so large a rate being so apparent. 

Having thus made every exertion in our power to carry out the directions of 
the Commissioners, and being in debt 3000/. for the supplies for the house, 
which we could no longer keep open without funds, and the time when the rate 
could be collected passing away, we saw the necessity of immediately altering 
the rate to an amount which it might be possible to have collected, and wo have 
accordingly struck a rate, the highest that in our opinion could be collected 
now, and which we expect to have in progress of collection without delay. 



The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians : — 
September 18, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor 
in Ireland, have had under their consideration the resolution of the Board of 
Guardians of Bantry Union of the 7th instanf^ substituting a scale of rates on 
the several electoral divisions of the Union for one adopted on the 29th of June 
last. 

The rates which the Guardians propose to levy are the following : — 

On six divisions, Is. 6d. in the pound. 

On two divisions, 2^. ditto. 

On one division, 3s. ditto. 

These rates, if adopted, would yield only 3500/., a sum not much more than 
sufficient to cover the existing liabilities of the Guardians, and no provision 
would remain to meet their prospective expenditure. 

The Commissioners, under these circumstances, earnestly request the Guard- 
ians to reconsider the amount of rate necessary to be levied in each electoral 
division of the Union. 

The Commissioners are of opinion that no less a rate than 3s. in the pound 
on each division of the Union would suffice for the vp^ants of the Guardians ; 
and the Commissioners strongly recommend the Guardians to adopt a rate for 
ordinary expenditure to that amount. 

by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 203 

At the same time, the Commissioners desire to acquaint the Guardians that Bantry Union, 
the Lords Commissioners of Her Majesty’s Treasury being strongly impressed 
mth the importance of giving every practicable aid to the Guardians of the 
poor in the execution of the duties which liave devolved upon them under the 
pennanent Poor Law system as amended by the 10 Viet. cap. 31, are pleased to 
determine that no repayment of advances made under the Temporary Relief 
Act (10 Viet. cap. 7), shall be demanded before the 1st of January next from 
any electoral division in which a rate equal to or exceeding 3.y. in the pound, is 
levied before that period for the purpose of defraying the current expenditure 
of the permanent Poor Law, and that in those electoral divisions in which the 
rate to be levied for that purpose before the 1st of January next is less than 3«. 
in the pound, repayment shall be demanded only to the extent of the difference 
between the amount required for the cun'ent expenses of the permanent Poor 
Law and the sum which a rate of 35. in the pound in sucb electoral division 
would produce. 

The practical result of this announcement is, that a rate, not less than 35. in 
the pound, will be required in every electoral division of Bantiy Union. 

In making the above announcement the Commissioners, in order to prevent 
any misapprehension, desire distinctly to state that the poor-rates will remain 
liable for the repayment of the advances under the Temporary Relief Act if 
the Guardians do not make the requisite repayment from the next rate or 
from the following rates, supposing that the rates levied are required for the 
ordinary expenditure. 



Extract from Minutes of Board of Guardians : — September 21, 1847. 

Resolved — That this Board having well considered the present state of 
this workhouse, as regards the state of its funds, and the necessity that exists of 
at once making arrangements for collecting such a rate as will create a fund to 
enable us to lieep this workhouse ojieii, and at the same time to guai’d against 
oppressing the rate-payers, and that, at a time when the landowners are in a 
state of great distress, having well considered their circumstances, we have 
agreed to make a rate, which we have every reason to say could be collected, 
but we now give it as our candid opinion, that it will be impossible to collect a 
rate of 35. in the pound. 

We would therefore respectfully recommend to the Commissioners to allow 
the rate struck on the 7th day of September instant, to be put in a train of col- 
lection, which we have reason to say will be paid, and, as soon after as possible, 
to strike a further rate of a like sum. This will, we trust, show the Commis- 
sioners that we are not actuated by any wish to depart from their instmetions 
or wishes, but knowing the state of tlie country as we do, we feel that we 
would be deceiving the Commissioners were we to hold out to them hopes 
which cannot he realized.

suggesting a rate according to the scale proposed on the 7th instant-, varying 
from 1.9. td. to 3s. in the pound over the entire Union. 

In reference thereto, the Commissioners desire me to state, that they wodd 
be unwilling to require the Guardians of Bantry Union to make any rate which 
could not really be collected ; but the Commissioners think, that they should 
not be justified in doing otherwise than insisting that the Guardians should 
make a 3s. rate. 

According to the strict provisions of the Temporary Relief Act no advance 
would have been made to the Guardians on the credit of the rates, unless the 
Guardians had resolved to make a rate for the repayment of the whole of 
such advance, and, unless the Inspector of the Union had certified that the 
Guardians were proceeding, with all possible despatch, to make and levy such 
rate. From a desire, however, to facilitate the introduction of the new Poor

Report from Mr. Galway, late Government Inspector, addressed to the 
Relief Commissioners, and referred to the Poor Law Commissioners. 

Bantry, September 29, 1847. 

It is my duty to state to the Commissioners the result of their com- 
munication of the 17th September, which informed me of the final determina- 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 205 

tion of the Lords of the Treasury in reference to the repayment of the advances 
under the Temporary Relief Act 

On Tuesday, September 21, 1 waited on the Board of Guardians, and made 
them acquainted with the nature of your communication. I endeavoured, in 
conjunction with the Assistant Poor Law Commissioner, to enforce a ready 
compliance with the directions contained in it. 

One circumstance in particular I was bound to draw their attention to. The 
present is the time for collecting a rate ; later in the year, it will be quite im- 
possible to do so. If it be preferred to strike only a rate of U. 6d. in the pound 
at present, unquestionably a much less amount of money will be collected than 
if a 3 j. rate were struck, notwithstanding that there might happen to be very 
many defaulters. 

If it be proposed by the Bantry Board of Guardians to levy a rate of 3^. in 
the pound during the ensuing twelvemonths, the present is the time most 
decidedly for laying it on. In January or February next, it would be idle to 
suppose they could collect a rate of L-. 6d. 

The result of yesterday’s meeting is, that the Guardians being unwilling to 
strike a rate of Sa. in the pound, conformably to the directions received from 
the Poor Law Commissioners, it would seem likely that the provisions of the 
Poor Law Extension Act are to be enforced in their regard. 



The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians : — 
October 2, 1847. 



The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor 
in Ireland have had under consideration the resolutions of the Board of Guar- 
dians of Bantry Union on the 28th ultimo, respectiug the rate which the 
Guardians propose to strike for the relief oi the destitute poor in Bantry Union. 

In reference to these resolutions, the Commissionei-s desire to state that they 
highly appreciate the spirit in which they were framed, and they thank the 
Guardians for the satisfactory assurance that whether they may continue to 
occupy the position of Guardians or not, they will collectively and individually 
give their best assistance in having the poor-rates collected. 

Still the Commissioners have to state that they would prefer that the Guar- 
dians should continue to occupy tiieir present position, provided that they wdll 
make sucli rates as the financial embarrassments of the Union imperatively 



require. 

The Commissioners therefore request the Guardians to reconsider their reso- 
lutions of the 28th ultimo, on the following grounds. 

As the rates which the Guardians propose to strike are not much more than 
sufficient to cover the existing liabilities of the Union, the effect of the course 
contemplated by them would be to make no provision for the relief of destitu- 
tion in the Union during the approaching winter, and thus the destitute poor 
would either starve, or would he thrown on the precarious resources of private 
charity. /• o • 

With regard to the supposed impossibility of collecting a rate of 3s. in the 
pound, the Commissioners have to observe that if the Guardians will at once 
make rates to that amount, and will individually set the example of prompt 
payment, the Commissioners do not anticipate that there will be any insuperalne 
difficulty in the collection. ^ i j.- ■ 

The net annual value of the Union, according to the Poor Law valuation, is 
41,829/., while the Guardians, since December last, have only collected abemt 
1533/. As the taxation for Poor Law purposes has been comparatively so light, 
the Commissioners cannot permit themselves to doubt that the Guardians 
would be able by extraordinary exertions to discharge their liabihties, and to 
place their financial arrangements on a satisfactory foundation. 

Under these circumstances the Commissioners feel bound to msist on the 
Guardians striking a rate of 3s. in the pound ; and if the Guardians, at a time 
when their liab'Uties amount to 32531., adhere to their determination of not 
levying a larger sum than 36001, the Commissioners wiU be under the pamtul 
necessity of exercising their powers under the ISth section of the Irish Relief 
Extension Act.

Great negligence was used, especially in one electoral division (Kilcrohane), 
the collector not having collected a sixpence, and the consequence is, the last 
rate of lOt/. in the pound has to be brought forward as an arrear. 

I was much surprised to find that the small occupying tenants in this division 
under Al. valuation, were entered instead of tlie immediate lessor. Mr. Craw- 
ford, however, had this altered previous to my arrival. 

Tenders lor collectors were opened yesterday at the poor-house, but there were 
none from either Kilcaskin or Kilcrohane, and I am afraid we shall not have 
any from the latter division ; and as it is most essential to put the rate in course 
of collection in that division simultaneously with the others, I would call par- 
ticular attention to the circumstance, for although I cannot detect it, yet I 
thhik there is some underhand work going on. The rate will be easily col- 
lected, since it is in a great proportion obtainable from the immediate lessor, 
and indeed, the immediate lessor is the principal party throughout the Union. 
I have weighed well the circumstances of the Berehaven mines, and since they 
received such enormous advances under the Temporary Relief Act for the 
division in which they are situated (Kilnamanagh), viz., 2,030^., I consider' 
they must pay the rate, viz., 1,200/., although a report is abroad, which I do 
not credit, that they were to stop work. It w'ould be a sad thing, as they em- 
ploy some 12 to 16 hundred persons ; but I cannot see how it can be helped, 
except, perhaps, it might be taken by instalments, say in three monthly ones, 
or any other way that can be suggested. 

I leave for Castletown to-morrow morning, and vdll next Wednesday again 
report. 

On setting tJie paupers to work on the 28th October, 34 women went out of 
their own free will. 

I am most anxious to finish a small road at the workhouse, and the "Vice-Guar- 
dians will employ the paupei-s, provided they can procure a few tools from the 
Board of Works, and which I propose writing for. 

Mr. Payne, J. P., agent to the Earl of Bantry, has said he will collect in 
Kilcaskin, and the electoral division of Kilcrohane is now the only difficulty. 

The Earl of Bandon, and Timothy O’Donovan, J. P., are the immediate 
lessors.

No Union in Ireland presents such facilities for drainage and other useful 
labour. 

In my opinion, it will be quite useless to attempt to relieve, or, I should say, 
assist, any division that does not exert itself ; and so I shall not do so, but rate 
after rate must be laid on until, by the pressure on all parties, tliey will be 
compelled to come forward. The principal part of the rate in tliis Union 
coming upon the landlord, he w'iE be put in mind of it by the first rate now 
about to be collected.

Captain Gordon, Temporary Inspector, to Mr. Twisleton t — 
November 20, 1847. 

Our house is full, and all parties who were entitled to receive out- 
door relief have been removed to make room ; and when the relieving officers 
know their duties, I do not see any difficulty, since the landlords must employ 
the ahle-hodied who are now in a starving state. I need not say what advan- 
tages could be gained, provided Lord Bantry got his first instalment under the 
Land Improvement Act. It would give us breathing time and make other 
landlords more active. 

The county surveyor having offered to lend us hammers and to jiurchase 
broken stone for the roads, I have suggested to the Guardians the advantage 
of putting the paupers to work ; and stone-brealdng is a good test, and as such 
recommended by you ; and, if we could only get a few tools from the Board of 
Works, we could find plenty of employment. 

With the exception of last night, the fishermen have been very successful 
and fish is very cheap. 

The late Board said they could not find collectors, nor could a 3^. rate be 
collected (owing more, at the time, than a I 5 . 6 </. rate would produce). I 
find that, I may say, more than three-q^uarters of it is upon the immediate 
lessors, and one of the late ex-officio Guardians has tendered his services as a 
collector and is appointed. 

The principal difficulty is Castletown, since there is no one there you can 
act through, the district being divided into parties upon religion ; and I would 
strongly suggest the propriety of sending a paid officer to reside at that place. 
I cannot visit it more than once a fortnight, and am fully employed in my cor- 
respondence about the necessity of lan^ords finding work for the labouifing 
classes, whom they must otherwise feed ; and I consider, that unless the landlord 
shows that he has done his best and applied for money, it would be per- 
fectly useless to attempt to assist his unfortunate paupers, except by giving out- 
door relief, and levying rate upon rate upon the electoral division, forcing him

Mr. Marshall, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 
November 6, 1847. 



I HAVE the honour to report, for the information of the Poor Law Com- 
missioners, that I attended a meeting of the Board of Guardians for the 
Skibbereen Union on Thursday, the 4th instant. The greater part of the day 
was taken up in examining the books of the relieving officers. Several of the 
Guai’dians could not remain for the general business of the Union, and left the 
meeting. A resolution has been, however, passed that the Guardians meet two 
days in each week in future : on Tuesday, for the purpose of admitting paupers 
and examining the books, &c. of the relieving officers; and on Friday, to trans-

• Mr. Marshall, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law CoMirassioNERS : — 
November 17, 1847. 

For the information of the Commissioners for administering the Laws 
for the Relief of the Poor in Ireland, I beg to report, that, with a view to afford 
as much room as possible in the workhouse, a scrutiny of the register has been 
made, and a number of those in the three classes, to whom out-door relief at 
prt^ent can be given, have been discharged, and orders given to the several 
relieving officers to select the most destitute among the able-bodied for the 
workhouse, till more accommodation he provided. 

Complaints have been made that the relieving officers are not making up 
their lists, or affording relief to the three classes for out-door relief, vpith suffi- 
cient expedition, and that the lives of many are in danger from want of food. 
To remedy this, and assist the officers, I have solicited the aid of the local 
Guardians ; and have suggested that they should also obtain the aid of the 
clergy and three members of the Relief Committees, who acted under the 10th

Vic., cap. 7, for tlie pui’pose of making out a list of the destitute persons of the 
three classes in each townland, and furnish them to the relieving officers for his 
guidance and examination when visiting their houses, hut not in any way to 
interfere with him in the discharge of his duties ; and that the local Guardians 
and the committees examine the books, and make any report they may deem 
necessary to the Board at their next meeting. By this arrangement those re- 
q^uiring relief will obtain it without delay, and much imposition will be 
detected ; and it will, also, have the effect of creating a greater interest in the 
proper working of the Poor Law in each electoral division. 

The rate collectors attend at the Board-room each Wednesday, when their 
accounts and books are examined. Directions were given the last day of 
meeting to furnish a list of all rates for which landlords are liable, that pay- 
ment might be enibrced immediately. Large arrears are due upon lands in 
Cliaucery, particularly in East and West Skull, and upon which a most mise- 
rable description of tenants are ; and some means must be taken to obtain the 
rates. Lists have also been ordered of arrears ; and when these are furnished, 
other lists will be made by classes owing rates over certain sums. A revision 
of the rate-books is much wanting in some electoral divisions, as frec[uent dis- 
satisfaction is evinced by those who consider themselves aggrieved. 

In order to obtain as much information as possible of the state of the Union, 
I have directed that returns be made to me of the number in each hospital 
weekly ; and am, also, preparing books, in which each of the relieving officers 
will keep a registry of the deaths in each electoral division, showing the 
names and ages, and deaths from what cause, which they wiU lay before me 
each week. By this means I shall know the state of each district, as I had done 
under the Temporary Relief Act. 

A meeting of the Board, was held yesterday, the 16th November, at which 
the relieving officers attended to pass their accounts, &c. 

Much distress pi*evails in some electoral divisions ; but still I would not re- 
commend out-door relief to the able-bodied except as a last resource ; for, if 
once opened, it would be most difficult to keep it within bounds. 

A much greater zeal is evinced by the holders of land this season than last 
to prepare i’or future crops. Sea-weed and sand are collected for manure very 
generally ; and, in order to promote individual exertion, I have endeavoured, 
at every opportunity, to state to the farmers that they have nothing to expect 
in the way of aid in any shape ; that those not able to support themselves, and 
cultivate their land, should give up before it is too late, tliat otliers, who might 
he able to do so, should take it, and not have so much waste land as was the 
case last season. 

Our agi-iculturist has arrived here from the Royal Agricultural Society, to 
give instructions in a better system of cropping, by which the resources of the 
district may be increased. I shall afford him every assistance in my power, 
and, after he leaves, endeavour to stimulate the people to attend to his 
advice.

Mr. Marshall, Temporary Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners: — 
November 25, 1847. 

On Monday last, I visited Ballydehob, for the purpose of seeing the 
relieving officer there, and of assisting in the arrangements for affording relief to 
the poor in East Skull ; and I took the opportunity of attending a meeting held 
there on that day for the purpose of hearing instructions given by Mr. Moore, 
who has been sent to this district by the Royal Agi-icultural Society of Ireland, 
at which a number of farmers attended, to whom I stated the necessity of their 
using every exertion to cultivate the land, and cautioned them against expecting 
any relief or aid whatever this season, either in seed or any other assistance, but 
that they should rely solely upon their own exertions, and not leave tlie land 
waste, as was the case this year. 

Next day (Tuesday), I attended at Drumdaleague for the same purpose, in 
order that every assistance might be given in promoting a better system of 
cropping and increasing the resources of the district. 

Both meetings were well attended, and beneficial results, I anticipate, will 
follow. 

On Wednesday, I visited and inspected the workhouse, and also inspected the 
paupers when at dinner, that I might see the quality of food supplied, which 
was satisfactory. In the evening, with the master, I visited the house which 
has been taken and fitted up as sleeping apartments for boys from 12 to 18 
years of age, and found it well adapted for the purpose. 

I attended a meeting of the Board of Guardians this day, when a Committee 
was appointed to select and rent additional buildings, in order to afford increased 
accommodation for able-bodied paupers. 

It is also intended to rent a house in the suburbs of Skibbereen, in which 
the children can permanently remain and receive education, as in the work- 
house, by which arrangement more day-room will be had, so much wanting. 
In accordance with the sanction of the Commissionei*s, assistants to the relieving 
officers will be appointed on Tuesday next. 

A deputation from Skibbereen waited on the Board of Guardians with a 
memorial, urging the necessity of giving out-door reliel’ to able-bodied persons, 
and in which they charged me with having prevented the Commissioners com- 
plying with an application made lately to sanction out-door relief to that class ; 
but I explained my reasons for giving an opinion against it, and that every 
means should be adopted to provide additional workhouse accommodation 
before such a ruinous step be taken, and read extracts from my reports to 
show that every suggestion had been made to meet the difficulty and afford 
relief to the poor as promptly as possible, with which they appeared better 
satisfied, and the Guardians had anticipated their views in the resolutions passed 
this day. 

I took the liberty of stating the danger of making a false step, and the diffi- 
culty of retracing it, and that no out-door relief ought to be given to able-bodied 
persons unless the reality of the destitution is tested by a task of work previously 
performed. 

A discussion again arose as to the necessity of paid guardians ; but although 
some may resign, several have stated to me their determiaation to continue to 
act and carry out the law to the utmost. 

The collectors’ books have been ordered to be ready by this day week, that 
the 3tf. rate be put in collection. The Commissioners’ directions with regard 
to collecting the new rate with the arrears, shall be strictly adhered to. 

When Mr. Wilkinson was here last week I suggested to him the necessity of 
having the paupers admitted at some other part of the building than by the 
front door, as should fever or disease increi^e in the district, much danger would 
be incurred to the Guardians and those visiting the house by having the paupers-
