The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians : — August 16, 1847. 

The Poor Law Commissioners have had under their serious con- 
sideration a Resolution which was passed by the Board of Guardians of North 
Dublin Union, on the 13th instant, to the effect that it is the unanimous opinion 
of the Board that rehef should he given to the able-bodied poor under the 2nd 
section of the 10 Viet. c. 31, and that the Commissioners be req^ucsted to issue 
an order accordingly. 

In reference to that resolution the Commissioners desire to state tliat they 
are not satisfied by the evidence before them that such a necessity as was con- 
templated by the Act of Parliament now exists for issuing such an order. The 
Commissioners believe that the Guardians will, on inquiry, find that there is 
vacant room in the workhouses of the Union for 400 destitute pemons, and l)y 
reserving this accommodation for the relief of the able-bodied exclusively, and 
by granting out-door relief to impotent workhouse inmates, and to widows 
having two or more legitimate children, the Guardians will probably have at 
their command sufficient workhouse accommodation for all the able-bodied 
men in the Union who are really destitute. 

The Commissioners are aware that during the past week, under the Tempo- 
rary Rehef Act, there were above 20,000 persons on the relief lists in the elec- 
toral division of the North City alone, but as the whole po 2 )ulation of that 
division at the last census consisted only of 97,065 persons, the Commissioners 
entertain no doubt that imposition must have been successfully practised on a 
very extensive scale, and the relief lists will afford no accurate indication as to 
the degree of destitution which really exists in the Union. Besides, the decision 
to teiminate operations under the Temporary Relief Act on the 15th instant 
proceeded on the assumption that the present being the period of harvest, and 
there being notoriously a demand for labour in the country, the able-bodied 
men might at once be stnick off the relief lists, and be thrown upon their own 
resouixes. The reasonableness of this assumption is shown by the fact that a 
similar coui*se was adopted in South Dublin Union, without material difficulty, 
a fortnight ^o. If, however, the North Dublin Board of Guardians at this 
precise time commence a system of out-door relief to able-bodied men, a favour- 
able opportunity will be lost for breaking through habits of dependence which 
have been inevitably fostered by the relief administered in North Dublin Union 
during the last four months. 

In conclusion, the Commissioners have to express their conviction that it is 
^ly by the most energetic and resolute action at the present crisis that the 
Guardians will be able to withstand the tide of pauperism which threatens to 
overwhelm them. If a population of only 97,065 persons attempt to maintain 
above 20,000 of their own number as paupers, the burden on the rate-payei"s 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 217 

will become almost insupportable, the well-being of the small shopkeepers will 
be materially affected, and no class will be more deeply injured than that of the 
honest independent labourer, the funds for whose remunerative employment 
will be diverted in many instances to the wasteful maintenance of the indolent 
and the false. The Commissioners rely therefore on the intelligence and 
activity of the North Dublin Board of Guardians for adopting such decisive 
measures as will prevent the necessity of granting out-door relief to able-bodied 
men in the Union at the present time. 



Oldcaaile Union : — Out-door Relief. 

The Poor Law Commissioners to the Board of Guardians: — 

October 19, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the laws for relief of the poor in 
Ireland, have had under consideration a resolution of the Board of Guardians 
of Oldcastle Union, of the 1 3th instant, recLuesting the Commissioners to issue 
an order authorizing the Guardians, under Section 2 of 10 Viet. c. 31, to give 
out-door relief to the able-bodied, together with a report from the Inspector, 
Mr. Flanagan, on the subject. 

The Commissioners at the same time observe from the return of inmates in 
the workhouse annexed to the Minutes, that out of the whole number, namely 
713, in the house on the 9tli instant, no less than 465 were children under 15 
years of age; and I am directed to call the fecial attention of the Guardians 
to the large preponderance of this class of inmates. 

The Commissioners rec[uest that the Guardians will cause a thorough and 
careful revision of the inmates to be made, with a view of procuring, if possible, 
further vacancies in the house, and especially of ascertaining whether there are 
any children in the workhouse whose parents are not in it, or are in employ- 
ment outside of the workhouse, and able to support such children. The admis- 
sion of children without their parents, who are bound to maintain them, is not 
only at variance with the provisions oi' the Irish Poor Relief Acts, but is liable 
to great abuse ; and the Commissioners strongly recommend the Guardians to 
scrutinize the cases in the workhouse, with a view to remove children whose 
parents are outside, and ableto maintain them ; and also to reduce the number 
of other classes, so as to make the accommodation in the workhouse as available 
as possible for the able-bodied. 

Mr. Flanagan reports that the Guardians have made exertions to procure a 
lit place to remove the children to, and the Commissioners consider such an 
arrangement, one which it is most desirable to adopt ; and they request to be 
informed whether the inquiries of the Guardians for such accommodation have 
extended to the whole Union, or whether they have been confined to the im- 
mediate neighbourhood of the workhouse.

Further Order authorizing Out-Door Relief. 

To the Guardians of the Poor of the Oldcastle Union ; to the clerk and 
other of&cers of the said Union, and to all other persons •whom it may 
concern. 

Whereas it has been sho'wn to our satisfaction that, by reason of the want 
of room in the workhouse of the said Union, adequate relief cannot be afforded 
therein to destitute poor persons not being persons permanently disabled, or 
destitute poor persons disabled by sickness or accident, or destitute poqr widows 
having t-wo or more legitimate children dependent on them, and it is expedient 
to authorize and empower the Guardians of the said Union to administer relief 
out of the workhouse to such destitute poor persons, for a limited time, as here- 
inafter mentioned. 

Now therefore, we, the Commissioners for administering the Laws for 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, do hereby authorize and empower the said 
Guardians to administer relief out of the workhouse, in food, to destitute poor 
persons not being persons permanently disabled from labour by reason of old 
age, infirmity, or bodily or mental defect, and not being persons disabled from 
labour by reason of severe sickness or serious accident, and thereby deprived of 
the means of earning a subsistence for themselves and their families, whom 
they are liable by law to maintain, and not being poor widows having two or 
more legitimate children dependent on them, for two months next ensuing 
after the date of this order. 

And we do hereby make the following rules and regulations as to the 
granting, ordering, and giving of relief to all persons who shall be relieved by 
the said Guardians, under the authority of this order, that is to say : — 

1. Every person relieved under the authority of this order shall be 
relieved in food only, and such ibod shall, as far as is practicable, be 
cooked food. 

2. Every able-bodied male person relieved under the authority of this 
order shall, so far as is practicable, be set to perform a task of work 
during eight hours at least of every day for which he receives such relief. 

3. No able-bodied person who shall be in employment, nor any part of 
his or her family, shall receive relief as a destitute person under the 
authority of this order. 

And for the more effectual administration of relief under this order, we do 
hereby authorize and direct the Guardians of the said Union to appoint so 
many relieving officers as shall be found sufficient, from time to time, to 
superintend the labour of such persons as shall be set to work, in pursuance of 
the regulations in this order contained, and otherwise to assist in the adminis- 
tration of relief under this order, as the Guardians, subject to our approval, 
shall direct. 

Sealed with our seal, this sixteenth day of November, in the year of our 
Lord one thousand eight hundred and forty-seven. 

(L. S.) E. T. B. Twisleton. 

W. M. Somerville. 

T. N. Redington.

few offers were put in at an exorbitant price. The Board expect to procure one 
house only, which will not contain more than from 30 to 35 or 40, and to which 
they intend transferring the infirm old women. 

They are most anxious, by the erection of sheds and other like measures, to 
increase the amount of workhouse accommodation, being fully sensible of its 
importance as a test of destitution, and they are prepared to adopt every means 
in their power for erecting these. 

Meanwhile, the house is now thronged, containing nearly 200 more than it 
was originally calculated for, and numbers are pressing for admission who 
nau^ be refused all relief unless the Commissioners be pleased, in the exertion 
of their jwwcr, to issue a limited order (such as I have suggested) for out-door 
relief under the 2nd section.

With reference to the death of Daniel Donohoe and Patrick M‘Evoy, I 
beg to report that I have made every inquiry on the subject. 

It appears that Daniel Donohoe came from Granard and requested relief 
from the medical officer of the Ballymacan dispensary, and that when in the 
very act of spealdng he fell down and expired. It does not appear that he 
solicited relief either from the relieving officer or at the workhouse. 

With respect to Patrick M‘Evoy, it appears that he and his family were in 
fever, and were supported by the neighbours ; and it does not seem that he 
applied for relief either to the Relieving Officer or the Guardians. 

The jury in both cases returned a verdict that they died from destitution. I

Mr. Barron, Inspector, to the Poor Law Commissioners : — 
November 27, 1847. 

I HAVE to report that I attended this Board on Tuesday, when I brought 
under their consideration, in consequence of the crowded state of the workhouse, 
the actual necessity of giving out>door relief, under the 1st section of 10 Viet* 
cap. 31. The Guardians admitted the necessity, but stated that they had no 
funds for that purpose, as they had entered a resolution on their Minutes, that 
the amount due to the contractor, Mr. Reilly, amounting to over' 600/., should, 
in the first instance, be paid out of the rates collected, and that the treastirer had 
received a notice to this effect. I tiien pressed upon the Guardians the expe- 
diency of their raising funds from their treasurer on their personal security, as 
he was willing to give them an advance on these conditions, which could be 
afterwards paid from the amount of rate collected; but to this pro])osition they 
would not consent, although I informed them that already two or three deaths 
had occurred in their Union from actual starvation, for wliieh they were, in a 
great measure, responsible, as they had neglected their duties us Guardians, which 
they did not deny. 

The new rate was struck on the 12th October, and no steps have since I)een 
taken to put it in course of collection. The relieving officers were a))pointL’d, 
and sanctioned by the Commissioners, and their securities wei’e peiffected ; but no 
steps were taken by the Guardians, to enable them to enter upon their duties ; 
they were furnished with their jirinted Instructions, but they never received 
their Relief Books, nor a copy of the Act. And although the depots ^vere 
appointed long since, at my recommendation, no houses have been taken for the 
Relieving Officers. 

A spirit of the utmost apathy and indifference appears to exist at this Board, 
which IS really lamentable. About 150 persons applied for admission into the 
workhouse, and there being no room, the master was directed to give them their 
dinner, and to discharge them. 

Finding all my efforts to induce the Guardians to obtain funds, and commence 
at once to relieve the wretched objects who presented themselves as recipients for 
T? r ^ Relieving Officers should be furnished with the 

Reliei Books, and a copy of the Act, which was done, in order that they might 
receive applications for relief in their different districts, and in order tliat their 
list might be submitted to the Board of Guardians at their next meeting, when 
Mnie arrangement might be made to obtain funds. I likewise instructed the 
Relieving Officers to hire a room for a week, to receive applications for relief, 
until the Gua^ians had an opportunity of hiring bouses for that object, and 
requested the Guardians to attend on next Board day, with a view of, at once, 
giving the reqiiired relief. 

1 directed the clerk to add the arrear (since, altliough it is considerable, there 
appears to be no other alternative) to the new rate, in order that the books may 
be signed at once by the Guardians, and the rate put in course of collection. 

It would appear that, among other neglect of duty, the collectors have not had 
their accounts regularly checked.

AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 

Such is the state of this unfortunate and truly neglected Union. Medical 
officers and contractors are readily voted, compensation tor losses and increase of 
duty, udiilst the people are dying from destitution ; and the Union is in a state of 
bankruptcy, witn. no credit whatever even with their treasurer, who would not 
make any advances, liowever small, except on the personal security of the Guar- 
dians themselves. I have not had the honour of meeting the noble lord, tlie chair- 
man of this Board, since I took charge of this Union, and the whole system seems 
to be one of the utmost mismanagement. 

A very strong feeling seems to prevail at the Board as to tlie necessity of having 
paid Guardians, and I apprehend, until the Commissioners adopt this course, the 
affairs of the Union will never be in a wholesome state. 

Mr. Kilhic, the gentleman who proposed the rate of the 3s. in the pound, 
according to the Treasury Minute of the 4tb September last, is most anxious and 
active to induce the Board to do its duty, and he has given me most valuable 
assistance. He has promised to aid me in all my endeavours to bring this Board 
to a sense of their duty, and to establish something like system in their proceed- 
ings. No exertion shall be wanted on my part to induce the Guardians to act as 
they ought to do ; and with that view I intend to attend the Board again on 
Tuesday. 

I regret to announce the death of Catherine M'Evoy, the widow of P. M'Evoy, 
from actual want, I have since received the depositions taken by the coroner, 
which I now forward. It appears that the screams of the unfortunate woman 
were heard at a very considerable distance, and no one would go near her until 
death put an end to her sufferings. I have made the necessary inquiries, and it 
is stated that she made no application whatever for relief to the proper authorities. 
The Guardian of the electoral division, Mr. Sheridan, has, I am informed, sent 
this poor woman’s only child to the workhouse at Cavan. The coroner tells me 
that much distress prevails in this district. The property of the principal land- 
lord is in. the Court of Chancery, and there are no resident gentry there. 

The Commissioners have only one course, to call upon the Guardians of the 
Cavan Union to perform their duty as Guardians of the poor, and if they do not 
do so at once to dissolve the Board.

The PoorL.\w Commissioners to the Clerk of the Cavan Union : — 
Novemhi?t"20, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in 
Ireland, have had under their serious consitleration the various reports which 
have been made to them of the distress and destitution existing in the Ciivau 
Union, and which have lately been the subject of several communicivtions from 
the Commissioners to the Board of Guardians. 

The Commissioners allude to certain i*epoi*ts made by constabulary officers to 
His Excellency the Lord Lieutenant, of inquests held within the Union, and to 
letters received by them from the Rev. Mr. Collins, of the contents of all of 
which, the Guardians have already been informed. 

From the verdicts given by a coroner’s jury, in three inquests, it aiijicars that 
Patrick M'Evoy, Daniel Donohue, and Catharine M'Evoy, lost their lives after 
much suffering,^ from want and destitution, having previously received no relief 
from the Guai-dians of the Union, or dny of their officers, 

The cases of Catherine M'Evoy and her son deserve especial attention, from 
verdict given by the coroner’s jury at the imjuest held on 
P. M'Evoy, on the 26th October last, which not only stated that the boy died from 
want of sufficient nutriment, but that in the opinion of the jury, the mother 
and brother were likely, if not relieved, to share the same fate. 

Hts Exc^lency the Lord Lieutenant having forwarded this report of the con- 
stabulary officer to the Commissioners, they, on the 30th October, sent a copy of 
that report to the Board of Guardians, calling the attention of the Guardians to 
the statements made regarding the surviving members of the family referred to. 

1 ins letter apjiears to have been read at the meeting of the Guardians, on the 
nd November, but the minutes of that date, and the subsequent minutes of the 
Guardi^s, do not show that any steps were taken by the Guardians, or any of 
their officers, m reference to the distressed state of Catherine M'Evoy and her 
surviving child. ^ 

^ On the 27th instant, the Commissioners received from the Rev. Wm. Collins, 
m ormation of two inquests in his neighbourhood, in which similar verdicts have 
een given, one of them held on the body of Catherine M'Evoy, the poor woman 
relerred to, as likely to perish if unrelieved, in the verdict of ' the 26th October, 
and in her case the jury found that Catherine M'Evoy died on the 23rd November 
irom destitution, and want of sufficient nutriment, and exposure to cold. 

e harrowing details of this latter case are now before the Commissioners, in 
a copy or the depositions taken at the inquest, which the Commissioners have 
revived with a report from their Inspector, hlr. Barron. 

rom this evidence it appears that Catharine M'Evoy was a widow, and that 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 225 

her two children were of the ages of eight and six years, respectively ; and there* 
fore there is no doubt that she and her two children were relievable out of the 
workhouse of the Union, under the 1st section of the Irish Poor Relief Exten- 
sion Act. 

The hut in which these poor persons died without relief, is situate in the 
Kilnaleek electoriil division, and the Conimissioners find that the appointment of 
the relieving officer for the district, including that division, was approved by them 
on the 23rd September last. 

With this stote of facts before them, the Commissioners have felt themselves 
bound to entertain the question whether the Guardians of the Cavan Union have 
discharged their duties according to the intention of the Acts in force for the 
Relief of the Poor in Ireland, or whether on the other hand, through default of 
the Guardians, the duties of the Board of Guardians have, to use the words of the 
statute, not been effectually performed. 

The Commissioners ibrbear to dwell on the previous management of the affairs 
of the Union, which they regret to say they cannot consider has been at any time 
satisfactory. 

It is sufficient to say that on the 31st October last, the debts of the Guai-dians 
amounted to 4471/., and that of a rate made in December, 1846, amounting to 
somewhat more than 5700/., there remained uncollected 1535/. on the 22nd 
November inst. 

In a report which the Commissioners have this day received from the inspector, 
Mr. Barron, they find it stated that Mr. BaiTon attended the meeting of the Guar- 
dians on Tuesday last, and brought under their consideration, in consequence of the 
crowded state of the workhouse, the actual necessity of giving out-door relief 
under the first section of 10 Vic. cap. 31. The Guardians, Mr. Barron reports, 
admitted the necessity ; but stated that they had no funds for the purpose, as 
they had entered the resolution on their Minutes that the amount due to a con* 
traclor, Mr. Reilly, amounting to more than 600/., should, in the first instance, be 
paid out of the rates collected, and that the treasurer had received a notice to this 
effect. 

Mr. Barron further states, that a new rate was struck on the 12th Octolier, but 
that no steps have since been taken to put it in course of collection; that the 
Relieving Officers appointed by the Guardians, and approved by the Commis- 
sioners, have perfected their securities, hut no steps had been taken by the 
Guardians to enable them to enter on their duties ; that the Relieving Officers had 
received their printed Instruclions, but not their Relief Books, and that althougli 
the depots bad been fixed upon, no houses had yet been taken for the Relieving 
Officers for the purpose of dispensing relief. 

The Commissioners gather from Mr. Barron’s report, and from the other 
information now before them, that a feeling of apathy and indifference regarding 
the administration of relief exists at the Board ot Cavan Union, which leaves the 
Commissioners without hope or confidence in the future proceedings of the 
Guarrlinns ; and they, therefore, feel themselves called upon to exercise the power 
provided by statute to meet a contingency of this nature, and to dissolve the Boai'd 
of Guardians. 

An order to that effect, under the seal of the Commissioners, is enclosed here- 
with ; and that order \vill be immediately followed by an order appointing paid 
officers to carry into execution the provisions of the Acts -in force for the relief 
of the destitute poor in Ireland.

Messrs. Robinson and Bates, Vice-Guardians of Cavan Union, to the Poor 
Law Commissioners: — December 21, 1847. 

WEheg to forward, for the information of the Commissioners for adminis- 
tering the Poor Law in Ireland, our report of the general state of the Union on 
our arrival, and the measures taken by us for counteracting the existing evils. 

We found 1245 paupers in the house ; 171 cases of fever, and that 332 had 
died in the house within the last six months ; a debt of 4000/. and upu'ards, not- 
withstanding which large balances were allowed to remain in the collector’s 
hands ; no rate made, no new collectors appointed ; most of the relieving- officers 
named, but no houses taken as depots, or means adopted for giving out-door 
relief, though nearly one thousand families were on the relieving officers’ books 
entitled to out-door relief under the 1st section of 10 Victoria, cap. 31, and frequent 
deaths had occurred outside the house, which were pronounced by jurie.s to have 
been caused by starvation ; cheques to the amount of 1745/. had been drawn on 
the treasurer, without any funds in hand to meet them ; consequently the credit 
of the Guardians was destroyed, and the house -was only kept ojien at the mercy of 
a contractor, who was owed nearly 3000/. 

The children in the house were unemployed, vaccination was totally neglected, 
no contracts for it being in existence in the entire Union. Fever on the increjise, 
and the ventilation and sewerage of the house in such a bad state as to tend in a 
great measure to the prevalence of disease. 

Such was the lamentable condition of the Union ten days ago, on our arrivid 
here to discharge the duties of Vice-Guardians. 

It would ill become us to give our opinion as to the causes which led to such a 
state of affairs ; but we will, as briefly as possible, detail the several steps taken by 
us to remedy these evils, and also our general prospects. 

We took immediate and summary steps to enforce the balances remaining in the 
collertors hands; appointed new collectors, at a reduced poundage, with undoubted 
security, to collect the rate within two months, under a heavy penalty. 

^ We made a new rate,^ which we are happy to state is now in course of collec- 
tion, without any opposition as yet being made to the payment. 

We filled up the vacancies among the relieving officers; received tenders and 
approved of houses as depots, in the most central part of each district ; examined 
the relieving officers’ application books ; and at this moment 824 families (coming 
under the 1st section of 10 Victoria, cap. 31,) are receiving out-door relief, This 
was not done in any instance without the most minute inquiry into the merits of 
each case ; this list, however, will be greatly increased when the districts of Ballin- 
teniple and Killeshandra, to which relieving officers were this day appointed, come 
into operation. 

On our arrival we found we were not in a position to admit any fresh appli- 
cants into the house ; we were, therefore, unable to afford relief to the crowds of 
able-bodied who applied for it. We have, accordingly, taken two houses in the 
vicinity, each capable of containing 100 children; also a large store, and are fitting 
up^the latter for the purpose of removing to it 100 fever patients. This will 
enable us to make room for 300 in the poor-house, and thereby test that number 
ot able-bodied applicants. 

We regret to be obliged to state that the applications for relief by this class are 
mos m^erous. We discovered that an address was about to be presented to the 
andlorus and occupiers by the late Board of Guardians, entreating them to exert 
themselves, _ and give extraordinary employment to the able-bodied at this mo- 
mentous crisis. This address was approved of on the 23rd ultimo, and ordered to 

^epared before the meeting : die Board being meanwhile dissolved, pre- 
vea ;it bemg . carried into execution. W!e have, after mature deliberation,

directed tills address to be published and distributed through the Union, in the 
hope of promoting so laudable and desirable an object, without which no exertion 
of ours can keep down a ruinous taxation, or ward off the evil consequences 
attendant on out-door relief to the able-bodied poor. 

Since our arrival here we have been waited on by most of the resident gentry 
and clergy of both jiersuasions, all of whom hailed the appointment of Vice-Guar- 
dians with delight, informing us of their inability to cany out those extensive 
measures of relief, ]irovided by the late enactments, from the discordant materials 
of which the past Board was constituted, offering us their cordial co-operation, 
looking upon us as the only means of affording adequate relief to the wretched and 
suffering population of the district, and saving the property of the rate-payers from 
confiscation by a judicious administration of the funds of tlie Union. 

We have reason to know that fever is greatly on. the increase throughout the 
entire Union, and ive are making arrangements to establish a temporary fever 
hospital in the Ballinagh and Arvagh districts, having received communications 
from the Board of Health as to the necessity of doing so. 

We propose immediately adopting measures to carry into effect the intentions 
of the I^egislalure as regards vaccination. 

We intend employing master tradesmen, with a view of instructing the most 
deserving of the boys in useful trades, and keeping the clothing of the establish- 
ment in repair. 

We also have turned our serious attention to the revision of the valuation of the 
Union, which has lately cost 300/., and we recommend tliat, instead of that large 
outlay for one revision, an active, intelligent officer be employed for that purpose, 
at a small annual salary. 

You will perceive by this report that the affairs of the Union are beginning to 
present a more liealthy appearance. We have entirely restored credit, and are 
now receiving tenders, at a low rate, from respectable parties who unlillately held 
back; and we hope in about a week to pay off our liabilities, and pay for our 
supplies ill cash. 

We hope we have not trespassed too long upon the patience of the Commis- 
sioners, and that the measures we have adopted may meet with their approval.

The Board of Guardians of the Cavan Union have- received and perused with very great 
satisfaction a statement lately published by the Bailieborougli Board of Guardians, of which 
John Young, Esq., the Member of Parliament of the county, is Clhairman, and addressed to the 
landowners and farmers of that Union. This able statement contains matter relating exclu- 
sively to the Bailieborougli Union, and which consequently is not of so much general interest. 
But it also contains suggestions upon the. general subject of employment for the able-bodied 
poor, which are applicable to the greater part of Ireland ; and the Cavan Board of Guardians 
have thought it would be most advantageous to have these suggestions published and distributed 
through the Union. 

The Cavan Board of Guardians cannot hope to be able to add to the force of the arguments 
so ably slated in the document which they now publish ; but they think it right to say that at 
this calamitous moment' provisions most happily are not dear, and, consequently, that employ- 
ment amply afibrded would almost entirely relieve us from our present distress. Farmers are 
neither rich enough nor have they work enough to give extensive employment at tliis season of 
the year. River-drainage, undertaken by the Boai-d of Works, must, of course, be in a great 
measure suspended during the rainy weather now to be expected. Land-drainage seems tlie 
only branch of industry which can at present supply adequate employment, and for it almost

Extract from the Statement of the BaiUohorough Board of Guardians. 

“ The Bailieborough Board of Guardians cannot conceal from themselves and from the rate- 
payers that as the season advances, the pressure upon able-bodied labourei-s and their families, 
and upon the holders of small plots of land up to one, two, and even throe acres, will become' 
more and more severe. 'I'heproduct of gardens is failing, potatoes are very higli in price, meal 
and other provisions can only be obtained by purchase, while the wages earned at harvest are 
becoming rapidly exhausted, and the labourer has no means of recruiting his funds. 

“ On the lltn October the following resolution was adopted by the Guardians, viz., That 

tocli Guardian make diligent inquiry in his electoi’al division, and obluiii as accurate informa- 
tion as possible, of any steps that may be in progress for providing employment for the able- 
bodied labourers of the district, whether by the outlay of private capital or by taking advantage 
of the liberal terms on which Her Majesty’s Government has decided to advance money lor 
reproductive works, and that each Guardian make his report on this important subject this 
day week. ^ 



_ “ The Board regrets to say that these reports state that, except in ono electoral division, and 
in s^e few partial instances praiseworthy in themselves, but not of any considerable amount 
as affecting the question at issue, no steps have been taken ; and so far as can be ascertained 
none are in contemplation, either by landlords or farmers, to increase the. amount of employ- 
ment, and ward off the evil consequences of gratuitous out-door relief to the able-bodied. No 
outragwhave disgraced this densely-peopled Union, no plunder of property has taken place 
—no threats even have been uttered, and wherever employment has been offered, tlie offer has 
been cheerfully accepted. The labouring men of the Union are ready and willing to work for 
their own sustenance and that of their families, and to give fair and honest labour for such 
moderate wag(a as shall enable them to live at present prices, and rescue them from the pri- 
vations which tliey are prepared to submit to rather than enter the workhouse. The Guardians 
hope they may he excused for pressing this point on especial notice. Many a poor hard-working 
man will struggle to keep out of the workhouse, but what follows? The family must submit 
0 want, to scanty clothing, to insufficient food; half starved and weak they lose heart and 
nope, they cannot do justice to any employer, or undertake a hard day’s work if they be lucky 
enough to have one offered to them. They become the ready victims and sum propagators of 
xn ectious and other malignant disease ; and under such trying circumstances it is rather to be 
hoped than expected that human nature will endure and abstain from all evil. If no exertion 
be made, no additional employment, offered, how small will be the security of property against 
depredation— (or the peace of the country against starvation and discontent — and for the health 
e ; community against so many causes and incentives to disease as must exist when hundreds 
01 lamilies are struggling in so great hardships. 

“ state however of the Union leaves room for better hopes, and is most favourable to

at the present moment. ^

AND STATE OF THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 229 

The pressinff evil is want of employment. No method for affording it is more obvious’ 
none better suited to the labourers of the Union, than draining. The land requires it ■, Govern- 
ment offers the money to do it on easy and liberal terms; and the able-bodied men only desire 
employment as wages, and, in every instance where it has been given to them, have exerted 
themselves cheerfully and honestly. 

“ Many tenants are anxious for the improvement of their farms, and would readily bind them- 
selves to bear their share in file repa yment of the money laid out ; in such cases tlie landlord or 
his agent might easily make arrangements satisfactory to himself and his tenants. 

“ Under these circumstances, and knowing they have done and are doing all in their power 
to meet the emergency, and give effect to the main provisions of the extended Poor Law, the 
Guardians feel themselves justified in calling upon all who have a due estimate of the duties of 
property to aid them in their efforts, and by providing additional employment for those who are 
able and willing to work, to convert, as, indeed, they have the power of doing, the pressure and 
apprehensions of the present moment into lasting advantage and security to all classes. 

“ The end is one of no difficult attainment, if the landlord, and rich farmers, or even half of 
them, come forward. The outlay need not be to any overwhelming amount, and ifjudiciously 
made is certain to be reproductive. 

“This view is stated with much diffidence, but it is prompted by necessity. The 
Guardians see no other mode than that mentioned of extricating the Union from great pressure, 
from perhaps ruin. Tliey hope committees will be formed and meetings held in every electoral 
division, to discuss the subject and make practical arrangements. Their opinion as to the 
necessity of this course is unanimous, and no time should be lost. It may be thought the 
Guardians exceed their functions in thus offering counsel. If so, they apologize fork; their 
advice is humbly tendered in the absence of other and perhaps wiser suggestions. Still they 
are persuaded the course they indicate may be safely taken; it requires a little exertion, calls 
for no sacrifice, but, on the contrary, must, if experience be any guide, result in gain to all. 
If the landlords and richer farmei-s choose, they can employ the able-bodied, keep down the 
rates, secure the peace of the Union, check the progress of disease, and rescue hundreds from 
misery, degradation, and sin. If they do not choose to exert themselves, the picture will be 
reversed; the taxation on the rate-payers will be ruinous, the demoralization of the labourer 
complete. Amidst suffering, discontent, and turbulence, what remains of property after the 
rates are paid, will be scarce safe from outrage, when life and health will suffer from contagious 
disease. In either case, whatever be the result, let those in whose hands, under Providence, 
the balance rests, recollect they have received timely warning from those on whom lias devolved 
the task — the no light or easy task — of administering the relief provided by the law for the 
destitute, and let them as they will, improve or reject the opportunity ; but according to tlieir 
own decision now, lot them hereafter congratulate themselves on having acted upon and profited 
by the warning, or let them blame themselves and none else for having neglected it, and with 
it their own best interest as well as bounden duty.”

Tlie Poor Law Commissioners to the Clerk of Mohill Union: — 

JDecember 8, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief of the Poor in 
Ireland have had under their serious consideration their recent correspondence 
with the Guardians of Mohill Union, the reports of their Inspector, Mr. Flanagan, 
the repox*ts of their temporary Inspector, Major Haliday, and other documents 
exhibiting the disastrous and disorganized state in which the Union is at present 
placed, chiefly in respect of its financial embarrassments, and of the deplorable 
state of destitution oi the labouring classes in the Union. 

Major Haliday, in his last report, received by the Commissioners on the 4th 
instant, represents the extreme difficulty with which a sufficient attendance of 
Guardians to transact business is obtained at the weekly meeting of the Board. 

He further reports, that sufficient funds not having been obtained by the col- 
lector of rates, the Guardians adopted no steps to enable the Relieving Officers 
to give either medical or any other assistance to those whom they were unable to 
admit into the workhouse, nor to procure additional accommodation, or to support 
the Fever Hospital lately managed under the control of the Board of Health. 

Major Haliday further reports, that on his inspection of the workhouse this 
week he found no improvement ; that the yards remained filthy and offensive ; 
many of the doors and locks insecure ; much glass broken ; a large proportion oi 
the inmates in rags, the master having no sufficient supply of workhouse clothing 
for them, nor materials to make them up ; the schools all but useless from the 
want of proper hooks, paper, j)ens, or ink ; and the hospital full of dysentery and 
fever. 

■With respect to the future attendance of the Guardians at the Board, Major 
Haliday’s report holds out to the Commissioners no propect of any improvement

Report from Messrs. O’Reilly and Duncan, Vice-Guardians of Mohill Union, 
to the Poor Law Commissioners -.—Becemhei' 20, 1847. 

1. Having now completed a week since our being placed in charge, as 
Vice-Guardians of the Mohill Union, under the Poor Law Commissioners’ sealed 
orders of the 10th instant, we beg to submit the following report. 

2. Our first care, on assuming our duties, was directed to the workliouse, every 
department of which we found to be in a lamentably neglected and disorganized 
state. 

3. The number of inmates, it appeared, was greater than accommodation was 
originally provided for ; and, from laxity in admissions, many of the inmates were 
improper subjects of relief. 

4. The building we found most dilapidated, and fast advancing to ruin ; every- 
thing out of repair; the yards undrained, and filled, in common with the cesspools, 
hy accumulations of filth — a violation of all sanatory i*e(juirements : fever and 
dysentery prevailing throughout the house, every ward filthy to a ino.st noisome 
degree, and evolving offensive effluvia ; the paupers defectively clothed, and many 
of liiose recently admitted continuing in their own rags and impurity ; classification 
and separation set at nought ; a general absence of utensils and implements ; the 
dietary not adhered to, and the food given in a half-cooked staui — most inadetjuate, 
particularly for the sick ; the meals distributed through the medium of onc-sixth 
the mimber ol vessels required, and uproar and confusion, the stronger securing 
an over quantity to the privation of the weaker, and the breakfast not (xtinpletely 
dispensed until late in the evening ; no contracts existing, no stores of provisions 
to meet even the wants of a day; the able-bodied not employed, and without 
restraint or discipline; the destruction of all description of Union property pro- 
ceeding rapidly, many hundred pounds’ worth appearing to be missing ; the chil- 
dren in the schools receiving no education or industrial training, in other rosjjects 
their neglected state painfully exhibited by their diseased and emaciated aspect; 
no means for the proper treatment of the sick, the officers ignorant of their duties ; 
coffins unused in the interment of the dead. 

5. These are a few of the defects remarked by us stated briefly in general terms'. 
The whole machinery of the establishment appeared opposed, in every feature, to 
the original intention, and almost no rule in operation, laid down by the Commis- 
sioners’ orders and suggestions, or exercised in any well-regulated workhouse. 

t. doubt not that the continuance of such a state of’ tilings, for a very 

limited time longer, would have produced a crisis attended with consequences pos- 
sibly entirely destructive to the institution, and ffital to the dives of a mass of the 
inmates. 

7. The condition of the children, both in. school-rooms and iiurseiy, so 

deplorably neglected, aroused our deepest sympathy ; and we cannot disguise from 
ourselves the melancholy fact, that the great mortality of the past few months, 
amongst that class paiticularly, might be attributable to causes arising from this 
neglect. i ; c e 

8. The officers (whose capabilities for eventually managing the house we have 
not yet been able to form a decided opinion on) attribute this great derilection of 
duty to the circumstance of their being left uncontrolled by the Board of Guar- 
dians, who, i'or a lengihened period, were not acquainted by personal examination 
with the irants of the house, no visiting or other Committee having acted, we are 
informed, for months.

9. The conduct of the officers, which we consider to have been most culpable, 
receives, perhaps, a slight palliation from the cause adverted to, as we can easily 
understand the withdrawal of the countenance and control of the guardians, 
inducing laxity and carelessness ; again, the money appropriated to the purposes 
of the establishment was certainly extremely meagre, but still even this is not suf- 
ficient to account for the abuses in their enormity. 

10. Funds . — In this department we find tlie Union overwhelmed with debt, a 
sum of 2455/?. lOi'. 11c?. being due to contractors, &c. ; its credit gone, and law 
proceedings against the Guardians in process, with the inconsiderable sum of 42/, 
in the Treasurer’s hands, which would be little more than adequate to purchase 
one week’s supply of food for the establishment. This sum could not of course 
be drawn to meet the outlay required for other purposes, hut your timely attention 
to our application for a loan of 200/ has afforded us the means of carrying out our 
plans of improvement. 

11. Rates . — This subject demauded our special consideration. We found a 
large sum of tiie last rates made remaining uncollected. The arrangement for the 
collection of the rate appeared to us totally inadequate, it being impossible that 
Mr. O’Brien, the rate-collector of the whole Union, could bestow on so large an 
extent of country the direct and prompt exertions which would alone ensure success 
in his duty. 

12. The valuation of seven of the electoral divisions iias not yet been completed. 
The rate-books have been prepared of the six divisions in which it has been brought 
to a close, and it remains but to have the arrears of former rates introduced into 
them to place them in a position for signature. 

13. We might here advert to the most unsatisfactory and illegal manner in 
which former rates were prepared. Independently of the books not being filled up 
in many particulars, the amount of each rate carried into the Union ledger, was 
assumed from data generally incorrect, and was not really tlie total of the sums 
entered against the names of the rate-payers in each electoral division which it 
purports to be. 

14. Accounts . — The late clerk having left the accounts uncompleted, the pre- 
sent clerk has not introduced any entries into the ledger, which, therefore, contains 
no record of any of the transactions of the half-year ending the 29th September, 
1847. Many of the books prescribed by the Commissioners’ order have not been 
kept at all, and others partially and defectively. 

15. Out-door Relief . — We found that one relief district was, from the sub- 
sequent disqualification of the person originally appointed, without a relieving 
officer. No houses to be used as stores for small quantities of provisions and the 
issue of rations had yet been hired ; and in re<ility no means were in existence for the 
dispensation of out-door relief, although the workhouse was already overcrowded. 

16. We now proceed to detail tiie measures which we have considered it expe- 
dient to adopt as remedial to the state of affairs already described. 

17. The highly valuable assistance rendered to us by Major Halliday, who has 
been most assiduous in affording the benefit of his experience, and in supporting us 
by his advice, we cannot over-estimate 

18. We decided almost immediately, after taking chai-ge, on closing the work- 
house against further admissions, until contagion could be arrested, and discipline 
and order restored. To effect this, we proceeded to separate the infected from the 
healthy, and to appropriate to them a separate ward or ^vards, \vhich we accom- 
plished by assigning one of the unused dormitories in the attic of the male wing 
to this purpose, as subsidiary hospital accommodation. We converted the adjoining 
attic dormitory into a convalescent ward; the place where the convalescents were, the 
probationary wards, being most unsuited for them. 

19. We amended the dietary for the children and sick, and prepared a new 
dietary table, which will be submitted for your approval herewith. We succeeded, 
by perseverance, in restoring silence and order at meals, and even with the few 
vessels, &c., at command, to have the meals prepared earlier. We are getting the 
wards and dormitories thoroughly cleansed and whitewashed. The boys have 
been set to clean and level yard and dig grounds; and separation has been 
enforced, so far as the broken locks will permit, and all the paupers employed, so 
far as practicable. 

20. The repairs of the bouse, ventilation, &c., according to Mr. Wilkinson’s 
plan, we at once contracted for with proper persons, we think advantageously ; 
and where workmen could only he had in distant towns, we sent there for them.

We made eveiy effort to procure a person to undertake the cleanin<j of the ces- 
pools, both by advertisement and otherwise, but without success ; however, this 
week we hope to succeed in our object. 

By defining the duty of each officer, allocating a collateral responsibility to the 
well-behaved paupers in the respective wards, enabling the officers really to see 
their way, and clearing off the confusion which surrounded everything, givin^^ our 
snpi)ort and using our personal exertions, wc have succeeded in removing, in part, 
the depression and apathy which seemed to pervade the officials, and induced a 
comparative state of efficiency, it would appear for a long time unknown. 

The whole economy and government of the establishment has received our 
personal superintendence during the week, and by that, principally, lias energy 
and activity been aroused. ° 

We at once ordered a quantity of indispensable utensils and requisites generally 
inexpensive, also supplies of clothing and trifling articles of furniture ; and, with the 
small facilities for procuring such this place affords, we hope by the end of the 
week to have made considerable progress in introducing them into use. 

Our main object is to place the workhouse, with the least delay, in a state 
which will enable us to admit the able-bodied and other classes, however few in 
number. Our arrangements which enable us to clear the probationary wards 
entirely, will, we trust, place us in a position to receive at next meeting a few 
paupers of the classes adverted to, if necessary ; at all events, to permit our offering 
the test of the workhouse to applicants for out-door relief, whose destitution is at 
all questionable. 

Funds . — The sum of 47/. of rate has been lodged with the treasurer durino' the 
past week, which, with the timely accession to the finances of the 200/. lent by 
the Britisli Association, we hope to carry us through, u'ith the limited measures 
we must only undertake until the new rate becomes available. We are keeping 
off the creditors of the Union, who are urgent and threatening, as well as -we cai^ 
and some slight additional confidence seems to have arisen in tbeir minds from the 
alteration in the guardianship. 

Wliere a false impression, such as their believing we were entrusted with funds 
irom Government, has arisen, we have at once removed it, and made jiublic the 
inct that the solvency of the Union can he attained, as well as the relief of the 
destitute accomplished, only by the payment of the rates, and that tlui interest and 
the duty ol all classes should therefore be extended to our support in the collection 
01 the tax.

Until we get tlie new rate in collection, we cannot feel that our functions are in 
full exercise ; then we shall bring our whole capacities to bear on the furtherance 
of the important object in view. 

The clerk appears to have fully inti'oduced the new orders of the Commissioners 
for the examination of the rate collectors’ accounts, the proper continuance of 
which will receive our earnest attention. We have failed as yet in seeing the 
revising valuator ; his being out through the Union, we presume, is the cause of his 
not attending to our letters. He appears to have occupied much too long time in 
completing the work, in which celerity is such an object, and we propose obliging 
him to bring the revision at once to a close, so that the remaining rate-books may 
be speedily prepared and signed. 

We ourselves have effected a useful improvement in four of the rate-books 
already revised, by rating the immediate lessor by name, in no case hitherto done, 
and thus facilitating law proceedings to enforce from him the recovery of the rate. 
The collecting books are in course of preparation, and will, we hope, be ready in 
time to meet the signing of rates. 

Additional TVorkhouse Accommodation . — Our most zealous attention has been 
given to this most important consideration, replete with local difhculties. We 
could not be more deeply impressed with the importance of procuring increased 
space for fever patients and children ; in fact, our whole prospects for the suc- 
cessful administration of the law, next to funds, depend on this. If we could 
relieve the workhouse of infectious dkeases, and acquire the space now occupied by 
the children, we would not fear battling with the pressure of destitution during 
the coming season, without the interposition of the Commissioners order sanc- 
tioning relief to the able-bodied, a measure, however, appai'ently financially 
impracticable. 

We propose making every inquiry during the coming week, and exerting all the 
influence we can bring to bear towards our object, and we hope we may be even 
partially successful. 

We have not yet had an opportunity of making arrangements with i-egard to 
resuming the operation of the temporary fever hospital under the Reliel Committee. 

It will probably be our course to devote a small part of the 200/. loan to defray 
the cost of such patients as it may be necessary to admit^to this hospital. 

Out-door Relief . — In consequence of our determination to close the workhouse 
at present against further admissions, we decided on placing funds, to a limited 
extent, in the hands of the Relieving Officers, to relieve any cases of sudden or 
urgent necessity coming within the clauses contemplated in the Commissioners 
order, such as they have hitherto been in the habit of sending provisionally to the 
workhouse ; this plan wm consider will prevent any disastrous consequences occur- 
ring, from the step we felt ourselves necessitated to take in closing the house. 

41. Proposals are to be laid before us at next meeting for relieving-houses for 
the storing, cooking, and dispensing food, one to be assigned to each officer. The 
position of the houses with x-egard to the convenience of the district, and their 
suitability in other respects, will receive particular attention, and probably also 

our personal inspection. ' , t v -rn 

42. We have advertised for an officer for the district vacant by the disqualihca- 

tion of Mr. Keon. The capabilities of the person we appoint shall he rigidly 
examined. . . 

43. ’Die competency of the present Relieving Officers to perform their onerous 
and important duties shall receive our searching attention, and subsequei^ reports 
shall convey our conclusions, both with regard to them and the in-door officers. 

44. Some of the members of the late Board have visited us. _Mr. Uodby (one 

of the former ex-officio Guardians) kindly offered us every assistance which bis 
position as a magistrate could afford ; and it appeared to be his feelings, m common 
with others, that the administration of the Poor Law here being placed under 
control which would insure its receiving more time and attention, was a step 
absolutely necessary. . , , 

Although disposed to he guided by the most rigid economy, we think we do not 
violate that principle when we assert our fears that the rate of remuneration to 
the workhouse officers (beneath average) is too low to have men of the attainments 
necessary for the offices ; and to keep them in a state of efficiency they must feel 
their situations to be desirable, which can scarcely be expected m the officers oj 
the Mohill Union, at the rate of remuneration they receive. It appears to us that 
the late Guardians scarcely consulted the same principles of ecoMiny when

Instructional Letter of the Commissioners to Boards of Guardians, as to 

the mode of Employing Able-bodied Paupers -where relieved out of liie Work- 

house. 

Poor haw Commission Office, JhcUin, 
SfRj December 24, 1847. 

The Commissioners for administej-ing the Laws for Relief of the Poor in 

Ireland desire me to call the especial attention of the Guardians of Union to 

that part of the order of the Commissioners, authorizing the Guardians to afford 
out-door relief to able-bodied persons in food, which requires that every able-bodied 
ruiile person so relieved shall iierform a task 'of work during eight hours at least 
of every day for -which he receives relief. 

The manner in which this important part of the order should be carried into 
effect, demands tiie immediate attention of the Guardians ; and the Commissioners 
now proceed to explain the result of their own experience on tiie subject. 

Most of the suggestions which have been made to the Commissioners have 
reference to the supposed advantage of obtaining productive labour in return for 
the relief afforded, and many of them involve the ]iroposal of employing the able- 
bodied apjdicants for relief in the cullivntiou of land ou the best terms which 
can be obtained by the Guardians from the parties occupying or owning such 
land. 

To every proposal of this nature the Commissioners consider objections to exist 
which are insurmountable, and they do not contemplate giving their approval to 
such proposals under any circumstances whatever. One obvious objection is, that 
such proceedings might interfere with the operations of the legislative measures 
expressly provided to facilitate the improvement of landed property in Ireland; 
under which measures labour will be employed and paid in the ordinary course, 
■without any disturbance of those relations which naturally subsist betw’een the 
employer and the employed, and wliich it is of the utmost consequence to maintain 
as far as possible undisturbed. 

Among the evil tendencies of a system which permits the recipients of relief to 
apply their labour to a profitable and productive employment on the property of 
private individuals, the following are perhaps the most prominent : — 

Firstly, Such a system tends to absorb the general stock of employment, and so 
to bring more labourers on the poor-rates. 

Secondly,' — It tends to lower the -market value of labour, to the great injury of 
the self-relying labourer; since the occupier of laud will not contract for the em- 
ployment of pauper instead of independent labour, unless he can obtain some 
advantage in the rate of wages. • 

Thirdly, It tends to spoil the industry and habits of the labourer, -who will not 
work with the same energy in return for relief, as when he has a bargain with a 
private employer to work for wages ; the continuance of his employment and the 
amount of his receipts depending in one case on his industry and the value of 
work, and in the other case on the necessities of himself and those dependent on 
him for support. 

There is no system of obtaining labour in return for relief from the poor-rates 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 




235 



AND STATE OE THE UNIONS, IN IRELAND. 

which, is Avholly free from the above olyections. The desideratum therefore is the Circular Letter. ’ 
mode"of employment which is least open to objection; and this will be found, as ' 

the Commissioners believe, in any such employment as shall be least calculated to 
attract labourers to itself, and thus dvtuv them away I'rom the ordinary employ- 
ments by which, they have been accustomed to maintain themselves. 

With these views, the Commissioners recommend the Guardians to establish a 
system of breaking stones by measure as the most suitable employment for able- 
bodied males i-equiring relief. The advantages of stone-breaking are, that it is 
easy to superintend and regulate it as taslv-work; that the materials are generally 
available, the implements of labour few and simple, and, above all, that it is less 
eligible to the labourer than most other employments, provided that it be vigilantly 
superintended, and that a full day’s labour be rigorously exacted from each 
recipient of relief. 

The Commissioners are aware that such a system cannot be established through 
a large Union without expense, and without great and persevering exertion on the 
part of the Board of Guardians ; but, on the other hand, the widely-spread distress 
which, ou the representations of the Guardians themselves, has led to the issue of 
the order authorizing relief in food to the able bodied, presents the two alterna- 
tives either ot such a system as the one now laid down by the Commissioners, or 
of a system of rations unchecked by any test or condition. But the latter system, 
even when administered with the greatest care and under the best control, must 
involve a profuse expeuditure, demoralize the population, and by making them 
independent of their ordinary employment, diminish the productive resources of the 
country and accumulate causes of distress. 

In every electoral division, ther-elbre, in which the Guardians find it necessary to 
avail themselves of the power to give rations to the able bodied, it is their impera- 
tive duty, in discharge of the trust wiiich they have received from the rate-payers, 
to provide a rigid system of task-work, and to appoint a sufficient number of 
superintendents of lalrour under that branch of the order which authorizes them 
to appoint such officers. 

These appointments should Ire made, not permanently, like those of the regular 
relieving officers, but for such time only as their sei’vices may be required, at a 
w'eekly rate of wages of about 10^., for ^vhich amount tiiere is no doubt that trust- 
worthy and suitable persons, able to render accounts in writing, may be obtained. 

The Guardians will have to determine the amount of labour to be required from 
each applicant for relief, and the amount of rations to be given him in return by 
the superintendent of labour after the performance of the task. 

The ordinary Relieving Officers will present the cases to the Guardians and 
take their directions in eacli case. The result of tlie decisions of the Guardians 
may be communicated by the Relieving Officers to the superintendents of labour 
in the following duplicate form : — 



Names of Applicanls. 


Daily Task of Work. 


Rations. 


1 Names of Applicants. 


Rations. 













The right-hand portion of the sheet will be detached in slips by the superintend- 
ents, and delivered to the parties employed in the form of tickets, entitling them 
to receive their rations from the contractor, or from the person in charge of the 
depot, as the case may be. Where contractors can be found to take on them the 
distribution of the rations, it is obvious that some trouble and expense will be 
saved in respect of depfits of provisions and the payment of persons to take charge 
of them. In either case the tickets brought in will be the vouchers to the Guar- 
dians for the consumption of so much food. 

The Guardians probably expect from the Commissioners some principles to assist 
them in determining the tusk of work and the amount of rations in each case ; 
and the Commissioners will observe, in the first place, that it is not necessary that 
the amount of rations should bear any direct proportion to the task ; on tlie con- 
trary, the order itself requires that each recipient should give a full day’s work for 



Printed image digitised by the University of Southampton Library Digitisation Unit 



Circular Letter. 



Miscellaneous. 



236 PAPERS RELATING TO THE RELIEF OF DISTRESS, 

every day for which he receives rations ; and it is manifest that the amount of 
rations must depend on the number of persons who, besides himself, are 
dependent on him for support. 

The justice of this arrangement stands on the following basis : the food is given, 
not as the price of labour, but as the relief of destitution ; the lultour given in 
return is the condition of receiving that relief ; and if the necessities of the recipient 
and his family are wholly relieved, it is just that he should give in return the full 
value of his labour, whatever tliat may be. 

The Guardians, acting on the above principle, will have to determine the amount 
of daily labour which may fairly be claimed from an adult nnJe of average 
strength; secondly, from an adult male of less than the average strength; and, 
lastly, from male applicants al)ove 15 years of age, but not yet adult, respectively. 
The ration, as already observed, will be in proportion to the number dependent for 
support on the person relieved. 

The selection of the places proper for the employment of the apjdicants in suffi- 
cient but not too great numbers ; the procuring of materials, and the conveyance 
thereof to each depot; the providing of such implements as it may be found 
necessary to provide for those coming to labour, are points which will necessarily 
have the attention of the Guardians in due course. 

The Inspector of the Union has been especially charged to afford the Guardians 
all the advice and iissistance in his power, to enable them to carry out the order 
with most effect and advantage, and the Commissioners request the Guardians will 
take the arrangements into consideration with the least possible delay. 

By Order of the Commissioner.s, 

To the Clerk of the Guardians W. Stanley, Secretary, 

of the Union. 



Miscellaneous. 

Mr. Stanley, Secretary to the Poor Law Commissiouers, to SirD. Le Marchant: 
December 24, 1847. 

By direction of the Commissioners for administering the Laws for Relief 
of the Poor in Ireland I have the honour to forward herewitli, for the information 
of Secretary Sir George Grey, a summary of a return, now preparing for jnluting, 
relative to the collection of poor-rates in the several Unions in Ireland during the 
month of November. 

The Commissioners have the satisfaction to state that this summary cKliibits a 
very considerable improvement in the financial condition of the Unions, — the 
rate collected during November amounting to 151,558/. ; the disbursements of 
the treasurers to 100,722/.; the balances in the hand.s of the treasurers of 
101 Unions to 105,860/.; the balances against the remaining 29 Unions being 
17,420/. ; and the rates remaining at the close of the month still to l)e collected 
amounting to 859,905/. 

Enclosoue.

PAUPERS IN WORKHOUSES;— 



\In continuation of Returns in Tkird Series of Poor Law Correspondence of last Session.] 



SUMMARIES of Weekly Returns of the Numbers of Paupers in the Work- 
houses in the several Provinces in Ireland, and Fever Hospitals connected 
therewith, from May to November, 1847, inclusive, and in the correspond- 
ing Weeks in the previous Years 1846 and 1845 respectively; showing 
the Amount of Workhouse Accommodation, Numbers of the sevei’al 
lasses of Paupers in each Workhouse, the Increase or Decrease thereof 
in each Week as compared with the previous Week of this Year, and 
also with the corresponding Weeks of the previous Years, the Numbers 
of Fever Patients, and of Deaths. — Also, 

SUMMARY of Workhouse Returns, showing the Number of Inmates of the 
Workhouses in the several Provinces of Ireland at the close of each Week 
in 1845, 1846, and 1847.
